This review is based on my personal experiences.
For the simulator fan:
I will start off by saying that I have both FSX and X-Plane 10, and that I am also a pilot in training in real life. I am relitively new to flight simulators but I would reccomend FSX over X-Plane 10 because it is very intuitive, easy to get flying, has great mechanics and loads of fun. X-Plane 10 also has realistic mechanics as well as great weather and detail in the cockpit, but is very hard to actually get started. I found it quite difficult to use, the contol menu baffled me with all the buttons and was just a pain to get running (I was completely new to that sort of thing). Then I got FSX on steam and it was extremely easy to get going. The graphics (especially in the cockpit) may not be as good as in X-Plane 10 though the scenery is still fantastic and I have had some very enjoyable 737 flights so far. The flight planner is also very simple and you can create a route which you can use in game in no time at all. When you launch the program, everything you need to set up is in the 'launcher' and when you click the 'fly' button, you're left free in the cockpit. FSX also has the addition of missions from an airline pilot role to rescue and military, which are fun and a nice touch. They are rated to a skill level so you know what sort of missions you will be able to do.
For a casual gamer:
If you are looking for some fun or you just want to try out flying aircraft, this game is great. However, it does require some understanding of aircraft(which you can learn as you play if you put the time into it) in order to get the most out of FSX. You can use the 'learning centre' in the launcher to get to know your way round the simulator and learn how to fly anything from a small single engine Cessna to a huge Boeing 747 airliner, and it is most enjoyable with a joystick. Mine just worked as soon as I started the game without me even having to change the settings. Compared to other simulators FSX makes it easy to get flying, just select 'free flight', pick an aircraft, practically any airport in the world, time of day, and weather and hit 'fly now'. I would not suggest getting this game if you just want a laugh, because it does require some time to fully get to grips with it and doesn't really offer any fun from messing about with a plane (crashing isn't any fun - I've tried). You may find it hard to understand all the features in the game (as I did), such as communicating with ATC or performing a landing with full ILS, but through time you get used to it.
Verdict:
This game is great for simulator fans and casual gamers alike. The graphics are not bad even by today's standards and it does not have many bugs, though the ones it does have are noticeable, but not game-breaking. You can get a lot of fun out of it if you stick with it and try to understand everything, and in my opinion is the best low-cost flight simulator on the market - perhaps even competes with higher-budget options. I would definately reccomend this game.

There is very little in the way of skill, many say it's an action game that plays like a puzzle game, but even then the only way to solve the puzzles is through trial, error and memory. The ai is very inconsistant as it will react differently on different runs despite you doing the same action. I found this in particular really kills the puzzle element of the game, it's like buying a jigsaw, and even though it has the same picture, the pieces will change shape each time you open the box, and the pieces are also trying to kill you. The difficulty is also very inconsistant, rather than easing you in with a gradual difficulty curve, the difficulty will randomly spike throughout the game. This is something that annoys me to no end, especially with how interesting the story is, it's incredibly annoying to suddenly have an inredibly difficult level come out of nowhere and act as a roadblock stopping me from continuing with the portion of the game I like. It feels very cheap, like the developers were concerned that the game wouldn't be long enough so they put in difficulty spikes every 4-5 levels to artificially add length.
Whilst i think the game is good and worth reccomending, just be prepared to spend a long time on a few levels having to go through some frustrating trial and error. I really like this game but it's far from perfect.

I LOOOOOVED this game in 1995.  It was the first thing I bought with my first paycheck when I turned 16 that year.  I love star wars, and I love doom.  Except this game had a better plot, cutscenes to support it, and some nifty tricks like jumping, crouching, and looking up and down.  Due to the last of those, the level design is genius!  You really have to explore, as keys are often hidden in little side areas rather than be guarded by groups of MOBs.  Back then it looked amazing, although 20 years later not as much.  Although, the graphics are really not all that necessary, as those mid 90's FPS's are all about gameplay and level design.  I miss this.  I cannot stand FPS games where basic enemies are bullet sponges.  I get bored if I have to put 8 or more rounds in every basic enemy.  These games are more "realistic" in the fact that you can clear the guards out of an area to perform your espionage, with a few well placed blaster rounds.  Only droids and hearty aliens like Gamorreans.  You may even get to punch a Kell Dragon to death ;).
The introduction of Kyle Katarn and the whole Jedi Knight series does not play like the followups.  He is not a jedi, and you get no lightsaber.  However, at this time period in Star Wars lore, the amount of Jedi is down to a couple tops, including a couple geriatrics and a 19 year old kid.  Getting to play a part in the rebellion to help dismantle the Empire is pretty cool for any Star Wars fan, and the gameplay will satisfy any retro FPS fan.
I do recommend looking into the XL engine.  It is a free fan made sourceport, currently in alpha.  It runs the game pretty well, and makes it much easier on a modern gamer.  Full mouselook, right click to use, and an overall refresh of the graphics.  Just textures, no new models or anything, but since the Jedi engine is not released, the guy had to build a new engine.

My first review, only because Civ deserves it.
The challenge every new version of Civ has is the legacy of the version before.  Each version of Civ is optimized over time with expansion packs, so they all start out good and become great.  When a new version comes out, the good of the new version doesn't live up to the great of the previous, highly optimzied version.
Is Civ 6 better than Civ 5 vanilla?  Yes.  Is it better than Civ 5 with the incredible expansion packs, Gods and Kings, and Brave New World?  No.
New systems:
Diplomacy - C+/B-: while it's not great, Diplomacy has always been weak in Civ so it's still a better score than I'd give other Civs.  Room for improvement here with expansions.
Religion - B-:  I like the effort.  religion is far more complex than previous versions.  The religious units and iterations of it though is weak and kind of a pain.  The major plus is the effort for a religious victory, seperate from a culture victory.  This can be improved as a system, the bones are here for something really good.
Districts - A-:  I love this system; I only give it a minus because I initially hated it.  Many people do, but that's because they don't understand it; it's a very complex system that's far deeper than it appears.  Setting up districts wrong can be really detrimental to a city; setting them up right can be ridiculously powerful, and it's not immediately obvious how to do it right.  Once I figured it out though, I really enjoyed the depth.  In particular, I found it made the cities more distinct from each other; in previous Civs you got everything you could; one city was pretty much another.  With the districts, I find myself specializing cities, making one a manufacturing hub, one an economic hub, one a religious city; they may all have other districts but in the end each city starts to take on a distinct feel, primarily due to the adjacency bonuses and correct setup of a district.
Otherwise, it's Civ.  It's AI struggles with stupid things like all Civs.  Combat is pretty much combat.  The economy section is what you'd expect.  The diplomacy side of things is mysterious so the AI often makes odd decisions, which most blame on poor AI but i find is really because the AI on purpose isn't always up front with it's intentions.
Personally I think Civ 6 is great, I love playing it, and I'll play a lot more.

Invisible, Inc. represents a retake on the tactical turn-based game.
Set in a dystopian future ruled by mega corps, you represent a convert group fighting corporate interests. The game opens with your HQ being attacked. Barely escaping and left with barely 72 hours, you're expected to get to the source of the attack and neutralize it, and save your organization's AI asset - Incognito - in the process.
Make no mistake here - unlike most turn based tactical games, Invisible, Inc. is designed to be very fast paced. Emphasis is placed on making strategic decisions on whether to explore each procedurally-generated map and harvest maximum resources, or achieve mission objectives with minimal risk. All the while, the Security Level rises at the end of each turn, and stacks more and more opponents against your agents.
Being the underdog, you'll find that fighting the enemy head-on isn't going to get you far. Stealth and speed is the mode of play here.
The game is also designed to address the propensity to "save scum" - instead of being allowed to save in game, players now have a choice to rewind the game a limited number of steps instead. "Beginner" difficulty also allows you to retry the level (regenerate map and start again).
Campaigns will not last more than a day's worth of play. Yet the game has great replay value - other than procedural maps always keeping you guessing, each agent made available to you comes with special abilities and you should alter your gameplay to exploit fully.
In a way, Invisible, Inc. tries to improve on turn-based tactical games and add a mix of roguelike. The result is interesting and definitely worth a try for those who enjoy turn-based tactical games.
As always, developer Klei did a good job with sounds and graphics to immerse the player into the world.
Pros:
- Turn Based Tactical game done properly.
- Replay value from different agent capabilities/upgrades, and procedurally generated maps.
- Fast paced game and incremental Security Level makes the end-phase of each map exciting (instead of boring).
- Rewinds offer a different way to avoid deadlocks/mistakes.
- Excellent visuals and sound.
- Good value, considering the cost.
Cons:
- Randomness and short game-length can be an issue - difficulty can spike, augments/tools you want may not be always available, etc.
- More back-story would have made the game more engaging for replays.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 picks up a ways after the first five episodes left off, putting you in the shoes of the other half of the first game's dynamic duo: Clementine. A bit older, a lot wiser, and a little bit more weary, Clementine soon finds herself entirely on her own for the first time in a while. She's learned plenty of new tricks, however, and Lee's demand that she keep going no matter what has clearly not left her ears.
While I still loved playing through The Walking Dead: Season Two as much as I did the first game, it didn't quite resonate with me as much this time around. It felt much harder to connect with the bulk of the new characters, between the pace at which they were introduced, the time spent with each of them feeling greatly reduced, and what felt like a lack of backstory for many of them. This was doubly troubling considering backstory was the motivating force for at least two, maybe three whole chapters. All but a small handful of the characters you did get to learn about felt fairly archetypical as well, rather than more nuanced, and several of the characters I thought I'd have time to learn to like had much shorter stints in the spotlight than I expected.
One thing I was grateful for was the lack of returning faces. Sure, there are definitely some familiar people who show up, and nods to the events of the first game sprinkled throughout, but it avoided being fanservice. Such returns were few, far between, and not overly hyped as the game went on; more of an "Oh hey, I remember that," before carrying on.
Characters new and old also suffered from a degree of stiffness in regards to their development. Whereas many of the first game's cast showed change over the course of five episodes, be it for good or for ill, while almost everyone in Season Two seemed much more set in their ways. Some cases could be written off as being hardened by their conditions for this long, but there was plenty of room for growth that never seem achieved. And, in one particular case, I spent the last episode and change yelling "Did you learn NOTHING?" at my monitor as a certain companion seemed to have fallen into (read: was written into) a rut of sorts.
Maybe it's not entirely fair to compare Season Two to the first one, as it is its own beast, but as a sequel, it's hard to avoid that sort of thing. Even with the drawbacks I've mentioned, it's still a great continuation of Clementine's story, and one worth seeing through to the end. In fairness, I'd say this trip is even more harrowing than Clem's original ordeal, which is saying quite a bit.

Though at first less compelling than its predecessor, The Walking Dead: Season 2 does succeed on all fronts. Its solid, eventually well-rounded narrative moves crisply along through the five chapters, each with its own distinct setting and challenges. Clementine is a welcome familiar face, and rightly serves as the moral and emotional center of her group of survivors.
The choices are as tough as ever, and their tests of Clem's character are sometimes heartbreaking, but that is nothing new for TellTale, who have built a formidable empire of strong, character-based narratives -- and have nothing to be ashamed of in this excellent sequel.
This is not Resident Evil or Dead Rising, so don't expect the undead and their kills to take the spotlight. The true heart (and guts) of the game is one young girl who is growing up in a violent, cruel world and trying to figure out how to retain her humanity when it would be much easier not to.

This is easily one of my top ten games.
My computer isn't top notch, but KSP runs very cleanly at mid-settings, and looks good doing it.  While the planets and moons are massive, the surfaces aren't intricately detailed with plant and animal life, but the geological structures can be pretty neat and provide some interesting landing and exploration experiences.  The Kerbols are simple but well designed and put a cute face on the infinite challenge space exploration poses.
Designing the most cost efficient and effective rocket or spaceplane in the vehicle assembly building can take a good chunk of time when you just want to try something new and different.  Sometimes it pans out nicely, while other times it just triggers a series of fiery explosions on the launchpad or runway.  Either way, it's a learning process and highly enjoyable.
Career mode is a lot of fun, it is a real challenge to make every mission a thorough financial and scientific success, and I find it very gratifying when everything comes together as planned.  I've put in a lot of hours and still haven't explored the entire available solar system, but I thoroughly enjoy getting a huge amount of gameplay out of a relatively inexpensive title.
If physics-based tinkering games are your deal, I think you'll agree that this is one of the best pieces of work out there.

Yes, this game is dated.  Yes, the controls are "weird".  Yes, the maps are confusing.  That said, for those of us who were fortunate to grow up in a day and age where this stuff was cutting edge, and weren't spoiled by games that assumed we were stupid and needed puzzles solved for us, this game still holds up as an awesome testiment to FPS history.
Noted as being "Doom with Star Wars Graphics", Dark Forces took gaming to the next level.  The voice acting was simply superb for the day, as was the cutscene detail.  We were drawn into the galaxy of Star Wars and told a story that closely ties to the origional movie trilogy (before Jar Jar).  You were made to feel as though you had a part in those movies, without actually being thrown into them.  This great story would be continued in Dark Forces II, but we're not here to talk about that.
For nostalgia purposes this game brings us back to a time when gaming was still searching for it's niche.  it's a time when "WASD" wasn't yet tied to a mouse as the "accepted" way to control a character.  You had to have both hands on the keyboard and learn how to multi-task your fingers, a skill that the youth these days would probably find confusing and too complicated.
Level design in Dark Forces, easily the biggest complaint against the game, was very well done in my opinion.  Every part of the map is used in some way.  It's either a place to pick up more shields and ammo, or has a switch, or has an item you need, or has a secret you've yet to uncover.  There is no wasted space, and it's up to you to figure out what to do with it.  Sure, you can run around a map for 15 minutes trying to figure out the next step.  For those who are used to today's games leading them around by the hand it can be a little frustrating.  For those of us who grew up with these games, solving the challenge can be quite rewarding and we wouldn't have it any other way.
Dark Forces was designed back in 1995, where the standard was DOS based gaming.  That said, in order for this game to function it's packed seamlessly with DOSBox.  I, personally, have never had a problem with games that are bundled in this manor.  The game is a perfectly emulated version of it's former glory.  There isn't any configuring required, unless you're one of those stubborn control freaks who needs everything to operate THEIR way.
The only hick-up I ran into was remembering that at the end of each level, when your mission is complete, you have to hit ESC in order to move on to the next level.  That information was included in the origional guide (as I recall), and will eventually pop-up in the game if you spend a long time waiting for the level to end by itself.  It's a minor issue that's resolved at the end of the first mission, and as such doesn't change my recommnedation.
If you've been spoiled by the high-end graphics and hand-holding of today's games then by all means avoid this title because it's not for you.  If you, like me, grew up with games like Doom, Heretic, Hexen, Decent, and Duke Nukem 3D then this is a MUST HAVE due to it's awesome storyline and great nostalgic value.  Its a testiment to early gaming and definately worth every penny.

I bought this game because I'm a big fan of two of their games, Mark of the Ninja and Don't starve. I would recommend this one, but not at its current price. Here is why :
It's a good little game, with  a great concept, that relies on a series of X-Com-like tactical missions that help you beat the final one. However, you cannot rush into the missions with heavy weapons and grenades. Here you have to reach the objectives by being stealthy and hacking into the mainframe accesses as fast as you can, because every 5 turns the security level increases.
I've had fun with it, and I liked the initial challenge, but ...
The campaign is far too short. I finished the Beginner campaign in less than 6 hours, in 4 attempts. What I liked in X-Com games was that you had to slowly improve your equipment, level up your roster and finally, after several hours, defeat the enemy against all odds. Here I finished the campaign in 2 hours, and some 6 or maybe 7 missions and with only one agent (the other one died in the third mission). I would have preferred a more rewarding game.
Also, each failure gives you experience, that will help you unlock new programs and agents. I've been a bit disappointed by the agents and more so by the programs I've unlocked (I've unlocked 4 agents and 2 programs).
There are a full set of options you can play with to increase the level difficulty, and the number of missions you can do before finishing the campaign, but now I have finished it, it seems a bit spoiled.
So yeah, I recommend it, but if you can find it at 5€, no more.

This simulator offers a complete package for newcomers to the genre.
Even without add-ons it's a nice looking game with a massive amount of content. Lots of different aircrafts and the whole world to explorer.
With free and bought add-ons and special hardware it can be expanded and customised to your preferences. (There are amazing high quality simulation planes available.) Making it into a popular flight simulator with serious enthusiasts.
But if you are getting started or are just a casual player you won't need that to enjoy this simulator. And important, it offers a good selection of tools to get started and learn how to fly.
To get in the air quickly there are tutorial missions showing you some of the basics.
The missions offer somewhere to start within all the possibilities of this simulator and are a quick way to try out all the different types of planes with a little guidance in operating them.
These missions touch on most of the available airplanes and different styles of flying. From basic take-off, taxiing and landing patterns, to flying sailplanes, helicopters, commercial traffic, air-racing and flying from aircraft carriers. The first tutorial missions will be easy for beginners but the more advanced missions keep offering you a challenge as you improve your flying abilities.
Nice about the first tutorial missions is that they tell you where to look at in the environment based on real world aviation skills. The briefing screen for the missions also tells you which articles to read for more detailed information about the current mission.
These articles can be found in the Learning Centre, a big library with documentation about everything concerned with flying and the planes. All edited to giving you real world information and the link with the implementation within the simulator.
Then there are the flying lessons. For me the best part to get into flying.
There are study materials available for the school and guided lessons, by an actual flight instructor! It's almost like a real flying lesson, where the instructor gives you part of the controls and you can keep practicing to get the hang of flying and, important, landing an airplane. Well, you don't need to read everything. You can pick most up listening to the instructor. But it's there and I think it’s good and useful in-depth information.
This game offers support for almost any type of controller. And you can add many devices simultaneously for separate tasks. I've seen people using a racing wheel. And there are fully functional cockpits being build and connected to this game.
But to get started you won't need much.
Not immediately intuitive, but after a short learning time it’s doable. I used to fly (FS2002) with the keyboard, it (still) works fine for normal flight, just be careful with fast/aggressive planes. And unless you build yourself a complete cockpit you'll use it for the special commands. Although many can be applied using the mouse in the in-game cockpit.
TIP: don't just press the keys,
them and be patient about it. A plane doesn't react immediately and pressing a key to much/long will make it move fast and hard to control.
I haven't done it yet, but you can use the mouse to steer the plane.
Now I tried using a Logitech F710 (it pretends to be a Xbox 360 controller). And it works surprisingly well. It is already preconfigured and the default settings offer the basics to start flying. For basic flying I'd say it might be even easier to use than a joystick, especially for helicopters.
I only have experience with a basic joystick with twist for rudder and an analogue throttle. It's a little more realistic and the throttle is great.
Just as with the add-ons: If you want to and have the budget you can make it as advanced as you like. But it isn't necessary at all.
Besides using the mouse to manipulate the controls in the (virtual) cockpit you can also use it to fly.
You'll just control the stick, but it's quite easy to use. This gives you good control, even with a laptops touchpad. Just keep track of the position of the small cross on your screen and remember the planes movements are indirect and most planes are a bit slow to respond.
Btw. Instructions on using the different controls and most anything else can be found in the Learning Centre.
My personal note on the currently available dlc on Steam.
These seem consistent with the base quality of the FSX. But you can find higher quality planes and scenery for free and you can create great flight plans in Free Flight.
I think they are a bit expensive and you'll probably won't need the extra content they offer.
I'd say: only buy them if you want to support the publisher for the work they do in maintaining this game.
And who knows what great DLC they'll add in the future.
And then there are so many aspects of the game that I haven't touched yet. If you get into it you can go as far ... well really far with added content, multiplayer etc. There is just so much more available.
But, my main point, you don't need that to have lots of fun playing and learning with this simulator.

The most enjoyable stealth game I've ever played. I'm not a fan of the genre due to its slow pace, often annoying cameras, unclear enemy vision/hearing cones, and repetitive AI dialogue (especially with AI that--after a mere 10 seconds--forgets you just killed all of their friends despite the pile of bodies and goes back to their patrol route like nothing happened).
Invisible, Inc. distills the ideals of the stealth genre down into an easily digestible, cartoonish, isometric game that manages to be challenging and rewarding without feeling cheap, and also solves a lot of control/camera issues that are found in full on 3D stealth titles.
My sole complaint thus far is that--much like in FTL or any roguelike really--the items you can find or purchase seem too random to where you can either get a bunch of really cool stuff, or a bunch of meh. At the very least the agency merchant (Monst3r) could sell more items whenever you're between missions. More often than not his shop is literally empty.
Aside from that, this is definitely another imaginative, polished Klei release and a welcome addition to my collection.

This sequel sits comfortably between Civilization Revolution and Civilization 5. As such, fans of the former will appreciate the cartoony style, but might be turned off by the slower pace and greater challenge. Fans of the latter may think this is too watered down, too simplified. I appreciate the fact that this game attempts to forge its own identity and improves graphics while still feeling like the other entries. While 5 had a huge focus on armies and various combat modifiers, 6 focuses more on city building. So while the combat has certainly been simplified, the cities reach a whole new level of complexity. Now, you have districts that each take up their own tile, and placement is crucial because of various terrain modifiers. For instance, a Campus will produce extra science when placed adjacent to a mountain tile. The Harbor district must actually be built on a water tile. The Great Pyramid requires a desert tile. Each wonder takes up a tile, so you can't just pile them all up in the same city.
There are so many government types in this one and I feel like they did a good job differentiating each one. You can mix and match various policies, many of which are not unique to just one type of government. Because of the new religion system, you can now have a Theocracy, which allows you to purchase military units using faith instead of gold. Faith is a new fourth commodity which is needed to purchase specific faith based buildings and units, but can also be used to unlock a Great Person early. One gripe I have is the fact that you can be very close to unlocking a Great Person only to have another player swoop in and buy it using gold or faith. This happens extremely often on higher difficulties, as if they have endless amounts of gold and faith available for that specific purpose. On the plus side, Great People are now split into different categories and there are buildings, policies, and research projects which allow you to obtain extra points in specific categories. So if you're going for a military victory, you can focus on getting Great Generals.
I think the new religion system is well designed, though it is one of the more time consuming winning conditions and it does get annoying trying to hold off endless waves of enemy missionaries trying to convert all your cities. Plus, other players get royally ticked off when you try to convert their cities. Now here's where it gets tricky: you need a Great Prophet to found a religion. Each player can only get one. But there are a limited number of them, and never enough for every player. So if you don't immediately start working toward a religion, you may miss out. Also, if another player does manage to convert all your cities, then it is impossible to get your religion back. Any missionaries or apostles you recruit are followers of the religion that city currently follows. So when your Buddhist city gets converted to Catholicism, your citizens become Catholics and the only way to turn them back is to recruit a missionary from one of your other cities that still practices Buddhism.
In other Civilization games, you use science to unlock new technologies. You still do that, but now you have Civics, which are unlocked through culture. This is cool because you can't just unlock everything through science alone and you're also not unlocking just one new thing at a time. In addition, you can speed up the process by meeting certain conditions. Another new system worth mentioning is amenities. In a nutshell, you need to mine, farm, or trade for shiny, valuable things to make your people happy and productive. The number you need depends on population. Otherwise, it takes forever to build stuff and they may eventually revolt.
So here's what I really like about this game: you have to plan. You can't just steamroll your opponents through military might. You have to make strategic choices not just in combat, but in where and how you build your cities, which technological advancements and civics you choose, trying to fulfill conditions to get them done sooner, and maintaining diplomatic relations so you can get favorable trade deals when your people demand more amenities.
What I don't like about this game is the fact that I have no interest in multiplayer and the AI "diplomacy" is a bit wonky. They declare war on you for the dumbest reasons. They get angry when they offer you a completely one sided trade deal and you turn them down. If you declare war on one player just once, you could find yourself getting repeatedly denounced for war mongering by every player for the rest of the match. Here's an ironic but annoying example: Ghandi declared war on me even though he was on the other side of the map and I hadn't done anything to him. He kept sending troops on boats and I kept sinking them. However, when you have battles taking place too close to a city, it creates war weariness, which lowers amenities. So as my production grinded to a halt, I attempted to negotiate peace with increasingly ludicrous offers and he simply wouldn't have it. Eventually, my people revolted, causing powerful barbarian troops to surround my capital and begin razing my farms and mines. So here I am stuck in a war I didn't provoke or start with the most unlikely antagonist and I can't produce troops, build up my city, or expand my population. As you can guess, it's more difficult to get a military victory now, but ultimately, it is for the better. It gives you more incentive to actually try to maintain peace and attempt other winning conditions. I would simply advise that you tread lightly when considering declaring war, because there is no coming back once you start down that road.
In conclusion, I consider this my favorite Civilization game, I consider it an improvement over previous entires in many different ways, and I definitely recommend it!

After featuring in a supporting role in games like Bioshock Infinite and Half-Life, it's nice to see the 'R' key finally recieving its well-earned spin-off game. Where it once occasionally helped out reloading for (respectively) Booker DeWitt and Gordon Freeman, it's now driving the action by respawning the protagonist every few seconds, like a crack addict with a defibrillator.
If the above paragraph hasn't made it clear, Hotline Miami is hard. But it's also exhalarating. The brutal 8-bit violence that permeates every level and the way the protagonist's spiralling insecurity combines with the aesthetic's is as chilling as anything found in American Psycho, but it works to create a visceral, perfectly polished game that I'd recommend in a heartbeat.
Speaking of heartbeats, one thing that takes some getting used to is the hyperactive speed the whole game moves at. At first, you plan and try to create a formula for getting through each room through trial-and-error, but in the later game when there are so many enemies to kill, so many variables, that it's better to get a shotgun/machete and dash from room to room, utilising razor-sharp instincts on a merciless rampage. And this is when the game really shines. Tension builds to an unbearable crescendo when you don't even have time to reach for the pause button because someone could shoot you from the other end of the hallway, when the mix of panic and excitement, the confidence from nearly clearing a room out mixed with fear of dying when you're so close to the finish, that you're in the shoes of a serial killer.
Each massacre is broken up with short interludes where you go collect pizza, or some other mundane task. They all take less than a minute to complete, but they help to give us witness to the killer's life when he doesn't have a mask, where he seems alien and socially inept, always being served by the same person who gives away everything "on the house," though it's never explained why (maybe there'll be a twist in HM2 where it turns out Miami's GDP is going through the roof so they just give stuff away because there's no room for more money). These sections become more and more bizarre as the game goes on, where his life of crime and his more domestic moments blur together. It's the kind of character study game where the story is made all the more chilling by just how fun it all is, like with FarCry 3 and Spec Ops: The Line. The pixely art style doesn't keep it from being gruesome one bit, and it's a lot to take on, but it's one of the most intense and compelling experiences I've had on Steam.
Sorry I couldn't get to properly talk about the brilliant soundtrack and psychedelic visual design, but I think it's something you should experience for yourself.

This game is my all time favourite; it has all the appeal of a retro game, whilst remaining fun, fresh, and damn well bloody. One of the goriest 2D games I have ever played, Hotline Miami never leaves you with a dull moment. With fast paced action, interesting mechanics, numerous weapons, and a deep underlying story, this is easily one of the best titles out there.
The music is somewhat strange at times, yet this all adds to the feel of the game. The first time I played the game, a combination of the music and visuals left me with a headache that lasted 2 days. However, once you get used to it, you will be dying to listen to the soundtrack again.
Whilst simplistic, the art style doesn't fail to attract your attention, and they have really captured the feel of a retro game. On top of this, they added a chromatic film over the game itself, causing an effect similar to that of LSD.
The gameplay is fast paced and unforgiving, a very fun feature allowing for perfection. The weapons you can find each time are randomised, allowing for a different experience each time through. Many mechanics are a learning experience, but once you get used to them they don't pose much of a problem. The only actual problem I have with the game is that occasionally the AI does game breaking things, such as leave a room that 99/100 times they wouldn't have done, or not chase you out of a room no matter how many times you try to bait them. Therefore, the gameplay regrettably only gets a 9/10.
Despite the unpredictable AI, this game is the best of its kind, providing a fun, fast paced and unique experience that will enthrall and excite you. I would definitely recommend this game, and it is a must have for any steam library.
A game about perfection - everything you do, you realise you could've done it a little faster, a little more accurately; things could've gone better. So you reload, you play again, you learn more. The more you play, the more higher you realise the limit of play can be. So you say to yourself: "Just 5 more minutes". Well, what better game to win the Steam award than this one, then?

Like any game this old, any recommendation is going to come with a lot of salt, and largely boils down to your personal tolerance level.
Dark Forces is basically Doom with a Star Wars wallpaper, though apparently it made a few technological improvements over Doom, such as the ability to have multiple floors on top of one another. This is just heresay on my part, I'm not a videogame historian.
The level design is fairly nonlinear and encourages plenty of exploration, but personally I found that the inability to look up and down (more than about 45 degrees either way, with really weird visual distortions) left me having only a vague idea that a floor was beneath my feet, which was incredibly disorienting and left me playing through most of the game with the transparent map screen plastered to my face (though I'll admit I found the way the map dynamically updated based on purely literal line of sight weirdly enthralling).
Like many FPSes, or indeed games of this age in general, the bosses ammount to little more than a single enemy that is both better at killing you and worse at dying. Can't really dock points there, it's not like you can expect elaborate boss mechanics in a game that slightly predates the notion of having to actually aim your gun at things.
While I still had enough fun to give this game a recommendation, do NOT try playing it without a walkthrough on hand. Many of the puzzles involve a sort of sideways moon logic that I never would have figured out on my own, even if I could fnavigate without staring at the map during firefights.

So, if your on the fence and wondering about the game and all the drama, here is the short answer;
If you like Shadows of Mordor, you will like Shadow of War. Period.
That being said, there ARE some things to be aware of;
The BAD:
#1 The so called "Online":
So, on launch, the game asks you if you want to sign up for Online, and it doesnt really tell you what all that is, excpet to say that they are going to "collect data".
DONT SIGN IT!!
The ONLY thing this gets you is the ability to buy loot chests, which you DONT need, and hand the publisher even more ability to spy on you, which you dont need.
You can click on accept, and the game will whine and tell you that will miss out on all the online content. Ignore it. It will also pester you to click on the damn TOS. EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. YOU. LAUNCH. Absolutely DONT click on it. Screw WB.
#2 Loot Chest cosmetics and Scolls:
If you dont accept the TOS, you will miss out on some cosmetic items (not needed) and some training scrolls that give you the ability to swap out skills on your orcs. The scrolls are handy, but you still dont really need them.
The other piece is that the "multiplayer" compenent. Apparently that only shows up in act three, when you have fortresses. The "multiplayer" component copies your fortresses and orcs and drops them into other players games as locations to attack. Actually sounds kind of interesting, but I am not anywhere near act three yet to test it.
Now, the GOOD;
#1 Nemesis 2.0:
The new Nemesis system is hands down the best thing about the game. Capatains are MUCH tougher than Shadows of Mordor. Some of the ability combos are downright nasty, and you REALLY want to gather info on higher level captains before you get a rude and fatal surprise.
Monolith did an outstanding job of improving an already damn good system. Kudos to them!
#2 Graphics:
Game looks fantastic, and with the recent Nvidia drivers, has run rock solid stable for me for 15 hours+ I have had zero issues with the game, which is great since I had noticible lag issues with Mordor a couple of times.
#3 World:
The game world is big and pretty detailed. They seem to be doing a decent job of streamling the less fun grind material, like flower picking, from Mordor out. There are still a lot of things to collect, but less of the "Go pick x of this type of flower and Y of this type of flower for an achievement nonsese. Thats a plus in my book.
There are quite a few quests, and some of them are locked based on required skills, which will require you to actually travel back and forth on the maps. Also a plus.
SUMMARY:
In short, if you like the overall game play in Shadow of Mordor, you will enjoy Shadow of War. They kept what was good in the first game, and seemed to have stripped some of the less fun fetch stuff out.
The Nemesis improvements alone are fantastic, and really add a lot of depth the the Captain encounters. Probably the best thing in the game so far.
Loot boxes and the online play stuff can be safely IGNORED. You get plenty of stuff that drops, and plenty of cash to pay for upgrades without even having to look at the marketplace.

Dark Forces... what is this?  It's an FPS from the DOS and PS1.  Don't back off the store page just yet, bear with me.  Is it canon? ... Yes it is, George Lucas just hit his head hard, and now somehow thinks the Death Star plans were taken by a bunch of plain old rebels and some blind dude.  Nope, it was Kyle, the one man rebel pain train.
This game's very doom-style, mixing together 2D sprites with 3D terrain.  You may also notice the way the X axis is locked, just like doom.  But wait, what's this... what happens if I use PgUp/PgDown... oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm looking up and down!  And there you have it.  This is a doom-style that also allows jumping, crouching, and looking up and down.  Have your fill of "innovation?"  Good, now let's talk about what we all really care about-- gameplay.
If you haven't already guessed, it's a Star Wars shooter leading up to the events of the Star Wars: Jedi Knight franchise.  You play as mercenary Kyle Katarn and it begins with a setting we'll recognize easily-- this is an imperial base.  Go steal the plans to the Death Star.  Then, the story takes a unique Extended Universe approach, as we follow the development of an Imperial super-soldier project, codenamed "Dark Troopers."  Your missions are to go into various places and carry out the assignment given to you, as you go deeper into the project and try to put a stop to it.
The level design is great... it has a good balance of puzzles, firefights, raids, speedruns, and more as you plow through stormtroopers and Imperial officers, as well as the occasional robot.  More than that, the levels themselves are very dynamic and overall, the use of elevators and moving platforms really add to the game.  Multiple weapons can be found, from Blaster Rifles to Thermal Detonators to Imperial Heavy Repeaters, and the sprites/texturing are still at least decent.  The game itself is completely solid, and visually it won't hurt to look at with the simple Imperial designs.
The only pitfall in this game is its technical updates, or lack thereof.  Now, I'm not the stubborn asshat I used to be, and I get it-- these old games generally don't have their source code laying around, not everything is preserved as it should be.  This semi-but-not-really excuses some aspects, like the continued lack of vertical aim.  However, what can't be overlooked are the basic flaws that take all of ten minutes to fix.  Why is DOSBox outdated?  The rerelease comes with the ancient 0.73 version of DOSBox, while the final version (0.74) is a
step up fixing many color issues and framerate problems, particularly in this game and other late 2.5D titles.  If you have any issues, check the bottom of this review for guides on how to update DOSBox, make it run better, and (optional) add controller support.
Overall: Rerelease, 7/10.  Game itself: 8.5/10, frantic Star Wars Extended Universe action with great level design and genuinely challenging puzzles.  It's definitely an odd one though, so if you're looking for some mindless mayhem by the likes of Doom or CoD, this is not the game you're looking for.

This game is much less of a turn-based combat/stealth game than it is, perhaps, a rather aggressive piece of choreographed contemporary dance. And much like a dancer, both the intense satisfaction of completing your routine and the sweat dripping from your brow as a result of doing so are key reasons why I recommend this game. Invisible Inc. is produced by Klei Entertainment, which should hopefully bring a smile to your face - they are the creators of the superb "Don't Starve", and I can confirm they haven't disappointed here either. I won't go into every reason for this game's success, but I will say that the gameplay, the style of which I have never really been a fan of, is tremendously fun and challenging, there is, much like Don't Starve, plenty of replayability due to the procedural nature of its level generation, and the visuals/audio are beautifully sublime, or sublimely beautiful, whichever you prefer. It also had the odd effect of instilling me with some sense of morality - typically a "tank" style of gamer with little regard for the fleeting lives of my computerized opponents, I completed my first playthrough without killing a single guard (with the exception of a walking-camera-droid-thing, and really, does that even count?), and actually frowned at the unlocked character I received afterwards, Shalem 11, because his special ability is the use of a sniper rifle. Life changing game. Thoroughly recommended. Now I'm off to watch all eight seasons of Dexter, back to back, to regain the complete desensitization to violence this game stole from me.

Sharing a game structure with X-Com, this smart, turn-based strategy game is an absolute delight. The game is part rogue-like with about an 8-10 hour campaign, but the replayability is high and encouraged. After you finish a campaign, you unlock agents and AI hacking abilities that fundamentally change the way you approach missions.
The game has some interesting mechanics that I'd like to discuss. FIrst, the hacking mechanic isn't like any game I've played before. It's a resource game, as you have limited power and have to accumulate it over time and draining it from consoles in the mission using your agents. Your AI can use the power to utilize her abilities, which neutralize firewalls and takeover devices, such as security cameras, turrets, corporate safes, power supplies to security measures or computers that control prison cells doors. It's just as important to the game mechanics as the stealth, although the stealth is probably the most intriguing part of the game.
Unlike most first and third person games that utilize stealth, Invisible, Inc. doesn't fall apart once stealth is broken. Agents investigate open doors, or aim their weapons at detected agents. You have one extra round to respond, whether that is to duck behind cover, take out the security guard guard with a gun, or stun the guard with the agent you have hidden behind him. Guards who detect abnormalities don't go back to their routine. They investigate the entire facility. Alarms aren't an On/Off switches. It's a constantly rising status that brings with it penalties every time its status is upgraded a level. It may raise the firewall level of protected devices, add extra guards to the level, or generally cause havoc, such as resetting cameras, but it's not a 'they know where you are' button like most games inflict upon you. No matter what happens, you can always recover, or at least evacuate whatever agents you have left. On easier difficulties, you can rewind the mission on critical errors, giving yourself an extra turn to react. It's a great beginner's tool, but later it becomes more fun to just roll with it.
I played through the campaign with no restarts and truly enjoyed my time. I plan to play through again to see more of the agents. I only used 4 in my first playthrough as that's all that's needed to fill out your roll call, but there are many more. I started with two and now have 4 to play on my second playthrough. I look forward to seeing what I unlock next.

Oh man, the memories! This was one of the first video games I ever played growing up in the mid to late nineties, and it has aged like fine cheese: pungent and stinky but delicious none the less. To those who actually remember the pre-sequel Star Wars era, this game does positiviely EVERYTHING right. The guns, the enemies, the locations, and of course the characters, are all done in a manner that is faithful to the Star Wars lore. When playing this game for the first time, everything feels new yet strangely familiar, which is EXACTLY how a Star Wars game should feel. You feel like you've heard the story before, but the manner in which it is being presented this time is unique and interesting. Atmospherically, this might just be one of the greatest examples of allowing level/character set the tone. Shiny Imperial starships feature well organized corridors patrolled by brisk, professional soldiers while filthy sewers are populated by dirty, grubby looking baddies with outfits that look like they've been cobbled together from trash and scrap.
Gameplay wise, the controls aren't as tight as they could be, only highlighting the fact that the platforming in this game is clunky at best. The story is no where near as long as it should be, and features only twelve missions. Despite its length, the story does do a good job of pulling you in and engaging you, even if it is a little corny even by Star Wars standards. The difficulty level is right about perfect, however. It is challenging without being impossible, yet simple enough that you rarely feel frustrated by it. That being said, the missions can feel a little bit confusing at times and you will occassionally feel like you don't know what you're supposed to do. Finally, the game's visuals haven't aged well and definately don't hold up to the standards that gamers expect out of a modern FPS. In all fairness, Datk Forces was on the cutting edge graphics-wise in 1995, and could look a lot worse. Its outdated graphical look adds a nostalgia factor to the game and give it an endearing quality that few retro indie games can match.
All in all, Star Wars: Dark Forces is most definately worth a play through. Whether you're a hardcore Star Wars fan or a gamer looking to play older games for the nostalgia factor, Dark Forces will scratch your itch and scratch it good. I would even recommend this game to any potential developers out there as a good lesson in atmospheric design. A true classic and an undeniable gem in Lucasart's crown.

A cool turn-based tactics where prime focus is on stealth. Even more - killing enemies is both hard to do and is punishable by missions becoming more difficult faster.
Game plays in a form of campaign set on an X-Comish world map where missions are randomly generated (as well as maps they take place at) and each corporation you fight has its own unique set of guards. You are racing against a clock to get more agents, make them more skillful and get better equipment before the final mission which puts a progress you've made to the test.
Missions have you sneak your agents to the objectives, avoid guards (as knocking them out is only a very temporary solution and can be hazardous to your progress if discovered), use gadgets to get out of sticky situations and hack into systems to turn odds into your favor. The clock however is ticking even there, making the game harder by the minute and your mistakes only speed it up. There's only 1 saveslot per campaign but you can rewind to a previous turn where you were out of danger - albeit only a limited number of times.
What makes the game even better and replayable is the ability to customize the campaign as you see fit - from a tough race against the clock to a more "classic" stealth gameplay where you proceed at your own pace and alarm level is raised only when you make mistakes punishing you with the greater difficulty increase instead. Even more - you can just set time limit to endless and do missions until you are tired with the current agency.

is a very well made roguelite twin-stick shooter that incredibly fun and satisfying to play that I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys roguelikes.
There are six different categories of guns; Bullet, Shell, Arrow, Laser, Explosive and Melee. Each one of them feels different and unique so there will be a preferred weapon type for everyone. The gunplay in the game is very well done, all the weapons feel like they have a weight to them and it is fun to mix different weapons to find the perfect combination. The randomized nature of the game means that players will get to experiment and experience all the weapons. Furthermore, it’s very satisfying to learn the how the weapons work and master the controls of the variety weapons.
There are a variety of character which have unique abilities such as rolling and shields and player also levels up their character through the run which will unlock new attributes, leading to some unique builds that will adjust how the player will play the game, meaning every run is unique. There is also daily challenges which will spawn a new run every day and you can replay the same map for a day and try to place on the leaderboard, rather than a randomized level each time, creating a variety of game modes.
Every stage in the game feels unique with new enemies introduced that you learn the patterns. The game has elements of Shmup games with a large amount of bullets flying towards you and can get overwhelming but it’s very satisfying find a path through the enemies and beat the level.
Even though the game can be very challenging, the difficulty curve is not too steep so that it doesn't become too hard for players too quickly, the player is always in a space where it is possible to fight out of any challenge.
The sound design and graphics both build a very unique atmosphere, the music often matches the settings perfectly and is very invigorating when fighting the enemies. The pixel graphics are very detailed and unique that gives the game great charm and character that is wonderful to look at, all the enemies are instantly recognizable and interesting to fight.
This is also a paragon of early access games. The devs have made over 90 weekly updates to the game that add new features such as weapons, characters, as well as adjust and rebalance gameplay. They listen to the community; they deserve some respect for their commitment to the game in a landscape of exploitive developers who want to release buggy, broken games to get a quick buck, such as DayZ and countless other scams.
started out a great game and has only gotten better over time as more things get added to the game, as it soon approaches its full release, it sets a standard for early access games on Steam and it is a shame that this level of dedication to a game isn’t seen very often. Overall, definitely worth picking up to support good developers and a great game, looking forward to the final release coming up soon!

Star Wars: Dark Forces was written off as a "Doom clone" on release in spite of its critical acclaim,
Indeed, it is hard to look at the game and not draw a parallel with the legendary shooter.
However, Dark Forces made a lot of innovations on the formula that is common place in shooters of today.
Dark Forces innovated with essential features like the ability to crouch, jump as well as to look up and down.
This game also made rounds for its ability to feature true room-over-room level designs with rooms intertwining within each other in impressive, multi-story displays of architecture.
Dark Forces also shot for a grounded, more realistic look taken right out of the movies in spite of the graphical shortcomings of the era. This was made possible with the game's wide selection of  level tiles that were rarely repeated.
Another aspect that helped the unique feel of each level was that no level was simply about traversing from A to B. Instead, you got a detailed mission briefing that gave you multiple goals that had to be seen through before heading out. These goals could be things like turning on the power of an area, planting explosives or infiltrating an imperial stronghold for information before making it back to your ship in one piece.
All of these innovations results in a shooter that was way ahead of its time.
Dark Forces is a truly unique title that shouldn't be missed by FPS fans and Star Wars fans alike.
As a fan of the latter but not the former, I was very happy that I decided to play this game.

DISCLAMER: At the time of writing this review, I have 2 hours on the game. In reality I have much more, but I played it in offline mode because of traveling.
At first, I was gonna make this a stupid "Hurrr durrr this Star Wars and Doom 420/69" type of review. However, I really do believe a great game like this deserves an actual Pro/Con review. That being said, be prepared for lots of Pros.
+ The environments of this game are some of the best I've ever seen in an FPS. They are all unique and encourage exploration, which makes every level memorable.
+ Lots of different enemies, all faithful to the Star Wars lore. You've got your Stormtroopers, Commanders, Probe Droids, Dark Troopers and many more.
+ Lots of memorable characters from the Star Wars universe. Mon Mothma, Boba Fett, and even Jabba the Hutt are all there.
+ The guns are also all faithful to the Star Wars lore (You might even find a few in other SW games), and are really fun to use as well. Thermal Detonators, Repeaters, Fusion Cutters, and even the Imperial blaster rifle are all super cool and fun.
+ Puzzles are thought out well, and are at that just right difficulty that you wont find too hard or easy.
+ SECRETS.
+ Every mission has its own briefing, which tells you exactly what you need to know, no bullcrap.
+ Story takes place just before and after the Episode IV, so a big plus for me and many others. And its also super cool because YOU ARE THE ONE WHO GETS THE DEATH STAR PLANS.
+ This is an FPS done well. Its so fun to blast the hell out of everyone. The gunplay is VERY fun.
+ Creative obstacles. No, really. There was one room that was pitch black, with 4 Stormtroopers. The only thing that created light were all the lasers flying around, sorta like flying flashlights.
+ You can use you fists to kill everyone. HOW BADASS IS THAT?
- The story. I mean there has to be a story, right? Except it feels so rushed and there's no point to it, because you only objective (except the level with the death star plans) is to stop the creation of Dark Troopers. Boring.
- The game is super short with less than a dozen missions, and lack of replayability makes it all the shorter.
- The ground feels like its ice, you keep slipping and sliding everywhere which makes it kinda hard to focus on a shot and do a bit of platforming.
- Lack of a manual. Thank Lord Vader for Steam guides, because it doesn't, ever, tell you the controls in the game.
- Obviously, everyone's con, the graphics. The game came out in 1995, and it has not aged well at all. If a younger gamer, or really any graphics fan picked this up, they might get turned off by the graphics. BUT THATS WHY I SAVED THE BEST FOR LAST. There is a mod for this game called DarkXL. It introduces lots of things like 1920x1080 resolution, rebindable controls, more options, being able to look up and down, a reticle, and it makes the game look fantastic.
This game gets a 9/10. If it had just been a bit longer, and if the story had been A BIT better, this would've been a solid 10/10.

Invisible, Inc. is a turn based game of stealth. The various components of Invisible aren't anything new. There's no new "wow" factor here. We've seen this before.
But it is an exceptionally well crafted experience. The mechanics of the game are simple - hide from your enemies. As a general rule you really can't kill them. But you can knock them out for 3 turns. All the while you're avoiding patrols, cameras and bots. You can instruct your friendly AI to turn off security systems and open safes, but you're always limited by power as to how much help the AI can provide. Meanwhile, there's a clock ticking that makes security get tougher every 5 turns, so you need to move with haste. Your operatives have limited skills, limited inventory slots and even more limited funds, so you're going to have some hard choices.
Put this together and you have a very tight package of gaming goodness. It's not hard to pick up but it does get difficult to master. Even on the easiest level the game is a challenge. On higher levels, you simply can't make mistakes and there's no save function here. You have a very limited ability to rewind to avoid a screwup, but limited is a key word in that sentence.
The "campaign" isn't very long - you'll finish it in fewer than 3 hours. But you mayl want to play this again and again since all levels are randomly generated and the various difficulty levels will always provide a good challenge.
Now my biggest problem with the game really revolves around the longevity. Even knowing the levels are random doesn't help what become some fairly simple gameplay mechanics. So while I found the game exceptionally well-crafted and worthy of your dollars, I'm not going to see a lot of long-term gameplay from this title in my experience.

is a very well made roguelite twin-stick shooter that incredibly fun and satisfying to play that I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys roguelikes.
There are six different categories of guns; Bullet, Shell, Arrow, Laser, Explosive and Melee. Each one of them feels different and unique so there will be a preferred weapon type for everyone. The gunplay in the game is very well done, all the weapons feel like they have a weight to them and it is fun to mix different weapons to find the perfect combination. The randomized nature of the game means that players will get to experiment and experience all the weapons. Furthermore, it’s very satisfying to learn the how the weapons work and master the controls of the variety weapons.
There are a variety of character which have unique abilities such as rolling and shields and player also levels up their character through the run which will unlock new attributes, leading to some unique builds that will adjust how the player will play the game, meaning every run is unique. There is also daily challenges which will spawn a new run every day and you can replay the same map for a day and try to place on the leaderboard, rather than a randomized level each time, creating a variety of game modes.
Every stage in the game feels unique with new enemies introduced that you learn the patterns. The game has elements of Shmup games with a large amount of bullets flying towards you and can get overwhelming but it’s very satisfying find a path through the enemies and beat the level.
Even though the game can be very challenging, the difficulty curve is not too steep so that it doesn't become too hard for players too quickly, the player is always in a space where it is possible to fight out of any challenge.
The sound design and graphics both build a very unique atmosphere, the music often matches the settings perfectly and is very invigorating when fighting the enemies. The pixel graphics are very detailed and unique that gives the game great charm and character that is wonderful to look at, all the enemies are instantly recognizable and interesting to fight.
This is also a paragon of early access games. The devs have made over 90 weekly updates to the game that add new features such as weapons, characters, as well as adjust and rebalance gameplay. They listen to the community; they deserve some respect for their commitment to the game in a landscape of exploitive developers who want to release buggy, broken games to get a quick buck, such as DayZ and countless other scams.
started out a great game and has only gotten better over time as more things get added to the game, as it soon approaches its full release, it sets a standard for early access games on Steam and it is a shame that this level of dedication to a game isn’t seen very often. Overall, definitely worth picking up to support good developers and a great game, looking forward to the final release coming up soon!

Well, as my eager and rabid fans know, I love The Walking Dead by Telltale. Had not Spec Ops: The Line been released in 2012, it would have been my game of the year. And so is the case with it's sequel. Had it not been released in 2013 along with The Last of Us, I'd definitely pick this as one of my favorite games, and an excellent sequel to the story set forth by Lee... albeit containing some problems.
The overall aesthetic from the first Walking Dead has been bumped up immensely. The textures and colors are a lot more lively in this game, as there's a lot more beauty and cruelty to take in. The first Walking Dead, while great, focused more on making it's colors look very grim and foreboding. But between the two color choices, I think Season 2 was a lot smarter. It's only an addition of some warm oranges or dark blues to change the temperature or urgency of a situation.
The story is more of The Walking Dead, but this time as Clementine. As you may be accustomed to. there are plenty of decisions to be had and just as many moral dilemmas to feel conflicted about. And I do like this. As a story that picks up near the end of the first game and just keeps telling the story, while still keeping the staples of it's predecessor and bringing back some old with some new in the story and gameplay is very nice.
Unfortunately, there are a few more flaws in this game than the first Walking Dead. The first and most obvious to me was Clementine's voice actress. Of all the characters in the game, she was voiced the most lifelessly and unenthusiastically. I eventually got used to it, and she did improve close to the end, but she hardly covered the emotional range that she could have. The voice work done for Clementine in the first game was much better, because she did much better actually sounding happy, sad, or scared. Melissa Hutchison just sounds bored most of the time, in this game.
The game also contains more technical issues, as well. Sometimes mouths don't sync up right. Sometimes a sound effect sounds like it was recorded in a jar. Sometimes the characters glitch a little before talking. I didn't noticed these problems as much in the first game, but they are far more noticeable in Season 2.
Despite these flaws, The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a must for anyone dying to find out what happens next to Clementine. Besides the disappointing lack of usage of characters from 400 Days and it's technical flaws here and there, Season 2 is a damn good addition to The Walking Dead.

Having owned the boxed copy of FSX: Deluxe as well as the Acceleration addon, I was originally on the fence when I first noticed FSX:SE on Steam. When it went on sale, I jumped on it simply thinking I'll have the convenience of a digital copy (installing from multiple DVDs + manually entering two serial numbers plus hunting down the latest patches and tweaks to get it to run on Win7 x64 is tiresome).
Little did I realize that FSX:SE isn't just the same binary distribution from the boxed DVD set, but has been updated. The source was modified to support Steam multiplayer and chat, rebuilt with VS2013*, tweaked to ensure Win7/8/10 64-bit compatibility**.
I haven't benchmarked the sim compared to its boxed counterpart on the same system, but it certainly feels smoother. I've cranked the custom details completely to their highest (texture size, terrain visibility, cloud detail, autogen, scenery density, traffic, etc) and haven't noticed any studdering or low frame rates. It might be placebo, but nonetheless it's nice to finally be able to run a 2006 sim flawlessly and smoothly, albeit on a 2014 PC (i7-4770K, 16GB RAM, Geforce 770).
Unfortunately, I don't own any additional payware test out with FSX:SE, but the free aircraft I've tried out thus far appear to work with no issue. I'm hoping to see Steam Workshop support in the future. However, I'm only concerned about the possibility that DTG might start reselling previously-advertised features as DLC (like they did with TS).
*I'll vouch for the advances in optimizations that MS's C++ compiler has undergone since VS2005. I've seen some cases increase ~10% in performance between VS2008 and VS2010 alone.
**Contrary to some info on the forums, the binaries are still 32-bit. While it no longer crashes or runs abnormally on Win7/8/10 64-bit platforms, there's still a 4GB limitation that might be problematic if one loads too many resource-intensive addons. I'm hoping DTG addresses this in a future update.

Klei took all the good things about round-based strategy from the big brother XCOM and added their experience with stealth games and some unique gameplay ideas to the mix and ... it works perfectly. To round it all up they got some rogue-like elements like permadeath for the agents and (depending on the difficulty) very limited possibilities to retry. But failing the short campaign (took me 5 hours on first try on beginner difficulty) will always yield some XP that unlocks new agents and abilities for the next round.
That alone would be enough for a great little game but Klei also shows again just how good they got with art and design. Artwork, sound design, UI - every little detail down to how the menus fade in feels just right and makes this good game a perfect one.
If you like stealth, and if you like round-based strategy, this is the game for you!
To the guys and gals at Klei: Fantastic work, I can't wait what you are working on next!

The Civ games have always had great opening sequences, setting the stage for something epic, challenging and somehow, fun. Civ 6 is possibly the first installment to deliver this promise, almost fully.
This is not the first Civ opening to move me to tears, nor is it the first that describes the hopeful, exploratory and often violent journey of the human race through an excellent montage of historical moments. It is not the first time that the theme plays on repeat, nor that my first session began sometime around 20:00 and ended at 14:00 on the next day. For some reason, the Civ series has always been able to magically turn the tiniest minutae of government and empire building into a deeply satisfying, personal experience. There's something about spreadsheets, I suppose.
Once I opened my eyes and made my way through the menu screen into the first game, and had played that a while, I realised this was finally the Civ I had been hoping for a long time. In other ways it reminded me of the very early instalments of the game, mostly because of the amount of time spent actually using workers for the first time since- I think- Civ 3, in which worker automation was implemented. But the sprawling cities I wanted to build were suddenly on the map, not quite as elegantly implemented as in other games, but more varied, and bursting with an approximation of lives. The map felt smaller, somehow, even a huge one, and locations somehow more memorable- maybe because I was taking up more space on it. The whole experience felt lighter, though not less deep than Civ 5- the game knows when to take itself seriously and when it can very well do away with all the weight of human history and just go with it, the history of the franchise might have something to do with it.
I am at the disadvantage of understanding a few languages spoken it the game: The historical leaders were, for a change, a pleasant interaction. Though cartoons, they are hardly caricatures of themselves. Played for character rather than comedy, and a lack of demotic, aramaic, whatever it is that Tomyris speaks and hindu, the leaders finally became memorable actors on the world stage, and everyone but the hero got killed in the end. Spoilers.
Somehow, this is also a very hopeful Civ. Looking- as some deduce from the lyrics of the theme- to the future, rather than back, this is a celeberation of what humans- however defined- can accomplish in the long term, while remaining schizophrenically addicted to simulatneously saving and preserving themselves. Where they might go, if just dreams came true. My map told stories for the first time, not only of battles fought, but of growth, discoveries, exchanges and losses. So this game makes me very happy- it is entirely new while remaining entirely itsself, throwing nostalgia for ages past out of the airlock and riding forward into a future.
Though, wierd thing about the music: the repeated orchestral renditons of several tunes associated with certain countries is beautiful, but the returning themes get a bit old after a few thousand years played in one go.
If you had to read this to know that this is a game to have played at least once, then good thing you got this far.
Update: After the first, somewhat breathless couple of playthroughs, I stand by my original opinion. It remains a very worthy adition to the Civ series, but feels, in its current state, somewhat lifeless- the world lacks the tension of the previous games, with many systems that gave the map a dynamic that went beyond where to plant your cities missing. Maybe the upcoming expansion will add some of these systems and improve the AI and give it some options to express itself in ways that do not include declarations of war.

Hotline Miami is one of those fantastic little games which come with a simple design and use that design to deliver a wonderfully complex and engaging experience. The year is 1989, the season is late spring, and the setting is Miami, Florida, during the infamous Cocaine Wars. You are "Jacket", a no-name-given murderer who takes out hits for a mysterious caller on gang members while wearing an animal mask to hide his identity. It is a violent, brutal, and honestly somewhat unsettling and disturbing experience, and the game relishes in all of it. Not relying on just ultraviolent gameplay, Hotline Miami also makes good use of a minimalist, surreal narrative; bright, gaudy, flashing neon colors; and a synthpop soundtrack that ranges from eeriely relaxing, bood pumping exciting, and nauseatingly strange all at once to express its unsettling message with excellent results. Each level is like a high, mixing excitement and violence followed by a down time in the form of the end-mission silence and tranquil, relaxing score screen. Tension is then built up again in the introduction of the next level with its unnerving music and telephone call delivering the next hit.
Gameplay is simple but effective: its presented from a top down perspective and you both strafe and rotate. At first you're only equipped with your bare hands, but taking down enemies allows you to pick up their weapons for your own use: cricket bats, golf clubs, knives, guns and more, as well as special unlockable weapons that are rewarded for high scores can randomly spawn throughout the level. Action is fast paced and furious: both "Jacket" and most of his enemies are one hit wonders, so gameplay isn't just braindead fighting. No, you must think ahead to plan your moves to account for the various enemy positions and their strengths and weaknesses (are they behind a door? Do they patrol? Do they have a gun or a melee weapon? What kind of gun? And so forth...) to plot your actions. However, the AI is simplistic in design and therefore a good bit random, so even the most methodical plan won't always go according to plan. This is the greatness in Hotline Miami's design: you'll never have the same experience twice, even if you were the most skilled player alive, there's enough random chance that you'll be quick on your wits at any moment's notice and adjust your plan accordingly. It isn't perfect, though: you can't drop a weapon next to another weapon without picking the other up (frustrating when you need to switch to your fists to knock someone over for an execution), and the AI is sometimes can be moronic beyond belief, or downright prophetic. I can't count how many times I was running behind someone to knock them over just for them to superhumanly turn completely around and club my face in, or shoot me with a shotgun point blank. The layout of a few areas in the game encourage this AI weirdness as well: anywhere with a lot of windows and open space, expect to get plastered by a shotgun from beyond visible range. These are only minor hitches in an otherwise solid experience, though.
The story is very minimalist, with a lot left open to interpertation (unless you play Hotline 2, which explains a few things). "Jacket" never speaks, and the narrative takes on an increasingly surreal and bizzare character as the game progresses: certain masks speak to "Jacket" at the start of each act, his only seeming friend somehow appears at every job in the local area, and eventually bodies of people he has killed start appearing in his daily routine. This combined with the psychadelic music and flashy neon visuals leaves you to wonder what, if anything, is "real" in this narrative - and unfortunately the game never really touches on it at the end, either. There is some conclusion to the story, but its an honestly unsatisfying exposition dump for the motives behind the mysterious individuals leaving messages on "Jacket"'s phone for why they're giving him hits to take out, and the surrealist story is left hanging. However, the story in this game is not the focus but rather an enjoyable aside and so the conclusion does not hurt the game much.
All in all, Hotline Miami is a star of an indie game, and a great example of how various elements of a game work together for a greater whole, even if there are problems. The music is some of the best made retro-style synthpop I've heard, and each track suits the mood and sets the stage for the action. Its fast paced, brutally violent, unforgiving and addicting game that I couldn't reccommend any higher. Give it a go!
