This won't be a long review, but I thought I'd encourage a few folks who picked this up, like I did, then ignore it for a while after bouncing off it. I, and a few friends, all bought this when it first came out, having gone back to Civ 5 numerous times. We played this a little, liking a few aspects, but, well, played like it was Civ 5 (or 4, or 3, or...) and thought it was pretty but not wonderful. I would strongly suggest you try again. We made ourselves play it again on our game night, and with a bit more time from having played Civ 5 found ourselves really enjoying it. There's some issues with AI, but it's not terrible. There's a few UI changes we'd also like to make, but there's some mods that can help with some of that.
If you're not enjoying it our combined recommendation is that if you give it a bit of time - after playing an earlier Civ - you might just find you like it.

Since  I intially wrote my review for FSX, I have discovered and rectified the issues I was having - all of which were down to the settings causing conflicts on my machine - and as a result I have now changed my recommendation of the game.
Pros
The in-game tutorials are very good - some of which are very challenging.
The ability to pick up and drop cargo from some aircraft adds a whole new set of challenges.
The interiors are far more detailed than they used to be on earlier MS Flight Sims and have more working controls.
Cons
Very large initial download if you have a slow broadband connection.
Some of the airports are somewhat lacking in detail - Heathrow looks nothing like the real thing other than the runway layout. For a more realistic feel you would have to buy additional scenery packs - an extra cost.
I have still to try out running some of my FSX compatible addons with the Steam version, but, from what I have read, it should not be a problem... time will tell.
Original post:-

I have been a real world aviator for the past 18 years. Back when I was training for my Instrument Rating, MS Flight Sim became more than just a game. It was an essential tool in the flight bag that helped solidify essential skills needed to fly in the IFR world. The end result of which saved me time and money obtaining my rating. I basically taught myself IFR flying. It was essential to understanding VOR radials and ADF tracking and intercepts.
After flying for a career for the past 8 years I'd never thought I'd have use for MS Flight Sim ever again. However, recently I dusted off my old copy of MS Flight Sim to help prepare for my Boeing 737 type rating. A company designed a fairly accurate version of the 737 with the correct system logic. It even included a fairly accurate FMC. Once again MS Flight Sim proved useful and was essential to understanding the systems of the 737 and cockpit flows. Hopefully the Steam version will allow for these add-ons.
My advice to anyone using MS Flight Sim as a training tool would be to treat it as just a game until you start instrument training and be prepared for many misunderstandings. My previous four year’s experience as flight instructor and chief flight instructor has taught me that those used Flight Simulators during their Ab Intio training developed bad habits that needed to be trained out of them. Once you have completed your Ab Intio training, it can be an excellent training tool.

If you're a fan of stealth games like Mask of the Ninja or tactical turn-based games like XCOM, you'll love this. You control a team of special agents who are trying to infiltrate a number of high-security corporation buildings to gather intel and gear. After 3 in-game days (approximately 8 missions), you're thrust into a climactic final mission that is nail-bitingly difficult, even on Beginner mode. Difficult, but not unfair.
That's really true of all of Klei's games. Every time you "fail," you learn more about how the game works. And in this one, much like Don't Starve, you also earn XP toward unlocking new agents and AI programs that make the process easier.
Maps are procedurally generated, there are lots of unlocks and several difficulty modes (including an Endless mode) so there's the potential for 100+ hours of fun gameplay here, easily.
If you like these kinds of games, you really can't go wrong. It's an amazingly polished experience all around, extremely challenging and tons of fun.

The reason why I picked up this game in the 1st place was because I saw a sequel come out. And damn right I did that. I have heard a little about it and did not take much notice, but when I started playing, that was it! What a game!
The big idea behind the game is to complete the levels fast, while you are accompanied by great music and massive killings. Planning your game is essential, kills are easy but you are no different. You die all the same as any other character. Bosses a bit tough and take some time to kill, which I actually dont like in such a fast phased games. Then you add masks to boost your abilities and if you cant do the round with one, maybe you should pick another one and it will be easy.
I am not sure if the game was originally made for consoles or not, but the controls on PC are rather good. Easy 6 buttons to use + mouse. The game is quite fast so you will have to move a lot.
For some games music adds some atmosphere and just a bit of story, but in this case the music adds 50% of your joy while playing the game. It just makes you want to move and... kill. Just the soundtrack is already enough to purchase Hotline Miami.
The visuals are amazing! So much blood. Everything is detailed, maps are not dull and boring. Characters animations are done very well too.
And now, the bad things that I have encountered. 1st and most annoying is when the dogs are running of the map. Just cant kill them to finish the round. Bosses are way too hard, and they break the fast phase of the game. Fallen enemies are the most dangerous ones.
Replayability is low. Now you can play 2nd game. Plus ones the story is finished, I dont see why would anyone want to play more of this.
So to sum up, I would recommend this game to everybody. It does not take long to finish, but you get a very good experience of being a psychopath. Its so much worth it!

LucasArts (rip in piece) took a step into first person action games with 1995's Dark Forces.
One thing that makes this Doom clone stand out is a lot of engine work. There are various differences in geometry, such as cliffs, pits, platforms, etc, and ambient lighting is colored, as well as colored fog.
Gameplay wise, you play as mercenary Kyle Katarn as he under takes missions for the Rebellion. From stealing the Death Star plans to escaping Jabba the Hutt's sail barge, the game throws you into maps, and gives you goals.
Unlike Doom, you don't just find the exit. You actually have objectives to do, and if you fail those objectives, you lose the level.
The voice acting is quite good for the time, the gameplay and maps are all great, and the game proved that LucasArts could craft amazing story lines with it's own universe. The Dark Forces series remains one of the best Star Wars series availible, and I would recommend this game to pretty much anyone that likes Star Wars.

If you are buying this steam version because some people said it’s smoother and gives more FPS, you’ll be disappointed because there is no enhancement whatsoever apart from the return of multiplayer.
I own a boxed version and have acceleration with service parks including lots of add-ons. I get a reasonable FPS in my windows 7-64bits but just like every fsx simmer you never get enough. So when I read the feedbacks here about how it was improved, I decided to give this steam version a go. I bought it yesterday, download took like an hour or so and installation was smooth. I have made few flights now, the truth is that the only difference is that it is a combination of Gold Edition, Acceleration and Service park, and that Multiplayer is back, also uiautomationcore.dll was added to the main directory for windows 8. Performance is exactly the same as FSX Deluxe Edition with Acceleration and service park without any add-on or tweak.
I have to admit that I am not very sad that I bought this steam version, but this is because my boxed version is almost cracked and I think it’s a good idea to have a digitally signed one saved at Steam library. Another thing I’m hoping for is that since this simulation is very old and therefore do not take advantages of new and better graphic cards and systems and Microsoft no longer provide updates, hopefully with steam re-releasing it now future updates will be a possibility, if not it is going to be a waste for those who have boxed version already.
As for those wondering if existing addons will work. Almost all addons that you can normally copy and paste into FSX will work in Steam version, Mine worked, I have never installed any which needs installation yet. Also I installed this version in the same PC I already have FSX, both are working fine.
If you want to read the reviews, from the beginning there is a separate tab for positive and negative feedbacks, which I didn’t notice. The default is positive so make sure to check the negatives also.

I will say this: I hate games that are released unfinished, and Sega is the king of doing this. Yet despite this baffling behavior by it's publisher, Alpha Protocol has survived it's premature birth with love and attention from it's development staff. It is a game of cinematic espionage action-RPG, a unique blend of concepts, themes, ideas and writing that rarely comes down the chute from on high. With it's gaping bugs patched and it's casts applied, the game holds together, despite certain rough patches. With it's massive gouge in price, it may be worth looking into.

Ignore all the hate on micro transactions, I'm 7 hours in and have yet to see a reason for them, there are so many captains running around there are plenty of chances to earn good quality gear just playing.
The same enemy types are back from the first game, but they also added Olag-Hai - which are basically big trolls you can only counter 1/3rd of the time - when you do get a counter though you can "ride them" and smash them into other orcs.
The nemesis system is largely expanded and the amount of traits Captains can now have is far greater and more nuanced. You can still run over the majority with the same tactics - stun, vault, executions etc. But sometimes one will be enraged by executions, or enraged by seeing a fellow captain with low health. So you have to change your style, or target one captain first - which can be hard when there are 20 orcs swarming you.
The story seems entertaining so far, although I have been largely doing side activities - of which there are lots and lots.
If you enjoyed the first then buy it - it's more of the same with lots more variety and fun combat. Can't go wrong.

Star Wars: Dark Forces, is a old, odd, game. When I purchased it on Steam, several years ago now... I really didn't know what I was buying. Yes, I knew it was a Star Wars game, but the main thing that had me eyeballing it, was it's ridiculous cheep price. It was $0.99.
One of the first things that surprised me was that it was an older game, Dark Forces came out in 1995 for MS-Dos. Which is why this game uses a pre-programed version of Dos-box to run the game on modern machines. I've played it on several computers, it seems to run just fine.
Dark Forces is the first in the Jedi Knight game series, you play as Kyle Katarn, a young mercenary, a cross between Han Solo and Luke Skywalker. In the future games Kyle grows to become a Jedi Knight, but in this game he's just a mercenary.
Gameplay is fine, think of a Star Wars meets Duke Nukem 3D. Dark Forces falls in from the time where 3D shooters weren’t quiet all 3D yet, a 2.5D pixel wonderland where you explore and take down stormtroopers and the evil dark stormtoopers.
Do you have a lightsaber? Nope. But you really don't need to, Dark Forces has you play as a one man army. You're not a Jedi. You're a hired gun, and honestly it's better this way. You're not this over powered superman with force powers, mowing down enemies. You're a dude turned against the empire. You're not in it to be noble, you're out for vengeance. This could have turned into an interesting series, you have this character go deeper and deeper to the darkside basically by killing stormtroopers for the wrong reasons, yet fighting for the right of the rebellion.
Instead, they dropped that, gave you a lightsaber, and called you a Jedi Knight in the sequel.
Dark Forces is an older game, don't expect to be wowed by the story or gameplay. You might be in for a shock to discover, much like myself that the Theme from Star Wars is played from a Midi version. But that's because its from that odd period of time. No, FMV... that’s for the sequel. If you're a Star Wars fan, you'll want to play this, and probably the rest of the Jedi Knight series.

I previously wrote a review for this game shortly after it entered Early Access. After leaving it for some time, I returned a couple of days ago when it was fully released. And holy hell, the game has been seriously, SERIOUSLY polished.
Gorgeous. Every character is stylised and are distinctive in their appearance, making telling your agents apart a breeze. The music is wonderful and frankly rather catchy. It doesn't intrude on your game, rather simply bolstering the experience. The tempo of the music speeds up as the alarm level rises, toying with your sense of urgency and driving you to get your agents out as fast as possible.
There has been some beautiful polishing here. Guards can be easily identified, along with their visual area - parts of the map that are in their cone of vision but behind cover are also easy to spot, making navigating the somewhat tricky rooms nicely intuitive. Cover is abundant when it needs to be, but never clutters the map.
Visual representations of information are good, too. Footsteps generate little echo pulses, rooms you have visual on are nicely distinguished from rooms you don't, etc.
The UI is clean, well-designed and frankly wonderful to look at. Abilities are easy to comprehend
The game is, above all, a challenge. The turn-based nature allows you to take your time and make planned decisions, but every mission has a propensity to go straight to hell  because of a guard walking into a room just as you're crouched over his mate's body rifling through his pockets. The game doesn't pull punches and you frequently have to make sacrificial decisions as to whether you want to risk everything on getting those lat couple of safes or play it safe.
The addition of limited rewinds (The ability to undo decisions) is a fantastic one. You can switch 'em off if you feel it's too cheaty, but the game only allows you to rewind a few times before you're stuck with your choices. You have a safety net, but it's made of dental floss and chewing gum.

Alpha Protocol, Obsidian's only original IP to date, is an RPG built on familiar mechanics with an interesting "Bourne Identity" style spy premise. Like RPGs of old, combat and dialogue are so separate as to almost comprise different games within the same narrative, but each is gratifying and reasonably well executed.
What distinguishes Alpha Protocol from similar stealth-action-RPGs are the branching choices. It is impossible to anticipate the consequences of your decisions, and even minor dialogue choices can potentially have game-changing ramifications.
The voice acting ranges from fair to excellent, and the graphics, although dated, convey the setting well enough. The soundtrack occasionally becomes repetitive, but its not a deal breaker.
Like all of Obsidian's work, AP remains very rough around the edges. Expect bugs, glitches, and design flaws to creep into your game every hour or two. If you can work through the flaws, there's a gem here that shouldn't be missed.

While I haven't had a chance to really dive into it fully yet, I can honestly say that this is a golden opportunity to play Flight Simulator X on current hardware. If you've ever been a fan of the Flight Simulator franchise from the recent years (Flight Sim '98, 2000 through 2004), FSX is basically the culmination of some of their best efforts.
Disclaimer: this game probably gives even modern gaming rigs today a run for their money with every single graphic option turned up to maximum. But with modern hardware (and even Surface Pro 3 tablets), those framerate-heavy moments hopefully won't steer you away from the fun to be had.
Of the things I've seen so far:
* Air traffic control is more integrated into the game than in FS2004
* Dynamic scenery by land, air, and sea
* Surprisingly cool special effects
* Really, REALLY good adventure/mission dynamics and experiences
I'll be paying attention to see how well add-ons integrate with this version of FSX. That should take care of some complaints of "my town doesn't look that realistic". (I took a flight over areas where I live and work, and major and regional roads are represented, so you can theoretically fly to a reasonably close proximity of your town.)
Sure, even a game like FSX has its shortcomings, but lack of scenery "authenticity" aside (they did a FANTASTIC job with stock scenery included), this is a world-class conversion and provision of the franchise. Get this game through Steam and let them take care of all the compatibility issues for you!

Many call this game just a Doom clone, but of course it's not as simple as that. Like most games from the early days of the (partial) 3D first-person shooter genre, Dark Forces builds on what was established by its predecessors. It takes Doom's formula, uses it as the foundations and creates something new and improved (just like Doom did with Wolfenstein 3D). From a gameplay perspective it is quite similar, but a number of key features have been added which were quite new in 1995.
In addition to all the typical stuff you'd expect from a mid-1990s shooter, Dark Forces also allows the player to aim vertically (this can however only be done using the numpad; the mouse is used for horizontal aiming instead). Other features added by the Jedi engine are the ability to jump and crouch and a number of atmospheric effects. Some missions require the use of a headlamp, night vision, gas mask, special boots and other tools. The player can also throw thermal detonators (explosives).
Dark Forces is set in the Star Wars universe. Since it is a licensed production, everything from the visuals and sound effects have a distinct feel. If you enjoyed the original trilogy of Star Wars (episodes IV, V and VI), this game will certainly make you feel nostalgic. The levels are slightly less abstract than Doom, but they are still very well designed and quite complicated, also forcing the player to think by adding various puzzles throughout. Dark Forces has a total of 14 missions and during the course of the game you will see aesthetically different environments.
Besides differences in gameplay and visuals, Dark Forces is also more story-focused than the Doom games. You play as Kyle Katarn, a mercenary recruited by the Rebel Alliance, one that used to work for the Galactic Empire. The plot begins shortly before the events of Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope, but gradually takes you past the ending of the film and takes place between A New Hope and Star Wars Episode V: The Empire Strikes Back. It's not masterful storytelling, but the simple plot and visually pleasant cutscenes make the game more engaging.
Overall, the game's numerous mechanical improvements and technological advancements make it a natural successor to Doom 2, adding variety to the Doom gameplay formula. Star Wars: Dark Forces was a brilliant game for its time; since then it has influenced other amazing titles (such as Duke Nukem 3D) and remains a classic.
NOTE: The Steam re-release of this game isn't entirely up to scratch. Upon launching the game, you will experience terrible performance issues (especially when there are multiple enemies on screen). It's nothing that a quick Google search can't fix, but it should be in-game from the get-go.

I have just started playing this game after it being recommended to me by a friend, and I thought I might mention a few of the pros and cons of this game so far. Baring in mind this is early access the cons are what I recommend for the final game and should be added in for a better experience.
Pros:
-8 Bit Graphics are cool, keep it that way. Fits the play style perfectly.
-A gradual difficulty slope that is easy enough for you to progress but difficult enought to make you want to come back for more, but I found that a few people (not including myself) found that it was more difficult than expected.
-Plenty of stages and levels to progress through, but it would be nice if you were to add more as people get better at it.
-Charatcers: the variety is great and all the special abilities and mutations means each run is unique and different from the last. It would be nice to see more for those who have played with every character and need something new.
-No micro-transactions at this time, baring in my it is still early access there is know means of putting money into the game after you have bought it, this is good!
Cons:
-Not full screen, The game runs in full screen but you have black bars along the side, please remove it as it is an ugly feature and the game would look cleaner and more atractive in a widescreen view. Though this isn't the end of the world it would be nice if the game had some graphics settings.
-30 FPS Cap!! What? Why? I am not sure exactly why the game devs have made it so the game can only be run at 30fps or less. Surely if the PC can run it higher (which almost any pc can) it should be allowed. This made the game feel ever so slightly choppy but it was fine overall.
-Co-op can only be done in a local network. Sadly this means I can not play with friends unless I bring my pc into the same internet as theirs or play split screen with a controller. Make a means of playing co-op online with people on steam. This would make the game more tactical as you would have to work together. I think this would be a great addition for the final game.
Summary:
Should you buy this game?
Yes, if you need some time to kill and are willing to pack in a few hours learning the characters and improving. It is worth the price especially as they have updated it over 90 times since the original release. This game has perma-death so expect to get annoyed throughout the time of playing it. Anyway I hope this review helped you make a more informed decision on wether this game is for you. Leave a like if it did, Thanks.

This is a wonderful story-based game.  A good storyline makes a good game.  In this game you play a famous book author, Alan Wake, who starts out his adventure on a vacation.  Things get serious when the characters in his stories come to life in what seems like a nightmare.  Soon, reality isn't what it seems.  This game plays like a cool TV series or playing a good book story.  It has episodes and Alan Wake narrorates his thoughts at times.  It's a horror adventure so there's scary parts.  You have to fight enemies, flip switches and find supplies to survive.  There are several things to find on your adventure like guns, ammo, book pages and flashlight batteries (you'll see why).  In other words the gameplay is like any other survivor-adventure.  But the storyline is real solid and leaves you wanting to find out what happens next.  At the time of this writing, Alan Wake is my #1 favorite story-based game.
Pros:
+ Storyline
+ Game plays like a good book / episode story
+ Cut scenes
+ Graphics
+ Soundtrack
+ Voice acting
+ Horror adventure
+ There's book adaptation to this game:  Alan Wake by Rick Burroughs

As much as I like to lament the rise of the linear, corridor shooter, Dark Forces' level design is a proper counter argument to the growing sentiment that Doom-era level design was inherently superior. The environments' visual simularity makes it hard to differentiate areas you've already explored and the maps sprawl and twist with hidden nooks and crannies that, in most games, would be secret areas but, here, are necessary to find and explore to progress.
If this sounds like it's going to be a negative review, I've misled you. Complaints on level design aside, the story is pretty great, especially for a shooter from this era, and the gameplay is challenging and frenetic at times. Your movement speed is akin to an F1 car and the weapons are satisfying in a Doom rocket launcher sorta way. Blasters shoot with violent rapidity and mowing down stormtroopers doesn't get old quickly.
I played through the entire campaign on medium when it was new (I'm old), and played through about half of it on easy here. On easy, I would finish most levels with max armor and health, on medium I remember things getting hairy a few times.
Worth it for nostalgia if you played it the first time and for morbid curiosity if you've never kicked the tires.

If you think this is similar to Overwatch, no, it is not. Probably some ability in some champions are similar but none of them are actually originates from each other.
Enough comparison of Overwatch and Paladins, this game is actually very playable and are recomended to all who likes to play class shooter FPS. But in this game you do not have the luxury of switching your role mid game like Team Fortress 2 or Battlefield. You have to adapt the game by using:
1. Pre-game Loadouts, a system of deck that can be purchased through coins (not that very expensive, mind you. I have completed all the characters loadout even before I reach level 30). The loadout might seems like a big deal for new players, but don't be afraid, that there are basic deck for each character that actually most cards are useful and are still used in competitive and pro-players.
2. Burn Cards (Items in-game purchase), a system of items with a UI lot similar to Smite (Another Hi-Rez product) that helps you adapt to the game as the pace changes. Items like Wrecker to counter Heavy Sheilds champions such as Fernando and Ruckus, or Cauturize for Heavy healers such as Grover and Mal' Damba. There are a lot more cards like reducing cooldowns and faster movement speed but these are your choice to change as many as you like in-match.
So, in conclusion, I like this game and have a very different experience of playing it in comparison to Overwatch, different pace, different procedure to tackle each match, different abilities for different champions, so why be afraid to try? It is not just some ripoff, it is actually a very loveable game.
P.S: Mind that this game is a BETA game, so expect to have some minor bugs (nothing game breaking).
Thank you for reading this review and good luck to Hi-Rez in making this game another success in follow up to Smite.

There is a money collection system for buying weapons, armor, and accessories through the black market to enhance your chosen perks. The aiming system was biggest weakness, the enemy AI could have been improved, and the bosses seemed overpowered, but overall there was really very few issues with the gameplay, and the execution is top notch. The game also offers a lot of replayability due to its diverse story paths. This is a must buy.

So if you enjoy a decent story and dialogue get this game (was 2$), but don't expect anything great combatwise.

Hotline Miami is one of those games that will stand as a gem in Gaming (with games like Shovel Knight). Hotline Miami has been out for 3 years. I played through it and had fun doing it. Especially when I played the side-story about that biker you kill (semi-spoilers).
Here are the 2 playable Characters:
Jacket (main story only, some spoilers)- Jacket has the choice of masks. He is the only playable character and never speaks (not a single line). However, he is a good character because he has no real traits besides being subscribed to 50 Blessings, Going insane, and having a girlfriend he saved after killing a group of Russain Mobsters. Honestly, I feel Jacket is pretty relatable if you know where he's coming from.
The Biker (side-story, spoilers)- This is the story where you aquire the secret ending (if you find all the pieces). Now, the story of the biker starts with him wanting out of 50 Blessings. You head to a Chinese Resturant and kill Mobsters. You then head to another Russain Mobster Safehouse with arcade machines. The Biker moves fast, has only one weapon, and has 3 limited throwing knives. If anything, he's a nice fast weapon. When you get to the Phone Company Mission, you kill Jacket (this is conflicting as Jacket kills the Biker, but it could be that both of their minds were seeing things by then, which is pretty understandable). In the end, you find the 50 Blessings group (composed of 2 Janitors at the Golden Truck club) and you put in the secret puzzle here. And when you do, you get the secret ending. You have the option of not killing, killing one of, or killing both of the 50  Blessings creators, leading you to the credits once you leave.
As for gameplay, it's a nice top down view, with visually appealing graphics and loads of secrets (secret masks, puzzle pieces for the secret ending, achievements, stuff like that.) The game itself is fun. I really had fun when playing it. It felt pleasing because I loved to kill the mobsters, it felt fun to just stab a mobster with a knife (which is op in the 1st game if you just swing and are moving fast, this was nefed to swing slower in Hotline Miami 2.) I give Hotline Miami lots of credit for being a game I enjoyed a lot.

I have been playing FSX for 5 years now. I am not a pilot, I just always enjoyed games that aloowed you to fly.
That said, FSX is an awesome experience for players looking for a good flying experience, all the way to real life pilots looking to practice their skills without paying for it in fuel. This game actually has the largest map ever, it's Planet Earth. The shear number of places to go and things to see is insane. Even for a game that is 8 years old, it still has scenes of absolute beauty.
This isn't an easy game. You throw on full realism, a crosswind, and a major thunderstorm... good luck making it off the ground. The physics of this game are beyond good. The controls leave you options as well. You can use keyboard and mouse, or a gamepad, or a joytick, or a full blown yoke, rudder pedals, and throttles. Whilst the full setup is a little spendy, I myself am saving up for one to experience flying in a more realistic manner, the Attack 3 doesn't cut it.
When gamespy went down, FSX multiplayer went with it. I suck at piloting, my joystick doesn't cut it for me. So in multiplayer I tried out being an air traffic controller. Let me tell you, I found my niche. I got hours upon hours of enjoyment guiding players to their runway, destination, or gate. Ground, Tower, Approach, Departure, Center, you name it, I loved it. Then gamespy happened. I was said. Now with Dovetail getting rights, I am happy to be able to try out my ATC again.
Speaking of Dovetail, cudos to them for wanting to continue one of the world's most storied game series. Hopefully they don't use the same sales model as Train Simulator, because that would suck. But alas, the series is being developed again. I for one cannot wait to see a new version with even more up to date graphics and physics that take full advantage of today's powerful computers.
Just a rock solid good experience. 10/10

Classic Microsoft Flight Simulator X, what more can you say? Great realism and complexity, some new aircraft thrown in the mix, with the promise of add-on packs and the possibility of Steam Workshop content. This is the best flight simulation game on the market, and Steam is brilliant for acquiring and releasing this well-loved classic. I'm an M-Soft F-Sim vet, I fell in love with the series with Flight Sim 2000, then 2002, I've owned the tin box edition of 2004: A Century of Flight for years. Never got to play X until now; the mechanics are vastly improved, as are the graphics and the quality of the missions.
In the first mission I played, I took mid-air control of a Cessna flying towards a small airstrip set on a peninsula in Alaska. I followed a Cessna Grand Caravan to the runway, and slowed my approach to give the Grand Caravan time to clear the runway. When air traffic control declared the runway clear, I aligned my approach and set the flaps to full. However, as I approached the runway I saw that my path would be blocked by a large cruise liner entering port. His path intersected with mine, bringing him between my plane and the runway just as I was slowing for the final stages of my approach. I increased throttle and pulled up, passing dangerously close to the gigantic liner; but having cleared the ship, I slammed my throttle closed and pulled the air brake in an attempt to land at a safe speed. I hit the runway and bounced once, twice, and on the third dip made contact with the runway and slowed to under forty knots. I then gently taxied to the airport terminal and parked next to the Grand Caravan that I had followed to the runway.
In my second mission, I took mid-air control of a Learjet over the mountains of Colorado, near Telluride. This is familiar territory for me, so I took time to appreciate the rendering of the scenery: deep valleys with low-lying fog at their centers, rivers carving their ancient paths through the Rocky Mountains. Then I was politely warned that I was flying too low and too fast, and needed to maintain an altitude of 12,000 feet to approach the airport, at a speed of 140 knots. I obliged the polite air traffic controller, and spotted the runway nestled at the top of a mesa ahead of me. I was told to increase flaps to full and extend my landing gear, but a problem with the landing gear triggered a buzzing alarm which would become the soundtrack for my panicked descent. I attempted several more times to extend the gear, but to no avail; the doors were apparently stuck. On my last attempt, with the runway in sight only a few hundred yards ahead of me, the doors opened and the landing gear deployed. I engaged the airbrake and pulled the nose back as I gently made contact with the runway. Following the ATCs intructions, I taxied to the left of the runway and parked next to two limosines. The celebrity cargo was safely delivered, and I was rewarded with a autograph that read, "Greetings from Telluride!"
The missions in this game are incredible and engaging, leaps and bounds ahead of the boring missions of the previous games. The heart of the game, however, is in simulating flights in real-time, and if you have never played a Microsoft Flight Sim before, you are in for a treat. You are given full control of the simulation, you can plan flights to anywhere in the world. Locations are rendered beautifully, and the graphics settings are flexible enough to run smoothly on most any gaming rig. The game automatically logs all of your free and mission flights.  You can communicate and plan with ATCs at any airport in your vicinity, even requesting an emergency landing if you need to do so. Using the flight planner, you can set starting points and destination points, and the game includes almost every airstrip in the world (even private strips). The game can be set to include in-flight emergencies, can require you to stop and refuel when you get low. Nearly every aspect of this game can be customized to suit your playing style.
In short, this is the king of flight simulation games, and Flight Simulator X was the final and greatest installment in this series. Do yourself a favor and learn to fly like a pro, Steam did the gaming community a service by reviving this amazing classic.

Invisible Inc. is yet another of a consistent line of solid games that set Klei Entertainment apart as being developers who truly care about providing a meaty emergent experience for the audience.
The premise is this: a team of underground hackers must physically infiltrate corporations in the 2070s to gain weapons, cracking tools, and other cyberpunk goodies while on a quest to find a new home for their repurposed European weather AI. Except it doesn't detect weather anymore. It breaks safes, converts enemy robots to your cause, disables laser barriers, and occasionally makes you wonder whether it's becoming sentient.
The game successfully subverts a thorn in the side of stealth games by randomizing the corporation maps and only allowing for a certain number of "rewinds," essentially a reload of a save. In older stealth games memorizing enemy patterns is a way to cheese the system but that's just not possible with Invisible Inc.'s robust design. Every new room you enter is a gamble, one that might end up with your valuable agent(s) dead.
I hope this game spawns a long line of sequels or imitators in the stealth-tactics (RPG?) genre.

I've held on to Flight Simulator X. I love this simulator to death. Of course, the simulator itself has been showing it's cracks and it's not as shiny as X-Plane or DCS, but make no mistake. There is a reason why a majority of the people play FSX over other Flight Simulator platforms. That said, I was quite surprised to see FSX live its legacy with a Steam Edition.
To be honest, I'm quite mixed about seeing the game on Steam. FSX is my little niche thing and it would be quite annoying (or amusing) to see some nine-year old flying like... a nine-year old, but with this release, the simulator receives a new lease of life as support is finally restored to a game that has long been thought abandoned by the publishers (We all know MS Flight sucked).
That said, I've tried and tested the simulator. For starters, the simulator runs quite well 'out of the box'. I then tested the simulator with add-ons as well. I had too. I've heard that this game has 'improvements'. So I've installed and tested ORBX YBBN Airport scenery with FTX Australia SP4. When I test for performance, I always test this particular airport. FTX is an amazing developer of add-on sceneries, but the Brisbane Airport (IATA:YBBN) is poorly optimized. No matter what setting I do, it just falls flat of expectation (Some settings are smooth, but it's below their recommended graphics settings). And I'm running an i7 3770k clocked at 4.2 GHz. I'm also using a GTX 660Ti. Just a note, the GPU is not necessarily the depending factor here. Usually, a better CPU leads to significant performance gains. CPUs needs to be overclocked (usually above 4.0 GHz) for optimum performance.
Unfortunately, it was no surprise that FSX:SE performed poorly in this scenery. Who was I to expect something short of a miracle? Unfortunately, this confirms what I've feared. The Steam Edition provides improvements (I will explain later), but you still need to tweak the fsx.cfg file located at the AppData\Microsoft\FSX folder. Some tweaks that I had to adjust were the Texture Bandwith Multiplier = 40 (It was set to 160), Set Affinity Mask = 15, Fiberframetimefraction=0.50 (default is 0.33), WideViewAspect = True, Regardless, it still performed like pizza in this scenery (I actually regret having this scenery), Just a note, while I've actually copypasta the entire fsx.cfg installed in my other hard drive, take caution in doing so. I noticed that the cfg file of the standalone and the steam edition are arranged differently. The [MULTIPLAYER] section of the cfg file is most definitely different.
Now I've noticed that some people in youtube have uploaded themselves playing the Steam Edition. I noticed one video where the person was using DX10. It's quite easy to spot when one is using DX10 even if they don't mention it. I found it quite odd. Everyone in to flightsim should know, unless you have Steve's DX10 scenery fixer, It is usually common knowledge to always use DX9. The reason for this is because while performance gains are realized in DX10, DX10 mode is inherently broken. That's why the ticker box is 'DX10 Preview'. Development was never finished. That said, I gave it a shot.
Here is where I was impressed.
Steam Edition performed phenomenally well in DX10. It's still not the homerun, but I was pleased with the performance. By this time, I had installed the ORBX Cairns Airport Scenery and compared it with DX9 and DX10. Brisbane performance was still kinda bad, but better. In both the Brisbane and Cairns scenery, I flew in the 3D cockpit of the default F/A-18 aircraft.
But you said DX10 performs well in FSX in the first place?
I did, but I was quite shocked with what I saw while running the simulator in DX10. Some of the broken things about DX10 have been fixed. One of the most annoying DX10 blunders is the opaque gray texture replacing the livery texture of commercial AI aircraft. That's been fixed. You could fly in the day with no problem. Flying at Dawn/Dusk, or night time can still be a problem though. The runway/taxiway still becomes opaque at dawn/dusk and the lights still disappear at these times. Cockpit shadows are still blunt. So while some DX10 blunders have been fixed, you may still require Steve's DX10 Scenery Fixer.
So do I recommend this game?
Considering that multiplayer is restored in the Steam Edition and DX10 performance is quite well, I'd definitely recommend this game, especially for the price. However, unless you're not into playing with add-ons free or paid, be prepared to modify the fsx.cfg, which I can say from experience, is a frustrating activity. Also, if you're in to add-ons, make sure you do have a Core-i7 desktop and a GTX 660Ti  equivalent or higher. Always overclock your CPU above 4.0 GHz. Memory with low timings also helps (although some will dispute that this is not necessary). It also helps to have an SSD if you plan to install FSX on a separate drive (FSX can take a long time time to load).
That pretty much wraps up my review, so Good luck and Happy flying to you all!
EDIT: So apparently, I had forgotten that my CPU is 4 cores, 8 threads. I was using the wrong value for the affinity mask. I changed the value from 15 to 85. Both DX9 and DX10 run better now. Brisbane is much better, but still gets some hiccups.

Paladins:
- Custom matches are limited, force you to sit through them, and are not good for practice.
- Terrible training room. Supposedly the hitboxes aren't even accurate.
- Casual or Competitive mode.
- Queue solo or with a friend in competitive. Funny because I play Competitive to avoid getting stomped by premades in Casual mode.
- Typical game is like 1-2 tanks, 1 support, 1 flank, damage.
- Queue times West Coast: 50-200 ping, wait time usually 1-8 minutes.
- Gamble with cosmetics.
- Hitboxes are utter trash. Headshot someone's♥♥♥♥♥and bodyshot someone's head why don't you. At least the damage modifier is something like an extra 30%, so it's not too too bad.
- Bugs are very prevelant.
- Always getting shot when running around corner.
- Characters are goofy in a characteristic way that grows on you. Every character kind of has something I like to say because the voice is just ridiculous. It sounds like whoever is voice acting is having fun with it.
- Maps are small, simple, and usually include 2 flanking sides.
- You heal by staying out of combat or by being healed.
- The Scoreboard at the end details EVERYONE, EVERYTHING. What it DOESN'T include (yet, I hope) is which player DC'd and got replaced by a BOT, though it's usually evident by their score and whether they drooled on walls.
- Very little content on Youtube for this game. Those out there are mostly cringe and the spokespersons of Hi Rez sound like they're just mimicking the raw essence of sport's enthusiasm with way too little substance. Perfect game for a Youtuber who's travelling West for open land.
- Has no voice communication at this time. Only a wide variety of amusing emotes to use.
- Play of the Game really should be skipped until it's not just a glitchy mess.
Overwatch in comparison:
- Custom matches are amazing and give you a multitude of options. Great for practice. I like to have Headshot Only against a bunch of Ana's to warm up.
- Dynamic training room.
- Quickplay or Competitive or Arcade mode. (Arcade has like 1v1 mystery duel, 3v3, 6v6 random hero, etc etc).
- Queue solo or with however many friends you want in competitive.
- Typical game: 2-3 tanks, 2-3 healers, 1-2 damage/flank
- Queue, West Coast, 50 ping always, instant-2 min average
- Gamble with cosmetics.
- Hitboxes are much much better. Headshots are way more deadly.
- Relatively bug free.
- Almost never getting shot while running around corner.
- Characters are goofy, except they try to be very serious. The voices make me cringe in pain because of this horrid concoction,: it all sounds so fake and the words they say are utterly redundant. For Mei, I think they just put gum into a re-tarded woman's mouth  and gave her statistically appropriate things to say. Ana rolls her R's way too enthusiastic in places there shouldn't be any R's, and the accent is very inconsistent. Whenever the characters speak in their home language, they sound like they rehearsed until they made up a phony little song of another language. I'd say: Paladins has fun being re-tarded, while Overwatch doesn't realize it is one.
- Maps are complex and huge.
- You get healed or by medpacks throughout the map. It pays much more to learn the maps in this game.
- The Scoreboard at the end details you only, and, vaguely, some info on a few others. I think this is to remove some toxicity of comparison. The result is a company preferring to keep people happy through ignorance, when really people should learn indifference to scoreboards because at the end of the day, more details = more information = good, always good. It's always good to know a frame of comparison, it's just not good to get affected negatively by it or to not know some champions have utility (Bomb King for instance usually has lower damage, but his stuns win matches). Sometimes I really want to know what happened, whether certain players got hardcore shut down, and to theorize as to why. Paladins gives me more information to learn the game very quickly, while Overwatch's vagueness gives me more time to blindly theorize stuff and at the end of the day still not know jack.
- Youtube is littered with content and theory.
- Has voice communication and a radial menu for passing basic information like health and ult state.
- Play of the Game is pretty polished and you can really discern someone's aim more accurately.
Verdict:
I'll probably keep playing Overwatch, despite having more respect for Paladins. Perhaps when it gets more polished I'll come back to it. Mainly I prefer the heart in the characters, the simplicity, and the open information.

Take XCOM's tactics and management, Deus Ex's stealthy cyberpunk style, mash em into a short-form roguelike. That's this game.
Despite being a very strange mashup of ideas, Invisible Inc.'s gameplay is very competent, balanced, and filled with tense, emergent situations you never thought you'd dodge (or fail).
Sounds great and looks great.
The story is short and consists of a cutscene, a string of randomized missions, a final static mission, and another cutscene.
There's not really a lot of story content, but the procedurally-generated missions are what you'll be coming back to play for. Lots of unpredictability, agents and items to unlock, and campaign difficulty options are there to keep things fresh.
I won't hesitate to recommend this game. It may not be for everyone, but it's worth a try.

Before i write this review  i wanted to say i wasn't sure if i should give it a positive or negative review. Obviously, by today's standards, this is a terrible game. But you also have to take into consideration that it was made in 1995. So it certinly wasn't going to be great. So, I'm going to write about some of the good and bad things about this game, I only gave it a negative review because i enjoyed many games made in the 90's. This game, however, is not one of them.
The only reason I bought this game was because of how much I loved Dark Forces II, So i figured I would enjoy this game just as much. But they're both completely different games.
First off: You will get lost VERY easily. There's never any clear indication as to where you're supposed to go. You do have a map but that really doesn't help. So you'll spend the majority of each level wandering around and going a bunch of places that don't lead anywhere. The game is also pretty easy combat wise. You'll almost never die, (although, i did only play the game in medium difficuilty) All you'll do is see something move and just hold down the left mouse button until he dies in one or two shots. It;s also a bit confusing at first. When i had completed all my objectives it didn't take me to the next level. Confused, i just wandered around for awhile figuring i had to find an exit. After awhile, i got a message saying i had to pause the game and click next mission. This was more than likely my fault i'll admit. It probably sent me that message as soon as i finished all my objectives when i wasn't paying attention. But it's still odd and confusing.
It actually has a pretty good atmosphere. At one point it was even pretty creepy. During the second level you have to go down this water drain and you'll end up in this really dark room in waist high sewage water. After i walked around for awhile i heard a sort of growl. It actually creeped me out quite a bit. As i continued i heard more growls but i still couldn't see anything. Until, finally, i ran smack dab into this octopus looking creature that emerged from the water my immediate response was to hold down my fire button until it died. It was actually quite jarring.
All-In-All, It wasn't a horrible game, it's just not a game for most people. If you like games like DOOM then you'll probably enjoy this game. But, if you're just a fan of Star Wars or just saw this and it looked interesting. I would suggest not buying it.

Interesting game with lots of new mechanics introduced. However, it has a lot of drawbacks and bugs:
1. Sometimes the game "crashes". It goes into exclusive fullscreen mode, which does not allow to maximize task manager on top of it and kill the task. So the game continues, but the only way to kill it is to log out of the session in Windows.
2. The game is not informative. Ususally, Civilopedia has enough information for new players to play the game normally, and various advisor windows (Civ 4 and 5) provide all information you need about units etc. In Civ 6, however, you don't even have a list of units! (you can click on name of one unit and see the list with all units under control, but this is terrible interface!). Some information is completely hidden from the player (like was your unit built in a city with barracks or without it?), and some information can be found on specialized resources or on forums (like how do you achieve Martyr promotion? how do you build national park?)
So overall: 3/10 for interface, 10/10 for game mechanics.

Have you ever wanted to play a game that's poorly structured, devoid of real action, strays from the main events which can be found within the history of the Star Wars universe, and lacks the ability to make the player (especially one who harbours feelings of such great affection and admiration towards the Star Wars franchise in its entirety) feel nostalgic? Well, if so, don't purchase this game, because, if you're seeking any of the above traits, you're sure to be disappointed - Star Wars: Dark Forces, is an exceptional work of game design. Though it is, in fact, the case that the game's graphics aren't of an overly high quality by the standards of the gamers of today's society, I can say that, despite this, it is still quite an impressive game; the various methods of, shall we say, "neutralizing" hostile units are all quite entertaining, and, though the game may be slightly old, the movement within the game on the part of the character is remarkably smooth. Never have I once found movement to be even the slightest bit, "laggy", no matter how vigorous my travelling has become. Look, I'm not saying this game is great - I'm just saying it's awesome considering the sale price, and that, for this, and numerous other reasons which I won't even begin to attempt to list, you should definitely buy it.

Hotline Miami is one of those games that will stand as a gem in Gaming (with games like Shovel Knight). Hotline Miami has been out for 3 years. I played through it and had fun doing it. Especially when I played the side-story about that biker you kill (semi-spoilers).
Here are the 2 playable Characters:
Jacket (main story only, some spoilers)- Jacket has the choice of masks. He is the only playable character and never speaks (not a single line). However, he is a good character because he has no real traits besides being subscribed to 50 Blessings, Going insane, and having a girlfriend he saved after killing a group of Russain Mobsters. Honestly, I feel Jacket is pretty relatable if you know where he's coming from.
The Biker (side-story, spoilers)- This is the story where you aquire the secret ending (if you find all the pieces). Now, the story of the biker starts with him wanting out of 50 Blessings. You head to a Chinese Resturant and kill Mobsters. You then head to another Russain Mobster Safehouse with arcade machines. The Biker moves fast, has only one weapon, and has 3 limited throwing knives. If anything, he's a nice fast weapon. When you get to the Phone Company Mission, you kill Jacket (this is conflicting as Jacket kills the Biker, but it could be that both of their minds were seeing things by then, which is pretty understandable). In the end, you find the 50 Blessings group (composed of 2 Janitors at the Golden Truck club) and you put in the secret puzzle here. And when you do, you get the secret ending. You have the option of not killing, killing one of, or killing both of the 50  Blessings creators, leading you to the credits once you leave.
As for gameplay, it's a nice top down view, with visually appealing graphics and loads of secrets (secret masks, puzzle pieces for the secret ending, achievements, stuff like that.) The game itself is fun. I really had fun when playing it. It felt pleasing because I loved to kill the mobsters, it felt fun to just stab a mobster with a knife (which is op in the 1st game if you just swing and are moving fast, this was nefed to swing slower in Hotline Miami 2.) I give Hotline Miami lots of credit for being a game I enjoyed a lot.

TL;DR: The game is fun, but it has too many problems for me to recommend as of now.
EDIT: The stuttering seems to have been caused by using an Xbox One controller, unplugging the controller and restarting my PC stopped the issue for the most part. The other issues mentioned in this review still stand.
I really really wish I could write a good review for this game, but at this point in time, I can't do that. The game is by no means a bad game, what I played was fun, but the game has some issues that can't be overlooked. First and foremost, this game has been nothing but a headache in terms of performance. It was all fine for the first hour or so, then issues started popping up. I started getting random 10-20 fps drops that would last about a second, and the longer I played, the more the issue seemed to persist. I updated drivers, restarted PC, tried different graphical settings, ran in admin, tried fullscreen,borderless,windowed,and max window, nothing fixed it. Then suddenly, it just stopped, but was replaced with another issue, extremely obnoxious screen flickering that would happen seemingly every time I would jump. The screen flickering is still happening as I'm writing this review, and the stuttering has made a comeback as well. Even if you're willing to ignore all the potential performance issues and take the risk, there's still other issues with the game, such as the obvious micro-transactions in a $60 single player game, buggy AI that will fail to see you when you're literally right in front of them, crashes, black screens, sound problems, AWFUL mouse/keyboard controls, etc etc etc. Wait for a sale if you're against the micro-transactions, wait for a patch if you don't really care about that, but want a working game.

The game itself is a fairly entertaining Assassin's Creed clone with Arkham style combat. I personally find it more fun than either of the games it copies. It's enjoyable to just treat the orc camps like a playground. I payed good money for this game so I'm going to put some hours into it in order to get my money's worth. Unfortunately, I absolutely do NOT recommend that anyone purchase this game unless it is deeply discounted. Let me explain.
You get one save file. One. They expect you to purchase an entire extra copy of the game with a separate account if you want another save file. That means my girlfriend and I can't each have a save. I refuse to spend money in this way. Also, micotransactions and day one "DLC" are present. Both of these things can be ignored, but they are a slap in the face to gamers. I honestly regret purchasing this game for these reasons even if it has fun game play.
Also, don't buy this solely for the story if you are a Lord of the Rings fan. This game takes Tolkien's themes and ideas and then let's drunken orc urinate upon them. This is a fantasy game that uses some location names and radom snippets of information from Tolkien's legendarium, but it is NOT a Lord of the Rings game. This is fan fiction level bizarre stuff.
If you like RPG games and you like a bit of action, this game is perfect for you. Usually I'm not much for tactical spy games, but this is blowing my mind!

The Walking Dead Season Two is another tour-de-force of engaging story-telling by Telltale Games.
Following on directly from the dramatic conclusion of Season One, Season Two is, in my opinion, an improvement in almost every single way; an impressive achievement given the already high bar set by its predecessor.
The game is all about the story, and once again the story shines as one of my most engaging and memorable gaming experiences. The pacing has, in my opinion, improved this time, with less emphasis on wandering around, which for me slowed the game down somewhat in Season One.
The cast of characters are richly detailed and believable; even if you may not always agree with their actions you can at least empathise with their motivations. As in Season One, the game quickly draws you into their lives, and knowing at the same time that those lives may be cruelly taken away.
With the exception of a few really tough calls, the difficult moral choices which you are faced with seemed to me a little easier this time, with a clearer sense of ‘right’ or ‘wrong’, however this might just be my own increasing familiarity and de-sensitisation to the endless horror of the Walking Dead universe. I hope that players new to this game will endure the same desperate, time-limited and morally grey decision-making which I experienced in Season One, and which remains the hallmark of this series.
Unfortunately (and this is my only criticism) crushing inevitability prevails: sometimes no matter what you do, you end up with the same outcome. I understand that to have realistically played out the consequences to every single decision the game would probably have never been finished. Sometimes, you just can’t save everyone you care about.
The graphics and interface have undergone an incremental improvement – the world is more richly detailed, gritty and intricate than before, but retains the same memorable comic book style. Although I play most RPGs with keyboard and mouse, I played the game with an Xbox 360 controller and it was again, a very intuitive and enjoyable experience, allowing me to give fast response times in conversations and interacting with the world. Scenes requiring urgent action or careful co-ordination have had another layer of difficulty added in the new interface, which I found more engaging and realistic than some of the button bashing sessions in Season One.
Once again, Telltale Games have produced a masterpiece of interactive story-telling, memories of which will remain with me for a long time to come. I am sad that for me, and for now, this story is over; and I envy those of you who have yet to write your own. If you haven’t already done so, play Season One first for the full experience – however, if you’re short on time don’t hesitate to buy this and see for yourself. Either way that’s one inevitable outcome you won’t regret.

Original review posted on October 26, 2015:
This game is amazing. It is fun and simple, but it is ungodly difficult at the same time. The premise behind the game is simple. You start the game with two characters, these being Crystal and Fish. All characters have two uniquie things. Their passive and their active. Their passive is just that; an ability that will run in the background, influencing your attack patterns and the drops for players. Their active is also known as their right-click ability. Left-click is the basic attack and the default movement is WASD. Just using the two starting characters as an example, I will show how different playstyles can be from character to character.
Crystal
-Passive: More base health than any other character.
-Active: A temporary shield that will reflect multiple bullets and protect you from others.
Fish
-Passive: Extra ammo recieved
-Active: A dodge roll
New review after multiple updates and a very particular mod release:
Ah, it's nice to be back to playing this game regularly, but now, there is an extremely different experience of which I must say I enjoy partaking in.
Now, if you have looked at the tags, it likely mentioned "Local Multiplayer" or "Local Co-Op," but that no longer matters(provided your computer isn't a toaster and your internet isn't an Explorer). There is now a mod(which has been mentioned in the latest news by Vlambeer, so you know it's good) called Nuclear Throne Together, and it does exactly what you think it does; it allows you to play online co-op(or even Vs. with some creative/idiotic friends), albeit at a few costs to the core game.
If there was one thing I absolutely loved, it was unlocking all of the characters(and what few B-skins I unlocked before save-editing them in, but that's a different story). The journey felt important, but sadly NTT takes that away by automatically unlocking all characters and B-skins(I know that it does as my idiotic friend hadn't even unlocked Steroids and yet, he was able to play Rouge with her B-skin using the mod).
While this certainly does detract from the appeal of the journey, the game is still far from kind and is honestly just downright vicious.
Now, since I have basically informed you to get NTT as soon as you start playing the game, I should probably give you some information regarding the rest of the other characters.
The first two characters unlocked, Fish and Crystal, I explained in the previous version of this review.
The next character, Melting, is unlocked by dying for the first time. He literally looks like a skeleton with melting flesh.
Passive-2 health, but recieves an extra Rad(NT's version of Experience) from every enemy(including enemies that don't drop Rads)
Active-Explodes all corpses on screen.
Next is Eyes, and he's a bit of an interesting character. Firstly, his passive only works on three levels(four, including 4-?), these three(four) being known as the Transition Levels. He's unlocked by reaching the first Transition Level, the Sewers(2-1).
Passive-See in the dark(allows him to see the outside boundaries of your FoV in the transition levels)
Active-Telekinesis(push bullets away, but pulls enemies and items towards you)
Next up is Plant, and boy-oh-boy, do I hate Plant. Plant is unlocked by reaching 3-1(I think), and I only ever unlocked him out of neccessity.
Passive-More speed(GOTTSA GO FEST!)
Active-Shoot a snare(traps enemies inside of it and acts as a source of light on the Transition Levels).
Ah, back to the characters I like, and next up is Yung Venuz(more commonly referred to in game as Y.V.). To unlock Y.V., try to pick up a screwdriver in the desert(1-1 to 1-3) and take it to 3-1(screwdrivers can be found almost anywhere, but it's easiest for them to drop in chests at the very beginning). At 3-1, there will be cars that will explode from too much damage, but there is one car in particular that stands out. Attack that car once with the screwdriver and press your activate button(for me, a mere keyboard user, it is E). You can thank me later.
Passive-Higher fire rate
Active-Pop Pop(shoot two rounds of ammo for the currently equipped weapon at the cost of a slightly delayed rate of fire)
Now, reaching 5-1, we unlock Robot, an interesting(but in my opinion, kind of boring) character to play.
Passive-Finds better tech(finds weapons of higher levels than what would drop on any other character)
Active-Eat your weapon(consumes the weapon currently equipped as the primary to give ammo for the other weapon).
Now, we arrive at 6-1, and here's where things get interesting. Steroids is up next, and he brings a whole slew of power to your arsenal.
Passive-Inaccurate(this is okay) and fully automatic fire(no matter what the weapon is)
Active-Attacks with the weapon equipped in the off-hand
Yes, that's right. As the load screen will tell you time-and-time again, "Steroids can duel-weild."
Okay, now we're getting into the spoiler zone, so read at your own risk.
Next up is Rebel, a character that can only be unlocked by defeating the Nuclear Throne and ending your run by sitting on it.
Passive-Restores half of damage taken when completing level(If she has 2/12(let's say remaining health is X and max health is Y) remaining health when you complete the level, you'll enter the next level with 7, as (Y-X)/2 rounded down in this case would be 5, so (Y-X)/2+X would be the overall equation for her passive.
Active-Okay, this one's a bit complex, so bear with me. On her first right click when entering a level, she will lose one HP and a minion will spawn. The minion will last 20 seconds before exploding, but there is a way to extend its lifespan. By right-clicking again, another minion will spawn, and this resets the timer for the first ones life(presumably, it heals them). However, every minion spawned after the first on a single level takes up two HP rather than one(you cannot kill yourself with this ability).
Okay, this next character is kind of strange. Horror is unlocked by defeating Horror, who will only spawn when you skip the Rad Canisters on two levels in a row(as such, it is easiest to unlock him on 1-3, but I have accidentally had him spawn in on 4-1 and proceed to end my run).
Passive-When choosing a mutation by leveling up, he will have 5 choices(as compared to the usual 4)
Active-Ability to shoot accumulated Rads in a concentrated beam as a tertiary weapon(all Rads used in this way will only be regained if they actually hit their target). Also, Rad absorption will be paused when this ability is being used, so keep that in mind).
Next is Rogue, and she is definitely the hardest to unlock. First off, when fighting the Nuclear Throne, destroy all of the generators(activated with the Throne's giant laser beam) and then kill the Throne. A portal will open up which leads to the Throne II fight. Beating the Throne II will let you loop, and that's how you unlock Rogue.
Passive-All Rad Canisters become ammunition for her Portal Strike, and she's chased by the IDPD
Active-Portal Strike
The last two characters in the mod, Skeleton and Frog, though playable in the original game, they are hidden. Skeleton is only playable by being killed in a Necromancer's circle, and Frog is only playable by saving the Golden Frog Pistol to a character(which is no simple task).
Skeleton
Passive-4 HP, slow
Active-Shoot for no armor at the potential loss of health
Frog
Passive-Can't stop, won't stop tryna make the booty drop. Also, he can't be effected by toxic items.
Active-Stops moving and begins charging a fart, which will poison anything that enters the toxic cloud
So, yeah, that's about it.

Nuclear Throne. I wrote a review about this game a long, long time ago. And now it's early-access state is coming to a close, and the finished product is within reach. Amazing, isn't it? To think this game was at first a simple Game Jam project, and has turned into one of Steam's finest games. Certianly something, huh? Well, let's look at the game in it's somewhat complete state and see what it has to offer.
The game is a bullet hell, in every sense of the word. Nuclear Throne is a game in which you play as mutants that were created or survivied the end of the world. Wether they be A Fish, A walking chunk of crystal, a person who's flesh is constantly melting, or a Gun God, you have a variety of characters. And even two new ones! While i've yet to unlock them it's glad to see that Vlambeer made new characters. However, I feel they're a tad hard to unlock seeing as I haven't yet, but hey I can't wait to do so. And maybe we can get even more new characters in the future, but that's wishful thinking on my part. As for the gameplay it's hectic as hell. You start off with only a revolver, your wits, and any secondary powers given depending on the character you choose. As you collect Rads, which is this game's equivalent of EXP, You level up and gain Mutations. Which can give you more health, deal more damage, and other perks. You're given a selection of four mutations (or five if you're playing as one of the unlockable characters) and they're all good. Sooner or later you'll get into the groove of the game and find your favorite characters, weapons and mutations. And your goal, Reach the Nuclear Throne. For now, let's touch on the story. It's amazing. The story is sprinkled bit by bit in every part of the game, and it's certainly interesting and it's hard not to get invested.
Nuclear Throne is the perfect game for when you want a challenge, but one that's fair. Nuclear Throne is like that one relative in your family that can reward you with a lot of cool stuff, but only if you work hard. You want to kill the Nuclear Throne? You have to earn it. You want your favorite mutation? Sorry, you'll have to deal with what I have now, and work hard with what you have. It's hard, but it doesn't treat you like a baby. The game is very balanced and while difficult, is not impossible. And you don't need to have the reflexes of a god to be good at the game. You just need to keep playing and improve. Which is extreemly rewarding. Nothing is more satisfying than geting farther in the game than you ever have, and nothing will ever compare to beating the Nuclear Throne for the first time ever.
The only two problems I have aren't game ruining. One small, and one a tad big. There is one NPC in the game that I feel is wholy unpredictable, and can be very hard to deal with because of that. Alligators. I feel like I can never tell when they're going to fire and they're range is kind of crazy. Sometimes they do nothing. Other times they go in guns blazing and it feels unfair. I can never predict what they're going to do. And unlike the Assasins, that while hard to deal with, you can learn they're patterns, the Alligators feel like they do whatever they want. And another thing about the game, is the reason it's so good. But is also it's worst enemy. Every level is randomly generated, besides a few exceptions. Which can make the game replayable for years to come. But can also make it unfair. Some stages can kill you simply because they overwhelm you in ways you can't fight back. Which is hard to deal with, it's hard to make a game random and fair and the same time. It's really hard, but sometimes I get a really good run going, only to have it stop because there are seven Snipers hiding behind Big Dog.
But other than that, I love this game. It's a wonderful time sink, and almost every run feels adrenaline pumping.
And Vlambeer, if you're reading this. Thank you. Thank you so much for making such an amazing game. I love the gamplay and I love the story. I honestly feel like the story is amazing and I love finding more about it. I feel like it'd be a dream if I got to interview any of you and ask questions, or hell even work on the game's story with you guys! But that's just wishfull thinking, and enteirly up to you guys. But I doubt it'll ever happen. But either way, thanks for making such an amazing, and timeless game. And I can't wait to see what you guys have in store next.

Hey, everyone! This is my first review and I'm brazilian, so I'm sorry in advance for any grammar mistakes.
Dark Forces I is a First Person Shooter developed by Lucasarts, it came out in 1995. In this game, the player takes control of Kyle Katarn, gun for hire and ex-imperial officer. I'm not sure if this game is canon, but we find out how the Death Star plans were stolen from the Galactic Empire - that's the first mission, setting the stage for Episode IV. After Katarn steals the plans and the Death Star is destroyed, the Empire develops a new weapon to unleash against it's enemies, and it's up to Katarn to investigate and neutralize the threat. One curiosity about it is that Dark Forces I is the game that introduced the ability to jump and look up and down.
My time with Dark Forces can be divided into three distinct eras: After it came out, my parents bought the cd for me to play. I found the concept of FPS - it was one of the first shooters I ever played, along with Doom and Wolfenstein 3D (the first game I beat) - very fun and interesting, and I'd already seen the classic trilogy. Shoot imperials, blow up facilities? Sounds fun!
I was very little (seven or eight, I think), and I used the in-game "cheat" which can be acessed in the options submenu: super shields. I didn't know that it was some kind of cheat, so I thought the game was too easy. The third level was difficult, but I managed. Until the sixth level. There was no way I could figure that puzzle out - I didn't even know there was a puzzle - and, after some game rage, I went to real cheat codes. Ah, the scum and villainy... I beat the game like that, using super shields and level skip whenever I got stuck.
In the second era, some good six years later, I was determined to beat all levels, but still using cheat codes - ah, the scum and villainy II -. I finally figured the puzzle out - didn't take long - and I felt really dumb. Was I a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kid? Maybe.
And we come to the final era. I've decided to give this game another try, this time without any cheat codes, and on hard difficulty. Not surprisingly, I died a few times, especially against some certain kell dragons. Damn it, that was hard. But I did it, and I for certain recommend this game, for nostalgic reasons, to see how the First Person Shooters evolved and to see how Kyle Katarn began his journey!

Invisible, Inc. is an exciting, in-depth take on the turn-based strategy genre. It has an incredibly deep atmosphere of cyberpunk infused espionage that steers you towards using cunning stealthy strategies to make any progress. Although, its focus on stealth isn't so restrictive that it doesn't allow a completely different playstyle if one is so inclined. Just remember: one wrong step and it is very likely game over – forever. You don’t get any checkpoints to revert to or retries when you fail a mission. While there are customizable options like that you can enable when you start a campaign, you’re basically looking at permanent death when you make a crucial mistake in strategic judgement in the regular campaign.
The short storyline is a neat and compact campaign with a well thought out and very satisfying beginning, middle and end. It has you navigating the whole globe infiltrating various corporations with the aim of acquiring high tech gear you will need on the final mission. There’s quite a variety of procedurally generated missions from which you can choose, but distance travelled matters in your choice as you run down the 72-hour in game clock every time you move to another mission. Even before you get in game you need to make strategic decisions on how you’ll tackle the order you do the missions in and how you will equip your agents. Even the levels on the missions are procedurally generated, so no two playthroughs of this game can ever go the same.
When you complete the campaign for the first time it will definitely leave you wanting so much more. Klei has you covered as their expectation isn’t that you just play the campaign once. This is where the unlockables deliver on your craving for more. With each playthrough, you use your experience gained to unlock new programs and agents. With up to four power programs, up to four hacking programs and up to 10 agents to choose from, there’s ample choice at your fingertips to construct tons of unique playthroughs.
When you've had your fill of the campaign in every combination you can think of, Invisible, Inc. really shines in the long-term replayability with its Endless mode. Endless mode is the same as the campaign except the mission difficulty increases past what they normally would in the storyline. That difficulty keeps on increasing as the days go by, but, of course, there is no time limit leading you to a final mission; you just keep on going for as long as you can handle it. Between the loadout combinations, procedurally generated missions and level layouts, I’ve happily put hundreds of hours into countless endless mode playthroughs. And that was before the full game was even released!
With all the gameplay praise, Invisible, Inc. also does not disappoint when it comes to its graphics, animation, music and SFX. The final release of this game is an incredibly polished work of art in all of those aspects. I can’t even put into words how perfectly the music and SFX fit the atmosphere of this game. Each corporation even has their own subtly different musical theme associated to them. The animations are smooth and the graphical style is crisp.
The only thing I don’t like about this game is related to the animations. My mind thinks very fast and I would like to be able to click on things and carry out orders in rapid succession. When I have to wait for every animation to finish before I can click on the next thing, I get quite annoyed. The game has a fast mode option to speed them up, but it’s nowhere near fast enough for my liking. I always feel like computer software should be the one waiting for more inputs from the end user, not the human element having to wait for the software to allow it.
Despite that, the bottom line is this: Klei Entertainment did a fantastic job with Invisible, Inc. and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys the strategy genre.
