Okay, let's write a real review. I'm updating my old one because of the Steam Award Nomination, Alpha Protocol is the game I gave the custom award which I named The "The most deserving of an Award" Award.
Because AP is that game. It was unsuccessful and sold on here very soon after release for a very low price, there is no sequel, not many gamers know it, though by now you find it mentioned sometimes exactly as that game that failed despite being interesting. And I agree with that. The gameplay is good: As an agent you go on missions following an interesting storyline about terrorist and intelligence activity, and of course there is a big conspiracy. There are different types of missions: A few that are only a conversation, where your answers influence the following story, and the larger stealth-action missions which can also be solved by shooting everything that moves. Also in those missions there will be decisions, which is the main thing AP took from Deus Ex and improved: Your decisions influence the story. They influence the outcome, they influence your allies, and they influence your enemies. And that is what makes the game great.
It won't be a totally different game on the second play-through when acting differently, but those decisions have enough influence on the story to really make you feel like you have an impact on the game world. Even though there is a "go through that or that door to chose what happens" situation (which can be missed and be buggy), that is not the only decision influencing the ending. It did not make the same utter mistake Mass Effect or DX:HR did.
But AP and DX: Hr share another mistake, and that are the bossfight. While the game itself can be played peacefully, the bossfights can't be solved without violence, and they are very hard if not having skilled up one weapon ability. They were an enormous mistake and probably what prevented that game from becoming successful at its time, as that flaw had to break the interest of the one target group that game had, fans of the original Deus Ex and Thief.

A very solid game, consistently developed through Early Access.  It is pretty well polished and I was thrilled to play through the full release version.
If you played or read about Mark of the Ninja (also by Klei), you know that they take stealth games seriously, especially in the way they provide interface feedback to the player and allow multiple paths to victory.
Invisible, Inc. is a great game in the squad-based-grid-tactics spirit of XCOM, and also in the I-can't-believe-they-killed-me-that-isn't-fair! spirit of XCOM...although just as with that game, as you learn and get better, you'll know that you are to blame, and the game isn't unfair, it is just difficult.
My favorite thing about this game, which came later on in Early Access, was the ability to really tweak the kind of game you want, including difficulty, Iron-Man-style, duration (endless mode), etc.  This truly gives the player the choice to play the level of challenge they like.
I recommend this game without reservation!

Space game that is both about space and a good game.
The good:
-Spaceflight is actually accurate, not fly-by-wire atmospheric flight (as in 99% of other 'space' games).  Proper orbital mechanics, though only 2-body simulation.
-All success is earned, no victory is given to the player.
-Possibly the most rewarding game I've ever played.
-Highly educational, the best way to learn astrophysics.
-Plenty of awesome mods, though none are required.
-Despite the apparently low end cartoonish graphics, is probably the most beautiful game I've played.  I never get tired of those alien planet sunsets.
The neutral:
-Nothing resembling a plot or characters, except for what the player makes.
-Challenging and unforgiving.
The bad:
-Can be difficult to learn, especially for someone with no physics background.
KSP is about as realistic as a space game can be while still being a game and not a simulator.  Good support from the developer and an awesome modding community make this a great game that will be around for a long time.
It's still better than X Plane 10. You should get it.

Invisible Inc is a turn based stealth game.  As such, it fits a niche that I haven't seen filled, and it does it quite well.  The turn system is very similar to X-Com, but without the randomness.  Actions are either possible and they will succeed, or they are not possible and you can not attempt them.  This is a good thing, and it eliminates the frustration found in X-Com where your sniper would miss time and time again on shots that had a 99% chance to hit.  While the AI in this game is not the smartest, the fact that every level is randomly generated, and you can't go back to a previous save when you fail, means that every playthrough will be different and still challenging.  During Early Access this game was incredibly good, but incredibly hard.  The release version now includes diffculty options and a story arc (a very good one so far, I might add) allowing you to ease into the game.  Once you are finished with the story in the game, you can play on endurance mode, where the game will just keep randomly generating harder and harder missions for you.  This was what the early access of the game was like, and I liked it back then, so I can see it keeping entertained after I am done with the story arc.

Turn based tactical stealth game, in a cyberpunk setting.
How could I not be excited about such a lovely combination?
The game heavily focuses on the tactical missions (well there is an in-between screen where you can upgrade your agents, but it's light, don't hope for any x-com-esque base building!) into procedurally generated maps (on an unique and flat floor). And let's be honest, procedural generation can give you harsh times, but you always feel you could have beaten it, if only you weren't so focused on that shiny loot! And that "rewind" function (limited use per mission) let you realize that, when coming back one turn earlier, you notice that you're able to make everything just going smoothly. Be aware that I usually swear by "ironman" mode, and yet I find this mechanic being as interesting to play as the rest of the game: you are able to come back only one turn earlier, so you must realize quickly that what you've done is going to put you in deep trouble before you can't go back on it anymore. It's really specific but it reflects well the general pace of the game, where you try to optimize your actions every turn but also have to think on longer term effects of what you're doing. Also know that your time is counted (in turns, not real time, unless you turn that option on in the beginning), so every decision count.
Story mode is very short (4-6h), but the game offers replayability, between very customizable difficulty settings with that campaign length that you might just set on "endless", the choosing of your starting team (2 out of 10 agents, with variants, that you'll have to unlock first, just by playing) and hacking programs and of the course the procedurally generated maps that made you never do twice the same missions (7 different objectives but never the same layout for rooms and guards patrols). And it feel very rogue-like, as its totally possible to screw it up and start from the beginning again. You might not play it for hundreds of hours though, but I guess you'll have a decent amount of time of thinking and fun, wether you're an hardcore tactician, or a more casual player. Just don't play it for the story, it's just there to justify the gameplay.
Now to be honest, I must mention its flaws too, which are not really surprising: an important part of the difficulty lies into the procedural generation of the map as I've already said, screen tends to be overcrowded with objects and icons sometimes (but you can rotate the map, lay down the walls or access a tactical map display) and guard behaviour looks very ridiculous at times, but hey, it's TBT meets stealth, what did you expect?

A truly underrated title. It has a really great conversation system, interesting characters, and excellent leveling up and customization, allowing you to go through the game with different builds.
It is not, however, without its flaws. The gameplay controls are not very responsive. For a game looks and feels like it should be a third person shooter, the actual shooting mechanic is very poor. The stealth mechanics are better than the shooting, but Splinter Cell this is not. And it a few mandatory boss fights, which are of course terrible in this style of game.
In fact, the game is very similar to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. They certainly both occupy the same genre of Steath/Action/RPG. The biggest difference is that DXHR has better gameplay, but far worse plot and character. Alpha Protocol has much better characters, plot, and dialogue/choices, but the gameplay is less polished.
That said, if you enjoy games with well written characters, interesting choices, and one of the best conversation systems ever in any RPG, then you'll enjoy Alpha Protocol.

TL;DR: The game is fun, but it has too many problems for me to recommend as of now.
EDIT: The stuttering seems to have been caused by using an Xbox One controller, unplugging the controller and restarting my PC stopped the issue for the most part. The other issues mentioned in this review still stand.
I really really wish I could write a good review for this game, but at this point in time, I can't do that. The game is by no means a bad game, what I played was fun, but the game has some issues that can't be overlooked. First and foremost, this game has been nothing but a headache in terms of performance. It was all fine for the first hour or so, then issues started popping up. I started getting random 10-20 fps drops that would last about a second, and the longer I played, the more the issue seemed to persist. I updated drivers, restarted PC, tried different graphical settings, ran in admin, tried fullscreen,borderless,windowed,and max window, nothing fixed it. Then suddenly, it just stopped, but was replaced with another issue, extremely obnoxious screen flickering that would happen seemingly every time I would jump. The screen flickering is still happening as I'm writing this review, and the stuttering has made a comeback as well. Even if you're willing to ignore all the potential performance issues and take the risk, there's still other issues with the game, such as the obvious micro-transactions in a $60 single player game, buggy AI that will fail to see you when you're literally right in front of them, crashes, black screens, sound problems, AWFUL mouse/keyboard controls, etc etc etc. Wait for a sale if you're against the micro-transactions, wait for a patch if you don't really care about that, but want a working game.
The difference between a successful launch or failed one is that whether the explosion is controlled or not.

This is like XCOM except it won't waste your time with huge maps and long drawn-out firefights across a ravine. It feels a lot more like dancing, as your squad scampers around guards and rooms, trading places / items / roles.
Very emergent qualities to the mechanics too -- you might make some noise to bait a guard outside, and he'll open a door and wander into your melee overwatch ambush... but then he left the door open, which means a hacked turret has line of sight to another guard in that room, and so the turret kills him -- the noise alerts other guards and raises the global alarm level, which shuts down your turret and spawns 2 more guards, etc. Things happen because of things, and almost every situation is avoidable if only you had planned ahead a bit better.
Anyway, this is an exceptionally well-done game. Highly recommended. (DISCLOSURE: I completed the campaign on all 3 base difficulty levels. I didn't pay for my copy of the game. I know one of the developers.)

A truly underrated title. It has a really great conversation system, interesting characters, and excellent leveling up and customization, allowing you to go through the game with different builds.
It is not, however, without its flaws. The gameplay controls are not very responsive. For a game looks and feels like it should be a third person shooter, the actual shooting mechanic is very poor. The stealth mechanics are better than the shooting, but Splinter Cell this is not. And it a few mandatory boss fights, which are of course terrible in this style of game.
In fact, the game is very similar to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. They certainly both occupy the same genre of Steath/Action/RPG. The biggest difference is that DXHR has better gameplay, but far worse plot and character. Alpha Protocol has much better characters, plot, and dialogue/choices, but the gameplay is less polished.
That said, if you enjoy games with well written characters, interesting choices, and one of the best conversation systems ever in any RPG, then you'll enjoy Alpha Protocol.

Imagine FTL injected with a heavy dose XCOM and sprinkled with the Mark of a Ninja's art style and stealth, and you get Invisible, Inc.
It's a very unique stealth/strategy rogue-lite game which borrows different mechanics from different games to create a one-of-a-kind experience. You choose two agents at the beginning of each campaign, and you're tasked with gathering resources (weapons, gear, agents) to prepare them for an end mission after some allotted time. You're given a map filled with different missions, and each one is tailored such that you're given something special in return. One mission may filled with credits to spend on items, while another may supply you with a third agent to help you. Deciding between these missions is crucial, as all of these assets you're sent out to gather are important to survive and succeed in the end-game.
The missions themselves are highly engaging, compelling, and challenging, and takes on a turn-based mechanic like in XCOM. It's a stealth game, so you either have to maneuver around enemies, or take them out silently. Everything in the game is a one-hit KO, so being spotted once is most likely going to lead to death, which is probably my favorite part of the game. It feels so engaging. Every turn matters, and the decisions you make have dire consequences if carried out recklessly, however, you must act swiftly, because every turn ticks a timer on an alarm, and the higher it gets, the harder the missions become (more surveillance cameras, more enemies, higher hacking costs).
The game is also a rogue-lite, so each subsequent run awards you exp which unlocks new agents and gear to bring along to the next one. You're also given an exhaustive list of different customizability options from changing the length of each run to changing how many guards appear on each mission to how many rooms there are in each mission. It's crazy! You make the game as hard or easy as you want.
The art-style is also gorgeous. Definitely has that Klei feeling.
The gameplay is so deep that it's hard to go over every single aspect of it, but for the price it's most definitely worth the price of admission. IT'S AWESOME.

Highly underrated, this is an experience where the choices you make actually matter, where your actions have reverberating consequences. A number of games boast of having a cool morality system but then end up being banal black-and-white scenarios, where good guys get a shiny sword and save the world, and bad guys get a demonic blade and take over the world for themselves. Alpha Protocol instead puts the emphasis on relationships and motivations, where you might undertake the same mission as someone else but your reasons and methods are entirely different. More importantly, allies and enemies alike will notice and react, and that's when you start to grasp what the stakes are.
While the combat might take a bit of getting used to, it's perfectly serviceable and, at later stages, quite satisfying. Better yet, the game will reward you based on your own style. Do you prefer sneaking around? Get through a few levels without raising any alarms and you'll gain a perk that makes you stealthier. Are you more of a crazy Rambo? Take enough damage without dying, and you'll gain a perk that increases your durability. Just like the story, the gameplay caters to your choices.
Have the patience and the deviousness to figure out how to play effectively and you can bypass the majority of the criticisms brought on by 'official' ratings. Espionage has never been this cool.

Another fine game from Klei to say the least. Had this since April of last year and I'm very pleased as to how the final product turned out. Yet another fresh take on stealth by Klei, this is a turn based tactical espionage game that features procedurally generated levels and permadeath(though there are mission retries on the lowest difficuly). It may not explicitly state this, but it is very much structured like a modern rougelike (a la FTL) with playthroughs lasting around the ballpark of a couple hours and a lot of variation between each playthrough. You create a team whenever you start a playthrough, selecting any two of ten unlockable agents(six of which have an alt form so technically 16) and two mainframe programs. There is a hacking element in the game that features resource management of CPU power that can be used to hack various devices such as cameras, safes, etc. There's also an alarm level that ticks every turn, Forcing a lot of different decisions(do I go after that nanofabricator machine and buy some gear or escape before things get too hectic?) and making the gameplay more dynamic. Overall, I love the gameplay of this game. Not many games can keep me playing for 70 hours(and I don't plan on stopping now) but Invisible Inc has enough depth and variation to keep me playing. Also, as with every game Klei makes, the artstyle of this game is wonderful. My only complaint I have is that the couple of cinematics they put in the game very recently could have been better quality. Voice acting is a little flat and it looks a little grainy. Overall I definately recommend this game.

After finishing this game, I really don't understand why it got such a panning - it's great!
I'll start with the not-so-good stuff first:
•	The AI isn't great, and
•	The boss battles are insanely unfair
That's it.
Alpha Protocol is an espionage RPG/shooter, but really - first and foremost - it's a great story well told. It offers choices that have real consequence, and it allows you to play it out however you see fit.
All out action? Sneaky stealth? A combination of both? You can tailor your character to suit your play style. I'm a sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at heart, so I chose a Specialist, with Stealth and Martial Arts as my lead attributes ;)
You want to kill everyone you come across? You can. Prefer to be non-lethal and just use a painful take-down instead? You can do that too. That assassin that tried to kill you, you want to kill or spare it? Again, up to you, and each choice will affect the story.
Conversations I found a blast, with usually 3-4 options as a reply - 'Joking', 'Suave', 'Professional', 'Tender', 'Taunt', 'Antagonise', 'Execute'...
Each response can have its pro's and con's, whether positive or negative, and affects how the other person will react to you in the future.
It looks pretty good, while not spectacular. The look is very 'clean', and there is a few clipping instances, but I really didn't find anything that marred my experience.
I'm not sure how many hours it took to complete, as the Steam hours counter didn't work on quite a few of my plays. I would say around 20-25, though.
I played the game using an Xbox 360 pad, so I can't really comment on the mouse/keyboard controls, but from what I've read, the pad is the way to play, really.
I paid £5 for this in the Steam Sale, but I really wouldn't have felt cheated if I paid full whack for it. It really is a shame it was received the way it was, and that the sales reflected this. I would have loved another slice.

Very very very very strong recommendation. I am a big fan of stealth, team based tactics and turn based strategies so this game is all I could ever wish for.  While it is an unusual combination, Inv. Inc. is a kind of game, which makes me wonder why has no one done that before.
Inspirations for this game are quite obvious – there is a lot of XCOM in there, as well as FTL and other rogue-lights. Don’t be misled though, as it is a game of its own. If you long for a lengthy XCOM campaign with base building, you won’t find it here. Also at the moment it is not a brilliant rogue-light. The score system has been removed from the final release, as it wasn’t well polished and forced players to play in very specific (often not practical) way. If you hope for leaderboards you won’t find it here (at least right now). Also the progression and items you get, while very well designed, does not have the FTL wonder and variation.
But let’s talk about the really good stuff. If you are into stealth, all you need to know is that it is the first game I have ever seen to expand (and not only replicate) mechanics introduced in Thief: DP and Thief 2:TME. Stealth is great but it did have some unresolved issues for years. Games’ quality mostly depended on the quality of level design. Way too often stealth’em ups were an exercise in patience and didn’t actually require skill. Often the most fun way to play was sneaking but either it was just easier to shoot your way through the levels or being revealed was punishable in either instant failure or unavoidable death. On the other spectrum, sometimes there really wasn’t much repercussions from being discovered, and sneaking felt kind of pointless.
Inv. Inc. solves those issues with a simple, elegant mechanic called alarm meter. As you infiltrate enemy territory the automatic alarm system detects your presence. With every turn alarm meter fills up by one point. Every couple points alarm level rises and new counter measures appear: extra cameras, new guards, higher level of security (hacking.) This forces you to be efficient, as the more time you spent on the level, the more dangerous it will become. Once you get to alarm level 6 you’ll be better running straight for the elevator.
But this is not all. Get spotted, kill a guard and the alarm rises as well. Thanks to that, your failings have repercussions and game punishes you for mistakes, but it is never an instant gameover (unless you do something really careless.) As a matter of fact my best experiences with the game were when things got hairy.
Add to that the way guard work – they follow their own stable patrol routines until you disturb them (be spotted or stun them – stunning does not take guard out of the game forever. He wakes up after couple turns.) When alerted they will be actively looking for you. They become unpredictable and dangerous. The ideal way is to ghost through the level. Even stunning a guard (and you will probably have to do it almost every mission) carries consequences.
That is about stealth mechanics. They are absolutely brilliant. The story is serviceable, mostly explaining, why you do what you do, but it does have some nice touches and is supported by great art-style.
There are a few game modes to choose from. There is the story mode, which is the main meat of the game. It has couple difficulty settings, to allow new players to get to know the game, without tearing their hair out, and some tough ones for those who crave for extreme challenge. It is a 72 (ingame) hour campaign, with a final mission at the end. You take on different missions and build up your squad in preparation for the final level.
There is endless mode, which removes final mission, allows you to go forever but the difficulty spikes beyond this of the story mode.
Time attack gives you a time limit on your turns forcing you to think quickly and make snap decisions.
Sandbox allows you to modify rules of the game (even remove the alarm system, which I don’t know why would you want to do….) and create as easy or as difficult experience as you wish.
It might not seem like much but between excellent procedural generation, roster of different agents and their alternative versions and programs to use (ha I didn’t even mention hacking! It is basic but well designed. Has more depth than seems at first and adds to the ever present resource management) you will be able to sunk hours upon hours into this game on a story mode alone. It is a game for those who like PLAYING games, and not only BEATING them.

This is an extremely slick turn-based stealth game. Despite levels being randomly generated, the situation never seems impossible thanks in part to an excellent arsenal of items, and an internal set of rules that are never hidden. Difficulty is fully customizable, and while there is an unlock system, it only affects your starting load out; all items and agents can be found during missions with the exception of two hidden agents that will require you to complete the story.
There are no dice-rolls in this game outside of level generation, and a few secondary effects associated with a few of the more advanced Incognita programs, so you aren't going to fail a mission because your sniper missed a shot. Instead you are going to fail because you got your agents too far apart, or you got greedy and used up all your hacking actions on that last vault before you discovered the security bot between you and the exit. Levels play like wonderful little stealth puzzles with a solution that depends on how you decide to handle the situation.
Easily Klei's best work thus far, and one of those "now I see why early access can be good" cases.

I have largely enjoyed Civ 6 so far, it perhaps isn't the complete package yet, like most Civ releases it tends to require a couple of expansions before fully rounded out and realised to its full potential.
Having said that, they have transitioned nicely to the new city tile system, with districts and wonders built separately outside of the single city tile, an idea quite foreign to previous Civ titles!
Multiplayer seems quite stable, without desync issues like 5.
As usual you will likely find you start more games than you finish but it's a good game for chilling out for several hours over Discord as you put the world to rights whilst growing your Civilisation.
The updates made to the game are slow but meaningful, adjusting the outright unreasonable AI from the initial release to a more strategic opponent and using the Civ's likes and dislikes system to a greater effect.
Overall it's a game i look forward to seeing how it evolves, perhaps with a world congress like system to spice up the late game, and with more Civilisations added over time to help bolster the numbers!

Star Wars: Dark Forces is pretty much Doom: Star Wars Edition. You're thinking "That's great then! What's the problem then?". Well, a lot actually...
The story starts off with a defect from the sith empire stealing the death star plans for the Rebel alliance, setting itself up for what starts off tieing in to Episode IV: A New Hope, but then goes off in it's own direction, including Dark Troopers as the Siths new method of ruling the galaxy, and you, the defect, have to stop them. Nice idea for a story, but the dialogue is so corny it's difficult to take seriously.
The core gameplay is Doom in a nutshell. Running around what are pretty much mazes, blasting stormtroopers that can hit something and occasionally collecting keys to open doors you found earlier that you couldn't open, with the occasional mediocre puzzle thrown in... and that's pretty much it. Backtracking is far too common in this game, which is a let down, and the platforming... Don't get me started on how bad that was...
The sound effects that we all know and love from Star Wars are there (no Wilhelm Scream though...) and the music we all know and love is there as well, including the music played during the Death Star attack from Episode IV.
One final note: Why did I have to look online for the controls to this game? Why wasn't there an option to access the controls ANYWHERE in the game? It would have helped me out in the first 4 or 5 missions. Playing around with the Gamma Correction in the options menu and shooting was not what I wanted to do to navigate dark areas thanks.

Klei delivers another quality game. One of their strengths is that they make you immersed in the theme of the game. They made you feel like a badass ninja in MoTN and here you feel like a mastermind in the craft of espionage in this roguelike turn-based strategy game.
Both games share another trait: Despite there being an emphasis on evasion rather than confrontation, the game gives you the choice to go for a confrontational playstyle without it being too difficult to achieve. This playstyle does have a "skill barrier" due to the fact that the lethal gear costs a healthy number of credits to obtain and killing guards raises alarm levels by a considerate amount. However, the option is there and that is what's important.
The amount of choice you are given from the get-go is lovely. With a roster of 8 different agents (6 of whom have alternate "archive" playstyle) with their own unique passives and gear, you can select two of them to start out your missions. There are many little synergies between them, and even on their own they bring hefty benefits to the table. The ability to attack twice in one turn is great for clearing out tough situations, revealing electronic devices behind walls and being able to unlock keycard doors without need said card key are all strong by themselves both early and late game.
You are given the ability to take over the enemy's electronic devices with use of Incognita, your intelligent SHODAN-esque AI. Visiting server farm locations to upgrade her is a must, the later missions' electronics require stronger hacking tools to take down quickly. The resource system for hacking is PWR, which is generated via the chosen generation tool at the start of the run and also be lifted in small amounts from enemy consoles within a building. Using hacking programmes costs PWR, and you have a variety of tools for the job. Managing PWR is extremely important late game due to the stronger firewalls and the cap on max available PWR, but it is well balanced. I only ever ran out of power due to my own poor choices.
There are different types of missions which hold their own loot for the taking. You can choose missions from a world map which displays the time it will take to fly to that location, mission type, the corporate name and the security level. You need to choose your missions with care. Are you in desperate need of credits? Visit a Vault. Need some advanced gear? Go to a Security Dispatch. Got plenty of credits to spare? Nanofab Vestibule contains stronger items available for purchase. Hacking feeling lacking? Incognita would benefit with tools from a Server Farm. There are additional mission types but you get the idea.
Missions themselves are simple at first glance. You avoid guard patrols and cameras, gain access to the mission loot while stealing whatever you can then you find the teleporter and get out before the security level rises so high it becomes impossible to deal with. You can hide behind furniture and machines for cover which allows for sneaking past guards, or you can sneak up behind them and knock them out for two or three turns.
I've had amazing fun with this game through Early Access and I hope it has huge success on full release. It's an amazingly designed game that Klei have put their love into, providing a bar which other Early Access developers should strive to come up to.

You know how you scroll through reviews to see a big red "Not Recommended" just to see some critical analysis of the game in question.  I know I do it and invariably I come across "this game should be done already" guy.  You all know him.  He's the guy who buys an early access game and then goes on to say the game has a lot of bugs and that it isn't worth the money in its current form blah blah blah.
Well here's the thing about invisible inc.  When I first played this game, it only had 3 characters and 2 or 3 mission types.  The items were limited to basically 2 different guns, some ammo, and med packs.  The hacking was a very simple system and you couldn't upgrade your hacking abilities.  The thing is though, I still had a blast playing it.  In fact, the game in that state was still well worth $15 in my opinion.
A left the game alone for a couple months as I moved and finding a new place for my PC was a bit of an issue.  But when I came back to this game, I found the updates were incredible.  A wide variety of characters with varied skills (6 or 7 I believe).  There are at least 5 missions types and they are suprisingly different in gameplay experience.  Detention centres for example contain a prisoner which may or may not be another agent to add to your roster.  Chief financial suites give you access to vault codes for future Vault missions.  The inventory received a similar upgrade.  Many items and even different types of equipment including augments which improve your characters functionality in their role by giving them unique passive buffs or abilities.  Equipment is no longer limited to guns and ammo but includes hacking aids, stim packs, gadgets like deployable cameras or sound traps, and alternative weapons like darts, tracers, etc.
What I am really trying to say here is that this game feels like it is a finished game with all the polish and content to justify its price tag and then some.  Technically, the game runs smoothly, the mechanics behave in a predictable manner without allowing the player to exploit them.  This allows you to plan ahead, and think of strategies that involve more than one turn.  There is nothing worse than having an awesome plan in your head, thinking it all through, executing the first 3 steps, just to have step 4 blow up in your face because the guard decided to turn around for absolutely no reason.  This is what I would call unpredictable mechanics and while a certain level of "randomness" or unpredictability can make the game more fun, Invisible Inc. is a game where once you learn how the enemies behave, the difficulty comes from having to use your brain and stay one step ahead of the game (not from throwing a random guard your way at the perfectly wrong time).
TLDR? This game is leading by example.  This is exactly how early access should work.  The dev's could have cut and run and moved on to another project months ago, and they still would have been less buggy and more fun than a lot of "finished" games out there *cough Looking your way Double Fine cough*.  Klei has shown me that a dev company can truly care about the experience their customers get and work hard to make sure that the final product is something they can proudly put their names on.  If any of the dev's read this seriously GOOD ON YOU!  More companies need to operate this way!

After being introduced to the series with Civ 5, I was very excited to get this game. Now, I think this game is even better than Civ 5. The way they've chosen to make tiles actually matter in this game is awesome. From district planning to wonder placement, to the limited number of builder charges, you have to think a lot more about your cities than before, and it makes peaceful expansion and growth much more interesting and exciting. Getting a +3 adjacency bonus on a district always feels good, and plopping a city in a particular spot for a terrain-specific wonder later on is actually pretty rewarding. I also enjoy that expansion is much more supported in this game, as compared to Civ 5, where building tall was almost the only way to go for a lot of players. All that said, there are areas where the game is lacking somewhat, like the Culture and Religious victories, and the lack of a World Congress. However, at release, Civ 5 was much the same way, and its 2 major DLCs remedied many of the problems and made it into a wonderful game, so hopefully Civ 6 will have the same treatment. And the modding community is already hard at work on this game, and many of the smaller tweaks and fixes they've made have already been incorporated into the game in official patches.

If you play heavily guarded levels, you will also experience some nice RPG-reminiscents, like the floating guardian. Reminds me of Eye of the Beholder.
So, what is the problem? IF you get to later levels, the guards heavily outnumber your team. It's not 2:1 or 3:1, that could be handable. But in the latest level, I played, I was outnumbered by at least 4:1, and of the guards woke up after one round already - he guarded the CEO of the company to hack. Dealing with a 3 turn cooldown on your main weapon, you are - let's say - always dead. This said, even in easy mode, which i was playing for about 12 hours now, the game always ended after 5 missions. Interestingly, by doing maps randomly, frustration about this is not as high, as expected, as you need to improvise.
I know, it's supposed to be a hardcore stealth game, but the difficulty is much to high, even after playing about 30 easy missions, in said 12 hours. However, I'd recommend this game to lovers of round-based, agent, difficult missions.

Star Wars: Dark Forces was one of the first video game entries to incorporate elements of the expanded universe. Built on an enhanced version of the DOOM engine, Dark Forces reset the bar for first person shooters. It introduces the lasting character of Kyle Katarn into the universe and proved that you don't have to be a Jedi or a starfighter pilot to make a successful Star Wars game. An epic storyline, combined with memorable characters and impressive level design makes this game a must have for any Star Wars fan, or those looking for a sense of nostalga about how far gaming has come.
The graphics were top notch at the time of release (1995) with smooth animation and distinct sprites and textures. Digital voice work is crisp and helps to give the characters a sense of personality. From the filtered 'halt!' of stormtroopers to the anamalistic groan of the Diagnosa as you wade through raw sewage, you will always know exactly what is hunting you.
Gameplay is standard fare for shooters of the time. you have a wide variety of weapons - pistols, blaster rifles, thermal detonators, along with more exotic weapons such as the fusion cutter or the assault plasma cannon. Health is non-regenerating and must be restored from medkits, along with shields.
Sound direction is excellent. The music features remixes of well known Star Wars tunes along with new music. Each tune fits the level it is attached to. Weapon sounds are unique, giving every gun its own feel.
Overall, this is a geat game for retro lovers. Solid gameplay, a memorable story that has influenced many other games in the franchise, and characters with actual personality makes this a good choice.
On the technical side, this game comes bundled with its own auto-loading version of DOSBox, meaning that it will work on modern systems. Confirmed functional on all systems up to Windows 7 64-bit, with reports of it working properly on Windows 8 systems.

Can I double recommend this game?
Nuclear Throne has quickly become one of my go-to favourite games of all time. After sinking over 100 hours into this game I'm still eager to play it for another 100.
This game is like a rogue-like, twin stick-esque, bullet hell arcade game, and it's freaking lovely. With active devellopers, a great community, and daily leaderboards, there's no reason not to play Nuclear Throne at least once a day. Not only that but the game itself just feels good to play. This game is comletely plot driven. Therefore, this game should only be played by people who finished the first Season. For those who did not play the first game, DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME. This review is for those who beat the first game, and are considering this game.
This game proves Telltale know how to take an old concept and keep it fresh - this game is very much just like the old one, but it gets rid of various flaws of the earlier entry, and instead focuses on the core of the game.
This time, you play as Clementine, which turns out very interesting. Although you are the same player making the decisions as the first game, you'd find your decision making process and the choices you make are different, all because you're a different character. I found this an amazing experience, and it just shows you that this game affects your decisions just as much as you affect its.
This game is focused on different things than the first game, as I said. It's a lot more focused on decison making than the first one. While the first Walking Dead game focuses just as much on puzzles, combat and classic-adventure-game mechanics, this game is all about the plot. It gets rid of boring or mondane mechanics from the first game, and make it a much more fluent experience.
That being said, it makes this game a lot less challenging and therefore, a little less rewarding. If you weren't a huge fan of the decision making in the first game - this game is just not going to be fun for you. However, if you loved the plot, the characters, or the dynamic decisions you make throughout the story, this game would be an extremely satisfying sequel for you.
In short, this game is fun and a great sequel to the first game. It takes down less fun things from the first game, and improves on the more core mechanics. If you loved the first game for the hard choices you had to make, you'd love this game. If you weren't such a fan of the choice mechanics in the first game, or the first game in general, this game won't change your mind.

Invisible, Inc is what I would describe as a "Cutting Edge" turn-based game.
The mechanics that govern how the player controls the character(s) during missions is top-notch -- I wish that more turn-based games functioned in this manner.
To be specific, each character can use their AP (action points) in any order with very few restrictions and the control system does not punish the player. This design philosophy sets Invisible, Inc apart from many other games of the same ilk and makes the play experience far more satisfying.
There is a Story mode with a unique scoring mechanic and there is also an "Endless" mode, the latter of which I found very much to my liking.
As someone who has been playing turn-based games for over a decade ranging from X-Com to Final Fantasy Tactics, I can assure you that this game has a very progressive control scheme. Give it a shot!

Alpha Protocol is a unique and very fun game. It's caught a lot of flak for the bugs that so often plague Obsidian products, but almost all of those have been patched out at this point; the experience has improved a lot. The game has a modern setting, so you get to play with all kinds of familiar looking but renamed guns, and a wide variety of armors, gadgets, and weapon and armor modifications. The skill tree works like Mass Effect 1, which the game resembles in the other ways you'd want it to as well. The combat is smoothly controlled third person with cover, the dialogue choices are made from a circular menu with option positions reflecting the conversational tactic, and the story is branching with many ways to change the outcome and the events on the way there. The maps are often more vertical than ME, though, and even the brown ones look beautiful. The game can get pretty easy if you ignore the stealthy achievements and just gun everything down, but has challenge if you want it.

Difficulty -  challenging to OMG WTF !?
Patience - I would say this applys. But it does not. There is a turn timer that increases security the longer you lurk in the       mission. So, this forces you to get what you can and GTFO.

now... GAMEPLAY
It's fanastic.
Movement/ Actions - Action Points system operated. I have no greivence with this. Feels like X-Com all over again.
LINE OF SIGHT ( LoS ) - THIS is the game. You rush around a corner, you probably just got your Agent get killed. You need to maintain a vigilence of speed vs caution. Guards and security devices have LoS too. Once spotted, you are most likely Killed on your next turn.
Rewind -  Nice feature. Lets you take your previous turn over again. BUT, you only get one.
Death of your Agent - When an agent dies, your life starts to suck. I have not confirmed it, but I think when your Agent is down, if you can carry them to the escape, you save them. OTHER STUFF....
Sound is good. You get to hear the guards on patrol. That's a nice little heads up.
Graphics. They work. Objects and animation is smooth. Details are not distorted or fuzzy.
Controls. you only need your mouse. THIS is deceptive, because there are no mouse control settings in the options menu. Just a keyboard key layout.

Cons:
-Poorly detailed terrain (but you do get the entire planet).
-Low speeds, even for commercial airliners.
-No crash effects, kind of boring this way.
-No co-pilot AI.
-VERY steep learning curve, but it is a flight simulator.
-No real air transit companies, but you do get real aircraft manufacturers.
-Cities are lifeless.
-No aircraft paint customization.
Pros:
-As mentioned, YOU GET THE ENTIRE PLANET!!!
-Several planes and helicopters to start with, each with a few paint variants.
-Every airport, big and small, seems to be included.
-Confusing controls, but you can easily simplify them.
-Real-time weather based on your location in-game and what it is really like there in real life.
-Static weather choices as well.
-Most major landmarks can be seen.
-Controller support (I haven't used a joystick yet, but you can).
-Air traffic controller and pilot voices, adding realism.
-Can listen in on radios to hear talking between AI aircrafts and AI traffic controllers.
-Great tutorials.
-Multiplayer.
-Sandbox mode, as well as missions
-Custom difficulty (unlimited fuel, or not, etc).
-Weather does affect the aircraft.
-Aircrafts look good.
-Well organized menus.
-Able to customize your voice and callsign.
-Able to customize your jets flight number.
-It feels like a real airplane/helicopter.
-Other aircrafts in the sky, landing or taking off.
-A million ways to customize the gameplay.
-Pretty good sounds, but I do recommend playing your music in the background.
Verdict:
-I have never actually flown a plane or helicopter before, nor will I. However, this game/simulator allows people, like me, to fly the aircrafts of their dreams! I wish that the cities were better, and the terrain looked like real terrain, but this is about the flying, and the flying is great! From fighter jets, which control like the ones in the ARMA series, to the commercial airliners, Microsoft Flight Simulator X provides a fun and exciting experience for anyone who wants it.
-Minor flaws like the lifeless cities and the lack of damage/explosions does hold the game back a bit, but the flying more than makes up for it!
-As I said before, the game has a huge learning curve and only real pilots will feel right at home. However, the game does provide several helpful tutorial missions that will get the rest of us in the cockpit in no time!
-Overall, I think that Microsoft Flight Simulator X is a very good game. Now that it is on Steam, I recommend that anyone who likes airplanes, helicopters or simulators should give this a shot.
-Balancing out the poor graphics with the amazing flying, I would give MSFSX an 8/10.

I've been extremely impressed with Invisible Inc. throughout it's development cycle.
Cyberpunk turn-based thievery.
a Turn-based strategy stealth game, something that I didn't believe could be executed with the same nail-biting drama I've come to expect from more 'genuine' stealth games. Though it's very nature as a Turn-based game deadens the intensity of hiding from a horde of guards; it is no less thrilling to be able to come out of it alive.
As of writing this review the story mode has not been fleshed out, and the setting is a not-too distant future, where people are cybernetically enhanced and corporations take the role of world goverment, all of this information being gleaned from item descriptions and what little character biographies you are given.
The game considers itself a 'roguelike' which generally means a mess of RNG and a hardcore, 'death means restart' mentality.  Which will put many people off in the first place, the game can SEEM to be unusually tough.  Though it does require a major alteration from general XCOM style tactics to be truly succesful at it.
Most of the gameplay revolves around controlling a squad starting with 2 units potentially up to 4 through rescue missions. Locating target computers or hostages and stealing the item, and then escorting them to the escape. Hacking in this game is a tool and not a minigame, interacting with secured devices involves using one of a variety of computer 'spells' paid for with power, gained primarily through unsecured consoles, to lower HP on secured devices.
One of the biggest conflicts that i've seen people have with the gameplay is the "alarm timer"  every turn a ticker increases indicating increases in cameras, hacking difficulty and eventually guards. Mind, that it takes 5 turn between, each increase in security.   Some people believe this to be unfair in a game that seems to be about being methodical, safe and discrete.    But this game is basically about being a thief, and good thieves don't drag their feet looting a location, you need to be able to quickly identify good enough hiding spots so you can check doorways to neighboring rooms, and prepare ambushes or simply stay unseen.
I only have 2 real complaints,  first is in regards to the tutorial not going over the mechanics involved in 'pinning' a downed opponent,  if you do not kill a guard he is KO'd for so many turns, usually 2-3.  But if you keep a unit on the same square as the KO'd guard the timer never lowers. It's possible to juggle 1 unit between 2 guards to effectively double the KO timer, giving your teammates time to loot more rooms. This is a very important skill for new players to learn and master
The only other complaint I have is in regards to guard vision cones, there is a difference between 'noticed' and 'seen'  Seen enters a 'guard overwatch' so long as the next action by that agent does not attack the guard, that agent is killed.  Noticed will cause a guard to come and investigate the location that you passed through; on the guards turn.   So it is very common for me to just walk up the edge of a vision cone triggering 6-7 "huh? what was that?" etc. before tazering the guard.    It's hard to believe that I can run down 3/4 of a hall towards someone in their peripheral vision without being spotted, even worse when I'm basically stomping my way there.
If you enjoy the thrill of creeping through a room full of turrets and armed guards, Invisible inc. will deliver in a style very familiar yet wholly unique

The only game I've played like this is FTL; you want to get your character(s) as much wealth, and therefore upgrades and equipment as possible in the run up to an absolutely nails-hard final mission. The unpredictability of the procedural levels has ended many of my games abruptly, dished out incredibly good fortune and most importantly, created tense stealth moments – I'm a fairly big Metal Gear Solid fan, they've captured that satisfaction of pulling off dangerously close manoeuvres around outnumbered and more dangerous enemies. Stealth is generally the order of the day, but there's success in gunning down your enemies, too, whether that's with your own weapons or hacking turrets to do it for you.
I see a few people asking why there's any reason to keep playing, for me the procedural levels and the range in different characters' abilities is keeping me going (at the time of writing, 6 characters, 5 with an alternative version). The continually escalating alarm, which gradually turns on more security cameras and deploys additional guards keeps the situation tense.
There's plenty I've barely explored, I haven't even tried all the characters yet and it's clear there's a wealth of upgrades for them and Incognita (the system you use to hack) that I've still not touched. I've completed the story, but I still haven't got into a vault yet...

This was one surprise of a game for me. The concept sounded good, but I figured it might be one of those games that you really need to invest loads of time into to learn all the various parts, skills, techs and strategies.
Far from it! The game mechanics are simple enough and there's not a lot here that will confuse people (although some perks are a little unclear as to what they do) but man, it will challenge you!
The game is challenging and your death and demise is ALWAYS your fault! There is no luck here. Laziness and lack of forethought will be your undoing. That's the beauty of this game. Randomly generated levels combined with solid game rules and permadeth equals loads of replayability and agonising consequences for screwing up.
If you like games where it's all about planning without the effect of luck, undpredicatble levels and the risk of losing with one mistake, this is for you.
It's not a shooter, in fact, that's your last and often unwanted resort. It's a stealth game to the max and it teases you with the random levels, as sooooo many times I've died just wanting to explore that next room, even though I've completed my mission and the exit is JUST THERE!!! Do you leave an unconscious agent so at least your game can continue, or or do you attempt to strategically resue them knowing that the gaurd numbers ar eincreasing and that they will find you eventually.

I really like how this game includes concepts from other games, makes it work, AND you have so much fun.
Introduction:
For example, <insert class here> you ride into battle WoW style 5v5, on a mount, and either head to objective or a vantage point, or whatever. The music is fitting for battle, and you unlock as you go cosmetics, emojis, etc. There is also a store so p2w? dunno yet. Simple interface, simple graphics, yet the classes have some depth due to the talents, perks loadout and type of class.
Gameplay:
Before and during a game, it gives you that MTG/HS feeling while choosing customized loadout and in game perks, pretty cool since you dont know what enemies counter your loadout "strategy".
The game is very rewarding AND is forgiving, leading to a fresh FUN experience! I HIGHLY recommend this game to all ages! It's pretty casual to begin with, there ARE some League of Legends style "locked" heros, which i dislike, and competitive. Allow me to define casual, Rocket League comes to mind, once you manage to score a goal, then you see someone fly and ariel a goal, you realize the skill cap is pretty high, ALTHOUGH if you just manage to score a goal, its still fun as 5 minutes will allow. Games take about 15-30, the client is fairly lightweight and easy to read and get going.
My experience was picking the sniper class, without even reading loadout, getting 17x killstreak, then i read the ablities, and was amazed that default sniper class has a teleportation (.3-.4s) delay AND slowing landmines(static) and deal minor damage), which made space for mlg type plays.
Enemy fleeing at 1hp? No problem, throw your tp thing and noscope420mlg him or 420mlg 180spin and commit to the "tactical retreat". ALL on short cooldowns, making them very useful from getting the payload from point A to point B, did I mention variety? I was getting outplayed by other classes in hilarious ways. The funniest has to be when a tiny fox on your team turns enemy into cute little pigs for 3 seconds or something, I lost it, and totally made my day. There is standard COD class (viktor), some invisible dashing girl, another one always shows up behind your back, some sticky bomb dude even MECHS [ARMORED CORE kinda] (ruckus), some other healing and tank classes.
I have only played 6 hours so far, and I can see I am going to spend many hours having FUN.
tl;dr
Miss the good ol epic KoTH battles? Paladins. "Fresh variety that includes elements from other triple a games? Paladins. Unique, yes. Cloney feel, no. Fun? Yes. Casual while highish skill cap? Paladins.
Install, launch q's are very fast, game is fun and comical, emphasis on fresh/variety to suit your playstyle do what you want however you want and still have fun.
Is it perfectly balanced? Not sure, I was not stun-locked for 7 straight seconds nor disabled for more than 2-3 seconds at a time, which is welcome CHANGE to the arena type of games so popular today.

The only game I've played like this is FTL; you want to get your character(s) as much wealth, and therefore upgrades and equipment as possible in the run up to an absolutely nails-hard final mission. The unpredictability of the procedural levels has ended many of my games abruptly, dished out incredibly good fortune and most importantly, created tense stealth moments – I'm a fairly big Metal Gear Solid fan, they've captured that satisfaction of pulling off dangerously close manoeuvres around outnumbered and more dangerous enemies. Stealth is generally the order of the day, but there's success in gunning down your enemies, too, whether that's with your own weapons or hacking turrets to do it for you.
I see a few people asking why there's any reason to keep playing, for me the procedural levels and the range in different characters' abilities is keeping me going (at the time of writing, 6 characters, 5 with an alternative version). The continually escalating alarm, which gradually turns on more security cameras and deploys additional guards keeps the situation tense.
There's plenty I've barely explored, I haven't even tried all the characters yet and it's clear there's a wealth of upgrades for them and Incognita (the system you use to hack) that I've still not touched. I've completed the story, but I still haven't got into a vault yet...
This is probably the best early access game I've bought into, the unpredictable content is already enough to keep me invested, the quality of the art and music is great, and it's created cool moments I want to tell other people about – a sought-after quality in games for me. If you like games like FTL and/or stealth you should give it a go.

Unfortunately, that’s really the extent of the effect you have on The Walking Dead’s narrative. Like in season one, picking sides causes people to react to you in different ways, but the plot still moves forward just the same. Decide to steal someone’s medicine or let them go; you’ll be in the same spot regardless of what you end up doing. Occasionally your choices will affect who lives or dies, but everything always ends up reverting to some kind of status quo. Moment to moment, The Walking Dead is thrilling, and it feels like your choices matter--examine it too closely and you realize that you’re merely given the illusion of choice. It’s no worse than the first season, but it ends up feeling more obvious the second time around.
Still, while the choices you make might not necessarily affect the overall story, they certainly affect how you feel about its numerous characters. I was worried that season two wouldn’t be able to deliver characters as compelling as the ones we got in season one, and that’s certainly the first impression I got when Clementine stumbles upon this new group. But over time, you get to know them and really connect with them as people. Luke attaches himself to Clementine as a surrogate big-brother, and the badass lone-wolf Jane teaches her how to survive at all costs. Even Carver, the megalomaniacal head of a budding utopia (and voiced by a scene-stealing Michael Madsen) feels relatable--his my-way-or-your-face-smashed-on-the-highway approach to leadership is extreme, but in the end, he’s only doing what he thinks he needs to do to survive in this harsh world. As in season one, season two’s cast follows a wide range of personalities, and each one is flawed in their own unique ways. They’re all capable of great acts of kindness as well as sweeping acts of betrayal--just like, you know, real humans are.
Unlike season one, season two completely sheds its extraneous adventure game roots. It doesn’t bog itself down pointless puzzles or fetch quests (people who remember finding batteries for a certain radio know exactly what I’m talking about). Rather, season two is constantly about forward momentum, as it propels you from one bleak scenario to the next. For the most part, this works in its favor--and whether you’re running from zombies or enjoying a brief respite, every moment feels deliberate. It really is a roller coaster ride of emotions (mostly depression), and Telltale has nailed the art of the cliffhanger in this series.
That said, season two’s pacing feels off. Major plot points are wrapped up by episode three, leaving the back half of the game to languish in this weird survival purgatory. There’s no real endgame--merely survival--and the last two episodes drift along aimlessly until the season's ultimate conclusion. The payoff is certainly worth it, as its exploration of the evils any of its characters are capable of finally comes to a head--I just wish it didn’t take so long to get there. Even with these pacing issues, season two is still worth playing, as there are some truly surprising moments that will make even the most hardened player reel in shock.
Season two also keeps its signature quick-time events intact, and if you hated them in season one, you’re going to hate them here, too. When you’re not navigating The Walking Dead’s myriad life-ruining decisions, you’re mashing buttons or matching on-screen directional prompts to avoid bandits or shambling zombies. Like the plot, these QTEs certainly feel like you’re doing something, and they definitely spice up the action, but they occur far too frequently, and your input is way too basic to be anything more than contrivance at best, and the red arrows have a tendency to blend in with all the action on screen, leading to more than a few frustrating restarts.
Even with its hiccups, season two of The Walking Dead is absolutely worth playing, with an interesting cast of characters and a narrative that is still sufficiently gripping despite its less interesting parts. It’s not quite game of the year material, and it doesn’t feel as necessary as season one, but Telltale proves that Clementine’s story is one well worth continuing.

FSX is a must if your interested in aviation in anyway.

For starters I will be playing this via DOSBox.  Because unless you have an old Compaq Presario 5528 with Windows 95 on it sitting in the closet, you will too.  Which means, that since DOSBox is pretty much a requirment to play the game, I’ll be including it in the aspects of the review.
As I have said before, and I’m sure, will say many times again.  I wont ever down an old game for its graphics.  If the game had bad or poor graphics, in relation to competition at the time of it’s release, I might.  But so long as things are at least par for its time, I wont argue it.
DOS Box is a neat little program that allows older DOS programs to run in the Windows environment.  It’s noting too fancy in that regard, but it does allow for a complete control customizing, something Dark Forces would otherwise be without.
Dark Forces graphics are great for its time, and a strain for the eyes now.  This is one of those games that I don’t expect a lot of people to go run out and play.  If you’ve been playing Battlefront II all weekend and then try to play Dark Forces.  Well, its gonna suck, plain and simple.  Especially if you’ve never played it before.  But again, this isn’t me saying this is a bad game, just uncontrollably dated graphics.
The story is excellent, giving the means to tell it.  There is the backstory, that unfortunately is not with the Steam version since it was in the original game manual.  But with a quick Google search can be found easily.  The meat of the story is told in short cutscenes and the mission briefings.  With the occasional comments from Kyle Katarn as you play.
I would absolutely love to see someone remake this game.  Using a modern engine, or ever just a less dated one.  Yea, it was tried, but that project was recently canceled.  It does strike me as odd though.  With Dark Forces being a landmark game.  For all gamers, not just the Star Wars nerds.  It seems like someone should have done this, and done it fully some time ago.  This is what people want.  If it could have been done with Doom, it can be done with Dark Forces!
The level design is better than I expected.  It doesn’t follow that flat maze and corridor style I was expecting it to have.  Perhaps I’m thinking too much about Wolfenstein 3D?  There are places that could use improvement, but then when isn’t there?  And they make great use of the multiple floors, remember that was a big deal when this game came out.  So of course, there are stairs everywhere.
Dark Forces is one of those games where you can take your time and take in the sites or just run for it.  Either way you play it you get pretty much the same experience.  A sit down with it, will show what gaming was like ten plus years ago.  You wont be blown away by anything by any means, but you might gain a little more admiration for the old school.
An excellent game for what it is, but unfortunately, doesn't hold up well to modern standards.  Which to be honest was completely expected.

Game is awesome. Instead of "reviewing" I'm gonna help you out with a few specific things. After 17 hours played so far,these are the things I find impt for people to know so far:
1) PRO: I see a lot of reviews (especially on metacritic) that solely complain about the micro transactions and nothing else. I got the preorder orcs that came in a loot box, and I got the game on sale, so after opening the preorder loot box, I thought "that was fun! All the orcs I got are super cool! Since I got the game on sale, maybe I'll use my saved money to buy some more loot boxes!" But then I started playing the game, and there is WAY MORE THAN ENOUGH orcs and gear and currency and everything in the actual game play. So much so that it actually made me change my mind from wanting to buy some loot boxes to not wanting to buy any. If you are someone who is worried about the game balancing, I can assure you that there is no incentive whatsoever to buy loot boxes.
2) CON: The fighting pits are something to worry about in their current state. I have had overpowered orcs lose and underpowered orcs win simply due to something dumb like one of the orcs never actually swinging their weapon during the entire fight, or never using their abilities like bombs. So you level 25 legendary will go up against a level 15 loser, and all the traits will put your orc at the best possible advantage, and then your orc just dances around feinting attacks, while the other orc deals 1 damage at a time until it eventually kills your legendary and wins. Most commonly the fighting pit will work like you expect, but this has happened to me several times now so I am simply warning you.
3) CON: Fighting pits again - when you start a fighting pit match, the enemy orc is generated at that moment. Since it is generated at that moment, it needs a place in the orc hierarchy to stand. I haven't tested it enough yet, but I have had an occasion where the enemy orc replaced one of my legendaries even though there were empty spots (from dead captains) in the hierarchy. So watch out for the chance to lose a good orc out of nowhere to some randomly generated one replacing it when you start a match in the fighting pit. If you put an orc in the fortress defense, it will be safe from this.
4) NEUTRAL: "Nemesis" difficulty really turns up the damage you take. (idk what it is like on other difficulties) So at the start of the game, you can be like 3-hit by grunts. Some orc captains can one hit you. A graug shows up? GG. Since the point of the game is to die, I don't mind this, but it is just a warning to people wondering what the difficulty is like. A major issue with it is that there are a lot more orcs out there, so you will be swarmed by 40 orcs, some with shields, some with bows, some with throwing spears, some that can counter you, and then 4 captains all at once, and then caragors and maybe even a drake. So much is going on that it is hard to avoid taking damage, which means a LOT of getting hit then running away to heal by draining a random orc, then running back until you get hit again, etc.
5) PRO: There is actually a lot of cool progression. For example, you can only have one upgrade per ability, so branding has been super annoying so far because I can choose to either add orcs to my team when I brand them, or to gain elf-shot ammo, but not both. It's frustrating because you start with only 5 elf-shots and like I said in #4, there's a lot of having to run away so the elf-shots are super important for triggering traps on your enemies, while dominating orcs is more useful more often because sometimes you're not using you ranged attacks in certain battles. ANYWAYS the point is, you can get more arrows when you get better bows. You can also get certain gear like a ring that, once you upgrade it, restores your elf-shot when you dominate enemies. So all the frustrating stuff becomes solved as you progress through the game and unlock and upgrade better gear. It adds a lot of depth because you can get better gear by sending death threats and targeting legendaries and junk.
It's egregiously broken in all sorts of different ways, but the things this game does right, it does so better than any other game of its type, and will spoil you rotten.

right im gonna start this off by saying this is my first steam review so if you see errors in what i say please tell me im open to criticism myself.
to start with lets go for the good things about the game, well to start off the story and lore is very dark souls-esque in the sense that the game will not just tell you what is going on, you have to figure it out through reading walls of text in character descriptions and item descriptions. for the most part the game never tells you whats going on leaving it mostly open to interpretation which i personally enjoy in a game.
Graphics: well it doesnt dissapoint, its no triple a title for sure but the art style is... well artsy, they were really creative with the character models and everything feels like a cartoon you would see on a broken TV in fallout only much more detailed and dynamic.
controls and bugs: bugs havent plagued me for the most part and the control system is easy to get a hold of, even so the keys are fully rebindable and its really allowing you to choose your own control set, the guards do seem to have a tendency of spotting me where i shouldnt be able to be spotted such as in an area labelled as hidden, but this happens so rarely it doesnt get in the way of your gameplay, either that or im salty about it, probably the latter with how many times i died.
AI and level design: well the level design is certainly unique, im unsure about it but i definetly thought each corp had a different layout for each building type, there were some reused things like desks etc. but these things are too mild to be considered an even marginal game spoiler. as for the AI those guards are smart, pathfinding is a bit iffy for your agents and the guards though, to give an example i once got deckard and told him to move to a safe thinking his path to be safe, he ended up running right through the guard's cone of vision and getting shot, the pathfinding is acceptable though as the developers implemented a screen that appears close to your cursor to tell you if you will be spotted on your current path.
now for the guards. their pathfinding is good for the most part with no real evident problems, except they tend to be wasteful of their AP. i once hid behind a safe and a guard stopped dead infront of the safe without going further and posing a further challenge, to be fair his patrol ended there but maybe the devs could be more creative to give them more reasonable paths, a guard hierarchy would be nice too, for example there is a guard captain and he co-ordinates the rest of the grunts making your job harder, i dont know about you but this seems like a good opportunity to me.
music and other story notes: the music isnt "gorgeous" per se, but its the perfect one for the genre, it gives me that original XCOM feeling of edginess when theres that one chrysalid you can never find and just when one of your guys sees it, BAM its gone, the only difference here is your the chrysalid.
and the story is definetly akin to that of shadowrun, minus the magic ofcourse im certainly going to say that what i found out about the story so far is compelling enough for me to keep digging.
reccomendation status: highly reccomended for strategy and stealth fans.

SECOND EDIT: The final game allows an excellent level of difficulty customization, from "filthy casual" to "brutal masochist." There's nothing really to add to the first edit I made apart from that. This game is amazing. Everything I hoped it would be when I saw the trailer and more. Without question the best early access game I've bought and the best game I've bought in 2015 so far. If you like tactical combat and a stealth based version of that sounds interesting you absolutely should get this game. You won't be disappointed. The developers seem to be actively working on it and I can see this becoming a classic like X-COM, it's that good.
The emphasis is very much on the stealth/combat missions, with minimal rpg elements, but that works fine in this context, and endless mode means you'll get lots of hours of play out of it (I certainly have).
STRONGLY RECOMMENDED
ORIGINAL REVIEW: This is a rogue-like, a fact which is mentioned absolutely nowhere on the game's store page. Ignore every other tag or adjective in the description as they are completely secondary to relentless, punishing rogue-like heart of this game.
On the surface I should love this game. Turn based tactical stealth? Count me in! And the basic mechanics are a lot of fun. The actual game side of it is really good, and I enjoyed it a lot. The graphics are really nice. If this were an X-COM style game I'd be giving this a thumbs up, because it has the potential to be an amazing amount of fun. Hell, it
an amazing amount of fun.
But it's a rogue-like. A rogue-like with the difficulty turned up to eleven. And that's what takes all the fun out of this game and stamps on it until it's no fun at all.
If you make a mistake, you get 1 do over/mission. Make 2 mistakes and you may as well delete your surviving agents and start over from the beginning. Not even joking. If you lose an agent, particularly after a few missions when you've spent some of your extremely scarce resources upgrading them, start over from the beginning. The mission difficulty ratchets steadily and if you've made any strategic mistakes with how you upgraded and equiped your agents, start over from the beginning. If you've even been a bit unlucky, didn't get the money or equipment you needed on the earlier levels because they didn't spawn, start over from the beginning. And that's the "Easy" difficulty level. I haven't even looked at "Normal."
EDIT: OK, I figured out how to get infinite money and power with Cheat Engine[1]. Once the punishing difficulty level is taken out, OMG how much fun is this game! I've been playing endless mode for hours and it is so good. Slowly building up your agents' gear and augments, leaning how to deal with the different situations. With the difficulty tweaked and/or getting rid of the nosave, permadeath BS I could see this turning into a cult game like X-COM. I really want to give this game a positive review because it does
. I just can't while I need to use 3rd party hacking tools to make it something other than an exercise in misery and frustration.
[1] They're stored as Doubles, and the memory address changes every mission, so you're going to have to either rescan every mission or do something clever with pointers if you want to cheat all the time.

Nearly 100 hours in, I think it's time I change my previously negative review into something that reflects what I really think of this game now.
Invisible is one of those games that is so unforgivably harsh, you will have a love/hate relationship with it, it will make you suffer, it will let you feeling miserable, but you will always be back for more.
You'll want to have the last word, but the game will argue with you even harder than the last time, then it will knock you down on knees again, and there you'll stand, bloody and defeated... untill you gather up the strength to lick your own wounds and then go back for another round... then another... and then another.
As you are mercilessly beaten up by it, time after time, you will learn its secrets one by one, such as:
Simple lessons, yet hard to learn and easily forgotten
Here I am now, finally admiting that this game is brilliant, not because it is simply "too hard to beat", but because it challenged me like very few games did, whilst teaching me its ways past its deathtraps.
I almost feel embarassed after reading my previous review, but I am going to leave it as it was, just so I can remind myself never to write reviews while angry, especially when my anger was caused by my own incompetence.
Well done, Klei. Well done.
*******************************
PREVIOUS REVIEW:
I simply love turn-based, tactical games. Add the word "stealth" to the equation, and I'm drooling all over it.
That's why Invisible is kind of a disappointment to me.
It delivers in mostly everything: artwork is superb, gameplay is smooth... you can improve your spies' abilites, you can explore the map, sneak past guards or knock them down, pickpocket them... you can hack servers, cameras... you can unlock safes and steal valuables... well, it's got everything really.
Everything... except that, because the maps are generated at random, half the time the obstacles spawn in such locations that you just cannot sneak past guards and cannot knock them out, not without losing one or more of your agents.
Other times, you are so ill-equipped agaisnt the vast amount of armored guards and high "disabling cost" cameras and other obstacles, that no matter what strategy you devise, you will lose.
And because playing this game has been such a frustrating experience, with sorrow I will not recommend it.
3/10
