Invisible, Inc. is a stealth tactical turn based game from Klei Entertainment, notable to me for
.
It isn't terribly fleshed out yet, but what is there -- the stealth-focused completely unforgiving rogue gameplay, agent trait management, equipment management, and 'Icognito' mode (the hacking mechanism) -- is really, really fun. Even if they don't add many more features (as I write this, in a week a major 'warez' based update is coming out) it's still a really enjoyable, deep thinking game. It has even taken the place of X-Com for the time being, for those times I want my turn based tactical combat fix.
Another reason it really came to my attention is the hard focus on stealth gameplay -- alot like Metal Gear Solid or Splinter Cell -- but with a charming, cartoony art style. Your agents will end up being found and mercilessly gunned down as your Central Operator expresses her disappointment in your performance. And then you begin again with a fresh new team, in a fresh new environment (did I mention its
which is something X-Com was never able to master) to raid, pillage and escape from various corporate facilities.
It's also a game that makes you say "Just one more turn" and staying up far later than intended playing it. If any of what I've said above peaks your interest, it get's a solid Recommend from me.
Try picking it up on sale for insane value, but it's totally worth the $15.99 it is now.

Alpha Protocol is one of those games that I have a kind of hate-love-relationship with. On one hand, this game has fantastic voice-acting (especially compared to some of the stuff thrown at gamers these days), a non-linear, thrilling story, interesting, complex characters, and a lot more. Some of these points are so strong that there are not even a handful of games able to compete with Alpha Protocol in those regards.
However, on the other side, Alpha Protocol has it's bugs and flaws. The controls are, at best, mediocre, and sometimes to be considered an atrocity. The overall graphics are sub-par considering what the Unreal Engine 3 is capable of. Despite this, UE3-typical issues like textures that are loaded far too late are still noticeable.
All in all, the story of Alpha Protocol is a sad one. Not because it's bad - no, in fact, I really do recommend this game to everyone looking for a thrilling espionage-action-game - but because it was confirmed that there won't be a sequel.

A turn-based stealth game, Invisble Inc. excels at both. Set in a not distant future, you have to infiltrate various procedurally generated facilities for different goals (5 different goals IIRC). One of the novelties is Incognita, your AI that can hack cameras and other security devices, as well as provide some distraction for the guards. You only start with 2 agents then you can upgrade them, free others, upgrade Incognita, etc... But Invisible Inc. is not for everybody: the game is very hard (even with the "door exploit"). There's no go back (game saves automatically for you) and every little stupid mistake on your own can mean having to start over, which is sometimes frustrating (OMG I left that door open, ZOMG I calculated the guard trajectory the wrong way, crap this agent was selected, I thought it was the other one, etc...). There's not even an undo button for your moves, so plan carefully. But it is also where the magic of this game resides: the tension of stealth + not allowing mistakes is a good combination if you're not easily frustrated. On the other hand if you have no patience, just skip it or you will end breaking your fancy hardware.
EDIT: Devs introduced a new "Easy mode" that is welcome for the frustrated masses :D

Played the game for nearly 40h (played some offline) so i would be able to rewrite the review fixing my mistakes and talking about things i did not talk about in the last one. I will be talking about Microtransactions at the end of the review. I will start my review by saying
Shadow of War starts where you left off in Shadow of Mordor. The game will also give you a small yet good recap of what happened in SoM to get you started for SoW if you haven't played SoM. This time the story is more on the entire Mordor instead of Talion doing things for his own needs. As Sauron sets his eyes on the entire Mordor, Talion and Celebrimbor decides to stop him. So far the story is more than just Sauron actually. As you progress through the story, you will meet more people learning more of the story and in a bigger scale. There's also parts of SoM that continues in SoWa. Overall the
The best part about the game no doubt. And oh my they just took the definition of fun SoM gameplay to another lvl. If you don't know what kind of game SoW is, it's an open world and kind of RPG game. I will talk about customization later. Remember that really good parkour in SoM? They just upgraded it to next lvl. With the speed boosts and new abilites you can traverse through the city so fast and such stylish/fun way that you will be surprised. They also added stylish double jump. The fighting is basically same but with new abilites and different gear you can also make it alot different than SoM. Riding Caragors and other beasts are bit easier than before and more beneficial. SoW is like the Sword version of Batman Ak games but much more fun and way more combos to do. The stealth is still an option if you want do it. Stealth is better than before. Much more accessible and different routes to take for a successful stealth mission. But fighting 100 Uruks in one time is still the best way to go.
This is what completely differs SoW gameplay from other games of similar genre. They perfected the nemesis system IMO. Giving you more reasons to use the system properly thanks to having bodyguards and fortress assaults. Also the insane amount of voice acting for every scenerio just makes the Nemesis System perfect.
This time they made the world with regions. so far i found 5 regions. All of them are really big and has atmosphere of their own. One with mountains, another one with snowy mountains then there's volcano/lava region etc. All of the regions looks really beautiful as well as big. Each region looks different and works different. But all of them will give you insane amount of fun and the nostalgia from LOTR movies. So far i'm loving the SoW world. When i look at the world map, there's more regions to unlock. More amazing places to visit and conquer.
Characters are well made with their own story. Now i'm gunna talk about the characters that i actually know something about/  I'm not sure about every last character but the key characters to the story has their story. Alot of them you can find while progressing or finding relics and whatnot. The really important characters like MC/MV have their story well written so that's nothing to worry about. Those who were in the LOTR universe has somewhat similar story but definitely good. Not the best game if you're looking to get attached deeply with characters but the feat is definitely there.
You can customize most of your gears including adding runes to them which are important unlike SoM. You can change your Sword, Dagger, Bow, Armor, Cloak and ring. Wide variety of gears are available in the game. This is not like other RPG games but good gears are necessary for survival in Mordor.
Insane visuals. The beautiful sights of cities/forts/landscapes to uruks and down to every last detail is really beautiful. I played the game at the E3 on console but the PC version looks same and believe me that's not a bad thing. The graphics is extremely good.
As like the first game the controls are extremely easy to understand and get used to even now that they've added alot of new options. Extremely well put controls and responsive. The game also lets you change every last one of the buttons to your own liking or change hold to toogle. Overall really good.

Ok, I just finished and I've split feelings towards the game. The end saved very much, what the rest of the game tried to ruin.
So, good things first: The end! Yep, I have to admit, I cried. At least at 2 of the 5 possible ends. Finally Telltale games was able to reach to my deepest feelings and touch them. thanks for that! Nearly as good as the end of season 1.
But that's it already about the good things. Now to the bad or better disappointing things about this game.
1. Setting: To chose Clementine as the main character put Telltale into some trouble. On the one hand, she is still a 12 year old girl. Sure, she has gone through a lot of s***, but still, she is only 12. And still, she has to handle all the stuff, the adults are supposed to do: Fix machines, mediate between childish adults, take important decisions for the group and even kill humans. Sure, this things need to be done by the player, otherwise there would'nt be anything to do. But this does not work for Clementine. They just took the concept they had for Lee in season 1 and put it on Clem. That. does. not. work. It's unlikely, and that is sad. Could have been much better.
2. Decisions: You think, you decide how the story goes on? You are wrong! Only the very last two decisions of the very last episode have an influence on the ending. All other decision do barely change anything. sure, sometimes a follow-up scene goes a little bit different, but the result will always be the same. And as soon as you have realized this, you stop to care. that woul have not been so bad, if Telltale would not claim, that the game adjust to the decisions the player makes. It does not!
3. Characters: Honestly, most of them were indifferent to me. Characters in Season 1 were so much better and so much mre connected to me, that I didn't even care, if one of the died.
4. Skipping: Why can't I skip the credits or scenes? That's annoying, especially if you want to replay a scene.
So, do I recommend the game? I do because of the ends, but still the thumb goes down. Because Telltale can do it better and I want them to do it better the next time! Especially I want to have the feeling, it REALLY matters what I do (was good on season 1, but bad on GOT and TWAU). And I don't want to play the super tough Killer- girl, I want to protect the little girl! Please do it better next time! I know you can!

Analysis of the game
Graphics 10/10,
Game runs at 100 fps on all ultra settings with a 1060GTX 6GB and an i7 8 core.
Story 9/10,
Story is Middle Earth lore.  Yeah it's not canonical but the movies are far from canon as well.  The team worked with so many people from the Tolkien groups, they got everything down pretty much to a T.  It lines up with Tolkien's letters about the books as well.  Only disappointment is no lip-sync in game, minus cutscenes.  Really detracts from the experience.  The prerendered cutscenes are annoying bc continuity errors arise with the armor, but you can get over it.
Value of Microtransactions 6/10,
They're only good early on, you need to grind in this game either way.  Don't buy them, you can spend 1 hour in game and get about the same value out of it, compared to purchasing ANY loot box.
Music 8/10,
Still haven't heard the iconic death march theme from LOTR, but the music is still great, even though it seems to be a remaster of SOM's soundtrack.
Audio 9.5/10,
EVERY ♥♥♥♥ING CLINK IS AUDIBLE IN BATTLE AT THESE LARGE SCALE INVASIONS, VOICE ACTING IS WONDERFUL ACROSS THE BOARD, THE SILENCE WHEN YOU DO AN EXECUTION ON A CAPTAIN ENHANCES THE DIRE NEED OF SURVIVAL.  There are, HOWEVER, several animation cancel audio glitches, but I'm doing some crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥and it's mostly excusable.
Controls 8/10,
Pretty much the same as SOM, with new abilities.  If you hated the clunkiness of jumping around, it's not your game because that still exists.
Gameplay 10/10,
I live for this♥♥♥♥♥♥  Everything is so interactive.  EVERYTHING.  The characters, the environment, the deaths, the SCRIPT.  If you don't want to buy the game, go find a friend who did and borrow their game.  The Nemesis difficulty brings immense joy, because THINGS ARE ACTUALLY CHALLENGING.  And yes, this is an RPG, there is grinding, there was a little bit of grinding in the other one as well, but this is fully fleshed out.  PLAY THIS GAME!
Multiplayer ?/10,
Haven't been exposed to all of the multiplayer, /I think/.  I did online vendetta's, which let you go into another person's fort and ♥♥♥♥ things up because they killed another player.  I full cleared 3 fort's captains so far.  The actual objective is only to kill the captain who got the killing blow.
NOTE.  The microtransactions WILL NOT help you late game,  ONLY grinding will.  The microtransactions are basically a scam for the people that need mirian, because mirian in the game is harder to grind than the general contents of the loot boxes.
TL;DR:
This is a good game, it sticks to loads of things that weren't EVEN MENTIONED IN THE BOOKS, BUT IN THE TOLKIEN LETTERS.  The gameplay is good, the controls are basically SOM+, all of the audio is great, and it looks FANTASTIC.  Buy this game, play this game, have a child with this game, steal the child in court so you can sell it as a sequel to this game.

Both Walking Dead games from Telltale have been the most compelling, story-driven games I have ever played. The gameplay makes it feel like a movie yet the consequences of your actions and the things you cant control make the narrative much more powerful. These games are extremely immersive, if only because your investment into the relationships you build (which is 90% of the game) makes the attachement and inevetable seperation have much more depth.
Im inclined to praise the first game over the second, only because it was easier to immerse myself as a middle aged black man then an 11 year old girl. You play as Lee in season 1, while you play as Clementine in the 2nd. Im glad they kept clementine around as she is in the first game, that alone carried over the investment you created in the first season.
These games are extremely impressive, extremely emotional and artistically beautiful. Some moments you connect with characters, and it makes a lasting impression on you. Some of the more horrowing events do the same.
I hope anyone who picks these games up feels as deeply as I do about them.

I can't recommend this. Spoilers follow.
Mostly because the majority of the game reviews are positive already. But lemme be real here. The game's not bad. If you liked the first one, chance are you'll like this one too. It's got some great moments, and some memorable and crazy choices.
However, I never felt like the cast of characters developed as effectively as the first 'season'. You're quite literally thrust into the group and very few if any relationships develop as a result. Additionally, characters die *so* fast, that after part 3 I felt myself pullling away knowing it was very likely that no one would be left alive by the end. I get that losing characters is dramatic, and can certainly be very effective, but when you watch this many people in your group get killed, I couldn't help but find myself pulling away. This is a weird comparison, but Modern Warfare 2 suffered from a similar issue, CoD4 had a pretty effective moment where one of your player characters dies, so what does the sequel do? Tries to pull that♥♥♥♥♥♥two more times. It's just dumb, and immersion breaking.
I also can't help but note but there seems like there's even less interactivity then the first season. I enjoyed some of the quieter moments in one, particularly when you were given a limited number of food items and had to decide who could eat that day. In this, nothing. Dialog choices, jamming on Q action scenes, and a rare minute or two where you walk around and examine three different things in the environment. I know this is a lot of people's big complaints about these telltale titles, but I never thought about it in Season 1 or Wolf Among Us as I did in this. It made me feel like user interactivity mattered even less than it already does, which, let's be honest, isn't all that much anyway. Which could be fine, but it needs to maintain the illusion or it fails at what it's trying to portray. It's no longer your story.
Another little thing, but there are multiple time jumps in this story, with the first one being, what, sixteen months? That's ridiculous to me to think that nothing of importance happens in all that time. The series has never been great regarding supplies, no one even has a ♥♥♥♥ing backpack, but are you kidding me I'm just supposed to shrug off sixteen months being like 'and they were fine and nothing happened'? ♥♥♥♥ you.  I don't buy it.
The multiple endings definitely helped, and I pretty much enjoyed the entire ending sequence, albeit it does get pretty ridiclous. Overall, I would probably still say I liked it, but I think a person should go in with tempered expectations while playing it. It really can't compare to season 1.

Shadow of War starts where you left off in Shadow of Mordor. The game will also give you a small yet good recap of what happened in SoM to get you started for SoW if you haven't played SoM. This time the story is more on the entire Mordor instead of Talion doing things for his own needs. As Sauron sets his eyes on the entire Mordor, Talion and Celebrimbor decides to stop him. There's also parts of SoM that continues in SoWa. Overall the
The best part about the game no doubt. And oh my they just took the definition of fun SoM gameplay to another lvl. If you don't know what kind of game SoW is, it's an open world and kind of RPG game. I will talk about customization later. Remember that really good parkour in SoM? They just upgraded it to next lvl. While not being as strong of a season or as solid as season 1, season 2 serves as more of a character study of Clementine. A focus at developing and exploring the possiblities of it's main character is what season 2 holds close to. The player, now actually given control of Clementine, has in a way even more of a responsibility to keep her safe in all forms. The game's community strives to protect Clem and the people she learns to care about, but with varying degrees of sucess seeing how it's The Walking Dead. The concept of building a character and handing them over to the player to further their development is an interesting one. This concept is put into season 2 and drives the player through it, nearly a social experiament. But with the game it gives each player an experiance that this is their own story, or their version of the game almost as if it's a show and the player is given the directors chair. Some key or even just passing choices and actions can carry over from the first season to the next seamlessly. Almost making the player keep consistancy with those choices made. What's clever is that even then, it's the impact and memory of Lee that has people keep Clem with a state of mature thinking, and how to stay alive rather than the games plot. It's the game allowing the player to think and act on what Lee would want Clem to do in certain situations, not the game itself forcing it. Which is a considerable achievement for it.
What doesn't carry over the seasons is the feel of the story and characters, which is an inevitable side-effect of having different writers. It is still noticeable that these writers did know the responsiblity they had for the season, but there's almost no way of seeing these seasons as anything but separate, and not 2 parts of a whole. Looking back in retrospective, the game has this feeling of needing a new location/set piece for every episode. Not so much that it has a sense of feeling rushed or having a fast pace. More of the thought of "What's the rush?" And by the end you have this feeling of either that it doesn't feel big in scope or of "not a lot really happened in the grand scheme of things"
New characters don't have this sense of attachment or proper depth that they should have, and some actions made by them just seem out of character for them, to the point of frustration (Looking at you Bonnie and Mike). Some characters are built as if they will at least have something happen with them, but then just getting dropped (killed) for presumed shock value or heartbreak, but it just brings disappointment. Some characters that bring great impact as it goes along aren't introduced early enough to gain that attachment for later events and big choices. At least the stand-out for me being Jane.
The balance of threats is at least still prominent as it usually is in the franchise, until surprisingly dropped halfway through. The pacings faults seem to carry over into the finale, as the ending/cliffhanger that leads into the last episode doesn't make it feel like it really is. It lacks that smack of urgency and dread that season 1 had so well. Instead, episode 5 starts and goes on as "just another episode"
The overarching devastation that lingers on the series is still here as usual and the big ending seems to go for a greater sense of despair or melancholy rather than sorrow and heartbreak. With one of the different endings mirroring season 1 gracefully.
There's plenty of iconic "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moment in this and one scene that will make the game's R18+ rating pretty clear.
It's, as to be expected, a solid continuation of the story. And the ending gives Telltale plenty of opportunities to do many things with characters that are known to be alive for each different playthrough, and with people that have simply disappeared or have their status' as unknown. But it's of course nothing compared to the pure quality of season 1.

I have only played this game for a small amount of time, and I do have a few other things to try out for it, but here is my review on the game, Invisible, Inc.
First thoughts, this game is challenging and even sometimes unfair because of how hard and tricky it can be to complete the objectives, not just partially, but completely.   It is very punishing for if you make mistakes, such as not looking before entering a room, or for not closing the door behind you as you ran pass it.   However, this game is somewhat like a game of chess.  You have to think ahead, plan on what to do if certain events occur, and know when to stay down and wait, and when to be aggressive and go for the push.   With that said, this game will not do well for those who play without thinking, or jump first, look second.
Gameplay:   Invisible, Inc. is a top-down isometric game that is turn-based, meaning that after you do whatever it is you do, the enemy has their turn to do whatever it is they do.   Also, this is a rogue-style game, so you will die often, and when you do, you will start from the very beginning.    In terms of mechanics, you pick to play with two agents who each have their own little niche in things.  One agent has better movement ability, so he can move farther and let others move farther too.  Another agent can scan for computers and electronics in a certain radius.  Aside from that, the agents all have their own, slightly unique, stats.  The stats are broken down to Stealth (affects movement), Inventory (storage space), Anarchy (affects stealing traits), and Hacking (affects hacking skills).   You earn money to buy upgrades.
There are also items and weapons that can be used to assist you in the break-in.  These range from lethal weapons such as pistols and rifles, to non lethal weapons, such as paralyzers and target marking guns.   There are also tools to be used in helping such as an invisible cloaking device, items to instantly hack a computer or camera, or a noise distracter to draw the attention away from you.    With storage being limited, you have to think wisely about what to buy/take and what to sell or not take.
Aside from tools and weapons, there are collectables to steal that will fetch a nice sum of money, an even hostages to rescue, who can help reveal more locations for you to break into.
Graphics:   Just looking at the pictures on the store page should give you a good enough idea on what to expect.  IMO, the good thing about graphics like these, is that they are unique enough to give it its own style and not rely on 'super 4k HD parallax & mega bloom" style of graphics, and thus keeps the focus on the game itself, rather than the looks.   And of course, people with weaker performing computers, can easily run this game.
Sound/music:   Not many sounds or music things going on but the current sounds that are heard, are good in that they make it easy to tell what it is that is going on when you hear it, like the sound of quick loud footsteps means a target is running, instead of walking.  Or the Alert, target spotted, sound played when you get spotted.   There is very little variety, if any, music, but that keeps the atmosphere focused.  Personally, I wouldn't mind there be more styles of music, or a music style change after the guards have spotted you for the first time (kind of like how payday the heist was)
Other thoughts:   This review will be updated sometime after the big big update that is set for sept. 30.   Since there are hints for new things coming, I will most likely change this if it adds more stuff to the game.  Until then, I would like to point out that this is an EA game, and it is clear that it is not complete.  What I mean by this, is that the story mode of this game, is short.  After you complete, you unlock Endless Mode.   And after playing through it a few times, there is nothing much to do.   The levels are randomly generated I believe, and that does give it a nice 'new ffel' to things, but the building tiles used for each 'unique' place, are pretty similar and it can be repetitive.    Also, being randomly generated, there are times where the AI or the setup of the guards, is just outright, impossible to counter, and usually ends up being a game where you either all die together, or one person makes a break for it, but make sure to not get spotted, or else you have one action to do before you get shot.
Overall:  This is a great turn-based stealth game that has a lot of potential, and in my opinion, is an example of an EA game, done right.   Hopefully this next update will add the amount of stuff that it is showing.  Til then, I'm just going to try out new things and see how it goes.

Let me start this off by saying I give this game a 5/10.
tl;dr
Game is buggy (for me). I had to find work arounds, including breaking my immersion in-game by making decisions that didn't fit with who I wanted my character to be, in order to keep it from crashing. Currently stuck in an 8-times-replayed crash trap and cannot complete the game. Only buy this game during a significant sale, or if you are prepared to possibly deal with extreme bugginess.
(NO SPOILERS)
I thoroughly enjoyed the first Walking Dead game, and like many others, it brought me to tears in the end because the story was so beautifully written. This sequel to the first game also brings me to tears. The reason not being the beautiful choice-based storyline, but rather the fact that I have experienced numerous crashes that take me completely out of the immersive gameplay.
I have tried just about everything to combat this: Changing graphics resolution, playing in-window instead of full screen, taking completely different choice paths because they appear less buggy (I didn't want to make the in-game decisions that I had to, but they were necessary as a "work around" to the frequent crashing), and the uninstall-reinstall of the game. Some of these have been temporary fixes, and have gotten me all the way to the 3rd chapter of the 6th episode.
The issue is, now it seems I can no longer progress to the finale of this game. At the point where you are tasked with getting a couple members of your group to come back next to the fire, every time I move on to convince the second person (no matter who I choose first) the game will crash. This part is at the end of chapter 3, and every time it crashes, I have to start from the beginning of the chapter and sit through about 10 minutes of decision making. I have played through this part 8 times now, and every time it crashes.
As stated before, I don't think that there is any work around for this one, and I will not be able to complete this game. This is a complete shame, because the entire rest of The Walking Dead: Season 2 is wonderful, and takes you on the series' famed emotional ups and downs. But there will probably be no closure for me, and others, with this story line.

I tried to play this game as top down shooter. You know, the one designed for mouse/WSAD or twin-stick.
That was a mistake - I died instantly on the first level. I was mad at this game - I was playing shooter so I wanted to shoot. Not keep dying and dying.
Everything changed when I changed my perspective. It's not a shooter - it's a brutal real time chess-like game. Where you die. And die. There is a lot of dying and restarting in that game.
Basically your objective is to either retrieve something from level or kill everyone. The trick is you are not a powerful hero. No - you can be killed with one shot, just like the enemies. So you have to plan your approach. You learn the levels and what can on them. If something unexpected happens you have to quickly adapt...or die. Rinse and repeat.
Enemies can be killed...brutally. Even with it pixel-art graphics it's a violent video game. You can stab, throw various object (knifes, bricks), shoot enemies with a guns, throw your gun, punch enemies to death or...kill them with boiling water.
Graphics - it's nice pixel art. Very detailed, but the some screen effects (wobbling?) can tire you eye quickly.
Sound - sound effects are good (punches, gun shots). There is no voice acting, so you have to use your imagination.
Music - very good electronic soundtrack by various artists. I listen to it to this day.
Story - story is delivered through interactive cut-scenes (all in game engine). There is plot twist, but no spoilers from me. Just now, that this is a good story.
Overall - I really like this game. It provided good story and good game play. Mask mechanics add variety to it and you can also try playing for high-score.

I have to say, Hotline Miami is probably the most fun I've had with a game of this scale in a very long time. From its gritty story, stylish visuals, awesome music, and absurdly fun gameplay mechanics, it'd be quite a loss to not experience the game for yourself. So go play it when you get a chance!
Story: You're a man who's out to, uhh... "clean up" the city. And you do a mighty fine job of it.
Visuals: It's a top-down perspective, and there are a lot of crazy glowing neon backgrounds. The stages themselves are mostly building interiors or urban settings, reflecting a bit of how you'd think the underworld of Florida looked circa the 1980s. I would say that it fits the narrative of the game well, and it sure didn't detract from it.
Audio: While there's not too many sound effects that you'll be focusing on (gunshots, stab/slice sounds, doors opening, wood cracking), the music stands out quite a bit, as it melds with the 1980's "neon and crazy" visuals that are present throughout the game. Moreover, the music is just plain nice to listen to by itself if you're into it!
Controls: While the controls may take some getting used to (I use a 360 gamepad for games when it's available), that's exactly the ticket. You get used to them FAST. You use one stick to move, one to aim your character since you can face 360 degrees, you have a button to pick up and throw items, a button to fire the weapons, and you can click the sticks to lock on. As stated earlier, by principle of playing the game, you learn the ins and outs of the controls fast.
Gameplay: The gameplay is divided into two different kinds of segments. Smaller "story" type segments where you learn a little more about what's going on, and just outright "game" segments, where you run about doing all sorts of stuff. You control a man wearing masks, and your goal is to usually clear a floor of a bunch of enemies by taking them out by any means necessary. Your score rolls higher if you use a lot of different types of kills. You can go from punching a guy, throwing a knife, shooting a gun, THROWING the gun, and a bunch of other crazy stuff to make the process flow a lot smoother. By the end of each mission, you're tasked with bailing out of where you are and taking off. On the other side, your character can generally only take one hit of damage before dying. You can, however, restart a mission as many times you need to.
Difficulty: While the game was much harder when I first played it a while back, it did get a little less absurd the more I played. I guess it has a decent enough curve, but I guess there are some people who would find it very difficult. So to be fair, I'll say it's moderately difficult. The one-hit deaths may be a factor that makes the game difficult for some, but you do get checkpoints in levels so that you can get back to where you were faster.
Fun Factor: Quite a fun game. There are times where the game gets a bit difficult, like a certain mission towards the end of the game. But in its occasional harsh difficulty, it still managed to do is be fun. There's just an odd joy in playing as a fragile human blender running around taking out a bunch of mobsters with extreme prejudice. Even when it gets to the point where you'd think they're starting to use your own strategies against you. For me, fun is a value in games that I seek out beyond presentation, pretention, and theory. Because pretending you're having fun is just not a way to spend your time.
Replayability: I'd say it's got quite the replay value. While the story campaign has a definite ending, you can always go back to earlier played chapters and just have at it. You may unlock something new in the process or find something you didn't see before. O you can take on the chapter in a more (or less) efficient way than you did the first time. You can go as unnoticed as you possibly can, or you can take on the mission guns (or throwing items) blazing. Considering how addictive the game can get, it's pretty easy to see why anyone would go back to play it again! You can even just go back and play it for absolutely no reason at all; you're bound to have some fun.
Would I recommend? - Yes.
To who? - Those who like relatively fast-paced action games.
Any possible detractions? - If you don't like ridiculous, pixelated violence, this game may not a little outside of your comfort zone. For anyone else, I really can't say there's anything negative to take away from the experience.
Numbered Score - ?/10 - In my own personal system of numbered ratings, a "?" is given to a game I put in the realm of "To give it any number would be a disservice to myself and its creators." While opinions definitely vary on how good a game is or is not, the "?" is merely my sign of respect.

EDIT: After buying a few loot boxes with mirian(In-game money) I've gotten several legendary orc captains, several decent training orders(Olog gang, level ups, Make captain legendary) I did get a few common and epic captains aswell, but the chance of getting good stuff is VERY high.
I've finished the game, and I suppose it's alright, story is a little...I dunno.
So far: Nurnen, Cirith Ungol, Gorgoroth and Seregost are the only forts you can take, Minas Morgul/Ithil doesn't entirely count, but it is an extra region to explore and do stuff in.
Pit fighting is pretty cool, easy way to level up your orcs who have fallen behind and need some extra training, however it is a slippery slope. I had a legendary Olog that outleveled a common captain by 15 levels get killed, so it is very unexpected. Legendary captains are considerably mroe difficult to take down, but not impossible.
Still greatly enjoying the game, looking forward to attacking peoples forts, and they mine. I have to admit though, I am a little upset that there are so few forts. I thought there would be like, idk, 9? But four seems quite low. I mean we are in MORDOR, and there ought to be way more than a measly 4 forts around for us to conquer.
Wish Monolith made it a little more complicated. It is all pretty straight foward, attack a fort, and the region is yours. Kinda lame, wish there was a bit more to it, like, capturing outposts. I don't mean disabling them, but legit capturing them. Maybe add a thing where if you don't capture the outposts there is a chance for the fort you are attacking to get reinforcments, with a Warchief or someone leading a force to attack your rear.
That aside, it is said that they want to expand the map, which can be cool I suppose. Question is, in what direction? In the Shadow War stage, Talion seems to be able to traverse through mordor, and out of it, judging by the games lore, so perhaps instead of expanding westward to Gondor, maybe east and South, for Harad and Umbar? Just a thought.
All in all, it is a pretty solid game, very fun. Highly recommended. Lootboxes aren't shoved down your throats, nor are they a requirement at all. They simply are like, little care packages to bolster your forces, and enhance your gameplay a bit, though you don't need to spend any cash, just use the in-game money and you will be fine.
WARNING: Do not get carried away with it, though. You need that money for fortress upgrades, aswell as upgrading your attack forces. When you've got the silver to spare after leveling up your forts to your hearts content, then go at it with the loot boxes, rack up those training orders and legendary captains.

As a long time lover of the Civ series, this game did not disappoint.
I've never had so much fun learning about history and the new "unpacked" cities mechanic is such a fantastic natural ensurance of a more realistic experience.
The visual and audio aesthetic is beautiful - the art manages to be modern while still maintaining a classic and stylised appearance and I find myself sometimes just relaxing with all the UI hidden, looking at a nearby vista with my city in the background.
Diplomacy has come a long way since the previous installments in the system, exposing the various metrics required to have harmonious relations with all met civilisations, and espionage feels tightened up. Spies now have very specific contextual actions to consider, making their placement often times a really crucial decision in the mid-late game.
Religious combat is a fantastic way for 'peaceful' civilisations to still have the fun of fight-strategy while never receiving the warmongering penalty that is usually incurred with combat, and the UI surrounding the religious system has been overhauled (in a patch) to make more sense. The end result is a really polished and what I used to find a quite annoying mechanic is now one of my favourite aspects.
Overall I think this is the perfect game, and am aware that I'm being as subjective as hell because of the joy this game gives me.

The second season doesn't quite reach the lofty heights of the first, but it remains an excellent experience.
After a rather wobbly first episode, which relies too heavily on cheap techniques to have emotional impact, the second episode is a stellar return to form - possibly the best episode of any Telltale game. From there, the game tells a strong and compelling tale, with plenty of memorable moments.
The one bugbear (aside from some wonky and in one case buggy controls) is the thin veneer of choice. I was so bothered by the death of one character that I planned to restart the episode - until I learned that the character would die later in the episode anyway. There are few consequences for decisions, and even the big consequences (like saving a character) are undermined by the game finding a way to kill them soon after. The first season at least had the culmination of your choices on display in the final episode through the people who chose to join you - the second doesn't even have that, and instead essentially offers a multiple-choice ending.
Hopefully the third season will take the choice/consequence system much further.

True stealth games are hard to come by, most are faux sneakers and often enforce a shooter game play. Invisible Inc. is not one such game, it punishes violence. Not familiar with turn based games, the learning curve is fairly steep, but having an affinity for stealth gameplay helps in learning the game. The noir atmosphere and graphics are gorgeous and traditional stealth gameplay elements are adhered to strictly. There is no apparent story of import, but that doesn't bother me, however there are some flaws. Pop up features (peek/door) block other pop ups (# of turns) depending on camera angle. A limitation that is presumably found in turn based games is the need to change the camera angle often, and sometimes to no avail as the rooms are very difficult to see and observe where your character is. There is no restart button or in-game saves so you must fully commit to a mission until completed which is very difficult in these fog of war maps. Most of these flaws can be forgiven as it is an independent game with a small development team. Invisible Inc. is an ambitious, but flawed, early access sneaker that pushes new boundaries for the genre.

Invisible, Inc. is both frustrating and a ton of fun. First, you have to accept that you will die, and you will fail. Like many rogue-like games, it rewards multiple playthroughs and doesn't pull any punches when it comes to the situations you are put in. You will be outnumbered, you will make mistakes and you will accidentally walk into a group of guards with no way out.
What you will also do is learn. You will learn when to be cautious and when to run like a maniac. You will learn when to take a guard down and when to sneak by quietly. You will balance the rewards of exploring the whole level versus the lives of your agents.
The game is well developed for an early access title and Klei once again doesn't disapoint. Graphics are sharp, mechanics work well and the interface is easy to use and intuitive. Updates are made regularly and the developer does an excellent job of keeping the community in the loop the way an early access title is supposed to be.
If you like turn based strategy, stealth with a more realistic approach and a challenging game, definitely pick this up.

I hit the 50 hour mark so i kinda have to write a reveiw. Let me just start out by saying that this game is not for short tempered or impatient people. This game will beat you senseless only to help you back up and give you a band aid. Nuclear Throne is honestly one of the best games ive ever played. Its a retro pixel art, fast paced, rouge-like game thatll break even the most hardcore gamer's spirit. Now let me get this out of the way Nuclear Throne IS NOT a game that intentionally makes you wanna rage its actually a very well balanced and fair experiance.
Nuclear Throne has you picking from 2 mutants from the very start, more can be unlocked by reaching certain stages or doing special actions and each mutant has its own unique passive and active ranging from being able to perform a dodge roll to shooting out a beam of radiation. Speaking of radiation every time you kill an enemy they will drop rads when picked up these will fill a bar at the top of the screen when filled  you will level up, this allows you to pick a mutation at the end of the level mutations are vital to your success they do things like raise your max health or increase pickup drop chance or even upgrade your active abillity or specific weapon types. When you reach level 10 aka your ultra level you can pick one of 2 ultra mutations specific to your mutant thatll which will greatly upgrade your active or passive or even add another extremely powerful passive.
The game has you fighting thru multiple stages collecting rads and weaponry thatll help you reach and defeat the Nuclear Throne. Now let me just say this game has an abundance of weapons to choose from. From triple machine guns to plasma cannons or even lightning hammers this game has no shortage of ways to cut down your foes. your gonna need those guns to if your gonna deal with some of the enemys in this game. Enemys come in a vareity of colors shapes and sizes. Theres one thing that Vlambeer does extremely well and thats making things feel really good. every gun you shoot feels so nice and every hit sound is so satisfying. There is nothing better then the noise you hear when you smack a cop with a shovel. This game is an excellent example of how to make good "game feel".Everything has weight and the game and the feedback the game gives you is so nice and meaty. but of course lets get this back on track
Now this game isnt gonna just let you get to the Throne, no, its gonna make you work for it. youll be fighting thru hoardes of bandits, rats, robot snow gorrilas and dogs made of pure radiation. But all of those are small potatoes compared to the bosses in this game. Now let me just say that this game does bosses really well. each boss has its own attacks and patterns you have to learn and know how to counter. even after youve done that its still gonna be a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to get past some of them. but when you do its very rewarding and satisfying.
Now the last aspect of this game id like to address is the soundtrack. this game has and amazing one. right from the start the music really sets the pace for the game and is just all aroud the perfect theme to kick butt to. from the desert to the labs this game has a soundtrack that really holds its own. It has its own unique theme but at time has a bit of a hotline miami/ payday vibe to it and just really keeps you in sync to whats going on
In the end my hats of to JW Rami and all the other wonderful people who helped shaped this game into what it is today it may still be in early access but the games nearly finished and i think it should be this winter so defenietly get this game now or when it releases. But if your waiting for it to go on sale, it wont until its officially released. Only downside is that its still has some annoying kinks in it that need to be fixed but im sure theyll be fixed by the time im done writing this reveiw 9.5/10

Pros
Middle Earth: Shadow of War is a solid sequel. Better graphics, larger world and more content, all while keeping the fundamental elements that made the first game great. The nemesis system, which is one of the primary features that set the first game apart from other games in the genre, has been drastically improved and expanded upon. You have far more control over your ever growing army of orcs and the game feels less about your individual strength and more about building the power of your military force as a whole. Combat feels more fluid and visceral than ever before. Shadow of War also introduces more character customization, not only allowing you to choose new abilities from skill trees but also change your weopons and armor. Once you level up your character a couple hours into the game the battles turn into beautiful flowing sequences of bloody and gratifying violence.
Cons:
I know a lot of people have been turned off by the microtransactions the developers have added to the game but if you are a player's that likes to sink a lot of time into your games than I would not be concerned. Everything you get via microtransactions can be obtained in game simply through grinding. Personally, I am not concerned about sinking in the necessary time to earn in game content needed to progress. If others want to skip ahead by buying some loot boxes that is their choice.

The entire Walking Dead series from Telltale has excellent atmosphere, voice-acting, pacing and tension...
...and also a very bad habit, similar to the TV series, of passing the Idiot Ball around for the purpose of moving the plot forward.  This time around, it's doubly frustrating because a lot of the time, the Idiot Ball is passed directly to YOU.
Perhaps it's because the WD franchise, in general, maximizes character strife and situational tension through liberal use of this particular trope.  But a game revolving around player choice is bound to be hamstrung, when the player's choices are between "stupid/moronic/get yourself killed and then pick one of the first two, dumbass".
Mind you, I say this even considering that Clementine is a little girl (Lee isn't, but at least in Season One it happened less often).  Sometimes, it's perfectly reasonable for her to carry that ball.  There's NO such excuse for NPCs who've managed to survive the zombie apocalypse for over a year, only to get everyone killed by pulling a first-week-rookie stunt.  Like, say, having most of the lights on in your highly-visible mountaintop retreat without bothering to close the damn curtains.
Pretty sure "these schmucks were really asking for it" was not the emotional response the writers were looking for.
So while I enjoyed this game for its story, I ended up being repeatedly and severely annoyed by its gameplay.  I honestly think it would have been better as its own Walking Dead spinoff TV show, so at least *I* didn't have to be personally involved in passing the Idiot Ball around.

Invisible, Inc. is a challenging, turn based strategy game that has you move your agents through extensive randomised levels to get valuable money and resources off powerful corporations. Every level is guarded with guards and CCTV cameras, with an alarm level that increases over time to send in more units, activate more cameras and make hacking more expensive.
I’ve had had a mostly positive experience with Invisible, Inc. However, it can be frustrating when you fail, as you have to start again. Invisible, Inc. has many unique features: hacking, strategic combat, stealth and looting.
-Hacking
A massive part of the game is hacking. You will need to hack a lot to progress through the game. Among the things you need to hack are: CCTV cameras, laser barriers drones/robots, Corporate safes, turrets and generators, executive control panels, console/camera databases and nano-fabricators (shops).These are the most important thing you have to hack but there are many more. To hack you will need Power (PWR). You will slowly get power through ‘Power drip’, a program provided to you by your agency. You can also get power by hacking console, which usually give you 2-3 PWR per console, but be careful, some consoles are monitored by security.
-Combat
To take care of security guards, you will have a Neural Disrupter by default. The Neural Disrupter is a melee weapon to stun enemies for 2-3 turns. You can get upgraded versions from some nano-fabricators. Other weapons include pistols, dart guns and rifles. Killing guards with heart monitors will raise the alarm counter by 2 bars. An agent can go into melee reaction so if a guard goes past, the agent will knock them out and keep them pinned. Alternatively, your agent can go into overwatch, so if a guard/drone goes into it’s line of sight, He/she will shoot it. If your agent is firing bullets the guard will be killed. If they’re firing darts, he will be knocked out. Drones cannot be knocked out and are unaffected by darts/ Neural Disrupters, but some can be hacked.
-Stealth
Stealth is vital to the game. It is nearly impossible to go in guns blazing and succeed. You have to stay in cover to avoid the enemy’s line of sight, otherwise your agent will be shot. If your agent is shot, He/she will be critically wounded, however, the other agent can still get to the elevator to exit the level or revive the wounded agent with medi-gel. By default, Deckard will have a cloacking rig, enabling him to be invisible for a turn if he’s out of sight. An upgrade version can be bought from some nano-farbricators.
-Alarm Counter
The alarm counter will increase over time but certain events such as a guars getting killed or a security-monitored console being accessed will increase it too. As the alarm counter rises, it will reach levels (1,2,3,4,5,6 etc..). At these levels, the mission will get harder as hacking will cost more PWR or more guard are called in.
I highly recommend this game as it’s a lot of fun to play, But I suggest that you play the tutorial as it teaches you a lot and without it you’ll probably fail the first mission.

Easily one of my favorite games of all times.
I'm a big fan of rogue-likes but, until now, I have not really been a big fan of bullet hell games. The game is exciting from the first second, the action is fast and chaotic, and the difficulty ramps up steadily.
Each run can last anywhere from a couple of minutes to 30+ minutes. It takes seconds to randomly generate a new floor so it keeps you in the action and always keeps you guessing. The entire environment is destructable so using explosive weapons, destroying certain objects, or enemies can greatly change the landscape of a floor. That along with the corpses staying on the floor, by the end of the 3-4 minute long floor, it really looks like a huge battle had just occurred.
On the surface, the characters may seem pretty similar considering most of them all start with the same weapon, have the same movement speed, have the same amount of HP, and can hold the same number of weapons. Once you spend a couple of hours with a character you realize how unique they actually are and how easily you can create some pretty unique character builds by applying new mutations. Mutations are earned after reaching a new character level and can greatly enhance or modify the single run you are on. Mutations range from higher max HP and max ammo, to modifying weapons, to more utility based like allowing you to break through walls.
A ton of secrets, easter eggs, and unlocks are scattered throughout the game. Bosses are challenging and fun. Mini-bosses and stronger variations of common enemies tend to spawn periodically on certain floors to keep you on your toes. There are a TON of weapons to find in random drops and random chests. Each weapon is unique and has it's own pros and cons. This makes it more interesting and there are very few instances where one gun is a hands-down upgrade over another gun because a more powerful version may have a slower fire-rate or consume a lot more ammo.
Nuclear Throne is addicting, exciting, super fast-paced, and amazing fun. I currently have over 200 hours on record and don't anticipate ending that anytime soon. Highly recommended to people who enjoy shooters, bullet hells, rogue-likes, and fast-paced games in general.

I'm not terribly far into the game yet, but I feel confident enough I'm getting my money's worth that I'll write a quick review now. Mainly to do a bit to counter out review bombers who only play enough to write a review without actually giving the game a legitimate chance. I'll update the review, and potentially change my recommendation, once I've seen the "true" ending. Until then I'm not even going to respond to anything or watch any discussions due to the number of spoilers being thrown out by trolls.
The game has excellent graphics, and playing on High with a GTX 1070, AMD FX 8350 and 32gb of RAM has a very stable framerate of around 80-100 with no noticeable dips or freezes that I've seen.
The combat is very much like the first game but significantly harder (at least on Nemesis difficulty, which I started with), in part due to the limited nature of upgrades. Each ability gets one upgrade, think Diablo 3 rune system, but you only can pick one upgrade at a time to use it seems.
Fighting on Caragors seems a lot clunkier, and that spirit glaive thing is also clunky, which I very much dislike, though all Caragors can stealth now (not had a chance to try Dire Caragors though). Enemies routinely attack in pairs which is nice, and dodge (spacebar) prompts are more responsive than the last game. Ranged enemies are legitimately dangerous, even the grunts (maybe less-so on sub-Nemesis difficulties). Graug are okay though my stay on one was brief. I am very much enjoying the usage of Drakes in combat. The gameplay surrounding them feels amazing, from fighting to riding them.
Elf-shot and focus is depleted very quickly early in the game but bows (better bows grant more elf-shot) quickly come your way alleviating some of this problem. Focus as well has use in melee and stealth skills, making it more in-depth than just an archer pool. I'm playing with aim assist off though so that might be adding to my early difficulties with elf-shot and focus. Though if you want to have an archer-focused playthrough or anything like that I suspect you're in for a challenge given that drain will not, without a particular upgrade, give you elf-shot.
The physics are buggy, enemies have a bad tendency to go flying about 8-12 feet in very unrealistic manners, but I've only seen this maybe half a dozen times in 5 hours of playing now. I've also seen some weird... "crumpling" in the physics of Talion's cloak resulting in it freezing in odd positions, but I've only seen this twice and it quickly fixed itself with a simple roll.
Mild spoiler, I don't like what they're doing with Shelob. It seems too strong a turn from her "character." I can appreciate her being seductive and manipulating. It fits with the whole spider theme. But the way they're going so far with her being some sort of anti-hero just seems wrong.
Largely a non-spoiler, but it seems the new "towers" in this game have Eyes of Sauron above them, instead of the old silver towers which fit better with the Wraith. The look of these Eyes comes across as... cartoon'ey, and I feel cheapens the menacing nature of the Eye of Sauron. The Eye should be saved for something more momentous than what amounts to a mini-game version of AC2's Ezio Auditore "memory syncing" at the tops of those towers. It feels wrong.
I do like how Talion feels more connected to the world of Middle Earth in this game than in the past one. He's meeting people, and making his mark on the world rather than bullying around orcs in an area no one else, save the human's slaves of the region, could give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about.
It's too soon to really comment on microtransactions, but they feel completely irrelevant to me. I am quickly amassing a huge sum of in-game currency and loot from all the orcs I'm killing, and this likely won't change as things progress. Even if I do need loot-boxes to get by in the "end game," it seems absurd to think I'd need to pay real money for anything given how quickly you can amass the in-game currency.
Anyway, this was an "early impressions" review. I'll update it at a later date.

I feel like I've put enough hours into the game now to form a solid opinion on it, and I really enjoyed it.
First off it feels very similar to the first game combat wise. It's still fun and engaging, though I saw a lot of recycled executions from the first game in this one. Not a huge issue, but I thought they'd put a little more effort into that aspect to set it apart from the first. In any case there are new executions and brutalizations, so it's not all too terrible. A good way to explain this one is
A good way to explain this one is "The first one but on crack." There are tons of Uruks everywhere, huge patrols, Caragor riders, slavers, convoys, camps and wildlife. The regions feel very alive and diverse. There are elemental Graugs and big packs of Caragors walking around that do their own thing. I think they did a great job at upping the ante on this one and making it feel like a much larger scale than the previous game.
Mobility is the huge improvement in this one. You can now "Sprint" using some of your focus in your focus meter (Which regenerates over time now) and It just made traversing the regions more enjoyable. Your mobility in combat is improved too, which makes for some really cool fights in higher level gameplay. They added lots of quality of life improvements too, like arrows being able to be picked up just by walking over them, Shadow Branding and stealth interrogations were added too. They made dominating enemy captains less of a hassle as well. I also noticed that some traits I saw constantly in the first game were absent in this one. ( As far as I know ) I never ran into a captain that could be killed instantly by stealth, and I never ran into a captain who could be killed instantly by ranged. I actually appreciated this, as it kind've forced you to interact with the captain in some way, and made the game less of a breeze at times, since a lot of people complained about the first one being too easy, this might've been a way of them forcing the player to challenge themeselves.
The story was great. It kept me interested and some of the cutscenes were INCREDIBLE. I enjoyed the questlines more than the ones in SoM personally. The ending was great, though I'm on the fence about the whole ACT IV thing, and I'll refrain from any spoilers. But I don't mind the aspect of the Shadow Wars, it's just the fact that we are held from a final ending behind all of the Shadow Wars. From experience these battles aren't too difficult as long as you're well equipped, and they aren't exactly impossible and aren't a grind, but I feel like devs shouldn't hide a true ending of their game behind tons of hours of gameplay. My campaign was done at around 30 or so hours when I started the Shadow Wars and I'm at about 51 hours now. Today I just reached Stage 8 of the Shadow Wars. I looked it up online today and there are 20 stages before the actual ending. That's cool and all but that's over 40+ hours after finishing the main story to get the actual ending cutscene. 20 stages just feels like overkill to me. I do want more gameplay and hours on the game, but why not just give us the cutscene at the actual ending, and put us in an endless sandbox when were done with constant attacking forces on captured fortesses? I know theres a petition for Monolith to make this a thing, and apparently they're already working on it, but it was just kind've a bummer to find out how much I had to play to get the ending I've been waiting for. (Yes, I know I can just look it up and watch it, but I wouldn't feel satisfied with that. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )
On a more positive note, the nemesis system is amazing in this game. The Uruks all have their interesting traits, and they're a blast to encounter and meet. They all feel like their own cleverly thought out characters, and you'll grow attached to some of them and want to keep them safe and alive at all costs. I had a few Uruks die that I really liked and it actually made me sad lmfao. You actually care about your army, and not a whole lot of games can do that, especially with randomly generated characters.
I played through the whole game without spending a dime, and I have plenty of Legendary and Epic Uruks from just playing the game. I didn't need the Micro-transactions at all personally, and I enjoy going out and hunting the highest level Uruks and recruiting them, but I can see how someone who doesn't want to spend that time playing would want to buy some of these loot boxes. They're practically pointless if you actually want to play the game how it was meant to be. Which makes me wonder why they're even in the game in the first place.
Either way, the game itself is a ton of fun. I'll be playing it much much more in the future and I've definitely gotten my money's worth. Especially worth the money if it's on sale if you feel uncomfortable with the full price.

Updated review. If you are going to buy this game, Please take the time to read this list of WTFs. I compiled this list over the course of about 3 hours of gameplay, and each was observed at least once but typically many times. If the list included terrible things from memory, it would not fit here. The game has been out for over a year as of this writing.
The UI is so terrible in so many ways, but the worst is how it ACTIVELY attempts to mess up your units' moves. You can turn off the unit auto advance, but -UI of course- the act of selecting the next unit doesn't really speed you up and is just as unpredictable as the auto advance, and sometimes acts like there are no more units left, only to tell you over and over that you need to end your turn, only then to tell you that you can't end your turn, you must move more units.
Other civs can butt in on your turn, causing your movement click to do something you didn't intend.
Unit selection auto advance is slow, arbitrary, and often selects one unit, gives you time to start moving it, then as you click, it advances to a DIFFERENT unit which then gets the movement order even if you had been holding down the click with the prior unit.
Unit selection will shift on its own after you manually select a unit, sending the unit the game wanted selected to the spot you tried to send the manually selected unit.
Auto end turn will auto end while you're planning the move for a unit, creating a difficult to get rid of route plan for a unit which it will use to try to make you mess up other units' moves and sometimes just doesn't move the unit you set a direction for.
If a unit has 0.5 moves left, and there are zero tiles available to move into with 0.5 moves, the game still makes you decide what to do with the unit (wait 1 turn, because there is literally no other choice).
The notification toasts on the right hand side of the screen try to trick you into making a unit move to the tile beneath the notification icon, because there are only two ways to get rid of them - leave them there for several turns, or right click (move) them, and the game may pretend the notification wasn't there and send a move order.
When you are deciding on which policy cards to use it, #1 doesn't tell you what the calculated benefit will be, #2 darkens the borders of the screen making most of your totals impossible to read so you have to CLOSE THE POLICY WINDOW to find out what your base yields were in order to take a guess at how much you will benefit!
One AI will offer you a trade, and as you Accept or hit Esc ANOTHER AI will butt in with a trade causing you to accept a deal because your finger was just that milisecond touching the *click* for accept when the next window popped up, or causing you to reject a trade or offer or even a gift you didn't get to look at. If you navigate correctly, then it will wait a bit before showing you the next AI's offer again.
Sometimes it shows you the WRONG LEADER when it's offering you a trade, and changing a trade item causes it to show you the correct leader. You like Scythia but hate Norway.. Scythia offers you a trade where they wants lots of good stuff, you're tempted to accept, but you want a different resources, you adjust the trade to get it, and BAM it was actually  angry ol' Harold who hates your guts about to get your supplies.
Icons often overlap each other making it difficult or impossible to see what yields are unless you adjust the UI to show or not show some things.
Icon overlap can make it impossible to select other things in a tile, such as when you have several units in a city and it doesn't cycle to the next option when you click again.
I like how the NPCs have real personalities and act in predictable ways and even the most warmongering of them will love you Forever and be your best friend and ally and neighbor all game long if you play toward their likes and avoid their dislikes.
You spend a lot of time closing out requests from civs that in the same turn but separate popups denounced you, inform you they are going to kill you, ask how you would feel about trading (not demanding) them your niter (gunpowder) and iron for 3 gold now plus 1 gpt for 30 turns, then another trade request asking (not demanding) to trade them a luxury. NO! I don't plan on helping you build musketmen that you will use to destroy me. Nobody does. Nobody will.
It acts with complete disregard for the history of its own actions in a way that's just annoying and adds Tons of clicks, which the UI of course tries to use to trick you into moving units into terrible places.

(you know here comes a rant from someone who screams i played CIV NEGATIVE 10, but so be it. the things that follow are sadly true and i wish they were not). I'm trying SO HARD to like this game. You shouldn't have to try (so) hard to like a game, so I don't think I like it.

The Walking Dead Season 2 picks up right after where Season 1 leaves off. Clem, now living with Omid and Christa, set off to survive on their own. While it is much advised to play Season 1 first, you can enjoy Season 2 without having played Season 1 prior. There will be some story elements spoiled in doing so.
I'm pretty bummed you can't skip dialog in this game. I wanted to replay the whole game, but this alone made me think otherwise. Adding to that is the fact that you cannot skip credits either. Considering you'll see the credits five times in a playthrough, this decision makes no sense whatsoever. And you still cannot save/load your games at will. It's like the game conspires against you trying to replay.
The sound and graphics are pretty much the same quality as the first game. The quality of writing may have gone down a bit, as many options they provide are less thoughtful this time around. Characters change attititudes over small things, and some characters are outright useless. That said, it's still an enjoyable read, and certainly enough to keep your interest to the end.
I give Season 2 of The Walking Dead a 8.5/10. It flows at a nice brisk (albeit liner) pace, and does a good job keeping you entertained to the end. My main criticisms are outlined below in the spoiler section.
***SPOILER SECTION***
I have a theory that Telltale games supports the Novikov self-consistency principle. This idea states that any changes a time traveler makes is history all along. Thus the past cannot be changed, and attempts to change it would result in an event to ensure consistency. Try replaying any chapter and select new choices. Same outcome, right?
Unfortunately, because I was aware of my inability to actually influence the story, it removed much of the immersion and I stopped caring about what I picked. Every time I saw "[This person] will remember that", I saw it as a death sentence. What was the point in remembering your choices when the NPC is going to die a few scenes later? What was the point in being a good samaritan if you are going to be attacked anyway? Why should I save anyone at all? I mean I'll still do it, but I already know it's pointless. I get that they want to create the illusion of crafting your own story by presenting timed responses, but it's obvious nothing matters.
While I appreciate Telltale for trying to tell a solid story, I had trouble suspending my disbelief when most of the remaining humans have have become crazy, corrupt, and/or traitorous. Those that aren't are promptly killed off or slowly corrupted. Why is it always man vs man anyway? No one tries to go on the offensive to cure the zombieism any more. Even if there's no cure in the end, it's something that people should never stop pursuing.
There's a consistent pattern that goes on in the entire Walking Dead universe. Main character finds a (usually friendly but not always) group . Group starts to fall apart. Deus ex zombina. People die. Move to new location. Repeat ad infinitum. The "move to new location" part I find amusing because whenever someone mentions "settling" it always ends bad and they must move. And I'm pretty sure this is because staying in one location would be boring to watch, play or read. If this were real of course people would like to settle. But that would simply be boring to write about and experience.

The chart showing your responses compared to other players is interesting, but flawed. A number of decisions are virtually no-brainers. Why would I not climb in the ticket booth when it looks and sounds empty? Decisions that sound dangerous to Clem don't work because we know as players the game will not kill you for it. Typically the only way to die is to fail at a quicktime event. The good decisions have two seemingly good outcomes, or are hard to figure out the lesser of two evils. For example, the option to rob Arvo was a good choice, since you could certainly use the meds. Instead most choices are to be nice or mean. At the very least, if we're given mean choices, I'd like to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥doing it. For example a choice between saving the baby or shooting the Ruskies. You bet I'd shoot Arvo if given the chance (though I'm sure they'll try to spin some tale to make him sympathetic next season). One choice I wish I picked differently was chopping off Sarita's arm, because chopping it off was definitely a bad idea. Of course she'd scream and alert the whole mob if you did that, but I didn't have enough time to think it through. It still doesn't matter, but the option and urgency here was good.
While a majority of decisions do not matter, surprisingly you can make an actual fork in the game at the end. I did appreciate this a lot. However, I'm fairly certain the fork will converge right away when Season 3 rolls out.
Walking Dead Season 2 is still a good game, I just wish we could make an appreciable difference in the story and the world.

I feel like I've put enough hours into the game now to form a solid opinion on it, and I really enjoyed it.
First off it feels very similar to the first game combat wise. It's still fun and engaging, though I saw a lot of recycled executions from the first game in this one. Not a huge issue, but I thought they'd put a little more effort into that aspect to set it apart from the first. In any case there are new executions and brutalizations, so it's not all too terrible. A good way to explain this one is
A good way to explain this one is "The first one but on crack." There are tons of Uruks everywhere, huge patrols, Caragor riders, slavers, convoys, camps and wildlife. The regions feel very alive and diverse. There are elemental Graugs and big packs of Caragors walking around that do their own thing. I think they did a great job at upping the ante on this one and making it feel like a much larger scale than the previous game.
Mobility is the huge improvement in this one. You can now "Sprint" using some of your focus in your focus meter (Which regenerates over time now) and It just made traversing the regions more enjoyable. Your mobility in combat is improved too, which makes for some really cool fights in higher level gameplay. They added lots of quality of life improvements too, like arrows being able to be picked up just by walking over them, Shadow Branding and stealth interrogations were added too. They made dominating enemy captains less of a hassle as well. I also noticed that some traits I saw constantly in the first game were absent in this one. ( As far as I know ) I never ran into a captain that could be killed instantly by stealth, and I never ran into a captain who could be killed instantly by ranged. I actually appreciated this, as it kind've forced you to interact with the captain in some way, and made the game less of a breeze at times, since a lot of people complained about the first one being too easy, this might've been a way of them forcing the player to challenge themeselves.
The story was great. It kept me interested and some of the cutscenes were INCREDIBLE. I enjoyed the questlines more than the ones in SoM personally. The ending was great, though I'm on the fence about the whole ACT IV thing, and I'll refrain from any spoilers. But I don't mind the aspect of the Shadow Wars, it's just the fact that we are held from a final ending behind all of the Shadow Wars. From experience these battles aren't too difficult as long as you're well equipped, and they aren't exactly impossible and aren't a grind, but I feel like devs shouldn't hide a true ending of their game behind tons of hours of gameplay. My campaign was done at around 30 or so hours when I started the Shadow Wars and I'm at about 51 hours now. Today I just reached Stage 8 of the Shadow Wars. I looked it up online today and there are 20 stages before the actual ending. That's cool and all but that's over 40+ hours after finishing the main story to get the actual ending cutscene. 20 stages just feels like overkill to me. I do want more gameplay and hours on the game, but why not just give us the cutscene at the actual ending, and put us in an endless sandbox when were done with constant attacking forces on captured fortesses? I know theres a petition for Monolith to make this a thing, and apparently they're already working on it, but it was just kind've a bummer to find out how much I had to play to get the ending I've been waiting for. (Yes, I know I can just look it up and watch it, but I wouldn't feel satisfied with that. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )
On a more positive note, the nemesis system is amazing in this game. The Uruks all have their interesting traits, and they're a blast to encounter and meet. They all feel like their own cleverly thought out characters, and you'll grow attached to some of them and want to keep them safe and alive at all costs. I had a few Uruks die that I really liked and it actually made me sad lmfao. You actually care about your army, and not a whole lot of games can do that, especially with randomly generated characters.
I played through the whole game without spending a dime, and I have plenty of Legendary and Epic Uruks from just playing the game. I didn't need the Micro-transactions at all personally, and I enjoy going out and hunting the highest level Uruks and recruiting them, but I can see how someone who doesn't want to spend that time playing would want to buy some of these loot boxes. They're practically pointless if you actually want to play the game how it was meant to be. Which makes me wonder why they're even in the game in the first place.
Either way, the game itself is a ton of fun. I'll be playing it much much more in the future and I've definitely gotten my money's worth. Especially worth the money if it's on sale if you feel uncomfortable with the full price.
