It's tough to say whether or not I could recommend Hotline Miami. On one hand, the music is phenomenal, the visual presentation is great, and the gameplay is addicting, albeit somewhat rage-inducing. The game sucked me in at first with its questions of "Who is leaving the messages?", "Where are we right now?", and the ever-popular "Do you like hurting people?" The game threw me into the fray, taught me how to hurt people, and initially, I felt like the game was planning to reprimand me for these blind acts of violence. The anticipation of that concept is what sucked me in to the game: that longing for knowing more, and that desire to uncover whatever themes may lie beneath the surface. Unfortunately, that's not the sort of experience that was ultimately delivered.
Hotline Miami is almost the polar opposite of Spec Ops: The Line. Whereas the latter insists that narrative is what drives a game home, the former holds that gameplay is most important above all else. And they're both right, in their own ways. There are games that greatly benefit from an intricately crafted plot, but there are also those that hold their own simply by their fun mechanics. There's a place for both of these kinds of games in our world. So if you're looking for a game where gameplay is paramount, then you can't go wrong with Hotline Miami. It really is worth the experience. But if you go in looking for something deeper, you may leave disappointed.
The ending of Hotline Miami is what ultimately drove my decision to not recommend it. It's not that it's a bad game. On the contrary, I think it's a fantastic and unique piece that handles the hardcore arcade theme very well. The downside, for me, was its intentional facade of deeper themes and an intriguing story, all of which evaporated when the game pulled the curtain in the final chapters. I understand that this was their point all along, but that doesn't change the fact that it left a bad taste in my mouth.

I don't normally write reviews for early access games but in this case I will make an exception as, even in alpha, Invisible Inc is a blast to play. It is both one of the best roguelikes and best stealth games I have played.
Invisible Inc is a procedurally generated, stealth-oriented, turn-based, science-fiction roguelike set in a world run by corporations. The player is tasked with leading a team of secret agents on a series of missions to steal and hack everything they can from the corporations. As each mission progresses it becomes more difficult, with additional security being added in the form of more cameras, more guards and better software firewalls. The player must make the choice of staying to get extra loot or leaving while it's still safe.
Invisible Inc is an alpha in the purest sense; it is largely feature complete but missing a lot of content. While the mechanics of the game are mostly in place and polished to a fair degree, there is still a lot of content to come, like new agents, new corporations, more tech and more programs. Even so, what is currently in the game is very fun and certainly enough to keep you going for many hours.
Buying games in early access is always a risk, but going on Klei Entertainment's previous track record this is much less of a risk than most. Klei are a company who have proven their ability to make quality games, with regular updates, and to ship on time, many times over.

The graphics on a technical level are a step up from the previous game, though are leave just a bit more to desire. After playing through The Witcher 3 and it performing the way it did, this game is tougher ro run and doesn't look quite as good. Having said that, it is pushing a whole Hell of a lot more enemies on screen, which is an okay reason to reduce my performance. Having said that, there's a lot of control of graphical options and you can turn off things like Motion Blur and V-Sync if you do not like them.
The story is okay, it's passable. The main draw here is of course the gameplay and the Nemesis system. Everything is improved and expanded upon over the original. More things are now included in the Nemesis system and the orcs have more things that they will 'remember' in the new system. The combat is great. Fighting dozens of orcs at a time is just as fun as it was in SoM and we're now given even more techniques to us in killing the orcs. This game uses a lot of the keys on the keyboard as you start to unlock the multitude of skills. The action is very responsive, still a similar system to that from the Batman Arkham series, though there are times when there's just so many enemies that I'm fighting that I'll end up moving on to a different enemy than the target that I actually wanted to attack, but it's okay and doesn't completely ruin the combat.
Shadow of Mordor was my favorite game of 2014 and I tried really hard to not get too overhyped for Shadow of War, but I still did. Despite that, and all the controversy over the loot boxes, it's looking to be one of my most favorite games of 2017, if not the top dog again.
Speaking of the loot boxes, they're a joke. They did not ruin the game at all. You don't have to grind for gear at all. I'm progressing through the game casually and I'm still getting plenty of solid look. I've gone against orcs that were 4 times my level, and while they were challenging, they were not giving any indication that I was stuggling due to not buying loot boxes but because they were simply meant to be encountered later. Despite that, I still killed them in a matter of a couple minutes since I know when to attack, what to attack with, and when to dodge/parry.
So yeah, just play the game, ignore the loot boxes, and just have fun.

Garry's Mod! A fun, very flexible sandbox game mod that came out almost over a decade ago. I remember as a young kid seeing Gmod videos on YouTube and thinking, "Man! This looks so cool, what is this?" So, in 2010, I signed up on Steam and got Gmod. I first played it on my mom's laptop, and boy was it fun. So far I've gotten over 5k hours poured into the game.
Sure, it's had slight bumps in the road, but the community stands firm and is fun and enjoyable. Gmod comes with many tools to build and invent contraptions to your heart's desire. And with Workshop support, you're able to download lots more content at any time, making the experience much more interesting. Though, I won't say it's all that great. The Gmod Workshop has some issues with poorly made content here and there, and mediocre saves and builds. Aside from that, it's still a very good game.
The multiplayer depends on the users. RP servers are fun and interesting, sandbox offers lots of flexibility. Anything else is up to the player to find out and explore. Honestly I say to anyone who loves sandbox to get this, I literally grew up playing the game! So much to do and see in this game. And if you are in to animation as well, Gmod allows you to make films, such as stop-motion. But yes, this is a great game and I hope any future person getting it will enjoy it greatly for years. Here's the problem. The game is amazing, but there is a fundamental contradiction. Random generated levels are very good thing when you have the time to traverse and explore them. But when you have brutally limited time for the whole mission and for the K.O. of the enemies (many of which you are forced to attack, because of generated level setup), and on top of that you have a cooldown on your attacks, the whole experience starts to feel like playing a lottery of what level you get generated and hope for a lucky one, because very often you will stuck on a simply unfair setup.
With such pace-pushing time-constrains we shouldn't be limited with attack cooldowns and what not. We don't have time to make a good approach. We need to act fast, but our actions are harshly limited. I think that The Alarm Level should not rise with time (I literally enter two empty rooms and the Alarm Level is rised). It should rise only with actions (when we are spotted, attack a guard, etc.) For example if a guard stands up after a K.O. he should call his supervisors and that will rise the Alarm Level (rise it a lot). Also every hack could rise the Alarm Level. I though about percent chance (of hack rising alarm level), but I don't think chances are a good game-design anyway. So you could go kinda back to the old Alarm System with more points to rise so it could accumulate with more actions. I know the game is closing to release with every day and your design-decisions are more and more permanent, but you shouldn't let your game-development Alarm Level to force you into rushing a room full of media cameras and armed consumers, because this will not be a successful mission.
I have a lot of respect for you at Klei Entertainment. You did a great work with Shank (1 & 2). Don't Starve is not my cup of tea, but its genuinely good game nevertheless. And I absolutely love Mark of the Ninja. So I bought Incognita (before you've renamed it to Invisible, Inc.) right away. It was a pleasure to see how the game shapes and evolve. Now I hope you will address the issue somehow and make the game less chaotic and more reliable.
P.S.
I gave thumb-down only so Klei could potentially see this when they scan for criticism. Otherwise the game have all my fingers up. I just hope it will be improved even further.

This game is a gem that is getting polished bit by bit.
GAMEPLAY:
Stealth Combat: Challenging but without the frustration of random number generators (abilities have cooldowns instead). Hide behind doors and desks, distract guards, and knock them out for a few turns before they regain consciousness.
Hacking: Manage your energy power vs the cost of hacking into firewalls. You can gain from dispensed terminals in a level and from producing it yourself based on the particular tool you decide to use (ex. Power Drip = +1 power/turn vs Power Fusion = -5 power + 3 power for 4 turns)
Fast-Paced: Every turn you spend in a level, the Alert meter fills up. There are 6 Levels in the meter with various consequences (ex. Level 1 Alert = more cameras turned on, Level 2 = added firewalls)
Various Objectives: Rescue prisoners from detention cells, steal artifacts and cash from corporate vaults (my favorite), steal advanced gadgets and equipment, steal corporate intelligence; then make it back to the extraction point.
RPG ELEMENTS:
Characters: +4 characters to choose from each with their own unique abilities and stats (ex. cloak vs rifle). 4 Different Statistical upgrades which include Stealth, Hacking, Inventory, Anarchy. Each level of a stat gives a character an additional benefit (ex. Stealth = +1 to movement points).
Incognita: Upgrade the hacking tool you use on a mission when you pull up the tactical 'incognita' map interface.
ART & ANIMATION:
Just look at the screenshots above. Animation is basic with more fluidity and variety to come (early access).
NOW I'm just waiting on technical and balance refinements and additional story elements.

A satisfying sequel & finale to the 'Shadow of' franchise.
Was a great experience - to follow on with Talion & Celebrimbor's storyline and what becomes of them. Interacting with new characters such as Shelob, Carnan, the Witch King & Nazgul -  and the Balrog were also fantastic.
Monolith developed their Nemesis System and Ability Tree very well, along with a basic item/gem system to compliment the extra levels in the game. The introduction of the Drake, Olog'Hai and other mosters were a welcome addition to the sequel, adding some more diversity, unique fighting and carnage.
Fortress Seiges - an interesting new concept with customisable options to strengthen yourself as the attacker or defender.
Microtransactions - hidden away in the main menu, not in the slightest bit invasive to the game. The amount of grind was fair, and did not seem at all like it had been tilted to encourage MT interactions. You earn a LOT of 'in-game currency' as well as some premium currency simply by playing through the game.
------------------------------------
All the positives aside, the few things that bothered me:
- The Uruk voices. Some of them just sounded like Dwarves from 'The Hobbit'. The voice did not at all match the menacing looking Uruks...
- A bit much dialogue. They've added on anything from 2-7seconds of Dialogue for each Uruk introduction which I feel negatively impacts the experience. I feel the dialogue pre/post fortress seiges is a bit much. Something simpler and more 'shock and awe' would be suitable..
- Acts I, II, III and IV. The first two acts progressed at a decent pace where the story was quite enjoyable and we interacted/developed an attachment to the recurring characters. Act 3 simply felt rushed in my opinion - the 'break up' I simply did not see coming despite their casual disagreements.
Act IV felt lazily done. The... 20? fortress assaults we have to go through quickly became tedious and to be honest did not feel a part of any type of storyline. That act had plenty of room to improve.
------------------------------------
All in all - Well done to Monolith for creating a fantastic game and it was great to see how you developed your beloved Nem system. Was great to continue & finish Talion/Celebrimbors story. Thank you for fairly implementing MT's as I believed you would - despite the blind hatred you received for doing so.

Since playing Civ II all the way to Civ VI, I must conclude Civ VI is both intriguing and disappointing. Civ V with the packs is a better game. Civ IV was better in some ways, also, such as more commonly able to use an artist as a border bomb to expand territory aggressively and strategically. It takes a good amount of time to get the hang of Civ VI with exact placement of districts to your benefit. What I would like to see, overall, is the AI be improved. It is very disappointing as a solo player. Going to King level and above makes for too much of a disadvantage to play. How about reconstructing the entire intelligence of the game so there is better personality-based leadership by the different civs? *Instead of* being penalized, create Civ VII with AI that actually works well! Too many times there are troops aimlessly milling about doing nothing on the part of the AI. If they are at war, it "should be" with aggression and calculation at the right time. Why would they not be programmed to mass on a city, with ranged pieces behind them, in organized fashion? The Trade screen should be blown up in AI to allow for random chances to have better trades to *our (the player's) advantage on occassion. Always feel like I am being shafted when not dealing with Allies. How about Allies more often ask to agree on research project together with us a bit more often? In the start of the game, all too often at Prince level, I feel with default settings the Barbarians raid a bit too aggressively on workers. Is there a way to have this be a bit more random, as opposed to calculated? In other words, if I create 2 cities, have two warriors, a slinger, a scout, and an archer, the warrior gets killed, and I don't have time currently to build whatever troops as I am constructing a building, why be penalized by the AI, as they look at my troop count? Seems close to 100% of the time the AI punishes a civ for having a low troop count at the start of the game. How to balance time to create a good troop count with buildings? Not easy as a programmer to do, true. This is why I always favor placing the civic bonus of +5 to troops dealing with Barbarians at the beginning of the game. I'd much rather keep the precious resources of production count and the time spent in raising that troop, than to give a bonus to getting veteran status to my scouts in the beginning of the game.
The game *does flow *very well* in terms of bonuses towards technology advances and earning civics, in that awards are given for half the research by doing/creating specific items (ie, have three archers, build two bombards, build two universities, two banks, etc. etc.). This forces you to play in a way that balances your civ, which makes for something closer to a reality-type of civilization creation game. This definitely is a thinking person's game, and consuming. With patience and building up my civ carefully, in a balanced way as described above, I nearly always am winning the game at Prince level sometime between turn 50 and 100 (depends on too many factors, esp. starting place allowing for city growth or not). Main thing is getting frustrated by the penalites of the game at higher levels. Folks, somehow, Civ III was an amazing game for me, as I was able to tie the game at Deity level AI (and that's when I gave up that game for good). Civ IV was crazy fun for civ development, and as I say, the culture bomb. With Infantry ready, artillery, a railroad to my opponent's border, and tanks in the back ready to charge, maybe with a couple of those cross country skiing troops ready at the hills, it was a lot of fun to drop the culture bomb at the end of that railroad, have the tiles go inwards, and have full troop movement for those newly possessed tiles in my culture, and then +1 tile into the opponent's territory. A great, fast way to take down a city! Nevermind if that city happened to be on the coast, then thow in a battleship as well. OH! That reminds me, Civ VI is LACKING in a cruiser. Fellas, make the call, bring the cruiser back. City-States in summary: learn to use them, and learn your civics advantages. Often times I find have 3+ City-states on my side immediately around my civ makes a big difference if another civ decides to attack me, and the main thing by far, let's say if you are the controller of 4 City-states at least, are the civ bonuses, followed by critical resources if you don't have them, such as coal. You are about to have a sucking game if you are even with another civ on your border and you don't have coal when they get it. The difference at that point in the game is surely a game changer, if you've survived to that point. One note on that idea: if you do not have iron, and you are Trajan of the Romans, you can still build your legions...City-States come in handy for resources. My advice if you are Trajan (my over all favorite for the game up to the mid-game): build 4 cities well, keep enough troops to stave off attacks, then just go for it with Legions and catapults, with archer and horse, and choose a civ on your border to conquer. Maybe the AI mistakenly attacks you, then your warmongering penalites are not as severe. The Legions are *tough! With the defensive bonus from ranged attacks, they can take down one city after the next.
Religions: Top 5 only are what's allowed, else you've lost the race. A good idea for a game. I like the advantages of using apostles to boost the civ's religion's advantages to a total of 4 advantages from baseline of 2, once a religion has been reached for you to choose, if you beat out the other civs to acquire one. TRADE: you should get most of the max level of caravans used throughout the entire game. A good way to lose the game long-run is to ignore trade routes. Maxing out the trade routes, of course, is all to your advantage. Balance routes with gold, etc vs. growth for a slower-growing city. If you have a slower-growing city, consider long-term two caravans from that city to *your cities, in particular, your capital and second fastest or fastest growing city. This will bring the most food resources back to your starting city, and thus you can continually grow that city. International trade is *always a bigger risk: barbarians, and civs at war with you. The trade off is not necessarily better, looking at the numbers. If you are on a large continent, might be best to have most trade routes on that continent...so you can build roads on the continent as the trade rout is built...so eventually you can use those roads to conquer. Again, this is why I like Trajan so much, as each city starting out gets a road automatically built instantly back to the capital. If possible, place a ring of cities around the capital, and, voila! Instant defense of the capital. I have had fun with other civs: Egypt, France, Greece, Babylons for my type of play all do well. Wonders: If the AI is suggesting to you, in your best production city, to build a new type of Wonder, and you choose not to follow up right then and there, but build something else that takes time, like a University or bank, then just be warned that is the AI saying to you another civ very well may be building it and so the competition is on! (Unless you know you are way ahead in science, then your chances are different). Have fun. For now, I need to place this game to the side and focus on...life...with real people.

"Alan Wake."
A review by Richard Valkinsenn.
"It was wild and dark and weird, even by my standards."
Alan Wake is Remedy Entertainment's fourth game ever made, and serves as an excellent and unique survival horror game with equal emphasis on both gameplay and story influenced heavily by the works of Stephen King. As the titular character Alan Wake, you will make your way through a small town seemingly overrun by hostile, shadowy monsters known as the Taken while struggling to piece together the events that brought this situation about. Needless to say, this game's got its fair share of twists and turns.
The voice acting and visuals on display here are top-notch, as the writing on both the campaign's story and its characters is both memorable and intriguing and the game's visual and artistic design still hold up to this day. And it's not everyday that you see both story and gameplay mix together and even compliment each other as seamlessly as they do here. Throughout the game, light is your best weapon and your greatest ally, and darkness is your absolute worst enemy. As mentioned before, you'll have to deal with shadowy enemies called "the Taken." However, defeating them requires methods that border on spoilers, so they won't be mentioned here. Even then, this mechanic ties very heavily into the game's overall narrative and surprisingly never really does get old. At least during the first few playthroughs and some nostalgic replays.
Then we get into some of the more negative aspects of Alan Wake. While it's gameplay, narrative, and characters are all top-notch, once the game's been completed once, that's pretty much it. There's almost nothing to be gained from a secondary playthrough that hasn't already been explored the first time around. No real substantial secrets litter the game's environments, and there's no real surprises to be had the second time around. Worse, there may not be any real sequel anytime soon. Why that's a problem is something players will have to find out as they play the game.
Even then, Alan Wake is, by no means, a bad game. It's an amazing and lengthy journey from start to finish with many twists and turns to be had, along with some excellent writing on it's single-player narrative.
Final Verdict:
I loved it.
Until next time, this is Richard,
Signing off.

A fair few people seem to have bounced off this game which is why I decided to write this review. Yes, the initial learning curve is steep. You're likely to get squished the first couple of times you play until you get a better feel for exactly how far you can push it before you are putting yourself in danger. I can see that would put off some people, but it just means that when everything finally 'clicks' then the satisfaction is incredible.
This is a game that lends itself very well to creating instances where you are in awkward situations, often of your own making (e.g. opening doors you thought were safe but, oops, turns out a wandering guard is right on the other side), but you are given all the tools you need to create awesome solutions. When a recent mission went astray and two out of three of my agents were KO'd, it was up to my last guy to run around kiting enemies into the range of turrets I had hacked onto my side, taking their cash to buy an extra medi-gel, then cloaking, running past the remaining guards, reviving my two downed agents and everyone legging it to the exit. It was easily my favourite moment in games this year because I had created this impossible situation, and then come up with my own equally unlikely solution.
Once you've worked out how to play with the AI, and you figure out how to use the toys the game gives you in the form of different agents (you start with 2 available but can unlock 2 more) and items like EMP emitters, paralyzing drugs and cybernetic implants, if anything it gets too easy - but the joy of manipulating the enemies and the environment doesn't go away, and leads to so many incredible moments.
IMHO, very strong contender for game of the year.

A fair few people seem to have bounced off this game which is why I decided to write this review. Yes, the initial learning curve is steep. You're likely to get squished the first couple of times you play until you get a better feel for exactly how far you can push it before you are putting yourself in danger. I can see that would put off some people, but it just means that when everything finally 'clicks' then the satisfaction is incredible.
This is a game that lends itself very well to creating instances where you are in awkward situations, often of your own making (e.g. opening doors you thought were safe but, oops, turns out a wandering guard is right on the other side), but you are given all the tools you need to create awesome solutions. When a recent mission went astray and two out of three of my agents were KO'd, it was up to my last guy to run around kiting enemies into the range of turrets I had hacked onto my side, taking their cash to buy an extra medi-gel, then cloaking, running past the remaining guards, reviving my two downed agents and everyone legging it to the exit. It was easily my favourite moment in games this year because I had created this impossible situation, and then come up with my own equally unlikely solution.
Once you've worked out how to play with the AI, and you figure out how to use the toys the game gives you in the form of different agents (you start with 2 available but can unlock 2 more) and items like EMP emitters, paralyzing drugs and cybernetic implants, if anything it gets too easy - but the joy of manipulating the enemies and the environment doesn't go away, and leads to so many incredible moments.
IMHO, very strong contender for game of the year.

This game is brutal, I'll put it simply.  If Ironman XCOM is a game you love, then you wwill love this.  It has a very interesting blend of stealth and savagery - you can't just crush everything because, if you do, you'll be dealing with it for the rest of the mission.  And on top of that, the big badddies will destroy you.  Not even the big baddies - one shot, one kill in this game (or at least your agents die that easily).
Pros:  It's gorgeous.  Absolutely beautiful.  Rotating the map, being able to turn on "Incognita" so that you can see the grid and hack the cameras, freeing prisoners, sight cones - combined with the excellent graphic design, this game feels like a legitimate, true spy game.  On top of that, it's in Early Access, and it's this good.  These are the games that deserve Early Access, the games with proven, solid gameplay.  I already feel like I've got my money's worth out of this, because even though I only have 3 hours logged, I know that I have so many more available.  The procedural generation is astounding too - the rooms are almost always believable, and some times you have to figure out whether something is worth attaining, or if it's impossible for you becaus you just need that one piece of gear.  I love it already.  Their Alarm mechanic breates new life into this game, much like Meld did for XCOM.  Further, just because this is Early Access, I should mention that there actually have not been any huge bugs or game crashes or anything like that.  That may change, but so far, it's incredibly stable, both in terms of gameplay and... electronically?  It doesn't crash and you don't have teleporting guys or anything like that.  I didn't even see any small bugs.
Cons:  Not many.  Sure, they are going to add more content, and I could see how addining additional spies would assist with that.  Same for bad-guys and rooms and safes and target sites.  But it sure doesn't feel forced, nor does it feel constrictive because of a lack of content in any way.  Once or twice your spies will spawn in a room with one door and you kind of wonder how they got there (the vents I guess) but that's ot a concern more as a "huh" moment.  It takes up a lot of my time.  It's kind of annoying that everything is credits, and that my spies develop no "experience" unless I spend money (which determines your score) on them.  However, from a design stand point, this makes sense - now development is a decision, not a given; can you do without that upgrade to try and get an even higher score, or is it a small expenses for great rewards scenario?
You can tell I like this game if the cons have REASONS and aren't just there.
In a nutshell: This game is the XCOM of spy games.  Totally worth a buy, especially at 15 bucks.

I want to like this game.
I want to like this game.

You also die if you go fast.
People who love hardcore difficulty games will love this.
People who suck at them, like myself, will never complete a single stage after twenty tries.

A satisfying sequel & finale to the 'Shadow of' franchise.
Was a great experience - to follow on with Talion & Celebrimbor's storyline and what becomes of them. Interacting with new characters such as Shelob, Carnan, the Witch King & Nazgul -  and the Balrog were also fantastic.
Monolith developed their Nemesis System and Ability Tree very well, along with a basic item/gem system to compliment the extra levels in the game. The introduction of the Drake, Olog'Hai and other mosters were a welcome addition to the sequel, adding some more diversity, unique fighting and carnage.
Fortress Seiges - an interesting new concept with customisable options to strengthen yourself as the attacker or defender.
Microtransactions - hidden away in the main menu, not in the slightest bit invasive to the game. The amount of grind was fair, and did not seem at all like it had been tilted to encourage MT interactions. You earn a LOT of 'in-game currency' as well as some premium currency simply by playing through the game.
------------------------------------
All the positives aside, the few things that bothered me:
- The Uruk voices. Some of them just sounded like Dwarves from 'The Hobbit'. The voice did not at all match the menacing looking Uruks...
- A bit much dialogue. They've added on anything from 2-7seconds of Dialogue for each Uruk introduction which I feel negatively impacts the experience. I feel the dialogue pre/post fortress seiges is a bit much. Something simpler and more 'shock and awe' would be suitable..
- Acts I, II, III and IV. The first two acts progressed at a decent pace where the story was quite enjoyable and we interacted/developed an attachment to the recurring characters. Act 3 simply felt rushed in my opinion - the 'break up' I simply did not see coming despite their casual disagreements.
Act IV felt lazily done. The... 20? fortress assaults we have to go through quickly became tedious and to be honest did not feel a part of any type of storyline. That act had plenty of room to improve.
------------------------------------
All in all - Well done to Monolith for creating a fantastic game and it was great to see how you developed your beloved Nem system. Was great to continue & finish Talion/Celebrimbors story. Thank you for fairly implementing MT's as I believed you would - despite the blind hatred you received for doing so.

Invisible Inc is a very polished game, more so in fact than many of the games that get released on steam without early access. It has a beautiful art style with audio lending a fitting ambience to your teams role as corporate infiltrators. Furthermore there are little to no noticable bugs in the current content, a notable achievement for an early access game. That does however bring us onto the point of content, of which there is remarkably little at the moment.
Currently the game relies heavily on it's procedural generation to extend the gameplay experience with few options in terms of mission or agent variety available to the player. Furthermore one could argue the punishing difficulty the game demonstrates is based on the random element of the levels rather than any true difficulty with some missions being extra punishing due to at most 1 room in which 3 or more guards may have by chance built their route. I personally encountered a situation where an obbjective room was filled with 3 seemingly stationary guards which made it effectively impossible to access any of the items in the room forcing the mission to be scrubbed.
Furthermore noticable usability features such as a undo button remain absent from the game with  1 misclick representing the possible loss of an hours worth of missions. A lack of a between missions inventory screen or shop makes inventory management awkward and makes early missions excessively punishing as the game may make it impossible to effectively access a shop for several levels.
I'd say invisible inc represents one of the highest quality early access games available, it tempers the developers ambitions in the name of polish and stability while leaving room for those ambitions to be added later down the line when they can be added in such a way that maintains the high quality gaming experience. This is the level of product early access games on steam should be held too rather than the overly ambitious bug ridden messes that populate most of the category.

I bought this game when it first went Alpha due to my love of Mark of the Ninja and my liking of XCOM: EU. This game is supposed to be kind of a fusion of both, a stealth-based tactical RPG. I was dissatisfied with it for reasons I’ll list below but because its was extremely early Alpha I decided to just wait until it became more complete. Unfortunately it really hasn’t changed much.
Right now the game is a mess, people claim it is hard, but it’s all artificial difficulty to an extremely punishing degree. Unlike beloved stealth games like MGS, Thief, Splinter Cell, Dishonored, and Klei's own Mark of the Ninja this game actively punishes you for taking your time and being cautious due to an alarm system that’s constantly ticking up from the start of a level even if you’ve been completely undetected.  The procedurally generated levels also can throw you into unwinnable situations.  Even fans of XCOM: EU will be probably be dissatisfied because as I said this game punishes you for being cautious, which is the cornerstone of good XCOM playing. Your agents aren't nearly as expendable as XCOM troopers too which makes it even more ridiculously punishing. Stunning enemies is rather pointless because they just get up after two turns and shooting them just brings down the whole building on you. The only real way to beat levels right now is totally speed-run them (Which is even harder due to the procedural generated levels), which is not what a stealth game is inherently about; stealth games are about being taking your time and exploring your surroundings by doing things like studying camera locations and guard patrol patterns. Invisible Inc. just throws that all away and it really suffers for it.
This game as it is right now is just for masochists. But it still is very early in development and I really hope Klei turns it around because there is a lot of potential here to make a fun and fair game. The groundwork is all there.
I’ll keep this review updated when big enough updates come around.

"Over €15,- for an early acces, turn-based spy game? Nah... I don't think so."
My thoughts exactly. That thought turned out to be very, very incorrect.
After reading some reviews and figuring out I could miss the money, I decided to make the purchase. Boy, I am happy I did.
The game starts with a very simple tutorial which shows you the basis structure of the game. After completing this, you will see a world map with some locations on it. All of these locations are randomly generated maps filled with cameras, guards and other stuff which will work in your advantage or disadvantage, but most of all: loot. In each of these maps, the objective is to find the elevator, so you can escape and choose another area on the world, upgrading your characters and items and earning experience along the way.
My first couple attempts resulted in quick and merciless death, but after unlocking my first two rewards, I found myself getting further and further. And each time I played, I felt more rewarded by my actions.
I am not a huge fan of turn-based games, nor stealh games, but this game has already surprised me in a very, very pleasant way. I have never thought that turn-based could feel so stressfull.
Seeing that this is only the Alpha, I highly suggest you pick this game up. If you like to give yourself a fair but tough challenge, this is a must-buy.
(I highly suggest turning on fast mode, else you will be watching walking animations 30% of the time:))

I got this game as a gift from a friend.
Kerbal Space Program is possbily one of the funnest and funniest games that I have ever played.
The objective is simple, but reaching the goal is much more challenging. You are tasked to get to the Mun. While this may sound simple there is a lot of science behind getting things into orbit, space, etc. Anything and I mean ANYTHING can go wrong. The game does a fantastic job at helping the player understand each and every single little detail of rocketry, etc.
While it may be a snore feast to some "Yay going to the moon and space. Woo! *Goes back and plays a much more interesting game* " it's actually addicting and pretty fun. Yes there is no pressure or anything. The only thing you got to be worried about is your budget, reputation and the safety and well-being of your crew and workers.
There is an active modding community bringing in some crazy designs, etc. And a active community as a whole. If you need any help talk to the community they can get you to the Mun and back again.
There are some scenarios and a full-on training section which is nice. Helps the player even more, and a encyclopedia full of a lot of detail and stuff to assist the player even further.
Yes there is a lot of hand-holding here. But you are going to need it if you want to get to the Mun and back!
I recommend this game for the gamers who want to sit back and relax, However. This isn't the game for players who want to do more than just running a Space center and watching things going into space and things blowing up.

You realize that you are now the Miami God of Blood and Gore.

An extremely fun rogue like with twin stick mechanics.
Probably the hardest one of its type I have played so you need to be prepared to die a lot, mostly down to the fact of how quickly you can loose health in this game going from max hp to dead within in a couple seconds is not at all uncommon. But this difficulty makes the reward of getting far feel that much better.
The game plays like a twin stick shooter, has a huge variety in weapons and multiple mutations (perks) to choose from each time you level up. On top of that the game has many characters to play as, each one feeling unique, and creating its very own playstyle, this adds a lot of variety to the game which is vital in a game of this genre.
It has recieved a daily challenge mode too recently which allows you to compete against friends or the world on the same seed every day.
The soundtrack also deserves a mention being of the best in the genre, also a neccessity in a game which demands replayability.

Frame rate - it's constant, and has no performance issues, but it is locked to 30fps, I feel 60fps would of helped this already fast paced game feel even faster, but I think it deserves a mention. It is one of the only games where 30fps doesn't bother me though, so it does feel smooth.

Same guys as did Don't Starve (Klei apparently).
It's an isometric turn-based squad stealth game (and a very good one at that).
It doesn't feel like Early Access, at least the bad kind, or rather, it feels like a full AAA game that is still getting updates, so far (e.g. think Payday 2, FTL in terms of quality since FTL is indie).
It's a roguelike if you use the very open definition, in other words, it has permadeath(agents are irreplaceable and you can "lose" the game) and proc gen.
re: proc gen
The levels so far seem to be intelligently designed, like a puzzle. Haven't come across anything unbeatable yet (not counting the guy who posted the screenie of a level not possible to reach the exit, heh), but certainly difficult (Heavy blocking a vault with 2 guards inside it first mission, detention centre with 2 patrol guards and a Captain inside, double Heavy patrols, etc). I'm guessing that there's some general rules followed for placement of stuff, besides the obvious (no guards in starting room), and it seems pretty well done so far, the missions don't feel like randomness jumbled together, so good job. They feel like story missions even though they are in fact proceduraly generated. It's a bit like the generation of Binding of Isaac levels, except it feels less random than that even- I imagine it's  basically the same though, placing certain things with a small bit of patterning.
re: graphics, interface, music
I can never get tired at starting a fresh level and hearing the music start up, and then looking at Internationale's animation and grumpy face, good touch :)
Also the random blocks moving up and down and around in Incognita and the main game screen while playing a level. I never really paid attention to them before, but it's way better than a blank background :)
While I'm here, the interface is really great too. I'm playing fullscreen and I just realised how the interface never gets in the way of anything, it's never intrusive, and even though the game is in isometric view, I never have problems seeing anything or seeing where stuff is (I do switch to incognita for a broader view sometimes), I feel like I've always got a good view of the immediate area and the whole level, and it always feels like the interface elements are invisible until I need them, since they take up so little space. I also rarely feel the need to rotate the levels at all, I've played a ton of missions and completely forgot that I could rotate with Q and E that it turned out to be a huge surprise to me.
re: gameplay and balance
Both are great, keeping more entertained than the other half dozen games I purchased recently. It's a "hard" game, if you're a veteran at tactical turn-based you'll probably find it easy though (at least I think it's easy once you've got the game mechanics pat down).
Reccomend at base sale price Y/N: Y, if you're interested in this kind of game it's a fair deal in terms of gameplay(how much fun) & replayability(how many hours before you get bored) - or wait for an eventual sale, but either way.
I have a low threshold for getting bored, I get bored by games really easy, so two thumbs up. Hope you enjoy it.

It's a bit light on content right now, but the core gameplay is a lot of fun. Basically a turn-based stealth roguelike, with the stealth mechanics done right.
What really makes this work is that the game provides all the necessary tools to make the stealth gameplay work - you have variety of scouting options including hacking cameras and predicting visible enemy routes, but they all have an opportunity cost. Due to the options to gather information, there's very little randomness outside of the actual mission generation (though there are plenty of opportunities to take calculated risks). You never feel like you were cheated by something you couldn't have accounted for or that winning is more luck based than skill based.
The balance is also very good considering it's still in Early Access. It does have a bit of a learning curve to figure out what works, but once you get rolling the missions are challenging but reasonable. The main difficulty is in how greedy you want to be - there's a soft time limit in each mission, and plenty of optional loot; usually you can't afford to try to get everything, so you have to make some tough decisions. But the game keeps scaling in difficulty, so you can't leave behind too much loot...
Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys stealth games.

I am thoroughly convinced this was supposed to be a TV mini-series and not a game. Because as a game, it has mechanics that grow tiresome after the second or so chapter. The mechanics never evolve, grow, or change enough for the player's attention to be maintained. There are SOME moments of brilliance, but they are few and far in-between. The game's plot is the high point. The story is intriguing and it's all formatted as a telivision series (with 'previously on Alan Wake' recaptions at the beginning of chapters, and end of chapter vocal songs). The game's plot was strong enough that a novel was made of it, and I await the TV mini-series I hope gets made. The plot is the ONLY thing that will keep you going in the game, and there's a sense of satisfaction and anticipation gained when a chapter is completed. I can't recommend the game for its gameplay, but it's story is formulated interestingly enough for me to recommend it, if you can get past its mediocre gameplay, that is. It's a shame, because I really do love a good story and I feel there's something here, but you gotta keep me entertained between those plot elements with a solid gameplay formula.

Life is Strange is a narrative driven game that I would consider to be a medium length game. It isn't short like some first person shooter campaigns that last five hours and it certainly isn't as long as even shorter RPGs. It took me about 15hrs or so to complete the game. I wasn't trying to speed through it and neither was I trying to be a completionist. The story branches out into 5 different episodes which, to my knowledge, cost about $5 each with the exception of the first episode, which is free. I got this game on sale for about $5 for all the episodes, it was an amazing deal.
Let's talk about the negatives first. I should start by discussing the original review that I made which was a negative review. When I first bought the game I had issues being able to even navigate the menu screen. My steam controller wouldn't work and then even my mouse and keyboard wouldn't work correctly. The issue ended up being that I had my HOTAS (flight simulator joystick for those who don't know what that is) plugged in and the game recognized that as my input over mouse and keyboard or controller. I've never had an issue with this in other games so I find it really odd that I did here. While we are on the topic of the controls I should mention that while keyboard and mouse gameplay was generally fine, controller gameplay was not. Perhaps this was just an example of a steam controller having issues but I can't imagine it being any more fun with other controllers. Considering this is also released on console I expected better.
Graphically speaking the game has a much more artsy feel to it. It was a more detailed cartoon. Generally the graphics aren't bad and are rather beautiful in certain cutscenes. They certainly aren't great though, I personally found them dated even for a more simple art style. But it certainly wasn't a massive issue.
Next is plot holes.
I'm not going to spoil anything but I will mention that there are several times where characters are making decisions based on a belief in something with very little evidence. It honestly bugged me quite a bit near the end where the decision is essentially be selfish (if you believe the consquences with very little evidence) or make a really heart crushing decision. There aren't too many plot holes though and the little evidence is mostly my personal opinion, I'm sure there will be others that disagree.
Alright now the positive.
Character development. In an age when a lot of the AAA games aren't focusing at all on character development this game significantly stands out as a game that gets character development right. The fact that they did this and also did so while allowing such a large amount of choices is really impressive. You will get attached to these characters, especially Chloe. The voice acting is pretty spot on but occasionally the facial animations can be a little sub par. There was a time where David was talking but his mouth wasn't moving (probably just a glitch)
Gameplay. While I still don't like the controlls there is something that the game brings to the table I haven't seen before, rewinding time to change different decisions. It's the main story point of the story and it mostly revolves around this ability.
Story. It's sort of a detective story. But it also has a lot of high school drama that gets very real and rather dark real quick. It's not a cringy high school drama, it touches on a lot of really imortant subjects really well. I don't want to spoil the story but it touches on subjects like; bullying, suicide, security vs privacy, PTSD, loss of a parent, mental illness, sexual abuse (though indirectly), the power the rich can have over the poor, and other issues I can't discuss without spoils.
Overall I will recommend the game. Even if it doesn't become your favorite the price is fair enough that you get your money's worth. If you like purly narrative driven games then this is a must.

I got this game as a gift from a friend.
Kerbal Space Program is possbily one of the funnest and funniest games that I have ever played.
The objective is simple, but reaching the goal is much more challenging. You are tasked to get to the Mun. While this may sound simple there is a lot of science behind getting things into orbit, space, etc. Anything and I mean ANYTHING can go wrong. The game does a fantastic job at helping the player understand each and every single little detail of rocketry, etc.
While it may be a snore feast to some "Yay going to the moon and space. Woo! *Goes back and plays a much more interesting game* " it's actually addicting and pretty fun. Yes there is no pressure or anything. The only thing you got to be worried about is your budget, reputation and the safety and well-being of your crew and workers.
There is an active modding community bringing in some crazy designs, etc. And a active community as a whole. If you need any help talk to the community they can get you to the Mun and back again.
There are some scenarios and a full-on training section which is nice. Helps the player even more, and a encyclopedia full of a lot of detail and stuff to assist the player even further.
Yes there is a lot of hand-holding here. But you are going to need it if you want to get to the Mun and back!
I recommend this game for the gamers who want to sit back and relax, However. This isn't the game for players who want to do more than just running a Space center and watching things going into space and things blowing up.

It's a bit light on content right now, but the core gameplay is a lot of fun. Basically a turn-based stealth roguelike, with the stealth mechanics done right.
What really makes this work is that the game provides all the necessary tools to make the stealth gameplay work - you have variety of scouting options including hacking cameras and predicting visible enemy routes, but they all have an opportunity cost. Due to the options to gather information, there's very little randomness outside of the actual mission generation (though there are plenty of opportunities to take calculated risks). You never feel like you were cheated by something you couldn't have accounted for or that winning is more luck based than skill based.
The balance is also very good considering it's still in Early Access. It does have a bit of a learning curve to figure out what works, but once you get rolling the missions are challenging but reasonable. The main difficulty is in how greedy you want to be - there's a soft time limit in each mission, and plenty of optional loot; usually you can't afford to try to get everything, so you have to make some tough decisions. But the game keeps scaling in difficulty, so you can't leave behind too much loot...
Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys stealth games.

The nemesis system is back and has a bit more to do but not really too much of note about that. The story is pretty cool and despite the few incredibly forgetable characters it's servicable and will for the most part keep your interest. Effects for blending your ranger and your wraith are in my opinion way cooler than the last game but that's really just up to preference.
Now the bad things of which are pretty annoying and for the most part are just carried over from the last game which is super annoying. The fighting system is what it is which is a consolized system designed for the controller. If you use a controller with it you shouldn't have many problems but if you want to stick with keyboard and mouse you're gonna have a rough time from what I saw with my short attempt to use of that control scheme. Back again is the problem where you mean to hit one guy and it hits another which is incredibly annoying when you accidentally kill the Uruk you've been tracking and trying to bring to your side for 20 minutes. Parkour system is really fun when it works but often it doesn't and can screw up an extra mission goal when you accidentally jump down into a crowd of like 50 uruk forcing you out of stealth. Oh, and they made the same mistake as the last game by making it take about 5 hours (if you stretch it out like I did to enjoy it) to get to the part where you get to build your army. You know; that thing that is the biggest difference from the last game? This is super annoying and I wouldn't be suprised if people who didn't know to keep through it just quit because they thought they'd never get to build an army like advertised.
My biggest gripe to be perfectly honest is that the animations are ripped STRAIGHT OUT OF THE LAST GAME so you'll be looking at the same animation not only hundreds of times in this game but also be remembering it from the LAST GAME. WHAT WERE THEY DOING IF NOT THIS WITH THE 3 YEARS THEY'VE HAD??? I'm not talking one or too similar animations here but I can't think of one action moved from the last game to this that doesn't look identical to the last. This includes the stealth takedowns, the branding of orcs, and even the sword combat is absolutely no different than the last game. Come on guys. I can't confirm this but there's a rumor going around that the best ending of the game is only acheived through a 10-20 hour grind however aside from the fact that it can be made easier with the microtransactions this system of fully finishing the game has been in a lot of games even from 20 years ago so I'm not totally sure that this is really an issue.
Anyways I am still gonna thumb up the game because despite the flaws mentioned it's much better than Shadow of Mordor but don't expect a monumental change here, just a revamping of most of the stuff that made the first game cool. Hope this helps and if any new problems or positives come up I'll put them in this same review as an edit.

If you liked Walking Dead: Season 1, you're gonna like Season 2. It's just as good maybe even a little better because you play as Clementine. If you haven't played Season 1 here is more detailed review:
9/10 Points
So, the gameplay isn't something to get excited about: it's pretty much just point and click, also there is a fair amount of illusion of choice: they say your choices matter but that isn't really the case. But everything else is ♥♥♥♥ing great: the characters are strong and well written, the story is good and the voice acting is ♥♥♥♥ing great. So to conclude this into one sentence: If you like a story driven game - with little gameplay - but strong characters and a strong story than this is for you. If you like games where gameplay matters and story and characters aren't that important to you than will most likely not enjoy this game.

is violent, gritty, and unbelievably insane. Thankfully its pixelated art style obscures most of the endless brutality that is the core of the game. I didn’t hesitate to drill a roomful of people to death (that looks bad in writing) because I couldn’t see the brain noodles I was making. Between killing faceless enemies a story is alluded to, but upon completion it turns out to be almost nonexistent. Before learning that, though, I willfully endured countless bullets to the gut, pipes to the head, and dogs to my throat.
My character died more times than any other throughout the game. Early on, a lot of deaths came from fumbling the controls. The problem is that it’s hard to stay front-facing when your character can run in 8 directions, using WASD, while your top-half moves independently. It’s kind of like being in a tank where turret and tracks are separate. I eventually overcame my inability to actually face my enemies and became a reliable killer.
With the controls learned, I could focus on creating ridiculous combos. Soon my hard-won x5 turned into x10 and then I found the Zach mask—extended combo window—and something changed. It was hard to believe my transformation, earning x27 at best. I was a monster.
The mechanical challenge is Hotline Miami's bread and butter. There is a noticeable lack of story. The dialogue is disjointed and forgettable, and constantly alluding to something happening just beyond our vision. When I finished the game and epilogue, nothing was revealed except
Wow, really? Hotline Miami has more fill-in-the-blanks than storyline.
I guess I wouldn’t complain about an action movie lacking wit. Still, I can’t shake the feeling that the developers missed an opportunity to make this something memorable. Maybe the pending sequel will flesh out this skeleton. In any case, if there’s a brick throwing, double barreled, ‘what-have-I-become?’ sense of satisfaction pumping me up, I’ll be back for more.

So, I just finished the tutorial. Leaving with the basic tools of the trade, I selected a "Guarded" mission - from what I could tell, this was the one that was least likely to hand my♥♥♥♥♥♥to me through use of an industrial bacon slicer.
Spawning in with instructions to find the elevator and maybe steal a few priceless artifacts if I felt like it, I quickly explored the area with my two agents. They already felt very different - Mr Bond 2.0 galloped about the level like a majestic stallion in padded socks, crossing rooms in a graceful yet silent leap, whilst our resident lady-spy hacked computers from a mile away to fill the battery to doxx n00bs, celebrities, and any security cameras and safes that were unfortunate enough to find themselves in our randomly-generated path.
Flash forward - lady-spy was in the vault hiding behind a safe having disabled both layers of laser trap, waiting for the battery to fill just once more level to unlock the safe. James was racing for the elevator, dodging irritated patrols that had been knocked unconcious one too many times through a combination of electric shocks and homoerotic terror (disregard for lady-spy). It was halfway through the final room when I froze - fiddlesticks, I thought, lady-spy has the keycard for the elevator! In my haste, I had neglected to open it on the way, out of a combination of ignorance and moderate stupidity.
With the alarm level raising continuously, I had to double back. I carefully guided James to the safe, hands shaking, nose pressed up against the monitor, and brought lady-spy to rest behind a desk in the elevator room. Battery having charged, I grabbed the final priceless treasure and hustled my trench-coated♥♥♥♥♥♥back to the main room. Suddenly, the alarm level escalated once more, and a new guard was brought up into the elevator.♥♥♥♥♥♥
The new plan was simple. Lady-spy would run to the now-open elevator, knock out the guard inside, and James would then join her - his extra movement abilities would allow him to bypass any possible guards that noticed the commotion or turned around to view the kerfuffle taking place. Palms sweating, I navigated lady-spy to the elevator, in position to knock out the guard. However, much to my dismay, there was a second guard in the elevator whom I could not see, but immediately saw me and moved to shoot. I had one square of movement for cover, and ducked behind the elevator door for cover, readying for combat if a guard moved to my square. James was placed next to her, also ready to attack. They could take out both guards, and we would be free!
Alas, t'was not to be. Unfortunately, a third and fourth guard had heard our bickering. Elevator guards one and two were knocked out, leaving us with no defence when three and four riddled us with more holes than a swiss cheese at a double penetration party. I swore loudly at the computer.
Buy it. It rocks.

From the short time I have played I have to say this game is better in every way then the first.
It takes a little getting used to, as it seems to be more responsive then the first game so they take some adjusting of control setting and play style. Graphics are crisper and have greater color depth to them at least with the GPU (Radeon 390X 8gb) I am running on mostly Ultra setting and I sit at a good solid 70+ fps.

The combat is fast and smooth, on Nemesis difficulty it has a nice challenge to it, because the Uruk Captains are not as predictable as in the first game, they put up a real good fight because they adapt to your attack to a degree.

The Equipment and Leveling system is a nice change but can also take a little getting used to at least right at first.

I can honestly say that as of the few hours, the story feels very epic and very in line with the first game and fits well with in the Lord of the Rings World setting. I am impressed with the game Monolith Productions has put out they should be proud of their product, I look forward to many hours of play.
As of my few hours playing, I can say the lootcrates are NOT needed, unless you don't like a good challenging game, or just totally suck and if that is the case don't play on Nemesis difficulty.

I may add more once I get farther into the game but as of right now I highly recommend then game to anyone that liked the first or loves The Lord of the Rings Story Saga.

This is a game for creative and strategic minds, you will have the chance run your own space program where you will build spacecrafts as simple or as complex as you want or need.
In carreer mode you will be in charge of all the areas of your space program, this means you will have to take care of recruiting and training new engineers, scientists, and pilots, accepting new contracts, building the spaceships, choosing the right crew members, pilot the spaceships, run experiments to gain new knowledge and use it to research new parts, you'll also have to manage your space program's financial resources.
If you expect to fight aliens and protect the world from evil, this game is not for you. KSP is a game in which your only enemy OR your best friend is the laws of physics.
With the wide range of mods available from the huge KSP comunity, you can make your gaming experience as complicated or as simple as you desire. You'll find excellent mods that improve the visuals, add environment sound effects, add new parts to the game, add and AI pilot to your spaceship or airplane, provide flight assistance, and much more.
If you are only interested in building and piloting your creations with no limits, you can also do that in the samdbox mode.
One thing worth mentioning is that you must be prepared to learn physics principles in order to have any chance of surviving, this is not a game that depends on your speed with te keyboard and mouse, but it depends a lot on your knowledge, planning, strategy, and execution. One amazing resource is the wikipedia-style documentation available in the game, and of course, youtube videos.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike by the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service against the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii Territory, on the morning of December 7, 1941. The attack, also known as the Battle of Pearl Harbor, led to the United States' entry into World War II. The Japanese military leadership referred to the attack as the Hawaii Operation and Operation AI, and as Operation Z during its planning.
Japan intended the attack as a preventive action to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from interfering with military actions they planned in Southeast Asia against overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States. Over the next seven hours there were coordinated Japanese attacks on the U.S.-held Philippines, Guam and Wake Island and on the British Empire in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
The attack commenced at 7:48 a.m. Hawaiian Time (18:18 UTC). The base was attacked by 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft (including fighters, level and dive bombers, and torpedo bombers) in two waves, launched from six aircraft carriers. All eight U.S. Navy battleships were damaged, with four sunk. All but the USS Arizona were later raised, and six were returned to service and went on to fight in the war. The Japanese also sank or damaged three cruisers, three destroyers, an anti-aircraft training ship, and one minelayer. 188 U.S. aircraft were destroyed; 2,403 Americans were killed and 1,178 others were wounded.Important base installations such as the power station, dry dock, shipyard, maintenance, and fuel and torpedo storage facilities, as well as the submarine piers and headquarters building (also home of the intelligence section), were not attacked. Japanese losses were light: 29 aircraft and five midget submarines lost, and 64 servicemen killed. One Japanese sailor, Kazuo Sakamaki, was captured.
The surprise attack came as a profound shock to the American people and led directly to the American entry into World War II in both the Pacific and European theaters. The following day, December 8, the United States declared war on Japan,[18][19] and several days later, on December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. The U.S. responded with a declaration of war against Germany and Italy. Domestic support for non-interventionism, which had been fading since the Fall of France in 1940, disappeared.
There were numerous historical precedents for unannounced military action by Japan, but the lack of any formal warning, particularly while negotiations were still apparently ongoing, led President Franklin D. Roosevelt to proclaim December 7, 1941, "a date which will live in infamy". Because the attack happened without a declaration of war and without explicit warning, the attack on Pearl Harbor was later judged in the Tokyo Trials to be a war crime.

I loved Mark of the Ninja. Klei proved without question they can do stealth gameplay well, and I grabbed this game on the strength of that alone.
Be aware that the game is rough around the edges, and you're going to die a lot before you even understand how to play properly.
It's difficult to tell where rooms actually begin and end in some cases, and where line-of-sight is. Some elements of the background are easily mistaken for rooms you don't currently have LOS to. Also, when planning where you're going to move to next, it's hard to tell where you can be spotted from that position.
It's not clear whether an edge is a wall or a corridor you haven't been down yet. Considering that every move counts, you can't waste time exploring a wall that you thought was actually a pathway.
That said, you can rotate the view left and right with Q and E, which alleviates this problem somewhat.
It's not obvious when enemies are going to regain consciousness. It's two turns from when you knock them out. I'm not even sure whether than means they revive on turn two or on turn three.
It's not obvious at ALL where reinforcement enemies are going to spawn from, and it badly needs to be. More than once I've sneaked into the enemy spawn room accidentally, a guard has spawned the next turn and killed me.
Basically, it's difficult to get to grips with how the game actually works, so it's going to take some perserverence.
On the plus side, the game is very hard :) . It has the feel of a roguelike, where your own skill and experience makes the difference between success and failure. Also, it has permadeath.
Previously I'd complained that you unlock more abilities and whatnot purely from grinding. I was wrong. The unlocks are really just alternate stuff you can use, rather than things that are objectively better.
Very difficult, very tense, and there's a lot of potential here that needs a bit more polish. On the balance, though, it's probably worth getting.

The polish level for the final release is outstanding. Don't pass this one up.

I can highly recommend this to anyone as Hotline Miami is great game. The combat takes place from a top down perspective and you and your enemies go down in single shots. While I personally didn't care for the story, it is clear that this game is still one that can effectively weave a narrative.
While the game isn't that long, one full play through was only around 3-4 hours plus bonus levels. The price also reflects that, only being $10. This in my view was a good example of quality over quantity and an overall good value for money.
Finally, the developers are pretty cool, care a lot about their product and absolutely deserve to be supported.

This is a game for creative and strategic minds, you will have the chance run your own space program where you will build spacecrafts as simple or as complex as you want or need.
In carreer mode you will be in charge of all the areas of your space program, this means you will have to take care of recruiting and training new engineers, scientists, and pilots, accepting new contracts, building the spaceships, choosing the right crew members, pilot the spaceships, run experiments to gain new knowledge and use it to research new parts, you'll also have to manage your space program's financial resources.
If you expect to fight aliens and protect the world from evil, this game is not for you. KSP is a game in which your only enemy OR your best friend is the laws of physics.
With the wide range of mods available from the huge KSP comunity, you can make your gaming experience as complicated or as simple as you desire. You'll find excellent mods that improve the visuals, add environment sound effects, add new parts to the game, add and AI pilot to your spaceship or airplane, provide flight assistance, and much more.
If you are only interested in building and piloting your creations with no limits, you can also do that in the samdbox mode.
One thing worth mentioning is that you must be prepared to learn physics principles in order to have any chance of surviving, this is not a game that depends on your speed with te keyboard and mouse, but it depends a lot on your knowledge, planning, strategy, and execution. One amazing resource is the wikipedia-style documentation available in the game, and of course, youtube videos.

TLDR: This game was very obviously made with love. If you like science, building, space, or something different give this game a shot. Also check out the very well made Scott Manley tutorials to get started.
This is the first time I write a review for any game. I usually wouldn't unless something really compells me to do it. Besides the amazing physics and work the creators have put into this game throughout the years something happened today that made me love them even more. Very few times within the game did I notice the word "autosaving" pop up, and so I would remind myself to save whenever I wasn't in the middle of a mission (in space), and to be honest I don't even know if you can save while in space. Basically what happened: I was completing my very first orbit around Kerbin, I had managed to collect a bunch of science points while in space too and all in all I was going to fulfill a good amount of contracts (which give you money and science points) when I decided to start trying some function keys out. I pressed a couple of them to see what happened and after accidently taking some screenshots among other things the game crashed on me as I was descening back to the planet. Naturally I was heart broken that my very first orbit attempt was going to be successful and yet I would lose all the data. Although sad I opened up the game again to try and replicate the last hour (someone that knew what they were doing could easily do it in 10min or less). And lo and behold, all the contracts I had fulfilled while on my mission were fulfilled and all my science points and money were still there. At no point did I ever see the word autosaving but man my heart melted when I saw that my last hour hadn't gone to waste. This game was obviously made with love and very very intelligently.

I've had this game for a while know, ever since it was called Incognita, and I gotta tell you, this game has evolved massively since then.  It used to be a kind of turnbased rpg where the goal was more or less "complete goal X then leave the building" but now it is more of a roguelike, but it has an amazing twist on the genre.  Since you play as a spy, and most teams don't even start with weapons, you have to us stealth, hacking, and lock-picking to make it through the hostile buildings you find yourself in.  This might sound boring, sneak in and out while gathering anything you can, but it leads to some absurdly tense moments. Yes, microtransactions suck.
TLDR is that you should buy it at 40-30 dollars or even wait for the game of the year edition in like a year or so
Now that I've gotten that out of the way let's talk about the actual experience aside from the WB bullsh*t. First thing to mention is that the game is basically just the last game cranked up to 11 in terms of graphics (of the envirorments and orcs at least cuz your character's facial animations are plain garbage at all times) and amount of things to do as the map is LITTERED with dynamic mini quests and collectables. The nemesis system is back and has a bit more to do but not really too much of note about that. The story is pretty cool and despite the few incredibly forgetable characters it's servicable and will for the most part keep your interest. Effects for blending your ranger and your wraith are in my opinion way cooler than the last game but that's really just up to preference.
Now the bad things of which are pretty annoying and for the most part are just carried over from the last game which is super annoying. The fighting system is what it is which is a consolized system designed for the controller. If you use a controller with it you shouldn't have many problems but if you want to stick with keyboard and mouse you're gonna have a rough time from what I saw with my short attempt to use of that control scheme. Back again is the problem where you mean to hit one guy and it hits another which is incredibly annoying when you accidentally kill the Uruk you've been tracking and trying to bring to your side for 20 minutes. Parkour system is really fun when it works but often it doesn't and can screw up an extra mission goal when you accidentally jump down into a crowd of like 50 uruk forcing you out of stealth. Oh, and they made the same mistake as the last game by making it take about 5 hours (if you stretch it out like I did to enjoy it) to get to the part where you get to build your army. You know; that thing that is the biggest difference from the last game? This is super annoying and I wouldn't be suprised if people who didn't know to keep through it just quit because they thought they'd never get to build an army like advertised.
My biggest gripe to be perfectly honest is that the animations are ripped STRAIGHT OUT OF THE LAST GAME so you'll be looking at the same animation not only hundreds of times in this game but also be remembering it from the LAST GAME. WHAT WERE THEY DOING IF NOT THIS WITH THE 3 YEARS THEY'VE HAD??? I'm not talking one or too similar animations here but I can't think of one action moved from the last game to this that doesn't look identical to the last. This includes the stealth takedowns, the branding of orcs, and even the sword combat is absolutely no different than the last game. Come on guys. I can't confirm this but there's a rumor going around that the best ending of the game is only acheived through a 10-20 hour grind however aside from the fact that it can be made easier with the microtransactions this system of fully finishing the game has been in a lot of games even from 20 years ago so I'm not totally sure that this is really an issue.
Anyways I am still gonna thumb up the game because despite the flaws mentioned it's much better than Shadow of Mordor but don't expect a monumental change here, just a revamping of most of the stuff that made the first game cool. Hope this helps and if any new problems or positives come up I'll put them in this same review as an edit.

I put over 100 hours into SoM GOTY edition and platinum'd that biotch. So far I'm loving this game. It's more of the same, but on a grander scale and with many new features. Is there some clutter and an overall sense of video gamey-ness? Sure.
Are there meaningless loot boxes if you look in the game menu? Yes. Completely ignore them, like in all the other games that have this now. I'm pretty sure they're not going away. Some multimillionaire's kid will buy them; it does not concern me or the vast majority of players. There is so much in game loot it's not an issue. Read the Kotaku article on this.
Are there lots of items to collect? Yes! I like this! It's fun collecting Ithildin and memories and whatnot. Is the story fantastic? So far, not really, tbh. But I don't need every game I play to be a story-rich Witcher or a hands-off murky lore like in Dark Souls. It's just a good video game.
I'm playing this on i5-4690 with GTX 1080ti and 1440p monitor. Runs like a charm, rarely drops below 144 fps. Really happily surprised to see this level of polish on launch day. Graphical improvements are incredible from the first game. You can see the crazy amount detail in the characters' faces. You feel immersed in the cities as they fall under siege. I was about to get killed by an orc captain when a city guard stepped in at the very last second and gutted him, saving my life. It was exciting.
This is just a preliminary review but I think the game is great so far.
