Just to precede this, I played through Season 2 right after playing through Season 1. This game IS a very high quality game, but I would argue it palls in a lot of areas in comparison to Season 1.
This season contains a lot of the pessimistic wheel-spinning found in later seasons of the AMC show. I found myself attached to very few characters (the group dynamics seem elastically bound to pettiness- particularly in the form of faux heroes and self righteous stand-offs), especially in comparison to Season 1. Many realistic options to do the honorable AND SMART thing are left out to create unecessary (and again- petty) tension. Many people would probably argue it's realistic, but if I wanted something constrained only to the actions of your average joe-blow (yes- even in extraordinarly apocalyptic scenarios), I could play The SIMs.
Lastly, and this may be due to my playing one directly after the other,
In summary,
Pros
-Very high quality game
-appreciable change of setting
-Clementine is hardcore
Cons
-Very little character relatablilty (I barely cared about the death of a single person in Season 2)
-Group "teamwork" dynamics largely revolve around pettiness and non-cooperation
-Dialogue choices can be decieving. You'll intend one thing and it'll veer off to "you" saying something destructive.
-Quite a few easy choices are unrealistically left out that would be both honorable and intelligent.
-I found it a little weird playing as Clementine, given I was just recently Lee taking care of her, but that's not a huge point. It just made me feel a little seperated from Clementine's character as I had come to love it.
This game is still very good, but with that said, I am of the opinion that it is 1/3 to 1/2 the game that Season 1 was.

Workers now have charges instead of keeping them forever, Wonders have to be placed on, near, or next to a special district due the geography of where the wonders is actually in the real world. Bottom line: if you like building things, flying things, space, exploration, or hard-won achievment: play KSP. For SCIENCE!

A worthwile and almost necessary game for any geek interested in astronomy and space aeronautic engineering. The physics, though not perfect, are nearly spot on. Playing the game really makes you feel for the pioneers in the field like Wernher Von Braun and Russian rocket scientists Sergei Korolev. The feeling of building your own space program from the ground up with little funding and huge goals gives you a chance to appreciate the true difficulty of Space Travel by programs like NASA with harsh limitations.
Let's say you want to play the game like a sand box. You don't want these harsh limitations because you would just rather create absurd contraptions. Well, that option is available to you at anytime.
Okay, but what about the ability to roleback your mission if it fails. You can turn that off as well, which makes all the math that goes into space travel necessary. Before you try to launch your rocket, you better make sure it will actually launch, and when it doesn't launch and just bursts in the air I want you to put yourself in the feet of Sergei Korolev watching his attempts at launching Russian man to the moon failing. Every failure and success are huge moments.
Great game for science and space travel. Build your ship, test your ship, retry when things go wrong, get science when things go right. Want to land on the moon? Go for it. Are you interested in landing man on Mars? Try it out. Want to fly into the sun? Not smart, but you can do it.
Civilization games are always great, this is no exception.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike by the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service against the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii Territory, on the morning of December 7, 1941. The attack, also known as the Battle of Pearl Harbor, led to the United States' entry into World War II. The Japanese military leadership referred to the attack as the Hawaii Operation and Operation AI, and as Operation Z during its planning.
Japan intended the attack as a preventive action to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from interfering with military actions they planned in Southeast Asia against overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States. Over the next seven hours there were coordinated Japanese attacks on the U.S.-held Philippines, Guam and Wake Island and on the British Empire in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
The attack commenced at 7:48 a.m. Hawaiian Time (18:18 UTC). The base was attacked by 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft (including fighters, level and dive bombers, and torpedo bombers) in two waves, launched from six aircraft carriers. All eight U.S. Navy battleships were damaged, with four sunk. All but the USS Arizona were later raised, and six were returned to service and went on to fight in the war. The Japanese also sank or damaged three cruisers, three destroyers, an anti-aircraft training ship, and one minelayer. 188 U.S. aircraft were destroyed; 2,403 Americans were killed and 1,178 others were wounded.Important base installations such as the power station, dry dock, shipyard, maintenance, and fuel and torpedo storage facilities, as well as the submarine piers and headquarters building (also home of the intelligence section), were not attacked. Japanese losses were light: 29 aircraft and five midget submarines lost, and 64 servicemen killed. One Japanese sailor, Kazuo Sakamaki, was captured.
The surprise attack came as a profound shock to the American people and led directly to the American entry into World War II in both the Pacific and European theaters. The following day, December 8, the United States declared war on Japan,[18][19] and several days later, on December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. The U.S. responded with a declaration of war against Germany and Italy. Domestic support for non-interventionism, which had been fading since the Fall of France in 1940, disappeared.
There were numerous historical precedents for unannounced military action by Japan, but the lack of any formal warning, particularly while negotiations were still apparently ongoing, led President Franklin D. Roosevelt to proclaim December 7, 1941, "a date which will live in infamy". Because the attack happened without a declaration of war and without explicit warning, the attack on Pearl Harbor was later judged in the Tokyo Trials to be a war crime.

This is easily one of my most favorite games.  I originally played this when it came out on XBOX and was riveted by the story.  I couldn't put the controller down. The concept of using light to vanquish the darkness so that your enemies are vulnerable is a cool idea.  There is a lot to see and do.  Sit next to the radio and listen, switch on the TV sets and watch the programs.  The characters are interesting and developed.  Not to mention, there are some great songs here.  The game has serious replay value for it's comedic value alone.  I just can't say enough about the story.  One thing I do need to mention, is that I completely prefer playing this game with a keyboard and a mouse than with a controller.  Alan Wake can be a bit more artificially difficult due to the joystick and aiming - a problem not present with the responsiveness of a mouse. Some might not find the game appealing, but if you enjoy a good story, some spookiness and like to find extra content in a game, then this one is for you.
A must play! But, you must play the first one first as well as the DLC to get the full story!

In case you want to know about the positives and negatives of the game, instead of just seeing dozens of reviews only mentioning the loot box system, here you go.
Shadow of War is the sequel to 2014's Shadow of Mordor. There is hardly a comparison between the two as this is an incredible upgrade in regards to the original. I 100% the game on PS4 when it came and just played through the campaign on PC as I heard that your nemesis and allies would transfer over.
Let's start with the
Almost every aspect of that game has been improved, the graphics are nicer, the storyline and characters are not annoying so far, and practically every area of the game has been sped up and streamlined.
Interogating enemies does not require you to grab them and then wait for the animation to play out, it is now just draining them and the screen to select the captain you want is there.
The skills are phenomenal. Elven Grace will now work on walls as well, and pressing the left thumbstick will give a burst of speed without having to jump over an obstacle. I have had an endless amount of fun combining the slow-time-when-falling bow perk with the double jump to jump off of a tower, snipe a few enemies on the ground, then do a backflip onto a different building and keep running.
The combat system has changed, you build wrath to perform Talion's exections, which stays between fights and does not disappear over time unless you are injured. You also build rage to perform special Celebrimbor moves, where you enter the wraith world and can dispatch enemies with killer arrows and executions. Also added is a heavy attack, called Glaive, which will stun enemies in a circle around you.
The captain strengths and weaknesses are much more involved now, and you can see their strengths without interogating a worm, but not their weaknesses.
Also added is the ability to equip different weapons, armour, and
It is surprisingly optimised (for my build at least, don't have any friends with this game to check theirs) on day one. Maintain more than 60 fps on Ultra quality, except for cutscenes...
Now the
The game still uses prerendered cutscenes in many places, which is a sin to be honest. I hate when the game suddenly has a massive change in visual quality and the FPS drops because they rendered it at a lower framerate than your computer runs the game. Also dislike seeing Talion with completely different equipment than he had equiped before walking into a door for a cutscene. Just really wish games would stop using them, hopefully soon.
(While writing this I saw the 4k Cinematics pack, so I will get that. Still doubt that the framerate will be better.)
The Orc lip synch is not the best, and that is being generous. To be fair, the Orc appearances are so different I can imagine it would be difficult, but since the game zooms in on a captain when he talks to you it is noticeably off.
Last but certainly not least, the loot chests. Oh boy, WB. This is a full priced, singleplayer game that has purchasable item consumables. Always a bad idea.
Fortunately, these crates are entirely pointless and do not aid your gameplay in any way whatsoever. I tried a few and saw that I could easily get better items by running around killing Orcs. Still love how people are saying it is impossible to beat the game without buying them, probably the same people who say it is impossible to beat Contra without the Code, or are
.
If you like LotR and you like the gameplay from the Arkham games or Assassin's Creed, then this is likely a good idea to purchase. Fun, pretty, and interesting. Just do not buy the loot chests. For the love of God please do not buy the loot chests we cannot encourage this. They probably saw how much money Blizzard and RockStar get from purchasables and wanted to be like the big boys. Do not let them.
An edit addendum, for all the comments:
No, I have not finished the game. I also didn't buy the crates, where I pre ordered the game from gave me a few legendary crates, which literally an hour of gameplay gave me items vastly superior.
I am aware that the final act is supposedly incredibly difficult, but the crates are so pointless I cannot imagine them being of any use in it.
And before any one tries to nag at me for preordering the game, I do it when the pre-order is at least 15% off sale price and I know I'm going to get it anyways. Amazon Prime, my dudes.
An extra addendum: Wow, I didn't want to but I had to delete a few comments. Because you disagree with someone else's comment is no reason to threaten them or be incredibly abusive. Grow up guys, it's a game that had a very unfortunate decision implemented that does not affect the game (which is much better than I was expecting). It was a terrible decision, but it will not affect you in any way, so don't threaten or swear (excessively at least) at each other in the comments, alright?

In Alan Wake you collect manuscript pages, damn fine coffee in thermos and shoot stacked beer cans. Light is your key to survival against the dark forces, which try to stop you as you are looking for your loved one. Exciting!

Alan Wake surprised many of us by making it's sudden appearance on Steam, and this time on the right platform on which it belongs!

Invisible, Inc.  is a roguelike, turn-based, strategy stealth game. Moving past the buzzwords, it's a game where you move your units through randomized levels by observing the patterns of enemy movement and then avoiding them on your way to the exit point of the level. If you're lucky, you'll find some items or cash along the way. As you go further in the game, you face more and more dangerous enemies. Eventually you get spotted, die, and have to start again from the beginning. You do that last bit a lot, actually.
I've noticed a lot people assuming that the game is similar to Shadowrun Returns or XCom due to the isometric perspective. It really isn't, and if you go in trying to play it that way you will end up being frustrated. Invisible, Inc. is a stealth game and a roguelike. Combat is difficult and usually not an effective way to deal with enemies. Also, it is a roguelike, to the extent that word still means anything, and you will most likely fail a lot as you learn how to play, and sometimes just because the random number generator screwed you over. How much you enjoy it will depend on your tolerance for that sort of thing.
Also, this being early access, there's always the question of whether the creators are going to actually finish the game. Klei is a pretty well established company at this point, and they previously did a public beta similar to early access with their game Don't Starve. Personally, I think they're trustworthy based on that track record. Not that I'm an expert or anything.

The ending kind of felt like a cop out, with your final decision playing a huge role on the ending overall, but I couldn't have thought of a better way for it to end, and I was okay with it. This story carries such an emotion to it that it can be felt by the player, and getting even deeper into the story and piecing together the mystery revolving the plot kept me intrigued til it was solved. I have played similar games that relied on story as its leading factor, such as the TellTales Walking Dead series, and I feel this story matches some aspects of that game series, and in some ways even surpasses it. My gripes with the game are so miniscule compared to the positives that come with this game that they are barely noticiable at all. This game gets an easy 10/10 rating from me and I'm hoping that the studio that worked on this masterpiece continues to work on games like this and continue to amaze all who decide to dive into their wonderful journeys and experiences.

After getting nearly 13 hours in I thought I'd come back and talk more about the game, the customization and gear in particular.
As I said before the nemesis difficulty really tests your mettle. Not only do you get hit harder, but the enemy's traits are better, their levels are higher, and they seem to adapt quicker and cheat death more often. The single last chance can be a bit ridiculous at times, but not only is there a skill perk that adds one more, there is also insane gear customization that allows for you to cope with the higher damage.
I have my gear set up to give me health back whenever I can. Since I went out and killed all of the orcs I could before branding was re-introduced, I have very high quality gear that allowed me to get near full health from drains/brands, full health from stealth kills, full health from last chances, and smaller amounts from damage and such on weapons. The combo of jems and gear stats really allow for you to go for any build you want.
Not only does all of my gear give me health back in some way, the armor also gives crits a chance to add fire to my attacks, my bow gives health back to me (with a very small chance of full health on kills), my sword has a chance to do poison on crits, and my dagger gives might on throws and guarentees fire on stealth attacks. So I naturally cause a lot of normal fire that can be turned into balefire on melee hits, and always cause balefire on stealth attacks (Which is a super awesome effect to see!).
All in all the game is very good at allowing you to create fun and unique builds, but I feel it lacks a bit of weakness in the orcs. At times (in regards to nemesis difficulty) you can find yourself up against enemies 5 or so levels higher than you with few or no weaknesses and an intimidating set of traits.
During those encounters the "difficulty" of the mode shows some flaw as I've found myself fighting the same captain for 10 minutes or so because they've adapted to every move I can use and-or are immune or resistant to special things (such as elements and your wraith powers).
When you get in a battle like that it becomes a mad scrabble to find any little thing that can get damage off on the enemy, praying that they don't have the trait that allows them to heal themselves or that an odd trick you try in desperation doesn't enrage them.
I often find if I remember to open with the odd moves in mind (slide tackle, shoulder bash, glave attack) along side my normal combat orcs go down fairly quick, but if you are too intent on using a weakness or repeat the same move a little too often don't be surprised when the only move in your arsenal capable of catching the uruk off guard is a slide tackle or shoulder bash :D

I saw the reviews and knew this was destined to be a great game, but while the first episode was great, the gameplay wasn't the most complex and the story wasn't as attractive as I'd hoped.
Nevertheless, I bought the rest of the game by the recommendation of my friend and will not ever regret it. I would feel satisfied paying $60.00 for the game, as the experience is beyond amazing. I wasn't allowed to play video games as a young child, so when I first got the chance, I dove in with Skyrim. The magic and wonder in that virtual world made me awestruck and I cannot begin to explain how amazing that felt. After that I played countless other games, all being great, but none being eye-opening or moving; then the Witcher 3 came out and I thought no other game could ever top that.
I wouldn't say Life is Strange is better than the Witcher 3, but I would say that despite the high bar that's been set by the Witcher 3, Life is Strange has still managed to capture me and blow my mind. It was an emotional and philisophical roller coaster that I might not ever forget. The gameplay felt somewhat lacking, but it wasn't intended to be well featured, it was just a bonus to the story and artwork of the game's world itself. If the guys who made this keep it up, I will buy every single one of their games.
10/10 - Voice acting
9.5/10 - Story
10/10 - Visuals (not graphics intensive, but still somehow amazing)
10/10 - Soundtrack
8/10 - Gameplay (This wasn't their artistic focus though, so I wouldn't recommend making this a deciding factor)
This game will definitely hold a high place in my mental shelf and I will treasure the experience. I hope the rest of you out there who haven't gotten it yet make the decision to buy it. It is mesmerizing.

Strategy games live and die on the complexity and satisfaction of the countless decisions made within them, and it’s here that Civilization VI stands tall. Where its predecessors laid the foundations and systems of play, this is a game that refines and perfects them to a remarkable degree. It’s not without a couple of flaws – the odd diplomatic quirk and some religious spamming are its most notable – but Civilization VI gives the series’ 20-year Anniversary the hurrah it deserves. It’s a game that celebrates the genre while fundamentally improving it, and it comes in a package that is simultaneously attractive for newcomers while being exciting for Civilization veterans.

Well. It was about time I got to writing a review about this game. I think I can accurately say the positives and negatives about the game.  with my 600 plus hours into it. And heres what I think. First review as well, for my first game I ever bought on steam: seems fitting.
[h1[Pro's[/h1]
Very realistic, for the most part. You have to know what you are doing, and learn how basic orbits work and what not to really learn how to play the game.
Funny. This is that other part. The game isnt perfect, and you can mess around all you want with it, and do some silly things, like launch kerbals from the moon: not land and then take off, and not in a ship, but literally launch the kerbal from the moon. It was fun.
Satisfying. Once you set foot on the mun (moon equivalent), then a nice lil bit of joy and happiness rushes over you. You feel this giant accomplishment. And this does dwindle after every other landing, even on other bodies, but it is still there. And once you actually land back on Kerbin, thats almost as sweet.
Customization: Build rockets and stuff however you want: just need to make sure they work, engineer.
There isnt much inherently bad with the game. The only problem with it is this: personal drive. You have to want to go to the mun, Duna, or other bodies, or create that perfect plane that can take off from kerbin and go somewhere in space without a hitch. If you dont have that large drive, then the game is boring; No sense of direction, nothing to do really, things of that nature. So if youre gonna get the game, make sure to ask yourself: Can I set my own goals, and actually achieve them/want too?
EDIT: I did forget to mention the new career missions that you can do in career mode, thanks to one person who saw my review. Those can definitely extend the life of the game; I personally did not find them too much fun, but they are indeed there, and are fun for many others as well. :)
I have not actively played Kerbal Space program in just under 2 years or so. One of the updates wiped my save, unfortunately, which made younger me mad and not want to play it anymore. Now, I just dont care anymore to really play it on my own. I did what I personally wanted to do, which was to land on every planet, and a few moons, and make a space station. I did that, and I feel like I beat the game. Now every time I go back, its all just "Ya! I remember doing that", but then I just go play something else. I tell people that I love this game, and I truly do. Its just I already beat it for me. But I will still gladly play it to show friends the ropes, and just to make sure I still know how to do it.
Should you buy it? Yes, if you like sandbox space games. This is probably one of the finer ones out there. But make sure you have the drive to do it, otherwise you will stop playing it before you achieve anything. All the people that love this game have that drive, and are the ones that still playing it, that reach higher hours than I have. And I commend them for it. They have that drive that I have lost, for now. Buy the game though: Its fun to watch things explode :D

This is a game that I pick up and play every day - for about 20 - 30 minutes per day. Nuclear Throne is a "rogue like" top-down action shooter. The world you are playing in is procedurally generated, which, while following general rules, will vary every time in terms of layout and enemy difficulty.
The game is very much a bullet-hell/twitch based game; if you don't like fast-paced shooting action, this isn't the game for you. Some characters, like the Chicken, can slow down time and make the game a little bit more manageable while you learn.
As you shoot/slash/explode your way through the levels with one of a dozen unique characters, you gain XP for traits that power your character up and pick up new weapons to better shoot your way through the world. This also lends itself to a different experience every time that you play. When you die - that's it. You have to start over again. But it's not such a huge loss - since maybe you'll luck into that golden combination that gets you all the way to the Nuclear Throne!
The game is capped at 30fps, but I don't think this detracts from the gameplay at all. The visual style is unique, and very evocative of 16-bit gaming consoles.
I reccommend this game, as it is a great value for its price.

The next major game from Remedy turns out to be a smash as Alan Wake is an engaging thriller of a game that'll keep you enngaged from beginning to end. Taking cues from Stephen King and Twin Peaks, Alan Wake presents a decent tale that is very stylised with frequent narration from Alan himself. The presentation is outstanding with the game looking gorgeous and having a great creepy atmosphere with its various lighting and wind effects, although there is an over-reliance on forest locations for my taste. Also the TV show style structure provides great stopping gaps for playing and give a unique presentation to the usual game structure. Gameplay is fun with the torch and 3rd person gunplay working in tandem to provide a nice spin on the usual shooting gameplay. However it can get a little formulaic at points, with not enough enemy types with it only being Taken, Brute Taken, Fast Taken and Birds being the main enemies. That being said Alan Wake is still a great and intriguing game to play with it's compelling presentation and fun gameplay, definitely check it if it goes on sale.

SPOILERS FOR BOTH WALKING DEAD SEASONS ONE AND TWO!!!!
I honestly don't know what to think with this game. On one hand, the characters are very unique, likeable, and stand out a lot more than the cast of Season 1, but on the other hand, the story itself is a lot weaker than Season 1's campaign. The gameplay takes a dive too. Remember in Season 1, episode 2 when you had to sneak around the house, looking for clues about what the dairy farmers were hiding in the barn and where they were hiding Mark? Remember how it steadily got more and more tense as you uncovered evidence that something was seriously wrong and you're friend was in trouble? Then there you had to run down the stairs and blurt out the right speech option before Clementine ate human flesh, and if you panicked and didn't press anything, she ate it anyway?
There's no gameplay like that here. All of the tension is saved for cutscenes and decision points, inbetween you just have to wander around, talk to people and look at objects. It's as boring as it sounds. When there's a threat, the gameplay is reduced to "QTE to dodge and avoid" and "Mash the Q button to get away from enemies." It's a wonder my Q button wasn't destroyed from playing this. Thank God the characters and interactions are interesting enough to keep you going. (Well, except Sarita, anyway. She was as dull as dirt) The most dynamic and interesting part of the game, as far as gameplay goes, is in episode 1, when you have to sneak around the cabin to get medical supplies to treat Clementine's dog bite, because the people she found don't know if it's a "lurker" bite or not, and locked her in the shed until morning to prove she wasn't infected. You have complete control of Clementine the whole time, so you get to decide where to go next, whenever or not to spy on the others, what order to get the items, etc. After that, it's basically an interactive movie.
And you know that screen you get at the end of the episode, showing you the percentage of people who made the same or opposite choice as you? The choices suck now. There so much more trivial and less interesting from the Season 1 decisions. In Season 1, you had to choose who to save, Carley or Doug. You can choose whenever or not to let Ben die. In Season 2, you get to decide who to sit with at the lunch table and whenever or not to confide in a woman who turned you over to the sadist with an entire army. I can see what they were doing with this, they were trying to show you how you were changing Clementine's character as you played, but that doesn't really matter. Clementine's personality does not change because of your choices, and when it comes down to saving two people, one of them will die, regardless of what you chose. This game is BIG on illusion of choice, the only time your decisions will affect the outcome at all is the ending. And I do applaud Telltale for providing five different endings to this game, even if some of them are less satisfactory than others. What I do NOT applaud, is how they built up to the climax.
So get this: in episode 2, you find out that Kenny is still alive, and he gets captured with you by Carver, basically a rip-off of the Governor from the TV show. Kenny gets beaten half to death, losing an eye in the process to save you, and the whole time, the group uses you as a covenant to communicate with him as he becomes increasingly violent after Sarita's death. (His new girlfriend) He really doesn't get along with Luke, a dashing young man (Still too old for anyone to be shipping him with Clem, though. *Shudder*) you befriend early in the game, and they end up arguing over everything. Often, you have to choose a side in their arguements and attempt to appease them.
So, you would think that this is building up to a fatal confrontation when it's clear that Kenny is starting to go over the point of no return, right? WRONG! Instead, Luke is killed off for no good reason, and the combantant instead is Jane, a semi-likeable, cold, ruthless, emotionally confused woman who only shows up in episode 3, and barely interacts with Kenny at all until the time leading up to their final fight. This throws off the pacing and suspense of the game so much, it hurts! It was such a wasted oppurtunity! When two characters are so angry at eachother, they will stop at nothing to murder eachother in the middle of a blizzard, with an eleven year old girl watching, and you have no choice but to kill one of them, you better make that a strong dilemma. I am sorry, but between the uncle figure who risked his life for me time and time again, and the older sister figure, who let her real younger sister die, whom I haven't known that long, I am sorry, uncle figure all the way! If it wasn't for the fact that Kenny was a broken, bitter husk of his former self that was better off dead at that point, it would have been no contest at all. It totally should have been Luke. It made so much more sense!
All of this has left a bad taste in my mouth, tricking me into thinking this game, this story, was better than it was. Don't get me wrong, it's still an experience worth having, but they could have done so much better, without resorting to killing off the entire group to make drama. There's more than one way to make drama, Telltale! They use tragedy and tears into fooling you that this game has more depth and complexity than it actullay does. So, should you play this game? That depends on you. Do you formulate stronger memories from directly interacting with a story, or are you satisfied with just watching it? If you answered yes to the former, go ahead, buy it, but do yourself a favour, and wait for a sale. Do not pay 30 bucks for this smokescreen of sadness. If you said yes to the latter, just look up a let's play or the like.
Personally, I would recommend playing it just for the bear related easter eggs in the credits in each episode. You know, if you like bears.

Despite the controls, which seems to be a source of anguish in just about every survival horror game, Alan Wake is a solid game guaranteed to keep you playing 'one more checkpoint' or 'one more chapter'. I started it yesterday and played it the whole day (with my shutters closed of course) and it hasn't bored me yet.
The story is gripping and the characters are well-defined, even though the facial animation is so sloppy everyone seems to be suffering from a stroke all the time. And even though Wake is a geeky writer, it's extremely irritating to see him get winded, slowing to the speed of an octogenarian and gasping for breath every two seconds, even with crazy axe murderers chasing after him.
As always, with any computer game in the history of the world, driving is horribly implemented (steering with the WASD keys, in this day and age? Seriously?!), and the strangely skewed third-person perspective is a bit uncomfortable for first-person aficionados like me, but I suppose that's part of the survival horror genre.
I'm not gonna review graphics and stuff, because seriously, who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥as long as the game is good? (They're lovely though)
Still, those little things aside, if you like survival horror, this is a must-buy, and even if you're just indifferent to the genre, like me, it's still a worthwhile purchase - but wait 'til it's on sale again.

Out of every Triple A title I've played (a lot) this $10 Indie Game has been one of the best games I've ever played. This game, at first glance, may seem like a hyperviolent run and gun arcade shooter. It isin't. This game is a very well thought out strategic game with very, very minor stealth elements. The strategy isin't shoved in your face either. The strategic elements you create yourself.This game also isin't easy. You need to play through levels multiple times to get the best balance of map knowledge, enemy spawns/locations and luck to pass a level. Now of course you could play this like the original GTA, shooting everything in site, but you will die. Alot. Planning your moves, picking the best masks and discovering new tactics is what makes this game so great. The story from what I've seen is wonderfully simple and complex. What you may think is that you play an insane psychopath hell-bent for destruction. And you'd be right. But WHY you're a hell-bent psychopath is what makes the story awesome. Coupled with the best video game soundtrack of all time, this game offers alot. And honestly I'm more excited for Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number than GTA 5 PC.

The controls are generally smooth and what you would expect from the genre. Alan doesn't move quite as nimbly or shoot as professionally as a GTA-style character but that won't stop you from enjoying the game. Playing this game is downright fun.
I picked up my copy on Steam as part of the Alan Wake sale: $10 for AW, AWAN, and the bonus content. I don't think the bonus content is worth purchasing, but the bundle gives you AW and AWAN for less than their invididual sale price.

The atmosphere is awesome, the story is great, voice acting is omnipresent and really well-done, graphics are pretty good, and the light/dark mechanic is really interesting. The gamplay, though? UGGGGHHHHHH the gameplay!
Controls work pretty well on a 360 controller (didn't try keyboard), but the 3rd person perspective is horrendous. The way its fixed really starts to feel claustrophobic, and there were literally a dozen times where I was attacked before the game alerted me to an enemy's presence because of the perspective.
The only complaint I have about the graphics is that the 3rd person perspective (again) really fights you in close-quarters stuff. You will not be able to see anything with the flashlight if you stand even semi-near stuff.
The enemies (The Taken) are pretty cool, but they're not at all tough, and they have no AI to speak of. Appear, walk towards Alan, telegraph my attack, attack. In addition, they spout stupid educational factoids in super cheesy voices when they appear. No joke. "There are over 65 million pigs and cows in the world," and "most of us are skilled laborers" are a few of them.
The light/dark thing is really interesting as you're learning it, but you quickly realize that it's extremely shallow, extremely repetitive, and it gets EXTREMELY annoying near the end. Especially when...
The only way the game can increase the difficulty is by throwing more of the weak enemies at you. I don't know if this was their intentional choice, or whether it was due to laziness or lack of knowhow, but the "tough" enemy encounters where you are absolutely surrounded are just flat out annoying. The boss fights are pretty cool though.
I don't know if you're like me, but one of my biggest pet peeves in gaming is when some arbitrary event happens that takes away all your hard earned progress (guns, ammo, etc) halfway through a game. Imagine how overjoyed I was, then, to find out that this game does it at about 10% of the way through the game, and again at 18%, then again at 30%, then again at 41%, again at 53%, etc etc. Seriously, I didn't even beat the game (and wasn't always paying attention), but it happened EIGHT times to me. I suppose that's the only way of making people excited again to pick up one of the game's three weapons.
As I said before, I love the story in this game, and I really really really wanted to finish it to see where it was going, but the sum of the individual parts added up to a great story chopped up by a game that I just could not stand to play. I quit in chapter 5 (out of 6), and looked up the ending on the internet.
This game is not difficult, not scary, and not fun. I know others loved it, but I found it to be a very frustrating experience, since it's such an interesting idea/story let down by a disgustingly overwhelming number of bland, aggravating shooting sequences.

But what if you dont get the gun, and you passed up some pretty good upgrades on the earlier stages? Then you done and went ♥♥♥♥ed yourself right there. But what if you get the right upgrades? If you love metaphorically bashing your head into a brick wall to find out which one will break first, then this game is for you.
This game, being a rougelike, will kick your teeth in and throw you in at the deep end, and leave you to fend for yourself. After you get the hang of the movement, weapons and other such stuff, you might just reach the Nuclear Throne (Yes, it DOES exist.)
+There are many characters, weapons and mutations, allowing for many different combinations of favoured strategy, such as being a reckless murderer as Chicken.
+The developers are usually more than welcome to feedback about the update, seeing as this game is in early access at the moment.
+Co-op for pairing up to find the Throne.
-Co-op camera normally focuses on P2, forcing the players to stick close together if they want to explore the map.
-Cursed weapons are typically from the lower difficulties, dissuading players from picking them up most of the time.
-World 3 boss is almost impossible to keep asleep during World 3-3.
+/-The crowns, while giving some benefits, come with downsides that sometimes balance out the pros and cons, but more often than not the downsides are more hefty.
+/-Golden weapons don't have too much of an incentive to collect, except for being able to start with a different weapon, or just having more ammo upon the start of an attempt.
+/-The spawns still arent perfectly safe after recent updates, but they are much safer than before.
Tips:
Be wary around cacti, skulls, pipes, cars and other environmental obstacles when using grenades.
Crystal cannot block every type of damage with her shield.
Never forget about Melting's active ability to detonate corpses that destroy projectiles and damage enemies.
Steroids can fire weapons fully automatically, no matter what weapons he is holding.
If you eat a cursed weapon as Robot, you will take a large chunk of damage (As of now I can't remember the exact number, I think it's 7.)
Plant's snare can hold assassins in place, making them far less scary.
Tl;dr "THE STRUGGLE CONTINUES" forever.

The atmosphere is awesome, the story is great, voice acting is omnipresent and really well-done, graphics are pretty good, and the light/dark mechanic is really interesting. The gamplay, though? UGGGGHHHHHH the gameplay!
Controls work pretty well on a 360 controller (didn't try keyboard), but the 3rd person perspective is horrendous. The way its fixed really starts to feel claustrophobic, and there were literally a dozen times where I was attacked before the game alerted me to an enemy's presence because of the perspective.
The only complaint I have about the graphics is that the 3rd person perspective (again) really fights you in close-quarters stuff. You will not be able to see anything with the flashlight if you stand even semi-near stuff.
The enemies (The Taken) are pretty cool, but they're not at all tough, and they have no AI to speak of. Appear, walk towards Alan, telegraph my attack, attack. In addition, they spout stupid educational factoids in super cheesy voices when they appear. No joke. "There are over 65 million pigs and cows in the world," and "most of us are skilled laborers" are a few of them.
The light/dark thing is really interesting as you're learning it, but you quickly realize that it's extremely shallow, extremely repetitive, and it gets EXTREMELY annoying near the end. Especially when...
The only way the game can increase the difficulty is by throwing more of the weak enemies at you. I don't know if this was their intentional choice, or whether it was due to laziness or lack of knowhow, but the "tough" enemy encounters where you are absolutely surrounded are just flat out annoying. The boss fights are pretty cool though.
I don't know if you're like me, but one of my biggest pet peeves in gaming is when some arbitrary event happens that takes away all your hard earned progress (guns, ammo, etc) halfway through a game. Imagine how overjoyed I was, then, to find out that this game does it at about 10% of the way through the game, and again at 18%, then again at 30%, then again at 41%, again at 53%, etc etc. Seriously, I didn't even beat the game (and wasn't always paying attention), but it happened EIGHT times to me. I suppose that's the only way of making people excited again to pick up one of the game's three weapons.
As I said before, I love the story in this game, and I really really really wanted to finish it to see where it was going, but the sum of the individual parts added up to a great story chopped up by a game that I just could not stand to play. I quit in chapter 5 (out of 6), and looked up the ending on the internet.
This game is not difficult, not scary, and not fun. I know others loved it, but I found it to be a very frustrating experience, since it's such an interesting idea/story let down by a disgustingly overwhelming number of bland, aggravating shooting sequences.
The real superpower in this game is how fast these kids can send text messages.

I feel like the developers were so focused on telling the story that they forgot about the "game" element. It reached a point where the only "gaming" elements that were left were the "shooting gallery" sections.
Let's not even talk about the fact that they make a 10 or 11 year old girl shoot a full ammo clip in a row, beyond it being unrealistic, I feel that they could have found a more interesting plot that didn't involve making Clem a Rambo Junior.
I actually re-winded the game and opted for the opposite choices from the previous play trough and it was just pathetic. The last game you could sometimes get somebody killed or choose who to keep in the team, this time they might as well just used a “press any key to continue” mechanic.
So if you are a real fan of "the walking dead", the story is ok.... really just....ok.... but you are better off watching it on YouTube and save your money for a real game.

"You did not reach the Nuclear Throne"
If you love metaphorically bashing your head into a brick wall to find out which one will break first, then this game is for you.
This game, being a rougelike, will kick your teeth in and throw you in at the deep end, and leave you to fend for yourself. After you get the hang of the movement, weapons and other such stuff, you might just reach the Nuclear Throne (Yes, it DOES exist.)
+There are many characters, weapons and mutations, allowing for many different combinations of favoured strategy, such as being a reckless murderer as Chicken.
+The developers are usually more than welcome to feedback about the update, seeing as this game is in early access at the moment.
+Co-op for pairing up to find the Throne.
-Co-op camera normally focuses on P2, forcing the players to stick close together if they want to explore the map.
-Cursed weapons are typically from the lower difficulties, dissuading players from picking them up most of the time.
-World 3 boss is almost impossible to keep asleep during World 3-3.
+/-The crowns, while giving some benefits, come with downsides that sometimes balance out the pros and cons, but more often than not the downsides are more hefty.
+/-Golden weapons don't have too much of an incentive to collect, except for being able to start with a different weapon, or just having more ammo upon the start of an attempt.
+/-The spawns still arent perfectly safe after recent updates, but they are much safer than before.
Tips:
Be wary around cacti, skulls, pipes, cars and other environmental obstacles when using grenades.
Crystal cannot block every type of damage with her shield.
Never forget about Melting's active ability to detonate corpses that destroy projectiles and damage enemies.
Steroids can fire weapons fully automatically, no matter what weapons he is holding.
If you eat a cursed weapon as Robot, you will take a large chunk of damage (As of now I can't remember the exact number, I think it's 7.)
Plant's snare can hold assassins in place, making them far less scary.
Tl;dr "THE STRUGGLE CONTINUES" forever.

Wow, what a game. I had been watching this for years after its initial announce, and was floored when it became an X360 exclusive.
Now that it has made the transition to the PC, I have to say I'm quite glad to have played it.
The storyline is a cross between Stephen King and Rod Serling, and makes very conscious nods to both. The soundscape is vibrant and alive, and communicates very clearly what is going on to the player.
The map design is absolutely gorgeous and organic. Things flow naturally and seem right. It isn't on Valve levels of feel, but it is damned close.
Graphics are pretty fantastic as well. Sure, textures could be sharper, but things are presented almost flawlessly and the overall impression of many of the scenes is awe inspiring.
The flashlight mechanic is pretty enjoyable to be honest, and can lead to some seriously tense fights.
The two Special Features episodes are excellent additions that are much more difficult than the main campaign.
Get it on sale, and definitely play it.

I actually bought this on release played for about 10 hours. It was buggy and very counter-intuitive so I stopped.  i picked this up again a few days ago hoping it would've been fixed after a year gone by. But no! This is still a mess of a game.
Civ 5 by the end was really a masterpiece IMO. Sure there were still some problems with diplomacy, AI and some balancing issues in regards to victory types possibilities, but overall all was great. The game mechanics (religion, diplomacy/trade, spying, etc) we're easy to use/understand with easy to find UI panels with the info you needed. Also, the overall map and city UI were simple, clear and easy to understand.
And now we have Civ 6...
It's like the developers just took everything that was good and done right with Civ 5 and took it out. Just for the sake of replacing it with new more complicated game mechanics that don't work. Because, you know, more complicated=better right??? Here are a few examples:
1-  The city UI screen is a clusterf%&k. They added so many city mechanics (districts, housing, amenities) that this thing will give you a headache. There is so much information that you will need a magnifying lens to be able to read it. Oh, and gone are the days where you could just scroll to see what you had already built, now you have to go to a sub-panel to find it which is really inefficient. Then there's the buying tab overlapping the main city info tab, so you can't see the latter unless you close the other. The whole city UI is just a cluttered inefficient tedious mess full of sup-panels. And since this is where you'll find yourself about 50-75% of the time during a game, this is just unacceptable.
2- Housing and city growth. So now along with making sure you have enough food for citizens, you need to have enough housing for them.
3- Happiness. In Civ 5 this was a rather easy to manage general stat for your entire civ. Now they changed this to a city mechanic tied to amenities. So basically now this forces you to micromanage every freaking city individually for happiness.
4- Diplomacy/trading is more complicated, frustrating and broken then ever. At least in Civ 5, you could usually get a 1 for 1 resource trade, now good luck with that. And the Ui panel is s%#T. They took out the deal history tab, so now there's no easy way to see what current deals you have with what civ. I mean wtf???
5- Many scroll over pop-up info is badly written, vague or just wrong. For example, one of the community hub district bonuses is  '+2 gold from each adjacent river tile'... Wrong!!! It should say '+2 gold if at least 1 adjacent river tile' . Now it doesn't seem like a big deal, but I've found several of misleading and false infos like this throughout. And the worst is, I found posts regarding some of these that go back to 2016 after release and they still haven't been fixed!!! It takes five secs to rewrite these c'mon!
6- Bugs and crashes. I've been playing for 3 days and, a year after release, this game has crashed several times.
So overall, they took a great game with clean UI panels and screens,  with complex yet easy game mechanics,  and gutted it of everything good just for the sake of change. They made every aspect of this game more complicated and tedious and all of it behind a frustrating, inefficient and time-consuming UI that just weighs the whole gaming experience down. I don't mind a complex game, but the UI has to be ez to use and infos ez to find and understand, which is simply not the case.
It seems that these developers went the opposite of the gaming industry's trend. When games like Battlefront, WOW, and others are dumbing down, simplifying UI and making their games more accessible to gamers (not saying it's a good thing btw) they went the opposite direction. Over complicating things and making it a chore even for hardcore civ fans like myself.
Anyways, that,s my 2 cents on it.  :P

Preliminary review:
The game offers incredible options for PC, the game goes into very nitty gritty details about your graphics card, and how each settings pulls on your hardware. Even by pure PC game standard, this is above and beyond anything I've seen before.
The game offers dynamic resolution scaling, it works well to keep you at a fixed FPS if your hardware struggles.
Cinematics are pre-rendered, which is great for people with lower hardware but can feel a bit out of place for people with good hardware.
As far as the game goes, the gameplay is very similar to Shadow of Mordor, but we get A LOT more tools to our kit. While in Shadow of Mordor, most progression was unlocking abilities that we should have had in the first place, this game gives you most of the staple abilities from the get go, only locking certain ones behind certain points in the story. The city really gets into too, it does summarize Shadow of Mordor... a bit too quickly. It wasn't a problem for me since I played the previous title, but someone jumping straight into Shadow of War might get a bit confused at first.
Will update once I have more time to play, but so far, the first city is great, that's one thing the first game lacked.

This would get a "meh" review from me if there was such a thing on steam, but given that it asks me whether I personally like/recommend the game or not the answer is no.
The core of the problem for me is that the game seemed to be all about trying to get me to relate to a teenage girl for whom socializing is scary and the popular kids are all jerks, which I just couldn't do. To be fair, I think the fact that this turned me off the game so much indicates that the writers at least did a good job of doing this. The "rewind" mechanic also felt like it encouraged this game's equivalent of save-scumming/optimizing for the "best" decision, which can get in the way of enjoying these sorts of games.
Attempting to not spoil anything, the story is mostly decent, but the ending felt a bit contrived and probably doesn't have as much impact as it's supposed to depending on your POV and your choices earlier on. Some of the events leading up to the end also seemed like they were just ramping up the drama for the sake of ramping up the drama and didn't feel like they would make any sense if you think of this as "a week in the life of Max Caulfield" rather than a game which is intentionally building itself up towards a climax: normally I wouldn't mind this too much, but the game puts a lot of effort into trying to make itself feel that way and it just felt jarring when events started picking up for no clear reason other than because we needed to get to some sort of climax.
That all being said, if you like adventure games and think you can relate to a main character who is introverted to a fault then this is probably a pretty good game for you.

The game's been getting a lot of flak due to news regarding it having microtransactions despite it being largely a single-player game with a season pass, with some hints of online PvP (not fighting other people, but attacking their bases and killing the AI they setup there).
I understand where this flak is coming from. It's a shame the devs or their publisher decided a game without free post-launch support needed both a season pass and loot boxes, but that's the way publishers are headed now.
I've played it a bit, got a bunch of loot from kills, killed an Epic tier enemy 13 levels higher than me without a problem, and opened up a couple chests I bought with currency earned in-game, rather than currency paid for with real money. I really don't see microtransactions becoming a problem. Shadow of Mordor got a bunch of criticism for being too easy, and basically allowing you to win every fight by only spamming deflect. Well, put that into practice, and you won't need to rely on paid loot crates to supply you with good enough gear to win fights.
Seriously, the game is really easy, and has three difficulty levels if you're doubting your ability to get through content.
So far I really like the changes they've made. Everything has levels and attributes now, like most ARPGs. It's pretty basic. One thing of a higher level has higher defense or attack than something of a lower level.
The main draw of the game is once again the Nemesis system, which is odd, because no other game that I know of has tried to copy it.
If anything, this game will fill the void in between now and Assassin's Creed: Origins.

As I type this review, I have 5 hours worth of time clocked in on this game and even now I still have an itch to play it despite having just stopped to type this. The game is fantastic and well deserving of the money I paid for it which was £9.99.
I'm not too sure exactly how to describe what the game is like but it's definitely in the same genre as the Binding of Isaac except instead of going from room to room and then down to the next floor, it's one big area full of enemies that you need to kill before going to the next level. Instead of tears, you use lovely guns of all shapes and sizes that do various nasty things. From the starting revolver (Katana/laser gun if you pick certain characters) to the shotgun that fires bullets out everywhere to the rocket launcher to the disc gun that fires out a rotating blade (Which can also hurt you) to laser based weapons to my personal favorite: The Sledgehammer.
The sledgehammer combined with the longer melee range perk and Corpses fly and hit harder perk, I can wreck enemies and it's so much fun.
Speaking of characters and perks, at the start of the game you pick a character to play as which range from all kinds of mutants that I'm not going to name off here. Just know that each character has their own special ability. One can roll dodge out of the way, One can use a shield, One can throw their weapon, One can explode corpses etc etc. My favorite character can eat his gun which replenishes ammo for various guns.  It definitely encourages trying everyone out to find the one you like the best.
The perks of the game work by killing enemies to pick up the green experience they drop until the meter in the left hand corner goes up a level and when you go into the exit portal, four options will appear for you to choose one from. These can be anything from some kills granting you hp/ammo to more melee range to some extra perma hp
I do have some issues with the game and it's that when you kill the last enemy, the exit portal pops up close by and when you get close it sucks you in. Sounds good? Yeah. Sounds good. But when I haven't finished picking up all the exp bits and looting the various chests, having the portal pop up to suck you in is quite the annoyance. Sometimes it even pops right up where you're standing so you just leave all the weapons, exp and ammo behind. If you run out of ammo and don't have a melee weapon on you then you may run for the nearest red chest and hope you don't die.
One of the other things is if you hit esc to pause the game while you're holding a direction then when you unpause, he'll keep running in that direction. The only way to fix it is to hold the direction and pause the game again. It's a minor thing but it can really screw you over during the more intense levels and when you're out in the open in general
Beside those, I love this game. Definitely try it out. If you're a fan of games like Binding of Isaac then you owe it to yourself to check it out.

Preliminary review:
The game offers incredible options for PC, the game goes into very nitty gritty details about your graphics card, and how each settings pulls on your hardware. Even by pure PC game standard, this is above and beyond anything I've seen before.
The game offers dynamic resolution scaling, it works well to keep you at a fixed FPS if your hardware struggles.
Cinematics are pre-rendered, which is great for people with lower hardware but can feel a bit out of place for people with good hardware.
As far as the game goes, the gameplay is very similar to Shadow of Mordor, but we get A LOT more tools to our kit. While in Shadow of Mordor, most progression was unlocking abilities that we should have had in the first place, this game gives you most of the staple abilities from the get go, only locking certain ones behind certain points in the story. The city really gets into too, it does summarize Shadow of Mordor... a bit too quickly. It wasn't a problem for me since I played the previous title, but someone jumping straight into Shadow of War might get a bit confused at first.
Will update once I have more time to play, but so far, the first city is great, that's one thing the first game lacked.

Featuring voice acting from an ensemble cast starring Corey Feldman, Karl Urban, John Cena, Keanu Reeves, Sharlto Copley, James Franco, Mila Kunis and Michael Pena as Fish.
Vlambeer delivers a gripping tale of self-discovery, love, and acceptance of the other, all underpinned by a prophetic warning of the dangers of the nuclear, climate change, and unregulated fracking. A must play.

The game is stunning. The sheer fun to play and learn orbital mechanics is the sole reason to buy it by any, even moderate space enthusiast. The vanilla game lacks numerous features, but the modding community is at its best supplying with the most of what you need (parts, scripts, missions, real stuff like solar systems, real mission equipment, mesh modifications, even interstellar travel). With little effort you can do space launches the right way; though scripted timed burns with the autopilot or proper plane fuel saving autopilot with altitude/heading hold etc., not the wacky space ride with thumb-rule throttle adjustments. Yet even these flights on manual will give you the feel of the orbital travel; a great teaching stuff.
Another great thing is that the developer really expands the game; some of the mod features make it into the game core; updates bring new stuff.
In the core the game is missing some concepts that might be bit lacking to hardcore space fans. The gravity computations model based on sphere of influence (you compute only gravity with the 1 object in which sphere of influence you're in; i.e. your craft is modeled either in respect to planet _or_ the moon), so not Lagrange points, halo orbits and perturbation instabilities. Creators are not planning to upgrade the model, as it would require core changes. Prolly that's why NASA is still using their own soft for sending probes ;)
The pros and cons of sandbox game are well known; you have lots of things to do, yet you have to set up you goals. Not much to write about, some like it, some doesn't.
I would encourage everyone to give this game a try; the creativity and shocking discoveries how the sky works will be very influential on you (whether you're 5 or 50).
+ Great teaching material (i would go as far as to make is optional tool for physics teacher)
+ Parts
+ Mods !!!
+ Freedom
+ Semi realistic gravity (no a StarWars-like "space")
- Simplified gravity model (no Lagrange points, perturbations and halo orbits)
- 1/10 scale might be too small for some
- animated kerbals-like world looks childish (no method to mod real humans)
- laggy when modded or with many parts flying (Unity-3D engine)
- sandbox game, so no big multi-mission objectives, you have to set these yourself

Wow... I just finished the game entirely, and it has to be the most powerful story game I've ever played. Let me list why.
(First part is from an artists perspective, scroll down if you just want the gameplay review)
I write a TON of stories and am fascinated by art. The amount of emotion revolving around the main character alone is incredible. I felt like I was in their shoes since the start. The way the game is structured, the episodes, the superpower- It all connects beautifully and incredibly. To think that there are people in the world going through similar situations in which they could have reversed time and changed something, it hurts. As much as it hurts, this game puts it in perspective as to how it would actually be. One little thing goes wrong and you destroy an entire city. Butterfly effect. I love the fact that literally every action can change the future. Perfectly and brilliantly laid out for a slightly old game.
I know there aren't very many hardcore 'artists' out there, so this section is for you. I find the gameplay to be extremely immersive, and the fact that every little action impacts the future, it adds onto that addicting and expectation factor. You may find yourself getting a bit emotional at parts (at least I did), but there is a thing called 'karma'. I think that gamers of all types will fall in love with this game, and the concept that you can rewind time and reality.
WOULD I BUY THE DLC FOR IT:
Ha, yeah. I bought the entire thing in a heartbeat; and it's only 5 U.S. Dollars. I find it impossible to play the first episode and not want to move onto the next ones right away. I suggest buying the DLC beforehand, as it takes a long time to download.
I thought I'd leave this in, just because I know that this game will heavily impact some people on an emotional level. If you're going through any type of drama or bullying, things will get better. You're worth more than what bullies tell you. Be happy they're targetting you; because they're so insecure about their lives that they have to push it onto people who seem better than them. Things will get better, and I know it's said a lot, but it's true. Stay strong.

The game offers incredible options for PC, the game goes into very nitty gritty details about your graphics card, and how each settings pulls on your hardware. Even by pure PC game standard, this is above and beyond anything I've seen before.
The game offers dynamic resolution scaling, it works well to keep you at a fixed FPS if your hardware struggles.
Cinematics are pre-rendered, which is great for people with lower hardware but can feel a bit out of place for people with good hardware.
As far as the game goes, the gameplay is very similar to Shadow of Mordor, but we get A LOT more tools to our kit. While in Shadow of Mordor, most progression was unlocking abilities that we should have had in the first place, this game gives you most of the staple abilities from the get go, only locking certain ones behind certain points in the story. The city really gets into too, it does summarize Shadow of Mordor... a bit too quickly. It wasn't a problem for me since I played the previous title, but someone jumping straight into Shadow of War might get a bit confused at first.
Will update once I have more time to play, but so far, the first city is great, that's one thing the first game lacked.

Multiplayer has been improved and optimized since Civilization V's popularity and with time and additional content, it may eclipse any older versions of the game.
It is a joy to watch everything come together as your civilization grows, from the strategic placement of districts to the tactical use of workers. The new changes to gameplay make your choices feel more important than they ever have, while also giving the player flexibity to work around bad starting locations and map generations. Civilizations have even more personality than previous titles with the inclusion of ethnic capital buildings, architectural design and unit variation. The amount of options in the unique leader abilities gives each civilization much needed flexibity in pursuing different win conditions. A must-try and definite on-sale buy for any fans or potential fans of the series.

At its core this game is a mystery game more than a walking simulator.  Great for mystery vets who pay attention to everything in the world around them.   While still being forgiving to players who arent walking Sherlock's due to the gameplay features that allow you to figure anything out one way or the other without having to care about anything in the game.  It is not an action game, but a story driven game similar to a telltale game with its choice mechanics.
The dialog and social dynamics as a slice of Americana are as real as can be like stepping into a modern Norman Rockwell painting.  The people feel real without that forced dialog or forced morality choices of other games.  No useless dialog preaching to the player makes this game a great choice for some real world escapism.  Outside the main characters, if there is a side character they can be interacted with or just ignored much like real life.  From the very start to the very end the same thing is there, no matter what changes, some things will always be there.
For any gamer looking to break up the monotony of same gaming, this can fill that gap.  Game can probably be completed in a couple sessions if just play right through like a rebel with no looking back.  If want to explore then there is alot of minutia to explore all excellently crafted fitting a real world setting which few if any games ever pull off.    Since the game can be completed quickly it has decent replayability to explore other options or just revisiting the world.
Being a story driven game makes it difficult to describe anything without spoilers.  Never bought into spoilers changing enjoyment a game, but google is a step away to get them.  Like anything in life even with spoilers of knowing what can happen, its always better to experience it than let life pass you by even if you know the final line or that crazy plot twist since its about the ride, not the destination.

Let me start by saying that in all the games I have played in recent memory, few have put me in control of a character as bad♥♥♥♥♥as a little girl. I mean it. The Walking Dead: Season 2 is essentially a simulator for kicking♥♥♥♥♥ and putting fools in their place.
Anyhow, I don't really need to go into the mechanics. You all played Season 1. If not, you've at least played a Telltale Games adventure before. If not, then welcome to video games.
Picking up not too long after Season 1, Clementine along with Christa and Omid make a pit-stop and -- surprise, surprise -- things don't go well. This is a theme in The Walking Dead, be it the comics, game, or TV show. If something good happens, two awful things will happen. If a character smiles, they'll be killed or eaten before you know it. This uncertainty shines in Season 2 -- in a way, moreso than in the first game. I'll get back to that in a moment.
Compared to Season 1, I didn't feel as much tension. I think the set pieces were more open, and the threat of humans and zombies -- particularly in the final two episodes -- seemed less than the original game. Also, despite the fractured state of the group in S1, we still felt like a group. These people were only a group in that they were clustered together, and I spent so much time telling them to shut up and work together, that I pretty much only cared for (not cared about -- there's a distinction) two characters by the end. Aside from Clem, of course. Toss in the fact that at any point, someone was going to disappear, and it seemed like even Telltale didn't want us to become too attached to folks.
To put it clearer, I didn't like the secondary and tertiary characters as much as S1, and the same goes for the setting, pacing, and plot, and -- as mentioned above -- set pieces.
So, I didn't like S2, right? Wrong.
This was still an enjoyable game, with interesting characters, compelling choices and action, and -- at times -- very good writing. Sure, it didn't captivate me like S1 or even The Wolf Among Us, but that's a knock against nearly every adventure game on the market.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game, and hope that you either find the same enjoyment as I did, or even more. Happy gaming!

The game's been getting a lot of flak due to news regarding it having microtransactions despite it being largely a single-player game with a season pass, with some hints of online PvP (not fighting other people, but attacking their bases and killing the AI they setup there).
I understand where this flak is coming from. It's a shame the devs or their publisher decided a game without free post-launch support needed both a season pass and loot boxes, but that's the way publishers are headed now.
I've played it a bit, got a bunch of loot from kills, killed an Epic tier enemy 13 levels higher than me without a problem, and opened up a couple chests I bought with currency earned in-game, rather than currency paid for with real money. I really don't see microtransactions becoming a problem. Shadow of Mordor got a bunch of criticism for being too easy, and basically allowing you to win every fight by only spamming deflect. Well, put that into practice, and you won't need to rely on paid loot crates to supply you with good enough gear to win fights.
Seriously, the game is really easy, and has three difficulty levels if you're doubting your ability to get through content.
So far I really like the changes they've made. Everything has levels and attributes now, like most ARPGs. It's pretty basic. One thing of a higher level has higher defense or attack than something of a lower level.
The main draw of the game is once again the Nemesis system, which is odd, because no other game that I know of has tried to copy it.
If anything, this game will fill the void in between now and Assassin's Creed: Origins.

The game is stunning. The sheer fun to play and learn orbital mechanics is the sole reason to buy it by any, even moderate space enthusiast. The vanilla game lacks numerous features, but the modding community is at its best supplying with the most of what you need (parts, scripts, missions, real stuff like solar systems, real mission equipment, mesh modifications, even interstellar travel). With little effort you can do space launches the right way; though scripted timed burns with the autopilot or proper plane fuel saving autopilot with altitude/heading hold etc., not the wacky space ride with thumb-rule throttle adjustments. Yet even these flights on manual will give you the feel of the orbital travel; a great teaching stuff.
Another great thing is that the developer really expands the game; some of the mod features make it into the game core; updates bring new stuff.
In the core the game is missing some concepts that might be bit lacking to hardcore space fans. The gravity computations model based on sphere of influence (you compute only gravity with the 1 object in which sphere of influence you're in; i.e. your craft is modeled either in respect to planet _or_ the moon), so not Lagrange points, halo orbits and perturbation instabilities. Creators are not planning to upgrade the model, as it would require core changes. Prolly that's why NASA is still using their own soft for sending probes ;)
The pros and cons of sandbox game are well known; you have lots of things to do, yet you have to set up you goals. Not much to write about, some like it, some doesn't.
I would encourage everyone to give this game a try; the creativity and shocking discoveries how the sky works will be very influential on you (whether you're 5 or 50).
+ Great teaching material (i would go as far as to make is optional tool for physics teacher)
+ Parts
+ Mods !!!
+ Freedom
+ Semi realistic gravity (no a StarWars-like "space")
- Simplified gravity model (no Lagrange points, perturbations and halo orbits)
- 1/10 scale might be too small for some
- animated kerbals-like world looks childish (no method to mod real humans)
- laggy when modded or with many parts flying (Unity-3D engine)
- sandbox game, so no big multi-mission objectives, you have to set these yourself

At its core this game is a mystery game more than a walking simulator.  Great for mystery vets who pay attention to everything in the world around them.   While still being forgiving to players who arent walking Sherlock's due to the gameplay features that allow you to figure anything out one way or the other without having to care about anything in the game.  It is not an action game, but a story driven game similar to a telltale game with its choice mechanics.
The dialog and social dynamics as a slice of Americana are as real as can be like stepping into a modern Norman Rockwell painting.  The people feel real without that forced dialog or forced morality choices of other games.  No useless dialog preaching to the player makes this game a great choice for some real world escapism.  Outside the main characters, if there is a side character they can be interacted with or just ignored much like real life.  From the very start to the very end the same thing is there, no matter what changes, some things will always be there.
For any gamer looking to break up the monotony of same gaming, this can fill that gap.  Game can probably be completed in a couple sessions if just play right through like a rebel with no looking back.  If want to explore then there is alot of minutia to explore all excellently crafted fitting a real world setting which few if any games ever pull off.    Since the game can be completed quickly it has decent replayability to explore other options or just revisiting the world.
Being a story driven game makes it difficult to describe anything without spoilers.  Never bought into spoilers changing enjoyment a game, but google is a step away to get them.  Like anything in life even with spoilers of knowing what can happen, its always better to experience it than let life pass you by even if you know the final line or that crazy plot twist since its about the ride, not the destination.
Rating for Mystery Game Fans: 11/10 Value: $24.99
Rating Non Mystery Game Fans:  9/10  Value:  $19.99
(Anything under $9.99 shouldnt leave any regrets....)

Sure you have, we all had it but this guy had it extreme, say for 3 years? Couldn't write a single paragraph, apparently.

The long anticipated follow up to Walking Dead Season 1 that won all kinds of awards and accolades from critics and gamers alike. So how does the sequel shape-up?
I did enjoy my time with the game, but honestly I’d have to say that the first Season was superior. The characterization was much stronger in the previous game, as more opportunities were given to see your party grow and develop. People like Ben, Kenny, Clementine, Lily, Carly and others were extremely memorable (So much so, that I remembered each of their names after 2 years since my playthrough). In Season 2, I have to admit, I had to look up several characters names just because they weren’t interacted with as much. Not to say that Season 2 doesn’t have interesting characters like Jane, The Person Who Returns from the Previous Season, and Rebecca, It doesn’t seem right that I can remember everyone’s name in the first Season, and yet hardly anyone’s name in Season 2.
Another thing I found worse about Season 2 is that it lacked…focus. Season 1 seemed to have clear events and was perfectly paced. I never felt a single episode was too long or too short in Season 1 (and in fact, wanted to play more of it.) Every event and interaction had a purpose and they didn’t stay around longer than they needed to. With Season 2 however, episodes 4 and 5 in particular seems to go on aimlessly. Some of the interactions in 4 could be cut and nothing would be lost. An Example would be the searching for supplies in the War Memorial. The Russians in Episode 4 also seemed to have no exact purpose or foreshadowing and came across as random to me when they appeared. Episode 5’s ending definitely did not need to be as long as it did, and its events definitely seemed to be a curveball in regards to the previous episodes. It definitely did not resolve the many hanging plot threads (which most likely will be saved for the next season).
Also, another thing I should mention is character deaths. I won’t go too in-depth about them to keep this a spoiler free review but…this time around the deaths are pretty forced. (An example would be a character deaths that occurred near the climax of the episode involving a Lake). In fact, the ending involves the death of a character that can be summed up as a misunderstanding. It was very anti-climactic and like the writers were trying to force conflict.
Finally, I should also mention that your choices really don’t matter in this game. It is a very good story, but every choice you make will just make a character say something differently or acknowledge that “You did say that, didn’t you!”. This criticism can also be applied to Walking Dead Season 1 as well, but I felt that in Season 2 it was much more apparent. You make a choice to save one character and they end up dying either way, even the exact way as the other choice. It’s something I thought Telltale would have improved on, but I guess not. Hopefully they do it for Season 3.
This is not a review that’s calling the game trash, but just acknowledging its faults. I did enjoy my time with the game, but it surely didn’t leave the impact that Season 1 did (though to be fair, that would be hard to top).
