So I went into this game a little skeptical. I'd heard plenty of times that people thought this game was amazing, and I wasn't sure it'd really deliver. The short answer: OH BOY did it deliver.
But if you're actually reading the reviews you probably want to hear more than that. So here's my two cents.
First off, I have to say that the story is incredibly awesome. At first I was a little put off by the overall "artsyness" but that quickly changed as I got sucked in. The complexity of the story gradually ramps up until the ending, which was, in my playthrugh at least, an absolute mindf*ck.
Why does it get so complex, you might ask? Simply put, the main character discovers she has the abilty to rewind time to a certain degree. This is used very well and frequently throughout both the gameplay and the story to create a rather unique and interesting experience. For example, it allows you to make chioce A in a conversation, check out how it goes, and if you don't like it, you can just rewind. This i limited, though. After you leave an area, you cannot reset your actions there, making your choices meaningful.
That brings me to another point. The game allows you to make a LOT of choices, ranging from what you choose to have for breakfast to deciding wether people live or die.
Something that is also important to mention is that at some points this game will make you cry like a little b*tch. Seriously. Prepare your feels.
Lastly, the protagonist and I have the same first name.
10/10, will definitely play again

One of the best stories you will find in a game.  Perfectly paced, amazing narrative, and the episodic format is done to perfection.  The greatest video game example of well executed psychological horror.
The game play doesn't vary from one episode to the next, but it doesn't need to.  It's a simple formula: expose the dark presence beings to light, and shoot them with your revolver, shotgun, or rifle.  It sounds like it could get stagnant, but it doesn't.  There are multiple different methods of exposing the dark presence to light (varying flashlights, flares, flashbangs, flare guns, spotlights, etc.), and the way you're presented with exposure keeps the game play fresh.
There's no real loot system other than picking up batteries for your flashlight, or ammunition for your weapons.  There are no stats to distribute.  There is no real map.  But that's not what the game is about.
I've run out of space, but I could write a review of this game that goes on for pages.  Just play it.

Don't listen to all the people complaining about this game.  In my opinion, civ 6 is a lot better than its predecessors.  At the time of this review I have 74 hours into the game, with probably at least another 100-200 more, and that is probably more than I put into all of the other civ games combined.
I wanted to write a review of my experience between Civ 6 and the previous civ games.  I have played the civ series from civ 2 to current, putting approx. 50-100 in each.
The 2 biggest issues with the civ games is that they ended up being repetitious & boring and most of them had a level of micromanagement that I did not like.  Of the previous civ games, I liked Civilization Revolution (PS3) the best.  Honestly, I was going to pass on civ 6 because I felt it was more of the same.  I bought it on the 50% off deluxe sale card.
Once I started playing it, I noticed there were a lot of concepts that were different, virtually all I like.  One negative I always had with the civ games is that you would create "mega" cities that had everything.  Civ 6 eliminated this because of the districts.  In order to build a library you need a campus district, a temple/religious district, etc....  The district takes up a physical tile, and has potential adjacency bonuses, which makes every city unique.
Wonders now have a lot of prerequisites.  If you want to build Stonehenge, you have to be next to stone.  Pyramids, you must be on a desert tile and on flat land.  Also, they take up a physical tile.  This also eliminates the mega city because even if you had all the prerequisites you could only physically build so many in a particular city.
The builders how have limited amount of uses and for me that is a good thing.  In previous civ games, I always either ignored the builders or deleted them because they were an annoyance.  Now, at least for me, they serve a better purpose.
The tech trees.  Now there are 2 with the standard science, but now also cultural.  So your culture points are used for more than just expanding territory.  And they both have boosts, which if attained, reduces your research time by half.  Most things you will do anyway, like farm a plot or kill 3 barbarians.  The other thing about the tech trees is that you can switch to research another tech/culture without penalty.  This can let you research until the boost is activated, then stop so when you get the boost, you get the tect/culture automatically.
The same goes for building units/districts/buildings or wonders in a city.  You can start building something, stop and start something else, and come back to it later.  In the case of districts or wonders, the tile will look like it is under construction.
The different bonuses that each civilization has makes them more unique.  France is geared toward culture, Macadon toward war.  For me, this a real positive.
The barbarians were overhauled and can really mess you up in the early game because they have scouts and can send units to wreak havoc.  The City States were also overhauled.  For me, this makes City States more useful (In civ 5 I would normally play with no City States because they were annoying).
Religion was also overhauled.  This makes religion a lot more interesting, but at the same time you can completely ignore it if you want to.
This gets into my only real complaint about the game.  The devs wanted to make war more undesirable so they created the warmonger penalties and Casus Belli.  This is a good concept, it just needs to get more flushed out.  It is supposed to keep you from just declaring war on everyone all the time.  What it ends up doing is the AI declares war on you, you defend yourself, take one of their cities (because they deserved it) and you get warmonger penalties for an extremely long time.
The same goes with the AI agendas.  These are characteristics that each of the AI's will have.  China, for example, does not like it when you build wonders.  And when you have more than them, they will pretty much hate you for the entire game.  When you are going for Domination victory, this is not an issue, but it is for the others.

Before I give you my review, I feel it is necessary to give a background about myself. I got Paladins in closed beta a while ago, when it was relatively new. I found it through a twitch stream and the streamer gave me a key, at the time I didn't realize how easy it was to get one, but was thankful regardless. I installed the game, played it, but was turned off quite quick due to my low fps. It was a few months later I got back into the game, figuring out the fps problem. I started really enjoying the game, and became a mildly competitive player participating in a few ESL matches and Summer Circuits under the Organization Voltage. I mainly played Bomb King, Drogoz, and for lulz, Pip. However, shortly after me and my bud Eclips3 were picked up, the Organization let the Paladins branch go, and we were ultimately a group of 5 players. We all went our separate ways shortly after, besides me and Eclips3.
[Why I quit]
A few weeks after, CB30 was released. I was so hyped for the update, and as soon as I could I downloaded it. I joined a game, and for the most part, was disappointed. There were some good things about it, which I will mention. However, the cons heavily outweighed the pros. Things I didn't like about CB30 include:
Removal of the Old maps - Without the big, open, maps, the game just didn't have that Paladins feel to it. They replaced them with new, smaller, more fast pace combat maps. That was a little disheartening imo.
The TTK - Dear god, I could write about this for hours. The TTK (Time to Kill) was severely lowered, making it almost impossible to escape when caught off guard. Before, a player had time to use his mobility ability, get behind a corner, rejuvenate health, and either fight back or regroup with the team. With the new TTK, that simply wasn't possible.
Mounts - One iconic thing about Paladins were the mounts. They were used to get from the base to the objective quicker, and were also used as a third person view to look around a corner. With CB30, those were taken out and you were very limited with your mount. Instead, they added portables and the mount time was forced meaning you couldn't get back on after it automatically unmounted you. They took a very unique thing in Paladins and watered it down, when no one asked for it.
Now there were obviously good things about it. I will unintentionally contradict myself with some of the good things I put about it, but I am merely saying they were good concepts, not that I liked them.
Makoa - Many people will say Makoa was a copy from Roadhog in Overwatch. As much as people want to compare the two, you can't expect games with a similar genre to have "inspirations" from the other if you will. Makoa is a unique character that has many unique abilities providing fresh gameplay and something different.
New UI System - Was way more designed, fluid, and less buggy than the previous UI. Props to them.
Faster Paced Gameplay - Although I didn't agree with it, it did seem good on paper. The biggest competitor with Paladins is Overwatch. Maybe to draw in more people they changed the fps style to a faster pace, lure in the people who couldn't afford Overwatch? Although the older players heavily shunned upon it, the new gameplay style could have been fairly worked with and made more fun, and that's where things got better.
Obviously, the cons heavily outweighed the pros, and I simply didn't see Paladins anymore. I saw a poor man Overwatch, despite (to my belief) Hi-Rez definitely didn't want to be compared to Overwatch. The games are significantly different, Overwatch is an FPS with MOBA elements, Paladins is/was a MOBA with FPS elements. Since I didn't see the game that way, I quit playing for a long time...
[ Open Beta Review]
And then, months later, I see Paladins has been released on Steam. And within 5 days, the game reached the top 3 F2P Games on Steam Store. Even 8 days after release, it is still top 3. However I doubt there is a chance it will top TF2, Paladins will just stay at the 3rd spot. With so many downloads, I was a little curious if the game got better. I made a post a few days ago wondering if it was worth downloading from Steam, and the answer went along the lines of, "with the growth of players, it's worth checking out again." I was curious, and decided to test that curiosity. As soon as it was downloaded and updated, I loaded the game. The UI was very impressive and dynamic. It was a little confusing at first having not played so long, but it was fairly easy to understand. I found a game relatively quick, something I didn't notice back when I played so long ago. The champion screen was also innovative, something I was fond of. I noticed competitive mode was locked until 12 or more champions were master 4, and despite me having so much experience in the game, I only focused on a few characters, which I was a little glad about considering so many have changed. Note I have tried every champion so I knew how they played and what they were good at. Wanting to try competitive mode, I immediately hopped on champions I never played much. I started with Grohk, and since the last time I played him, he changed completely. He is definitely not as big of a damage dealer than what he once was, but more of a support character and healer. I definitely dig the change. More characters worth noting that I now like in which I didn't like before:
Barik - Didn't like the feel to him, seemed to be a character that lacked compared to others. However, he is particularly fun now and with the TF2 skin you can get for him, a lot more new players are trying him out.
Ruckus - By far one of the worst champions I've ever seen. When I used to play, no one played Ruckus as, like Barik IMO, lacked so much. Had a slow windup for his rapid fire that barely dealt dps, felt really immobile, just a relatively boring character. He has changed a lot and is actually really good if you know how to use him, and he is a really fun champion now, something that I like.
I have tried others but I'll leave it at them two. The fps style is more or less the same as CB30, again, a style I wasn't fond of. However, it definitely seems they polished it making it way more fun and exhilarating to play. Mounts are back with some restrictions, TTK still somewhat low but definitely improved since CB30. The game felt like a sped up version of Paladins and didn't have the same Paladins feel I had prior to CB30, but this new Paladins has a version I like more than the old style. It is fast paced, but still slow. It is still relatively quick to kill, but still slow enough to escape, regroup, and fight back. Full on 5v5s are also a lot more exciting with the narrow map designs. I can definitely say I like the way Paladins is now, it has that vibe the old Paladins has, not necessarily in the way the game plays, but the aspect of fun. Coming back to Paladins was definitely a decision I don't regret and with the amount of players its raking in, I can't wait to see where it will go next. If you read the entire thing, I personally thank you. Leave your opinion in the comments and leave some discussions, I'm down to converse about Paladins. If you want to add me my IGN is: isotopeee
[TLDR]
Skeptical about coming back to Paladins after quitting when CB30 was released. Despite skepticism, came back anyways and wasn't disappointed. Innovative gameplay, UI, more players, and much more made the game more fun. Glad I came back...

This is a fantastic game.
Nuclear Throne is a frenetic shooter with randomly generated levels. Think Binding of Isaac with a post-apocalyptic mutant-cowboy bullet-hell vibe.
Keyboard and mouse controls are slick (gamepads are for consoles), though it is locked at 30fps. If you suffer simulation sickness, as I do, you may find it better to play in short bursts. Fortunately it caters for that.
Loot is random - as are the skills (mutations) you choose from each time you level up. There are a number of characters to play as, each with radically different styles and there are different modes to activate (crowns) which mean there's a seemingly endless variety of ways to play the game. (My personal favourite is playing as Melting with an explosive weapon and boiling veins). Better yet, there's a Daily Quest mode, which keeps you coming back and keeps you in contact with the rest of the community - who are decent and helpful and especially prone to drawing fantastic fan-art.
+ This game is hard
+ Daily quests
+ Inventive characters and design
+ Intuitive controls
+ Randomness means infinite variety and replayability
- 30fps
- This game is hard

That's not much once you fall into grinding characters you like. What really stands out about the game is the character customization, specifically the card abilities that other FPS games don't have. For example, I have a loudout (card combination) for my Pip that increases self-heals for however many team mates I catch in the area of my healing ability. It's more than just "Character A" versus "Character B." It's "Tank with defensive boosts" versus "DPS with increased damage off Ability X." This system gives the game a new depth others lack and better replayability.

I didn't play the first season of the walking dead.  Playing the 2nd season was less than exciting by not having any background on the whole environment of the game. Maybe if I'd played the first one I would not be playing the 2nd one.  This is the first adventure game, and probably my last, where I was constantly dreading the arrival of the endgame.  It was clear throughout the story that, no matter what choices you make through the game, you're not going to arrive at a happily-ever-after scenario.   Depressing and antagonistically so...but that's the nature of these zombie apocalypse stories.  The price on the game was right but I'm not a fan of lesser-of-10-evils outcomes and non-stop, pain-and-suffering, episode slogging.  If you're a hard core fan of the TV series, you won't see any of the characters you're familiar with.   If I was a fan of this genre of slow death via depression games I'd give it 5 stars.  I'm not.  2 of 5 stars is my rating because it graphically and physically handled the material well.   Barring that, the game would have been 0 of 5 stars.

It's a bit hard for me to write the review of KSP with the limited gameplay I have, but I doubt I'll play it a lot more. And that's the reason why I can't recommend a game for 40 Euro. 40 Euro is supposed to give me more fun than 15 hours.
So why do I give up? It is still fun, and a lot of things that I am nowhere near of achieving, but it all comes down to how fun I find the flight simulation to be. This part is crucial to your success. I have the capacity to build a rocket to take me to the moon, but I as a player am not good enough at piloting it (yet) because I find it boring. And a lot of the things I still can do feels like grinding chores for scraps (or play sandbox mode with endless resources but where's the fun in that?).
In conclusion, if you like flight simulation of space shuttles, go ahead and get this one. But if you don't, save your money. Watching your carefully crafted rockets explode at takeoff and later achieve a wobbly, elliptical orbit that eventually slams it into the atmosphere at astronomic speed is only that much fun before it becomes frustrating.
By hearsay, mods make things a lot better. But there's no steam workshop so I haven't tried them yet. If my playtime goes well above the 15 hours I have now, it's likely to be from playing with mods - and I won't change my recommendation based on mods.

This is a fantastic game.
Nuclear Throne is a frenetic shooter with randomly generated levels. Think Binding of Isaac with a post-apocalyptic mutant-cowboy bullet-hell vibe.
Keyboard and mouse controls are slick (gamepads are for consoles), though it is locked at 30fps. If you suffer simulation sickness, as I do, you may find it better to play in short bursts. Fortunately it caters for that.
Loot is random - as are the skills (mutations) you choose from each time you level up. There are a number of characters to play as, each with radically different styles and there are different modes to activate (crowns) which mean there's a seemingly endless variety of ways to play the game. (My personal favourite is playing as Melting with an explosive weapon and boiling veins). Better yet, there's a Daily Quest mode, which keeps you coming back and keeps you in contact with the rest of the community - who are decent and helpful and especially prone to drawing fantastic fan-art.
+ This game is hard
+ Daily quests
+ Inventive characters and design
+ Intuitive controls
+ Randomness means infinite variety and replayability
- 30fps
- This game is hard

This was a terrific follow up to an amazing game, and I can’t wait for season three.

[Life is Strange] is a wonderful game. I had a blast playing the full package, start to end. I heard the hype of LiS, but I was skeptical because it didn't "look" like a game; the studio behind it -- I've never heard of them, etc.
But I am a huge fan of games with a good, solid story. LiS delivers on that front despite the sometimes awkward (cringe) script depicting the supposed melodrama of hipster America/Oregon high school students.
_Cons_ would have to be those cringey moments of outdated slangs and references that you can't help but cringe or laugh that "I can't believe they wrote that." Graphics are more of stylish than realistic -- it has that instagram or painted look to it. It's not sharp like Telltale's, but the graphics and art direction (of hipster America) sets the mellow mood LiS is going for.
_Pros_ are obviously the story ep 1 - 5 goes for. My favorite was ep 4. There's plenty of emotional punches for players to enjoy and cry to :) I really like the statistics of which choices all the players who've played LiS have done. You can compare which camp you, the player, ended up in. That, I feel, adds to the replay value. Choices DO matter here (HUZZAH!!) from ep 1 - 5. The "inconsequential" choices do add up - not just the major choices, but the dialogue options as well.
As I played more and more, the emotional stakes went up; I felt for and were invested in the characters. The main story and emotional return from being so invested was enough to keep me interested despite the laughable lines here and there.

Note: This game is polarizing and I will give my best ability to not give an unbiased review.
What this game does right is captivating the audience into playing more. The game is set in an episodic story arc, weird for a video game, but Alan Wake pulls it off. It is not like The Walking Dead Episodic series, but instead each chapter is broken into the episodic format. At the beginning of each episode (excluding episode one) is a recap of the previous episode. If you are like me and you continue to play through the game, then the recap is not really needed, but it does keep the tone of the game. At times these recaps are helpful when it comes to remembering the plot or just returning back to the game. At the end of each episode, the credits roll and a song is playing. Once you skip or let the credits roll, the game will send you to the next episode.
The story overall is fantastic and the game’s writers knew what they wanted for the game. These writers are famous for writing the first two Max Payne games, so the majority of the story is told through Alan Wake, the protagonist, as the narrator. The story is about Alan Wake, a successful writer who suffers from writer’s block. He and his wife, Alice, go to Bright Falls, where they vacation to clear Alan’s mind. Then in their stay, Alice is pulled into the darkness and it is up to Alan to save her. Along the way Alan discovers manuscripts of his work in progress, Departure which tells a chilling story of events, and Alan realizes that whatever is on these pages will happen in the real world. This short summary of what is to come in Alan Wake.
The gameplay is a story of its own. The basic mechanics of Alan Wake are to get from point A to point B with enemies and puzzles to get in the way. Fighting enemies in this game are not in the traditional sense. The theme of Alan Wake is Darkness, and the ironically named Bright Falls is being taken over by the Darkness. The Darkness consumes people and Alan Wake has to shine light from his flashlight on his enemies to clear the Darkness from them before he can shoot and kill them. Not only does Alan Wake fight, but he has a dodging mechanic to where he ducks and weaves from his enemies that either attack or throw tools at him. This feature, like Max Payne’s shoot dodge, is used a lot to avoid enemies.
Now what this game does poorly is its character expression during cut scenes. The character development is awesome and the models are great, but when the characters speak, their lips and face are awkward enough to question the games programming, but it is not so bad that it takes away from the experience of the game. Another complaint is the PC port has a couple of glitches when I played, but Remedy remedied that (lol). Also the gameplay to a certain degree is a bit tedious. The running from point A to point B while doing rendered the same actions over and over is a little bit redundant at times, but there is enough variety in between these segments to make it not boring. Ultimately, the story is what saved Alan Wake from being a generic third person game to being a great experience overall. The story is what keeps you playing; the story is what makes you care for the characters; the story is what drives the gameplay home. You cannot go wrong with purchasing this game.

One thing that needs to be said about this game and I feel hasn't been stated by the developer or other reviewers well enough is this: this game is very very hard. It is probably one of the hardest games you will ever play.
The thing about this game is that it
be enjoyed by everyone, but the people that will enjoy it the
are the hardcore skilled players who want a challenge. I don't usually say this when reccomending a game, but if you are not very good at video games, you will probably not like Nuclear Throne. You can die almost instantly to just a small cluster of bullets, to one explosion, or something you didn't see which can leave you confused and angry. Trust me, that last one happens a lot. And when you die, there are no checkpoints, it's game over. Back to the very beginning.
In addition to this difficulty, the game has a ton of content that is only accessible if you progress very far. Meaning if you don't do well, you won't have as much of an in-depth experience as some better players will.
If you are a skilled player looking for a very challenging game that you will player for many hours, pick up Nuclear Throne. Vlambeer have done a great job at updating this game very often, so your money will surely not go to waste.

This is my first review of any game on Steam so, the short version is: BUY THIS GAME if you can because it is awesome and you'll have tons of hours of fun.
Now, for the long version...
Although I highly recommend this game, I must first start with the main negative aspects, which could make you refuse to buy it.
First of all, it is a highly scientific game, which will require of you hours and hours of watching youtube videos of other people explaining what is what in this game. The in-game tutorials aren't very helpful (at least for me), too short and barely scratch the surface. Luckily, the community is extraordinary and you will find a lot of help in many places. You will need to learn a lot of physics and other aerospace stuff to understand the game, which in its essence is cool but for many, a game is a reason to relax, not to learn complicated things. So, you will have to do a lot of research before you can play the game well. Its tutorials aren't going to help you very much.
Second, it is quite buggy even now, in 1.2. Especially if you use mods, it will crash to desktop a lot of times so save often. And even though it doesn't look much, the graphics require a good PC. But played stock, 4 GB of RAM are plenty.
Now, for the good part.
It is a hugely entertaining and educating game. You will learn a lot about how hard was it for the early pioneers of NASA to get a hang of launching stuff into space. Of course it is far from reality, but you will get a pretty good idea of it. At least, you'll get closer to it than with any other simulator. You will have to start from scratch, learning how to launch a rocket, how to build a plane, how to take into account the center of weight vs center of lift stuff, you will deploy sattelites built by your own hands (click by click), you will visit other worlds, plot courses that require enough celestial mechanics knowledge on your part. Your way of thinking will CHANGE.
If you are passionate about astronomy, this is your game. If you are passionate about astrophysics, this is your game. If you love building stuff, being patient enough to see them explode then rethink them, if you love learning thousands of things about planes and rockets, THIS IS YOUR GAME.
There are many detailed reviews about the game, here on Steam and elsewhere. The game is worth every penny so try saving some cash or just buy it, plain and simple. I've spent 60+ hours on Steam and at least 100 before that on another version of the game. I've barely scratched the surface. It keeps me up at night, making me plan for my next contraption and my next launch. So...
WARNING: It is highly addictive! At least, if you're into this kind of games. I uninstalled it and reinstalled it at least 10-15 times but I keep getting back to it. It is by far the most interesting, challenging and rewarding game (all together) I've played in my life.
Now... If this hasn't convinced you to buy it, just read the other reviews on this page. I'm just a newbie, but others have more comprehensive opinions about the game that will convince you this game is worth the money. I've got mine from♥♥♥♥♥at half the price but if I have had the money, I would've payed the full price or double. It's a lot of work inside a very beautiful game.
So...
As a final note: 95/100. Hard to learn, very hard to master, fun to play and addictive to discover its secrets. BUY IT.

This game is about strategy, flexibility, and timing
For example:
STRATEGY: You need to figure out how to kill four guys in one room armed with shotguns and crowbars with your bare hands (or a knife if you're lucky)
FLEXIBILITY: These guys will walk around the room, sometimes in a pattern, sometimes not in a pattern. You're going to have to deal with them if they start walking into a different room or turn around at the last second. It happens, be ready for it.
TIMING: When to bust in with a gun and when not to bust in with a gun. The difference is between life and death.
Eventually you will hone these skills (and probably more) to clear out entire floors of guys with nothing but a crowbar and a cheap mask from the dollar store.
That's gameplay, but I've got the say the style of this game is amazing. I love the music, the backgrounds, the colours, the masks, it's just got so much flavour and passion put into it. Also if you love digital blood, this game has you covered.
Overall this game isn't for everyone, but I highly recommend it if you like challenging games, being a badass, or dressup.

In a single playthrough, this managed to become one of my favorite games of all time.
I went in expecting a survival horror game with a unique light-based mechanic, and was quickly sucked into a compelling and real world from which I emerged feeling as if I'd lived the game, rather than played it.
The visuals of this game do an amazing job of reproducing the Pacific Northwest, in which I've spent quite a bit of time. The sound is perfect; enemies are scary, the voice acting is awesome and the music is so good that I purchased the soundtrack separately. (Poets of the Fall are awesome as always.)
I finished the game and spent several days just dwelling on my experience. I don't want to spoil the ending but it's... unconventional. Let the world draw you in and live it. It's worth every minute.
Lastly, this is not a much-too-common lazy console port. Remedy clearly cares about the PC gamers and patched this game quite a bit to add optimizations based on PC feedback. That's important!
[Edit: Just nominated for The “Whoooaaaaaaa, dude!” Award in the 2016 Steam Awards]

One thing that needs to be said about this game and I feel hasn't been stated by the developer or other reviewers well enough is this: this game is very very hard. It is probably one of the hardest games you will ever play.
The thing about this game is that it
be enjoyed by everyone, but the people that will enjoy it the
are the hardcore skilled players who want a challenge. I don't usually say this when reccomending a game, but if you are not very good at video games, you will probably not like Nuclear Throne. You can die almost instantly to just a small cluster of bullets, to one explosion, or something you didn't see which can leave you confused and angry. Trust me, that last one happens a lot. And when you die, there are no checkpoints, it's game over. Back to the very beginning.
In addition to this difficulty, the game has a ton of content that is only accessible if you progress very far. Meaning if you don't do well, you won't have as much of an in-depth experience as some better players will.
If you are a skilled player looking for a very challenging game that you will player for many hours, pick up Nuclear Throne. Vlambeer have done a great job at updating this game very often, so your money will surely not go to waste.

I’ve seen AI cities crank out units during war while still somehow working on wonders simultaneously even while being flat broke.

Maybe the AI has been sending apostles to convert your cities for the last 4,000 years even after you asked them to stop. God forbid you kill one of them on your boarder and cause one of their cities to convert to your religion. They will still be declaring war on your over it a thousand years later. Maybe they ask you to stop spying on them, three turns after you kill one of their spies in your capital. On and on.
No matter what leader you have or what leaders you are fighting or what victory condition you are going for there is only one path forward: Total War. You will cheese of someone no matter what. Going for a science victory and have a lot of science? That will bunch up someones panties. Same deal with cultural victories. We don’t even need to mention religion. You could be on the other side of the earth, having never met a civ and they will discover you, denounce you, and declare war on you within a dozen turns of each other.
"features", poor design decisions, abuses, and stupidity. If your city is completely surrounded by enemy units, you have a unit in the city defending, and you produce a second unit, bam, you just broke the game. You won't be able to end your turn because Civ 6 doesn't allow stacked units. You won't be able to move the unit because there will be no open space, so you are stuck, reload an autosave and do somethign different. That bug has been around since Civ 5 and they still haven't fixed it. There are also issues with moving units into the fog of war (double stacking when it shouldn’t) and rounding errors in combat calculations (an attack saying I should kill the defending unit yet it lives with 1 HP). I once eliminated a civ on turn 2 (yes, turn two), because it put our starting points within sight of each other. I captured their settler with my single warrior even though they started with extra warriors (which AI get start with ‘King’ difficulty). This is all before we get into production bonus policies that allow you or the AI to crank out certain types of units in 1-2 turns indefinitely during early game. It was even worse when the game lanuched. You could sell units for money even though they were half used up, about to get captured, or destroyed by the enemy.

Really boring. Once your cities are massive the end game is just a slog of micromanagement. Already researched all technologies? Well, you’d still going to have to select ‘Future Technology’ every turn for some reason. Want to bang out a bunch of units in a city? There is no production queue feature anymore so you have to select the next unit every time you finish one. Have a civilization five times stronger than anyone else in the modern age? Pericles is still going to declare war on you every 15 turns, even though they have 1 city and a spearman, because you had the audacity to be friendlier with city states than him. Once you pass a certain age every civ is the same, every game is the same, and it gets tired.
They almost never build any kind of navy (even though they "improved" that in the last major patch) and only seem to understand mass invasion. Set up a pinch point or have a well defender boarder and they will happily throw themselves into the meat grinder for turn after turn until they sue for peace. They don’t understand the strength and weaknesses of units either. You could have a line of spearman set up on your boarder and they will happily throw their horseman into it because that is the kind of unit they like building.

Here's the thing about Hotline Miami
You're going to die
A LOT
So I won't recommend this game if you don't have a good amount of paitence
This game is about strategy, flexibility, and timing
For example:
STRATEGY: You need to figure out how to kill four guys in one room armed with shotguns and crowbars with your bare hands (or a knife if you're lucky)
FLEXIBILITY: These guys will walk around the room, sometimes in a pattern, sometimes not in a pattern. You're going to have to deal with them if they start walking into a different room or turn around at the last second. It happens, be ready for it.
TIMING: When to bust in with a gun and when not to bust in with a gun. The difference is between life and death.
Eventually you will hone these skills (and probably more) to clear out entire floors of guys with nothing but a crowbar and a cheap mask from the dollar store.
That's gameplay, but I've got the say the style of this game is amazing. I love the music, the backgrounds, the colours, the masks, it's just got so much flavour and passion put into it. Also if you love digital blood, this game has you covered.
Overall this game isn't for everyone, but I highly recommend it if you like challenging games, being a badass, or dressup.

I bought this game back when it was in Beta, and even then, when it was just a sandbox game with zero "goals", it was still one of the best games that I've ever played.  If you are one of those curious types (curious about how things work) that likes to create and experiment and build things and test if they work...this game is for you.  I thought I understood how space travel worked, until I played this game.  Wow, this game will help you to understand space travel, orbital mechanics, physics, and more like only astronauts can.  It really is the kind of game that will make you smarter.  AND, it's a lot of fun.
There IS a learning curve, as you figure out how to construct the rockets, how to do multi-staging, etc.  I'd recommend to follow NASA's lead and start small.  Make a rocket that can get into orbit.  Next, go for something multi-stage that can get out to the Mun.  Then, try to get a lander out there and figure out how to land on the Mun.  Once you get to this point, you should understand enough to open up the whole solar system to exploration.  One of my biggest challenges that I gave myself was landing a craft on one of Jool's atmospheric moons, right on the beach, so that I could have an epic morninig view of Jool while I drank my Kerbilian coffee every day.
But really, this game is awesome.  The music is so pitch perfect and gives a sense of awe and wonder, kind of like the opening music of Blade Runner.  I have spent hundreds of hours just playing around in sandbox mode, thinking of a concept for a spacecraft and then seeing if I could build and launch it.  Building a super-heavy house-sized lander and trying to get it out to and land on Minmus... this kind of experimentation is what is so rewarding about this game.  A great game for  young kids who like to build things, in my opinion, but equally great for anyone who likes this type of game.
BEWARE:  it requires attention span and is not action packed.  Just be aware.

A classic in the making as far as the survival horror genre is concerned. You play the character of Alan Wake, a once successful writer who has hit a proverbial dry-patch as far as his creative juices are concerned. With his wife he embarks on a holiday, her attempt to get his creative talent back on track. On arriving at a beautiful spot at a lake on the edge of a forest, things start to unravel for Wake as he's plunged into a living nightmare. Tense from the beginning, this is brilliantly insightful story. You fight for your life as you are plunged into a world thats difficult to work out what's reality and are plunged headlong into a story you never wrote.. Gripping stuff that pushes boundaries. On the PC its visually top notch, especially for a game that was first released in 2010. Play at night in the dark with headphones on. Limited resources and a unique enemy concept make the game a real challenge, even in normal mode!
Its often on Steam Sale - if you see it for £10 or less grab it you wont be disappointed!

I bought this game back when it was in Beta, and even then, when it was just a sandbox game with zero "goals", it was still one of the best games that I've ever played.  If you are one of those curious types (curious about how things work) that likes to create and experiment and build things and test if they work...this game is for you.  I thought I understood how space travel worked, until I played this game.  Wow, this game will help you to understand space travel, orbital mechanics, physics, and more like only astronauts can.  It really is the kind of game that will make you smarter.  AND, it's a lot of fun.
There IS a learning curve, as you figure out how to construct the rockets, how to do multi-staging, etc.  I'd recommend to follow NASA's lead and start small.  Make a rocket that can get into orbit.  Next, go for something multi-stage that can get out to the Mun.  Then, try to get a lander out there and figure out how to land on the Mun.  Once you get to this point, you should understand enough to open up the whole solar system to exploration.  One of my biggest challenges that I gave myself was landing a craft on one of Jool's atmospheric moons, right on the beach, so that I could have an epic morninig view of Jool while I drank my Kerbilian coffee every day.
But really, this game is awesome.  The music is so pitch perfect and gives a sense of awe and wonder, kind of like the opening music of Blade Runner.  I have spent hundreds of hours just playing around in sandbox mode, thinking of a concept for a spacecraft and then seeing if I could build and launch it.  Building a super-heavy house-sized lander and trying to get it out to and land on Minmus... this kind of experimentation is what is so rewarding about this game.  A great game for  young kids who like to build things, in my opinion, but equally great for anyone who likes this type of game.
BEWARE:  it requires attention span and is not action packed.  Just be aware.
Not without its flaws but over all a really fun, engaging and entertaining game.

There are a lot of Easter Eggs in this game and tie ins to the media I listed above.  If you like story based adventure games pick this up.  It can be rather slow and controls take some practice, bear in mind this is a more casual laid back game with a few hair raising turns inside awaiting your discovery!

A game I recommend, but with caveats aplenty.
My biggest beef with LiS is that despite the entire premise of the game being "your choices matter so pick them carefully," there are only two endings and it depends entirely on the very last choice you make, leaving me questioning whether any of my choices really mattered much at all. Some of the choices play out in radically different ways than you'd expect, which is arguably an example of innovative storytelling and was exciting and interesting in theory, but sometimes just made me feel like I was being punished for trying to be nice or help people. YMMV.
Another big issue for me is that most of the substance of the game just seems to be about punishing the protagonist and her loved ones for no other reason than "the universe is nonsensically cruel". You do your best to mitigate (or exacerbate, if you want to have that kind of playthrough) the damage done, but as is required for the game to follow its prescribed plotline, most of the really bad things happen anyway and you're left reeling in the aftermath. All good stories need inciting crises and high stakes to be interesting in the slightest, but the plotline of LiS seems in rather poor taste given that most of the bad consequences happen to teen girls, an already struggling and vulnerable bunch as this game is quick to show; it's possible it could be one of those "drawing attention to real-life crises" situations, but given how much the supernatural aspects of the game keep being pushed, it comes off more as some sort of blunt reminder that "life sucks (especially if you're a teen girl) and then you die."
All the same, I have to say it's still a worthwhile experience more or less. The characters are enjoyable for the most part and have realistic issues to deal with, problems most of us have faced in some form or another, which makes all but the most "villainous" ones (for lack of a better description) sympathetic and likable to some degree or another. One of the game's strongest points is how the factors of lighting, music, and dialogue work extremely well together to catch you up in whatever mood is relevant to the current part of the story, whether that's nostalgia, sorrow, anxiety, etc. As others have said before me, the story escalates from minute one and then just keeps on escalating, far beyond what many would expect, so you're in for a wild ride for sure.

I bought this game back when it was in Beta, and even then, when it was just a sandbox game with zero "goals", it was still one of the best games that I've ever played.  If you are one of those curious types (curious about how things work) that likes to create and experiment and build things and test if they work...this game is for you.  I thought I understood how space travel worked, until I played this game.  Wow, this game will help you to understand space travel, orbital mechanics, physics, and more like only astronauts can.  It really is the kind of game that will make you smarter.  AND, it's a lot of fun.
There IS a learning curve, as you figure out how to construct the rockets, how to do multi-staging, etc.  I'd recommend to follow NASA's lead and start small.  Make a rocket that can get into orbit.  Next, go for something multi-stage that can get out to the Mun.  Then, try to get a lander out there and figure out how to land on the Mun.  Once you get to this point, you should understand enough to open up the whole solar system to exploration.  One of my biggest challenges that I gave myself was landing a craft on one of Jool's atmospheric moons, right on the beach, so that I could have an epic morninig view of Jool while I drank my Kerbilian coffee every day.
But really, this game is awesome.  The music is so pitch perfect and gives a sense of awe and wonder, kind of like the opening music of Blade Runner.  I have spent hundreds of hours just playing around in sandbox mode, thinking of a concept for a spacecraft and then seeing if I could build and launch it.  Building a super-heavy house-sized lander and trying to get it out to and land on Minmus... this kind of experimentation is what is so rewarding about this game.  A great game for  young kids who like to build things, in my opinion, but equally great for anyone who likes this type of game.
BEWARE:  it requires attention span and is not action packed.  Just be aware.

The graphics look good, not a huge improvement over Civ 5 but they do look nice.
The Civilizations are well planned, although some feel way more powerful than others like the Germans and the Australians.
The new boost system for technologies and civics is really cool and being able to switch between civics instead of having a set group of bonuses is awesome.
The different types of governments are unique and give powerful bonuses to whatever goal you have for the game.
Except for the mainstays like England, Rome, Germany and Russia, the DLC civilizations seem to be chosen at random. It's not really important though since you can use Mods to get around this, as long as you can slog through the billions of anime related civs.
When you select a site to build a district at, there is no cancel button or even a relocate button. This is ridiculous and should be changed as soon as possible. In multiplayer games, if you accidentally select the wrong spot the only way to solve the problem is to restart the entire game or just accept that you f'd up and play with a handicap for the rest of the game. If this seems like a balance issue, you can always add penalties to relocating them, (i.e. it takes half the production spent to relocate it to the new spot.)
The A.I. needs a improvement. Currently, a "higher difficulty" consists of giving the AI a bigger boost to their base production, science, etc. instead of a computer player that actually fights wars better or builds stronger cities. When the AI builds a city, they give almost no consideration as to how productive or successful they will be. They almost always build them right on the closest acceptable tile to their starting city.
When I play Civ VI, a lot of the maps have a similar feel to them and I don't get very many unique feeling games overall.
The AI seems predisposed to causing total war on any human controlled civilization that does not immediately send a delegation to them, the AI does this regardless of their relative technology level and likelihood of success.
The AI blames civilizations that get attacked, giving warmongering penalties even when they are defending themselves against a surprise or formal war declaration.
The Diplomacy screen for each civilization is  well done, but could use way more information such as the length of time you have been at peace, if you have been denounced, what turn it happened and when the denouncement will run out and what city states they are at war with.
Finding out what resources you are currently trading is a chore, if you look at the way it was done in Civ 4 it is incredibly easy to see the things you are trading but in this one you have to scroll through each resource in a huge list to see if you are already trading it to someone.
I'd rate this as maybe the second best Civ in the series, only because the AI sucks so badly - hopefully they will work on it for a while instead of releasing DLCs and scenarios.

3) I like that the cities are not easy to take down, especially with the barbarians coming out earlier and more aggressive.

5) I like the attempt of making the religion aspect of the game more relevant.
Cons:
1) The computer warfare AI is the worst. I almost want to spend the time training my 6 year old to play this game because I think he would be a better adversary than the Civ VI AI.

A game I recommend, but with caveats aplenty.
My biggest beef with LiS is that despite the entire premise of the game being "your choices matter so pick them carefully," there are only two endings and it depends entirely on the very last choice you make, leaving me questioning whether any of my choices really mattered much at all. Some of the choices play out in radically different ways than you'd expect, which is arguably an example of innovative storytelling and was exciting and interesting in theory, but sometimes just made me feel like I was being punished for trying to be nice or help people. YMMV.
Another big issue for me is that most of the substance of the game just seems to be about punishing the protagonist and her loved ones for no other reason than "the universe is nonsensically cruel". You do your best to mitigate (or exacerbate, if you want to have that kind of playthrough) the damage done, but as is required for the game to follow its prescribed plotline, most of the really bad things happen anyway and you're left reeling in the aftermath. All good stories need inciting crises and high stakes to be interesting in the slightest, but the plotline of LiS seems in rather poor taste given that most of the bad consequences happen to teen girls, an already struggling and vulnerable bunch as this game is quick to show; it's possible it could be one of those "drawing attention to real-life crises" situations, but given how much the supernatural aspects of the game keep being pushed, it comes off more as some sort of blunt reminder that "life sucks (especially if you're a teen girl) and then you die."
All the same, I have to say it's still a worthwhile experience more or less. The characters are enjoyable for the most part and have realistic issues to deal with, problems most of us have faced in some form or another, which makes all but the most "villainous" ones (for lack of a better description) sympathetic and likable to some degree or another. One of the game's strongest points is how the factors of lighting, music, and dialogue work extremely well together to catch you up in whatever mood is relevant to the current part of the story, whether that's nostalgia, sorrow, anxiety, etc. As others have said before me, the story escalates from minute one and then just keeps on escalating, far beyond what many would expect, so you're in for a wild ride for sure.

Having played Civ II, IV, and V I mixed feelings about this version. The graphics look great, and some of the new things like districts are nice, but VI has what I call micromanagment creep. In V you'd just let your builders do their thing and it was no big deal. In VI you only get to build so many improvements depending on buffs that you might have, and they disappear. Road building is a pita, where it was pretty simple in V. The leaders animations are overly cartoonish for my tastes. I cringe everytime a leader scene pops up. The worst thing to me is that the AI sometimes will blatantly cheat. Last night I was playing a game as Roosevelt (USA leader) and I was attacked by barbarians with the Rough Rider unit, which is supposed to be the USA's unique special unit. There are plenty of other documented cases about the flaws, and the blatant cheating by the AI in this game, so I suggest googling, "CIV VI AI cheats."
I'm going to say that I don't recommend this game because it is so long that it really is a single player game, but if you have a group of friends that you can actually play with, then the multiplayer is fun.

If you ever wanted something more from life, a story that could make you smile, laugh but also reach so far deep into your heart and mind so you truely felt the game connect to you... this is just that.
Every character is memorable, every action and decision feels heart warming or heart wrenchingly difficult to make.
The Walking Dead is not so much a game as it is an experience - gameplay mechanics its an action point-and-click which serves well for what it is: a truely interactive story where every decision DOES actually count towards something, sometimes its just something minor but every single step in the story is a step that YOU took to save, help or in some way try to survive because the characters you either do or do not agree with but you always want to survive.
About games like The Walking Dead, both season 1 and 2 ... you can't write a review, all you can say is this: if you want more from your games than a yearly FPS or a competitive multiplayer or survival-sandbox game... to not own and have experienced the amazingly well written stories by TellTale demonstrated as in The Walking Dead is a real loss.
Should you buy The Walking Dead: Season 2?
You should already own The Walking Dead: Season 1, the 400 days DLC AND The Walking Dead: Season 2 if you have any love for amazingly well written stories.

All in all a great game if you like insanely fast top-down brawlers, and don`t mind the brutality and trippy graphics.

Original review:
Awesome game, fantastic simulation but lacks polish, documentation and it's plagued by technical problems. It crashes in the most annoying, least opportune moments: when clicking on "Recover Vessel" and during landings in general so you lose whatever data you have stored from a long mission in a blink of an eye. I just did my second Mun expedition. I had about 100 Science stored on board and the game crashed as the landing chutes deployed. I am running the 64bit version.
Like many early access games it suffers from terrible documentation problems. Most videos and tutorials are outdated by several years and finding updated help takes a fair amount of internet searching. Their own Wiki suffers from "migration problems" - whatever that means, I guess it means it's outdated and broken . By its very nature the game is difficult and really needs well organized documentation which is, unfortunately, severely lacking.
If you have a video or tutorial out there that is applicable to older version of the game, please take a moment to delete it. It's not hepful any more! Same is happening with Elite and couple of other games. The internet is sfull of useless, outdated tutorials.
In game help is also abysmal. Forums are unhelpful either as most people assume you should know what you're doing and there is also a lot of inacurate and outdated information, most sticky posts are from 2014 and you have to sift through pages of useless posts to find the updated bits you need.
Controls need some work too. Precise manouver adjustment is impossible. I read there are mods for this, but something like this needs to work out o fthe box.
Frequent crashes and poor documentation really destroy the experience that could have been rather awesome otherwise. Knowing that the game may crash upon landing really discourages me from long expeditions.
The smartphone quality graphics don't help either. I know this game is not about looks, but seriously, the graphics need some work. RIght now it's something you'd expect to see in 3 year old smartphone game. Higher quality graphics would help with immersion, right now the planet surface is plain and ugly, smoke and light effects are laughable.
I wish I could give this game a neutral review, because I can't honestly give it Thumbs Up due to crashes, bad graphics and poor documenattion

Finally on its rightful platform, Alan Wake does not disappoint. Upon first loading the game, given you have the proper computer to run it, the graphics of this game will blow you away. The extra work put into this PC port shows very, very well. The music is also appropriately atmospheric without being afraid to switch to intense whenever needed and the licensed music really just rocks. Whereas some may be disappointed that this title isn't truly a horror game, rather than an action adventure with horror elements, the solid level design and especially lethally engaging storyline more than make up for it. The only true fault with the game is its limited enemy design, having hardly 6 enemies to fight throughout the entire game does wear a bit thin despite how hard the developers tried to change things up.

This is a followup to my season 1 and 400 Day DLC review.  I paid roughly 3 dollars for it.
Ever wonder what would happen if Telltale became so high on their own ideas and so disgusted by players influencing their first Walking Dead game, that they might just make a sequel with even less player agency?  If so, you must have an overactive imagination because not even I was able to predict this.
Again, I do not mind little choice so long as I like the story to a degree.  I have played quite a few games that were narrative based only with minimal gameplay.  However, they marketed choice and consequence...yet when it came time to make the game they seem to only have added consequence.  This game will make you look and feel like the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for the smallest thing.  Speaking of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, what is up with this cast?  This cast of characters is by far worse than season 1, worse than the first two seasons of the television show.  How do you even accomplish that?  I felt very little towards them when I finished the game.  Initially, I was drawn in by it all.  I even got an ending that I did enjoy...which funnily enough was one of the "least popular endings".  Yeah, I forgot to mention in previous reviews that these games have logistics to see if you made choices that fit with the crowd or didn't.
The best part of this game was Clementine, but she's not a very good lead.  Since she's a kid, she barely has any influence on what goes on around her.  I get what they were going for, but this is no good for a choice based franchise.  Her dialogue got mixed reactions out of me.  It's nowhere near the quality of season 1.
The writing in general varies from decent to downright awful.  I ask again, what happened?
I was genuinely excited for this game.  A sequel to a decent game.  One of my favorite characters from the first game playing the lead, an all new story to make at least some choices with, the possibility of more salt lick?  Sign me up!
Well...now I want my name off the list.  If you liked the first game and the DLC more than life itself or a lot more than I did, get this game.  I'm still going to recommend it to people who played the first season and want something to do.  However, it did NOTHING for me.  It did less than nothing.  What scares me is that from some of the reviews I've been reading of the Game of Thrones game, the Tales from Borderlands, and even The Wolf Among Us to an extent, not much has changed.  I don't think I'll be playing season 3.  If I do, then I'd buy that for a dollar.

This is the story of Jeb Kermin
Jeb wanted his entire life to become an astronaut. He'd look into the stars each night and think, "One day." With the arrival of the new Kerbal Space Program, Jeb didn't hesitate. He was the only willing pilot in the lot that offered to join. Jeb traversed dangerous missions of small hunks of metal launched at high velocities. Jeb endured it all, explosions, heat reaching the thousands of degree. Jeb endured.
One day, Jeb was offered a special mission. "We're gonna get you into orbit." said the commander.
Jeb crawled into the rocket, the rocket of Icarus. Strapping himself into the pod, he prepared the final checks before launching once more into Kermin's sky. As he exited the atmosphere and entered into space, as he had before, Jeb couldn't help but feel worry. Something was not right.
Looking at his live orbit map revealed a terrifying sight. Rather than circle Kermin, Jeb was destined to sail straight on...into space. Jeb's heart sank as the engines stopped. He had no fuel.
Time passed. Days. Months. Maybe a year. Jeb didn't know. His orbit map revealed finally a circle.
A circle around the sun. Jeb had entered space at such a velocity, he missed Kermin's orbit, and rather caught the sun.
He was to sail past three different planets, including Kermin, to orbit the sun.
Jeb felt no pain. He felt no sadness. Jeb looked on at the flaming ball of gas that was his new home. He smiled, for Jeb had the life he always wanted. To traverse the stars, see the planets.
Icarus had succeeded. History repeated.
Jeb was with the stars.
UPDATE:
Years have passed. All electricity in the pod have drained. For seemingly forever, Jeb floated high above the sun in a never ending circle. Tiring of the pod, Jeb prepared to make his mark on history.
Jeb strapped on his suit and ejected from the pod. He took a deep breath as he closed his eyes, letting go of the ladder holding him from safety. He drifted away, unsure of his destination. Unable to control himself, Jeb closed his eyes as he soared through the stars, drifting both higher and lower than the mysterious Eeloo, on the farthest reaches of the system.
A frozen tear drifted down Jeb's eye as he floated away, never once again seeing another planet. No Kerbin. No Mun. Only the Sun.
Jeb was unsure of what would happen. Jeb didn't mind. He would endure. He would survive.
Or Icarus would win.

Over a 1,000 hours played now. So i think I can post a review with a degree of credibility, even as a poor player of the game.
I really enjoyed this next evolution of Civ. And it is an evolution rather than an augment of Civ V.
Civ had to change (again).  While the addition of districts and other new features are far from perfect, they represent a significant investment in rethinkning the game rather than merely an upgrade of artwork and UI. And they offer a great platform to develop Civ into an ever more sophisticated franchise. Distinct, as it should be, from city and kingdom building-element seen in other 4x games. To a degree that Civ really warrants a genre of its own.
I'm glad that Civ hasn't followed the Total War and Endless franchises into greater focus on unit engagement. I'm sure that Civ VII will look to refine the new elements in the title and return demographic reports (please). But i really hope by Civ X, Firaxis have made greater strides to develop more sophisticated mechanisms to influence economy, culture, science and politics within the game.
That said there is a lot to enjoy in the game, perhaps without the voice talents of Sean Bean. Despite what you may have read go and buy a copy.

Making Clem the playable protagonist also puts her in the postion for YOU to control all of her choices, which means the devs couldn't give her any real personality to speak of. Worth checking out for people who are already fans, but I am on the fence about giving the series another shot in the inevitable sequel.

Even if you are tired of doing the same thing over and over, you can increase the difficulty by selecting different game changers (Crowns) that change the way you'll play the game.
Sure there are a few bugs in the game, but every game has them and sure, the game can eventually get repetitive, but so does every game. And you can easily adjust the difficulty by selecting different crowns.

To conclude this review, I would definately recommend buying Nuclear Throne if you are looking for something different and want a good challenge.

Season two also keeps its signature quick-time events intact, and if you hated them in season one, you’re going to hate them here, too. When you’re not navigating The Walking Dead’s myriad life-ruining decisions, you’re mashing buttons or matching on-screen directional prompts to avoid bandits or shambling zombies. Like the plot, these QTEs certainly feel like you’re doing something, and they definitely spice up the action, but they occur far too frequently, and your input is way too basic to be anything more than contrivance at best, and the red arrows have a tendency to blend in with all the action on screen, leading to more than a few frustrating restarts.
Even with its hiccups, season two of The Walking Dead is absolutely worth playing, with an interesting cast of characters and a narrative that is still sufficiently gripping despite its less interesting parts. It’s not quite game of the year material, and it doesn’t feel as necessary as season one, but Telltale proves that Clementine’s story is one well worth continuing.

Over a 1,000 hours played now. So i think I can post a review with a degree of credibility, even as a poor player of the game.
I really enjoyed this next evolution of Civ. And it is an evolution rather than an augment of Civ V.
Civ had to change (again).  While the addition of districts and other new features are far from perfect, they represent a significant investment in rethinkning the game rather than merely an upgrade of artwork and UI. And they offer a great platform to develop Civ into an ever more sophisticated franchise. Distinct, as it should be, from city and kingdom building-element seen in other 4x games. To a degree that Civ really warrants a genre of its own.
I'm glad that Civ hasn't followed the Total War and Endless franchises into greater focus on unit engagement. I'm sure that Civ VII will look to refine the new elements in the title and return demographic reports (please). But i really hope by Civ X, Firaxis have made greater strides to develop more sophisticated mechanisms to influence economy, culture, science and politics within the game.
That said there is a lot to enjoy in the game, perhaps without the voice talents of Sean Bean. Despite what you may have read go and buy a copy.

An entertaining hybrid of shmup and rpg tied together with reasonably diverting fluff and art.  The combination of shoot'n'dodge and character builder really emphasizes the complexity and importance of decision-making.   I like it.  It's a game to play with music pumping and wanting to get pumped up in 10 minutes- if you can make it even one play through.  I'd almost say it's an excellent lunchbreak speed-game in the sense of Strange Adventures in Infinite Space.  Semi-spoilers ah.. it's obvious that the draw is long-lasting complexity and high-skill ceiling, not tweests, right?
The shooting and movement is very well-executed.  Combined with the screen shake, the experience is intense and embracing.   The situations you find yourself in vary a great deal, a consequence of weapon variety, enemy attack types, and  character's and talents.
Balance, particularly for talents, is beta from my perspective.  I've been playing YV and Steroids, who both feature high-dps and emphasis on weapon combos, which could color my opinion.    The playstyle varies quite a bit between characters due to a variety of unique characteristics.  If I were better at dodging, I might prefer characters that are required to dodge more bullets due to comparatively low dps and talents that do little to shorten or ease a fight or improve my ability to panic spam.  Many of those heroes have traits that improve their resources.  Anyway, it is beta and balance is indisuptably a work in progress.
A significant example of the design philosophy is the cursed weapons available at this time.  If you pick them up, you can only exchange them for other cursed weapons.  You get more ammo for those weapons though.  This is a principle that pervades the game; even though talents are never generally bad, they are very often situationally useless.  What good is  a bonus to energy weapon damage or kinetic ammo supply if you don't have those weapons?    Optimization in specific utility (for short-term survival or situations that are not sustainable or easily achievable) or for general viability of your build are very important and I'd hazard most players will spent some time at the inter-level level screen, simple as it is.
It was worth it at $12 for me, but if you want it for less, it won't go on sale until after release.

It’s another one of those times when you curse Valve for not including the “Neutral” option. Life is Strange, while not being horrible, is not particularly great either.
In narrative focused games I look for three main qualities that will make my experience an enjoyable one or not. Those are: interesting, tightly held together narrative, likeable characters with interesting dialogue and interaction between themselves, and enough gameplay mechanics and player’s agency to drive some unique of qualities home. Life is Strange mostly delivers in the last element with its time rewind mechanics, leaving other aspects with much to be desired.
While not very impactful in the grand scheme of things, Max’s (main character’s) time powers bring enough novelty to mix things in certain situations. Wouldn’t it be interesting if one could have a power to erase their mistakes? The idea itself fuels both the imagination of many people and the game’s many plot points. While developers wasted a few opportunities which this concept provides they didn’t miss all the marks. You have some freedom in using the time rewind in very unique ways and often times it feels pretty fun to be able to “cheat” your way out of certain situations, like changing decisions after hindsight of previously unforeseen consequences.
Unfortunately both the overall plot and cast falls flat for me. Characters and the dialogue are the biggest offenders. The former are extremely one-dimensional, cartoon cutouts with names and bad teen-school drama personalities attached. Max is as bland as the next Ubisoft title, that rarely shows any characterization and spews incredibly cheesy one-liners that writers thought are cool and common for that age. Main character’s best friend Chloe also shows signs of being pretty cliché and unlikeable, but fortunately she is developed during the later episodes making her a little bit better in my eyes… just until she's becoming the most important plot device in the whole story near the end and it doesn’t happen gracefully.
The whole experience is made even more unrelatable with the web of pretty mediocre and forcefully hip dialogue. This circus ends up being quite hard to be attached to, especially when the plot’s pace is snail-like, logic behind its more wibbly-wobbly parts breaks apart under closer examination and all the
are all superficial as you would expect from a Telltale-like game. This is a real shame since some of the presented scenes, interactions and dialogue show signs of genuine effort and care put into them and it's for those moments that I kept playing until the end. This is why I labeled this review as “Neutral”. Despite everything, I still cared
for the cast, so I will give credit where credit is due.
Unquestionably one of the stronger parts of the game is the artstyle. I really dig the graphics which are humble from the technical standpoint, but still allow to present some quite impressive looking scenes with correct use of color, perspective and painting-like textures. Life is Strange looks pretty nice and no amount of poor music choices can change that. I’m absolutely not impressed by the licensed indie soundtrack featured in the game. Songs are sappy, uninspiring and make the game even bigger hipster-bait than it already is. Original soundtrack is mostly a-okay in the comparison.
In the end, I was quite unimpressed by the experience. It will certainly hit in the feels for no small group of people, but you need to be correctly attuned to it first if you want to get some enjoyment from it. It all depends if you like games in this style, like Oxenfree or Night in the Woods. Unfortunately, the latter example blows Life is Strange out of the water with more clever and relatable dialogue, so even between its peers Life is Strange ends up as a hard sale in my opinion.
The good thing is that the first episode is free. You still can rewind the time spend on reading this review and try it out yourself to form your own opinion. Maybe you will be more lucky than me?

This is about as close as you'll get to a proper solar-system space sim. There are others out there (Orbiter springs to mind) but this one defines the genre, really. Be warned... while it is extremely addictive, it also has a very steep learning curve.
Don't be fooled by the cute little green guys. KSP is a thinking-person's space sim... not an arcade/action game.
You can't just strap rockets onto a command module and go walking around on the moon. You have to plan trajectories, manage your thrust, fuel, angle of entry, rocket stages, the works.
It uses a decent (not perfect, but decent) physics model which gives a good idea of atmospheric interaction, gravity, thrust effects, etc... your rockets will flip, wobble, snap, explode and tumble uncontrollably far more than they'll fly straight... but mainly because you've messed something up.
When you manage that perfect launch, travel and landing, and watch your little fellow skipping about on the moon (Mun), the effort it took to get there, and all of the learning you had to do (and there will be learning) makes it all the more satisfying.
If you really want to know what this one is like before you buy it, go check out the Scott Manley Kerbal Space Program videos on YouTube. There are a lot of them, and not only are they entertaining, but they're a gold-mine of information about how to do stuff.
Graphically it is a bit average, but you can get a few decent (free) mods which improve this dramatically.  Ditto with audio, though there's a certain visceral charm in the "THUMP!" your engines give when you activate them.  Control is mouse and keyboard - but you'll be getting to grips with pitch, roll and yaw for a little while. It's not just point and click.

A few days have passed after I finished the game, and I'm still emotionally agitated. The story and the characters dragged me deep into the world that is "Life is Strange".
Similar to the Telltale games, Life is Strange is an interactive tale, which tells you a mostly linear story. The player character "Max" has the ability to turn back time for a few moments, or, later in the game, going far back in time to any moment in her life, by looking on one of her photos. This is quite similar to the movie "The Butterfly Effect".
You're playing a teenage/young adult character on a high school and therefore you're confronted with typically high school problems. Besides mastering your daily school problems, the main goal of the story is to find a vanished girl. This kinda reminded me of the "Veronica Mars" series, because you do all these little detective like stuff.
Another great thing in the game are the characters. I can't remember of a single dull character. Every person had a unique and interesting personality, even the story-unimportant ones. Especially Max' friend (or sidekick) Chloe will grow fond on you.
The wonderful Soundtrack alongside with the atmospheric art style lets you stare at the monitor and enjoy the little things in life (is strange).
Overall a clear recommandation if you like high school drama, with the theory of time travel ala Butterfly Effect.

- Mouse sensitivity does not seem to be saved. The value you saved is displayed correctly, but the sensitivity level is still set to Max (pun intended) and you have to re-set it after every load.

Pros:
- Everything else. Buy this, play it multiple times. It is worth every cent.

There is so much to love about CIV VI. The new multi-hex city development is fantastic, a vast improvement on the old ‘single hex’ city. You now have to plan, and think ahead as to how you will develop your city. The way builders now work, while feeling odd at first, now makes sense. Again, a huge improvement.
But, and I am afraid it is a big but. Diplomacy. Not only is it childish on occasions, as to why a CIV declares war on you, it blatantly lies to you. Then you get the ‘Diplomacy Spam’. Politely refuse to allow a CIV into your capitol, and they will come back almost every three or four turns and keep asking you. Not annoying and doesn’t break immersion? Try creating a custom single player game with the max allowed A.I. CIVs. It’s verging on unplayable. The full screen displomacy uses, adds to this frustration.
Then we have that old chestnut Religion. It’s just not worth the effort to create one. Your cities will get swamped relentlessly, as A.I. CIVs constantly swamp your land in order to convert your cities.
CIV VI has the potential to be the greatest CIV game ever. But right now, it’s a long way off and a missed opportunity.
As I have to either recommend it or not, I cannot in all honesty fully recommend it. In reality, its somewhere in between the two.
EDIT
One thing I forgot to mention. The initial civ starting positions. It’s ludicrous. You can have a huge size map but the civs will all be right close in to you. Huge swathes of land will be completely empty. There is no space.
Edit 2
Religion has indeed improved. That has to be said.
