There seems to be a preoccupation with the designers of this game to to place an overwhelming emphasis on scarcity, on play mechanics that constantly remind players that they will never get strong enough, wealthy enough, or cultured enough to feel like they've accomplished something. Everything in Civ 6 feels stifling and limited, from terrain limitations and population limits, to resource and ammenity scarcity and a lack of diplomatic options.
Putting aside all of the game's technical faults, the fundamentally broken AI, the arduous loading times, and all the other niggling glitches throughout, the crucial fault of Civ 6 is it's lack of imagination, scope, and grandeur. The graphic design is insipid and messy, with cities that never quite come together no matter how advanced you become and leader animations that look like a mobile game. You don't feel like you're controlling an entire civilization; you just feel like you're moving pieces in a board game, battling the AI or other players for points instead of societal progress in some form, be it culture or domination. Any feelings you have about the historical or cultural background of any of the civs or their leaders is pointless, as this does nothing for the game.
Civ 6 has a lot of problems, even more than I've laid out here in this rant, but it's biggest sin is that it's boring.

I know I'm going to get♥♥♥♥♥♥for this but here it goes.
I would put a neutral if I could for this game. As it stands I really really want to give it a humbs up but can't. Ever since it left EA, every time I update the game it gets worse. In v 0.9 rockets were really great to fly and planes were not. In 1.0, planes got much easier to fly, but rockets can't. Now neither planes nor rockets fly accurately. The aerodynamics and atmospheric physics models are so♥♥♥♥♥♥poor that every other aspect of the game is eclipsed by it.
- In real life, rockets with fins, (barring winds, etc) should go up, then come back down at the same orientation, or at 180 degrees depending on center of mass. In KSP, somehow my rockets end up moving sideways.. after deploying 4 parachutes and seeming stable in its orientation. Then it starting spinning everywhere. And that was just a little rocket. Last time I flew any bigger ones, they all had to do 360 degree flips before continuing up to orbit.
- In real life, things don't just fall apart in mid air at fairly low velocities. Things like an engine just.. falling off for no reason. Stuff explodes if it so much as taps the ground. Other stuff explodes for no reason. Kerbals can bump into solar panels and shatter them (learned that the hard way). Also, anything taller than the average house bends quite ferociously unless you cover it with struts. The cheats that stop this from happening end up making it more realistic until you bounce off the ground unscathed from a 50 m/s collision.
- The camera used to be fine. Now it wobbles like crazy even in smooth flight. How the hell do you manage to ruin the camera of all things?
- Speaking of wobbling, why do my ground vehicles constantly wobble left and right when I'm certain that the wheels are all facing straight forward? Or maybe they're just slightly off, it's not like they have an alignment tool to help.
- Pretty sure v 0.9 had more stock parts in many sections. The latest update made my favorite set of wheels a casualty.
- Mod support seems to be wavering
- Landing in water at a moderate velocity doesn't just completely destroy your vessel, it basically erases it from existance. All those costly science parts carrying data for your next research upgrade? Deleted, with no way of getting them back.
If I can't fly planes or rockets as is in the current verison I may as well uninstall... can't get a refund now (steam isn't showing my hours correctly, I have much more than ~26). The game forces you to micromanage stuff that you shouldn't have to worry about. The flight models are deplorable. Without mods, there are very few parts, so you can't use as much of your imagination as it looks like up front. It's not that the game is too hard, I'm okay with that. But difficulty shouldn't come at the expense of realism. It should be hard to design a system that can go from Kerbin to Jool, but it shouldn't be hard to get something to go straight up and down without tumbling to oblivion. I shouldn't have to cheat just so that my vehicle doesn't magically disassemble itself at perfectly reasonable speeds. If they fix the flight model, I'd give this a thumbs up because everything else can at least be shut off, modded or overlooked but if the core of a game is fundamentally broken, there isn't anything that can make up for it. I will update the review if it gets better.
Edit: Further, a handful of KSP developers left Squad due to long hours with dismally low wages. According to past employees, Squad treated them like dirt. These guys don't deserve the money, please help spread the word.

It’s another one of those times when you curse Valve for not including the “Neutral” option. Life is Strange, while not being horrible, is not particularly great either.
In narrative focused games I look for three main qualities that will make my experience an enjoyable one or not. Those are: interesting, tightly held together narrative, likeable characters with interesting dialogue and interaction between themselves, and enough gameplay mechanics and player’s agency to drive some unique of qualities home. Life is Strange mostly delivers in the last element with its time rewind mechanics, leaving other aspects with much to be desired.
While not very impactful in the grand scheme of things, Max’s (main character’s) time powers bring enough novelty to mix things in certain situations. Wouldn’t it be interesting if one could have a power to erase their mistakes? The idea itself fuels both the imagination of many people and the game’s many plot points. While developers wasted a few opportunities which this concept provides they didn’t miss all the marks. You have some freedom in using the time rewind in very unique ways and often times it feels pretty fun to be able to “cheat” your way out of certain situations, like changing decisions after hindsight of previously unforeseen consequences.
Unfortunately both the overall plot and cast falls flat for me. Characters and the dialogue are the biggest offenders. The former are extremely one-dimensional, cartoon cutouts with names and bad teen-school drama personalities attached. Max is as bland as the next Ubisoft title, that rarely shows any characterization and spews incredibly cheesy one-liners that writers thought are cool and common for that age. Main character’s best friend Chloe also shows signs of being pretty cliché and unlikeable, but fortunately she is developed during the later episodes making her a little bit better in my eyes… just until she's becoming the most important plot device in the whole story near the end and it doesn’t happen gracefully.
The whole experience is made even more unrelatable with the web of pretty mediocre and forcefully hip dialogue. This circus ends up being quite hard to be attached to, especially when the plot’s pace is snail-like, logic behind its more wibbly-wobbly parts breaks apart under closer examination and all the
are all superficial as you would expect from a Telltale-like game. This is a real shame since some of the presented scenes, interactions and dialogue show signs of genuine effort and care put into them and it's for those moments that I kept playing until the end. This is why I labeled this review as “Neutral”. Despite everything, I still cared
for the cast, so I will give credit where credit is due.
Unquestionably one of the stronger parts of the game is the artstyle. I really dig the graphics which are humble from the technical standpoint, but still allow to present some quite impressive looking scenes with correct use of color, perspective and painting-like textures. Life is Strange looks pretty nice and no amount of poor music choices can change that. I’m absolutely not impressed by the licensed indie soundtrack featured in the game. Songs are sappy, uninspiring and make the game even bigger hipster-bait than it already is. Original soundtrack is mostly a-okay in the comparison.
In the end, I was quite unimpressed by the experience. It will certainly hit in the feels for no small group of people, but you need to be correctly attuned to it first if you want to get some enjoyment from it. It all depends if you like games in this style, like Oxenfree or Night in the Woods. Unfortunately, the latter example blows Life is Strange out of the water with more clever and relatable dialogue, so even between its peers Life is Strange ends up as a hard sale in my opinion.
The good thing is that the first episode is free. You still can rewind the time spend on reading this review and try it out yourself to form your own opinion. Maybe you will be more lucky than me?

A few days have passed after I finished the game, and I'm still emotionally agitated. The story and the characters dragged me deep into the world that is "Life is Strange".
Similar to the Telltale games, Life is Strange is an interactive tale, which tells you a mostly linear story. The player character "Max" has the ability to turn back time for a few moments, or, later in the game, going far back in time to any moment in her life, by looking on one of her photos. This is quite similar to the movie "The Butterfly Effect".
You're playing a teenage/young adult character on a high school and therefore you're confronted with typically high school problems. Besides mastering your daily school problems, the main goal of the story is to find a vanished girl. This kinda reminded me of the "Veronica Mars" series, because you do all these little detective like stuff.
Another great thing in the game are the characters. I can't remember of a single dull character. Every person had a unique and interesting personality, even the story-unimportant ones. Especially Max' friend (or sidekick) Chloe will grow fond on you.
The wonderful Soundtrack alongside with the atmospheric art style lets you stare at the monitor and enjoy the little things in life (is strange).
Overall a clear recommandation if you like high school drama, with the theory of time travel ala Butterfly Effect.

It can't win because it's completely braindead when it comes to warfare. It will keep moving siege units around even though they can't fire & move in the same turn so they never fire (it's like it has no idea that the "no fire+move" rule exists), It took 6 months of patches until it could finally capture a single undefended walled city. If you have any units at all, the AI will never beat you in war. They really really need to go back to the "stack of doom" model from previous Civs since while those had their own problems, at least it allowed the AI to win wars through sheer numbers.
So that leaves non-war victories, and the AI is even more clueless there. It's seriously like the AI was programmed not having the slightest clue how victory conditions work. I'm not even sure the AI could ever win even if you went inactive and spammed the "next turn" button.
Religious victory? It will spam a ton of missionary units to spread religion (way too many, far past the point it's productive), but the religion portion is broken and so easily thwarted (declare war, instantly wipe out all religion units) that you'll never lose that way.
Culture victory? You have "culture", which is like research points for culture related tech advancements, but that must then be converted to "tourism" which is what makes a culture victory possible. While the AI is capable of pumping out a ton of culture (by cheating), it has no earthly clue how to effectively convert that culture to tourism. They decided to make tourism a sort of mini-game that's so unnecessarily complex that the AI has no clue how to do it. You must match similar works of art or artifacts by type and period to your different museums and you get a bonus for a matching set in the same museum but each museum only has so many slots and you can't transfer items until all slots in each museum are full and OH MY GOD why is this so convoluted? Just give me bonuses and forget this slot nonsense. On top of that, it seems like the designers meant for great artist works and wonders to be the primary source of tourism, but the biggest source is building seaside resorts to the point that you can completely ignore great artists until the invention of radio and just spam seaside resorts. Seaside resorts operate on a tile placement system that once again is too pointlessly complex for the AI to understand so it only focuses on great artists which never produce enough tourism on their own to win.
Space race victory? The AI can certainly pump out a ton of science to get the necessary techs. But you must then complete about 5 wonder projects from those techs and I've never seen the AI build more than 2 of them. I've had game where the AI finishes researching the entire tech tree while I'm still stuck in the industrial revolution age, and even then it never built even half of the space race projects. Even if it was capable of building them, they are extremely easy to destroy with war or espionage.
How about diplomacy? It all operates on a STUPID leader agenda system where the AI will have preprogrammed things that it will respect you for if you cover, and hate you if you don't. This system is laughably broken. One leader will respect if you've built a ton of cities, but then the usual "we don't like you expanding" penalty will kick in to contradict that. Also a bunch of the traits depend on conditions you can't possible fulfill early in the game. They will hate you for not having a lot of cities or a strong fleet or lots of wonders in the first 20 turns of the game! Even if you could sort out all this, they will hate you anyway because of the stupid "warmonger" penalty which is massive and impossible to recover from. +2 relations because of long standing peaceful trade? Now you have -30 relations because you declared war on someone else. It doesn't matter if you declare war on THE CIV THAT WAS ATTACKING THEM. You're still declared a war monger. Remember when Great Britain hated the United States for declaring war on Germany in WWII? Me neither.
There are a couple positives to the game. Districts are a nice way to handle city growth (even though religion and culture districts are kind of useless). The change to workers is nice. And....that's about it  :(
Bottom line: all the neat new features don't matter for anything if the AI is totally incapable of winning even on the hardest difficulty. It's braindead to the point that I swear even if you went AFK and had a woodpecker pound the "next turn" key, the AI still would never win. They desperately need to drop the "1 unit per tile" system as it's been a disaster for two whole games now that the AI cannot deal with. Next they need to simplify the pointlessly complicated victory conditions so the AI can understand it. Until they fix those, don't bother.

Do you like Civ V? Just play Civ V.
The mechanics of Civilization VI looked terrific on paper, but many were sloppily executed. I personally loved the implementation of un-stacked cities, it really made the placement of your cities important and added a completely new level of strategy to the game. The same goes for Wonders taking up an entire tile, adding on to the strategy of city placement even more. Having both science as well as civic trees was also a step forward in the series' game design in my opinion, it added a bit more depth to the progression of your civilization. Workers being replaced by the Builder unit was also a step in the right direction. By making builders spend charges to improve tiles instantly and then disappear after the charges were depleted got rid of the awkward "what do i do with all these workers" issue in the later stages of Civ V. But that's about where the pros end.
While the "agendas" idea for world leaders was a cool idea, it was very poorly implemented. I think it is absolutely absurd that I have several civs full out DENOUNCING me because I happen to have a city on a continent they are absent from, or because I don't control a lot of land, or get really involved in espionage, the list goes on. I could completely understand them disliking me because of these, but to full on denounce me seems a little too far. And even if I do somehow manage to line up with their main agenda, they have a second, randomly generated hidden agenda (apart from Teddy and Gandhi) that can be anything from a love of science or culture or income etc, etc. It is not uncommon to play through a game and see that almost every civ has denounced every other civ. It was a great idea, just very poorly executed.
After several updates, alliances are nearly impossible to make. The other civs' demands are outright ridiculous. They often demand you hand over at least 5000 gold and nearly your entire GPT amount, or want to declare a joint war against a civ they hate. Doing the latter will often brand you a warmonger amongst all the civs, even the one you're trying to ally.
Warmongering is mostly fine in this game thanks to both the deductions based on the era you're in as well as the casus belli system. My biggest complaint is that if, for example, both you and Teddy strongly dislike Victoria so you decide to declare war on her. Unless you perform a casus belli that reduces the warmonger penalty to zero, everyone including Teddy will dislike you for it. This was not an issue at all in Civ V, as friendly civs that disliked someone else as much as you cared not if you wiped them off the map.
All in all Civ VI is about five steps forward, and two to three steps back for the Civilization series. I cannot recommend this game in the current state it is in.

Civ VI's failure: The Two Salems
(This review contains religious references, but is addressing a failure of the game, not initiating a debate on the subject)
Civ VI has unfortunately joined the pantheon of other games which are simultaneously overtweaked and underdeveloped (Read Master of Orion 3+). But in having a selective view of historical fact, it demonstrates its ability to faor AI players over human players.
Case in point, and the reason for the title of this review, is that two Salems, and several other historical events of a similar vein, is the inability to kill Missionaries with forces defending cities. 2000 years ago, soldiers were involved the  removal of a key religous figure in one "Salem". Nearly 1700 years later, another "Salem" was at the center of another "religious persecution" at the hands of forces. There are more examples throughout written history, but apparentlly not where Civ VI's designers want the game to go, since you can't send city defenders after missionairies in the game.
This is just one of a list of flaws with the game, but  in short, if I could get my money back on this game, I would. Civ VI is a basic Civ 3 with an updated GUI.

It is a bit akward to rate "not recommended" in to a game I played so much...
So let me explain, from the view of a classic Civ player...
Cons
The AI is really stupid!.... ok, there is NO civilization game who wouldn't have a stupid AI (like enemies attacking without reason even if they are much weaker and commiting suicide, AKA civ1-3) Now they are the same, plus doesn't make much sense: They will declare war or firendship even if they don't get any benefit from it at all... and wouldn't match what they feel about you. This one is so far the worst: it is impossible to have any single civilization to ally with you if you defend yourself against a random attack, or befriend you if you decide to cede all your privilieges to any rondom former firnedly civ. To put it blank: diplomacy is totally broken!
Districts: I learnt to love the idea, even if you take out space to build farms, I see potential on the districts: but some of those are so underpowered that they are a waste of time! (pe the Industrial distirct gives so little production that is actually damaging to your economy)
Bad pacing! I hated from earlier Civ games that ancient eras where usueless, so fast they went.... At least in pre-civ V games you'll scratch a couple of turns where one of the most amazing military units in the world became useful during ancient times: the phalanx and the legion: Civ VI manages to make those just "meh" and if you select "marathon" pacing you'll make the military exactly the same,, but you'll be discovering flight while building a district takes up to 150~ turns... Making Civ V look like an amazing game!
The graphics.... I won't fall for the "I don't like the cartoonish" thing. I don't, but I consider the developers wouldn't be able to produce in just an acceptable amount of time some realistic 3D graphics... But then I have other questions: Wouldn't it be better to produce some high quality 2D like on Sim city4 or Simon 2 and make it accesible to slow end computers and faster in all computers? What is the point on 3D if you can't rotate anyway and it works like and old fashioned isometric engine? Well, at least the animations are quite cool....
Not balanced at all:  In previous games it was difficult to win unless you centered your civ to a certain task: war or science: here you have to center it around culture so any random civ won't beat you by culture even if you have all the economic and military cards on the game, or viceversa...
No palace upgrades and city views! After such a downgrade in game mechanics comparing to Civ V, I was expecting some good easy gratification respect Civ IV and V! no luck :(
The district mechanics is good, and I think it can really improve the game, but as it is it stands in: Buggy, faulty and meh, plus no palace and city view.... I'll stick to Civ I-III and sometimes go to V, but to enjoy VI you'll need mods... if you want to buy it I'll recommend to check the mods regularly and decide if it is worth. as a standlone product it is a big step backwards!

This is about as close as you'll get to a proper solar-system space sim. There are others out there (Orbiter springs to mind) but this one defines the genre, really. Be warned... while it is extremely addictive, it also has a very steep learning curve.
Don't be fooled by the cute little green guys. KSP is a thinking-person's space sim... not an arcade/action game.
You can't just strap rockets onto a command module and go walking around on the moon. You have to plan trajectories, manage your thrust, fuel, angle of entry, rocket stages, the works.
It uses a decent (not perfect, but decent) physics model which gives a good idea of atmospheric interaction, gravity, thrust effects, etc... your rockets will flip, wobble, snap, explode and tumble uncontrollably far more than they'll fly straight... but mainly because you've messed something up.
When you manage that perfect launch, travel and landing, and watch your little fellow skipping about on the moon (Mun), the effort it took to get there, and all of the learning you had to do (and there will be learning) makes it all the more satisfying.
If you really want to know what this one is like before you buy it, go check out the Scott Manley Kerbal Space Program videos on YouTube. There are a lot of them, and not only are they entertaining, but they're a gold-mine of information about how to do stuff.
Graphically it is a bit average, but you can get a few decent (free) mods which improve this dramatically.  Ditto with audio, though there's a certain visceral charm in the "THUMP!" your engines give when you activate them.  Control is mouse and keyboard - but you'll be getting to grips with pitch, roll and yaw for a little while. It's not just point and click.

Hotline Miami is an extremely violent action game, played from a top down perspective with retro styled graphics and an 80’s influenced visuals, soundtrack, and setting, which can get quite trippy at times. You play as an unnamed character that begins to receive mysterious phone calls from an unknown source. The calls simply tell you to go to a location and kill the people there (they happen to be Russian mobsters), and for whatever inexplicable reason, you listen.
This of course is the real beauty of the game, the top down, ultra-violent action. Once you show up at a location it’s you, your enemies, and the various weapons you have at your murderous disposal: fists, baseball bats, crowbars, knives, and an assortment of different guns. You die in one hit, and in most cases so do your enemies. This causes the game to often turn into a frantic adrenaline fueled rush of bullets and blood.
This means you will die a lot. You must clear stages in one life, dying will force you to restart the stage. Stages are not very long, so a successful run will go quickly, but the amount of dying will prolong your completion time. Despite the number of deaths you will incur, the game never feels very difficult, though that may be more the quick and short nature of the stages obfuscating the difficulty.
That said, things are not always a mad rush towards carnage. Success will require you to tactically plan how to eliminate all your foes. A gun will allow you to kill someone from a distance, but the noise of the gunshot will attract more enemies, who may be packing heat of their own. A quick rush towards them with a crowbar will kill them silently, but they may notice you and retaliate before you manage to bash their skull in. Or maybe you should slam that door into the other bloke in the room below you first and worry about this chap later. This balance of planning, sneaking around, and quick action helps make the game very enjoyable.
A few quick criticisms though, the game does not support properly support higher resolutions, as they will either feature black bars on the top and bottom and/or sides, or not display correctly at all. (The highest I could get it to run was at 1280 x 720, which still had black bars on the top and bottom. For reference, my monitor is 1920 x 1080). Second, the options lack any sort of things to tweak, so if you want to remap the controls, you’re out of luck. Thankfully, the default controls work pretty well, but it’s still pretty lame that you can’t change them even you want to. Third, and this pertains to the gameplay itself, while the levels themselves are great fun, the boss fights aren’t up to par, and well, frankly the boss fights suck. Which is a shame considering how much fun the levels themselves are to play.
All said and done though, Hotline Miami is a blast to play, and well worth your money. Go ahead, answer the phone and get to killing some mobsters.

In its current state, I cannot recommend this game at all.
2K and Firaxis have, quite literally, taken a page from Paradox's playbook. You're charged for each new civilization independently of one another instead of adding large-scale expansions like Civ V. Save your money, pick up Civ V or Civ IV.

A stirring and well-acted journey, Season Two of The Walking Dead may not deliver the breakthrough experience of the first season, yet it retains the emotional punch that makes this undertaking just as heartfelt and gut-wrenching as we all so fondly remember. Each episode builds upon the last, and we open with the slightly older and more experienced Clementine being once again ripped from the last vestige of Season One’s survivors. These initial scenes, when Clementine is truly at her most vulnerable, allow new characters and personalities to fill the void, and they are definitely a step up from those that we have love and lost before.
I would actually state that new characters such as Luke, Rebecca and the reprehensible Carver create a far bigger impression and provide a longer lasting memory. The performances by the voice actors is incredibly top notch, and the screams from Sarita during a particularly grisly moment are some of the best acting this medium can produce. By the end of Season Two Clementine and the other survivors will have experienced levity, horror, fear, love, friendship, anger and many other emotions beside, with a strong cast that have truly become their characters.
But among it all, there is Clementine. By the end of Season One you loved this little girl, and you wanted to protect her from the horror that has become of the world. Put into the spotlight herself, she thrives as a character in and of herself. Through the course of Season Two we see her grow, mature and even command the respect of those much older. She is strong-willed and can even have a lick of malice, depending on your actions. It’s a thrill to see her change and be changed because of the actions of others, and she can be both the voice of reason and the voice of spite.
As with Season One, the dialogue is the main gameplay element that will take up the most of your time. While engaged with the other characters there are usually four options and a timer to quickly speak. Staying silent is also an option, and what you say, how you say it, and if you choose to speak at all can place other character’s lives in your hands. You cannot mull over your responses, weighing the pros and cons over your eventual choice – the game’s dialogue is fast-paced and demanding, and can have an intensity that other games couldn’t even begin to touch. This dynamic is as much a source of tension as the ever-present zombies, and these choices do affect how some situations play out.
However, beyond dialogue, there remains a noticeable lack of direct interaction in The Walking Dead Season Two. Opportunities to explore the varied settings are far and few between, and these settings are much smaller than they appear at first glance. It’s hard to feel engrossed in the environment when you spend the vast amount of your gameplay ignoring it and talking to the next character to advance the plot. Quick-time events do vary the action on occasion, but the pacing of the gameplay is rather ho-hum.
Despite these concerns, Season Two is still a strong enough experience to merit your time. Clementine’s story is enough to carry the game through any interactive short-comings. The quality of the experience is measured through how torn you feel when a beloved character is inevitably killed. While Season Two doesn’t have the impact that Season One has made – it is another strong showing from the great storytellers at Telltale and comes highly recommended for anyone who enjoyed Season One.

Alan Wake is an awesome game; very linear but with a very cool storyline, a lot of interesting ideas & great music. The game is presented as episodes of a television show, with 6 main episodes & 2 special feature episodes, and this only increases the coolness of the theme. It's dark, spooky - sometimes outright scary - and the gameplay is creative. It also never stops evolving. The story keeps you interested while the gameplay changes here & there, never enough to make you feel you have no chance, but enough to keep you looking about, thinking things through and being tactical - especially when stressful moments arrive, like when your friends are trying to get a helicopter running and the shadow-infested citizens of the town of Bright Springs (or the Taken) start coming out of the woodwork in droves. The closest thing I can liken Alan Wake to is the first few seasons of the TV show Supernatural - intelligent, tense and moving between spooky & scary while retaining a clear air of cool.

I think the mechanics for 6 are the best of the series but the AI is certainly lacking. The AI follows a clear pattern at all difficulties: it sporadically declares war on players that violate its values. For instance, Barbarossa doesn't like players that contribute to city-states. The big issue is that the AI isn't programmed to be effective during war. It sends fledgling attacks, often without really much thought for logistics. It's too easy to fend off uncoordinated attacks from the AI and then sue for peace after 10 turns. Demands don't really work so intimidation in diplomacy never means anything. I also don't like that it's nearly impossible to recover a good reputation after 2 prolongued wars with an AI. I find that a good way to measure how good you're at with diplomacy is whether you're able to get away with a few wars without going below -200 likeability with the AI. 2 wars over 50 turns gets you down to around -120 around the medieval age. Every turn you recover +2 likeability. So, you'd have to wait 70-100 turns just to be in good favor with the AI. Nevertheless, even a slight infraction against the AI's values (take Barbarassa for example), would set even a likeable AI against you. Therefore, diplomacy is pretty much broken and binary.
I recommend the game for its mechanics and its overall playability. Functionally, it's a great game, but the diplomacy and the wartime AI make the game way too easy.

100 hours into Civ 6 (and a previous 400 in Civ 5) , I feel like for old fans of the game, and newcomers alike, there was enough in the intial release of this game to keep us all wow'd and interested while we wait for the next (free) DLC to improve on the games most universally frustrating issues:
- Diplomacy & Military stratergy. 2 cornerstones of any grand stratergy game. Ruined by arguably the worst AI Firaxis has ever released (to the point of making the single player mode a frustrating and tedious experience).
- All this also bleeds into how the AI controls religion and city states (like a hive mind, and nonsensically), two other major facets of whats supposed to give this game depth.
- As well as many basic map mechanic issues, like the inability to stack units now seems like a smart and tactical approach to where you should place your units, but instead, what its turned into (especially late game) is that the AI starts to move all their free roaming units in SWARMS. In particular religious units that you can't ban from your own lands. All creating a large amount of map traffic that actually begins to slow the processing of the game down too. It's infuriating.
All this has been crystal clear and apparent since before the first DLC.
As of Nov 7th 2017, none of these incredibly damaging issues to the game (and the brands legacy) have been fixed in any DLCs. But whats worst is there've been 6 DLCs to date, all releasing new characters, all costing a certain amount of money. It's nearly offensive that they expect us to pay for more content, before they've fixed what was basically an unfinished game to all those who paid full price for the original release.
Feels bad man, and will genuinely influence if I ever buy another game made by Firaxis.

Brilliant top-down rogue-like shooter - you choose one of the dozen available characters, each with different powers, and try to progress through levels by killing everything that moves. + Extremely solid and challenging action rogue-like gameplay
+ A dozen playable characters, each with a different ability
+ A ton of cool weapons and deadly enemies
+ Simple, yet effective graphics and sounds
+ Regular updates containing fixes, improvements and new content, with numerous new features to be added in the future
+ Local Co-op (online Co-op may be added later)
+ Fish can roll
Cons:
- Starting level spawns will occasionally cause you to die unfairly
- Limited UI (for now, it's being improved)
- Some minor bugs (e.g. problems with registering hits near walls)

Please note that this is a spoiler free review; no story elements, secrets or special weapons are spoiled.
Nuclear Throne is a top-down shooter, in which you control a mutant (or a fugitive running from the popo), with the goal of killing everything in sight, and finishing your journey to the fabled Nuclear Throne. In your task, you are aided by a metric ton of possible weapons, ranging from revolvers, all the way to nuke launchers, and anything in between. Generally, if you can imagine it, it's there. To those favoring a more hack and slash gameplay style, melee weapons are also present.
The character you pick will influence your playstyle significantly, as each of them brings an active, and a passive ability to the table. Currently there are 12 characters in the game, with 6 unlocked from the start. Five of the six starting characters are easy to pick up and play in terms of mechanics:
- Fish collects more ammo, and, as the loading screen kindly tells you a million times, "Fish can roll".
- Crystal starts with 10 HP instead of 8, and has the ability to encase herself in a hunk of crystal, reflecting shots
- Y.V. (Yung Venuz), the Gun God himself, has a faster rate of fire than the rest. His active ability is firing his weapon twice, with double the cooldown (affected by the fire rate reduction). He can also press B to airhorn, which should be a core feature in every game.
- Steroid has no active ability; instead, his passive allows him to fire two weapons at the same time, in exchange for worse accuracy.
- Chicken starts with a sword, instead of the usual Revolver. Her passive allows her to survive a lethal hit, by literally running around like a headless chicken. If she picks up health from any source, she'll survive, and take a -1 max HP penalty. She can also throw weapons Hotline Miami style, which is extremely effective in the early game.
Every stage, your main task is to blow everything the Hell up, and collect whatever you can to help you do that on future stages; radiation canisters (this game's experience equivalent), weapons, ammunition, medkits, and so on. Once you kill everything, a portal spawns near the corpse of your last slain enemy, and starts dragging you in. Enter, and you're whisked away to the next stage. (Possibly a secret area.. If you found one of them!)
If you've collected enough canisters to level up, you can choose one of four random mutations. All of these mutations are a large boon, that'll help you both short and longterm. There's quite the variety as well; each weapon category has it's own related mutation (example: Bolt Marrow apparently replaces your bone marrow with crossbow bolts [don't even ask how that's possible], causing your bolts to have slight homing capabilities; Laser Brain amps up the damage of your energy weapons, Long Arms increases your melee swing range, etc), as well as several more 'generic' ones (such as Second Stomach, which doubles the health you get from medkits, Rabbit Paw, which causes more items to drop, etc).
The mutations are varied, and powerful enough, that you have to make tough decisions when leveling up, however, there's not so many of them, that you can't aim for a specific playstyle.
I didn't talk much about the actual combat itself - that's because there's not much to talk about. It's extremely simple, however, that is a compliment in this case. The game is a perfect example of the expression "elegance in simplicty", as the game's narrow focus means that the action is fast-paced, exciting, and extremely hectic. Patterns are predictable, however, the sheer number of enemies you fight at times, coupled with the fact that you NEED to collect those radiation canisters means that you're constantly making life and death decisions, on the fly, under a split-second. Hesitate, and you can either lose out on an advantage you desperately need, or die. The weapons are, for the most part, satisfying to use, and most importantly, consistent.
One interesting thing is that guns themselves don't vary much in terms of raw damage output. A basic Shotgun deals the exact same damage per pellet as higher tier ones, a Revolver does the same damage per shot as a Minigun does, and so on (There are exceptions to this, however); thanks to this, even if you've never picked up a weapon, you generally have a very good idea on how much damage it'll actually do to whatever you point it at. Upgrades still feel extremely satisfying, however; despite the ammunition itself dealing the same damage, the overall damage output always increases significantly. You will have to combat the increased ammo consumption, but generally your mutations tend to help out with that.
Every third level, you will face a level boss. They will not be spoiled.
Rinse, repeat, until you reach the Nuclear Throne.
Simplistic. However, it is extremely charming. If you're not a fan of sprite-based graphics, look elsewhere. If you are into it, you'll dig the sprites in some cases; the mutants themselves are rather creative, and the enemy design is okay at worst, and "HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥WHAT IS THAT" at best. My personal favorite pieces of the art in this game are, funnily enough, shown in the first few seconds of the game: the character select screen. You get to watch your cast of mutants lounging around a campfire, doing their own thing (amusingly, their locations on the screen are randomly generated, too); selecting them results in a fighting game style character overlay. It's quite charming.
No shooty-shooty-bang-bang game is complete without sounds, and tunes.
The gun sound effects are actually surprisingly good. The audio feedback is excellent; even your starting weapon, the Revolver, sounds satisfying to use, higher tier weapons sound sufficiently devastating. It's a hard one to talk about without hearing the audio itself, so I apologize if the description is generic. Special mention goes to the sound effects you hear when you select a mutation - each of them have an associated sound clip, that's meant to represent the changes your mutant is undergoing.
The music... Oh, man, where do I even begin.
Personally, I'm infatuated with what the devs put on the table - or at least the idea of what they were trying to do. I sincerely recommend looking up the soundtrack on YouTube if you plan to read the rest of this section, as none of what I'll say make sense without.
The main theme itself is one of the most enchanting pieces I've ever heard in a game of this type. It's atmospheric, and it sets the mood perfectly well.
However, the audio quality drops massively when you actually enter the game; while the tunes themselves are extremely catchy, and complement the game perfectly, it is hamstrung by the low fidelity of it; synthetized, grainy sounding drums, generic, MIDI-sounding choirs. The guitar tracks, which are the only thing that sounds legitimately recorded, is excellent.
It's an interesting design choice that they chose all three bossfights to have the same main motif, with alterations on the track to more accurately represent the boss and the zone you fight them in. A nice touch.
I sincerely hope that they'll re-do the soundtrack before release, and pay someone to record a real drum track, as it's a huge flaw. Still extremely enjoyable despite that, if you're not an audiophile.

It's one of the most polished Early Access titles; for $12, you'll get a lot of value out of your money, if you're into this type of game. The dev support for the game is great, they DO listen to feedback, and it shows.
If this is your jam; buy it.

Telltale games definitely noticed the issues with the first game, because most of them has been completely removed from this "sequel"
Choices are now more easily visible, many of the action orientated elements of the first game has been replaced with Quick Time Events in shape of movement arrows you have to react to whenever they pop up.
The only issue I have with this, is that it's simply too easy to avoid failure.
One of the more interesting factors of the first game was that your failures would sometimes pave the way for what happened in the game, and this made for some more organic choice branching, whereas with this second instalment, I felt in control at all times.
As I addressed in the first game, the absolutely fury-inducing excessive interactions with useless things/people has been completely trimmed, almost too much in fact.
This means you will not be stuck at any point ever again. It's always very clear what you have to do, and whom to talk to.
I want this review to be absolutely bare minimum on spoilers, but obviously I have to comment on the fact that you now play as Clementine, which is a bit of a spoiler.
You see, Lee was a grown dude, and a big one at that, so his physical capability was often something that would come into play as you progressed. With Clementine however, you have to rely on wits and maybe the gullible nature of some more "pure" people.
It's undeniable however that an 11 year old girl can only do so much physically.
There is an interesting new approach to the character, because she has been hardened at this point.
Clementine is no longer a scared little girl, in fact her courage often surpasses that of grown men.
In terms of what development you can make with the character, you now have the option of playing a much more cynical, angry Clementine. And who could possibly blame her?
As for myself I chose to stick to the good pure spirited Clementine we had come to know in the first "season".
I must admit however, I feel like going with the more hardened, cynical approach would have been the more realistic choice, and trust me, you get plenty of opportunities to excercise those nasty kind of choices, or be a hero, if that's what you want.
It's as though, the developers wanted the story to be much easier to control this time around, but I do feel like the evident "this is what it would look like if it was up to the writers" appeal is more clear than ever.
As a result, I sort of felt that the story and therefore, the game, played itself way too often.
Maybe I will go for a second playthrough, maybe I won't, but if I do, I wanna make sure that I get to play out my choices with a character that has been broken in mind, rather than the sugar sweet, steriotypical hero.
I highly recommend you give this some thought as well, because otherwise you just might end up slightly disappointed, just like myself.
Clementine has a lot of emotional value to me and most likely everyone else that played season 1, but I can't help, but feel that she didn't make for the best kind of main character.

Life is Strange is an interactive movie in which you play as a teenage girl named Max Caulfield.
In the beginning of the story, Max has just moved to Arcadia. She is studying photography in one of the Country's most known schools: Blackwell Academy.
She is the typical introvert hipster with a polarized camera.
Life is Strange is very similar to Telltale Games' games. The decisions you make effect the ending of the story.
We are very familiar with these styles of games thanks to Telltale Games.
Messing with time is a very hard concept (Rick and Morty s1 ep11 and s2 ep 1) and could be very hard for the devs. However, Don'tNod Entertainment has done a very good job with Life is Strange.
The scenario is incredible. Life is Strange is one of the few games that almost made me cry.
The characters are so well written it feels like they all have their own personalities and lives.
And that's what it should be like. Side characters should be written just to be there. They should feel like real people (UBISOFT!).
The ending really shook me and I'm sure that it will shake you as well.
So in conclusion, Life is Strange gets a 10/10 from me and I highly recommend playing it.

A "brief" summary of Nuclear Throne:
A fast-paced action-packed rogue-like game about traversing dimensions, collecting radiation in order to mutate and strengthen yourself, and picking up insane weaponry to defeat your foes.
A run can take anywhere between 6 seconds and 40 minutes, or even beyond if you practice enough. The difficutly curve is sharp, the game is unforgiving.
The weapons range from machine guns and assault rifles to plasma miniguns and blood cannons
Mutations upon levelling can enable your runs in many different ways, but the real good ones come when you reach level 10, or level Ultra, where you get a choice of one of a couple of character-specific mutations  that make your run truly ball out of control.
Characters have their own passive and active abilities that define who they are. Passives can be something like more ammo, more HP,
, better weapons, more mutation options, etc. Active options range from telekinesis, to laser beams, to dual-wielding, to summoning allies to fight for you.
Overall, the game is hard, challenging, and fun, and a good way to spend either an hour, or your entire afternoon. It comes as a strong recommendation from myself and everyone I know who plays the game.

Overall pretty good. The game has a few down points but all in all I would give it 70/100 (50 is average). The game basically follows a group of people surviving the Zpocolypse like the show. It plays as an interactive story and the player makes choices for the main character. There isn't any gameplay really it is just point and click for I would say 75% of the game. The rest are small real time button mashes that you have to do, which are really kinda pointless in my opinion. The good thing about the game is that zombies are actually a pretty big part of the game unlike many "zombie" genre media that turns into nothing but soap operahs with a few zombies in the background as plot motivators. A qucik look around the internet and you will find that people get pretty emotionally invovled in this game, so thats always a good sign. For me, it wasn't as engaging but still well worth the time to go through it. Hard to say much else without spoiling the game for those who haven't played it.
For the not-so-good. I think the most fusterating part of the game is the controls. They are very loose and don't always work. The control scheme can be annoyingly difficult to manipulate at times. This is slightly better in Season 2 but the changes that were made to the HUD I feel were not nessicarily better, just different. There still were a few times where I died simply becuase the controls did not get recognized in time.
The other major issue was as with almost all choice based games there are often times when my personal choice just wasn't an option. You get 2 or maybe 3 choices and none of them are what I considered good so your left with just picking the least bad. That kinda kicks you out of the emersion a bit. This is particularly evident in Season 2 and it's ending. Probably from about Episode 4 and on I wasn't really on board with what was going on but there really is no option for what I would have done and that was pretty dissapointing. There are 5 different endings and while they all wrap up pretty decently, for me it felt like just watching a show I had no control over as the choices had to be made because the ones I would have done where simply not in the game. I was just going through iot to finish it after that point. That isn't to say the story is bad, it is pretty good, but not as an "interative" game that claims to be based on your own choices.
Some other critique I have is mostly in the way of graphics. Overall it is a good style and the game looks good, but there are gliches here and there and the animations are sometimes wonky. Nothing game breaking or really bad but a lack of polish nontheless. This is much improved in Season 2. The game looks and feels a lot better in the animation department. Although I would also have to say that running into invisible walls was much more apparent in Season 2 as well which was very annoying at times and for the most part fairly pointless.
So overall worth it. If you like this sort of game it is definitely worth picking up. If on the fence, it is worth picking up on a steam sale. I played it straight through and I guess steam didn't calculate all my time playing, but I think it was a little shorter than Season 1 @ about 10 - 12 hours total seems about right.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a satisfying squel to the critically acclaimed first season, released in 2012. The player takes on the role of Clementine, the child Lee took care of in the first game. While it adds and improves on some aspects of the first game (which was itself, near-flawless), it does perform less well in other ways when compared to its predecessor.
I would argue that Season 2 is a more thematically developed game than the first, exploring particularly what it's like to be a child in a post-apocalyptic world, though many characters seem less well developed and more two-dimensional than those in the first game. That's not to say there aren't interesting characters (Jane and Carver spring to mind), ad the game mostly compensates for these less memorable characters by putting them in much more interesting and tricky situations.
The moral choices in this game seemed much more difficult to make and tended to have unforseen circumstances. Unlike in the first game, by the end of Season 2, I actually wished I had made a number of different choices in the hope things turned out differently. This was much more interesting and realistic than simple "cause and effect" (which, in hindsight, the first game suffered from to some extent).
The dialogue interface has changed a little compared to the first game (honestly, I'm not sure which one I prefer), and the act of talking to secondary characters in moments of quiet is virtually absent. While this creates a much faster paced and more realistic-feeling game, this probably contributes more than anything else to the lack of characterisation when compared to the first game.
Finally on a side note, if you played the 400 Days DLC for the first game, the return of characters from that game in Season 2 is literally mind-blowing. I would highly recommend picking up that DLC before playing this game.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 picks up right where season 1 of the series ends. This time around we see the entire game through Clementine's eyes, something that really brings a new aspect to the entire series so far, if you ask me. After all, in many games we always play as an adult, especially in many games with survival and horror elements. So we get a different perspective with a child as the playable character. She has clearly been affected by the events of the last game, but the little girl soldiers on.
Through the entire game Clementine is challenged a lot. All from making those signature difficult choices that we remember from the last game, and also who to stay loyal with and so on. With all of these things we also get the emotional baggage that some of these choices causes. Some may feel that the game doesn't offer all that many choices like we remember from the last game, but it certainly has a good story, something that I feel defends the reason to why there aren't perhaps that many choices for everybody's liking.
From the first episode I could tell that Telltale Games put their hearts into the game and the result is of course of pure Telltale quality. If you enjoyed the previous game then you will love this a lot more. So go ahead and be a good sport. :) Click add to cart and enjoy the adventures emotional rollercoaster that this game offers.
Positive points:
+ The story is excellent
+ Hard choices
+ You can import your save from the previous season
+ The graphics are good, with the classic comic style from season 1
+ Multiple endings
+ Good voice actors that fit the characters
+ Old friends appear
Negative points:
+ May have too little choices for some
+ You may cry from the story (I don't find this negative, but some might)

You get a gun and a flashlight and that's it.  The entire game reminds me of the original Silent Hill--when Harry Mason is cast into the darkness after the alarm sounds-- so if you enjoyed the first game, you will love this.  It is everything that that the subsequent Silent Hill's should have been after the original.

This game has so much potential. So many refreshing changes that brings Civ into the modern era, like the excellent city grids, the divide between culture and science for progress etc. It's also a genuinely beautiful game, which is certainly a first for the Civ series. With the day span turned on, with the sun glittering in the waves during daylight and the cities, farms and temples lit up at night time the atmosphere is fantastic! But I can't wrap my head around why Firaxis still haven't fixed the warmonger system that ruins the entire game. Everyone seems to hate it.
As it is now you basically have two options on how to play the game. 1) Remain completely pacifistic. Never start any wars and if attacked, never seize any of the opponents cities. That way you can maintain friendly relations with other nations and pursue the different end goals like science win, culture win etc, but you will at the same time virtually shed the entire combat aspect of the game. Or 2) Play the game as a military game, where all other nations on the planet hates your guts throughout history. Even as a military game it becomes deeply flawed, since everyone will hate you if you are succeful. Military alliances etc are virtually impossible, because it will be you agains the world.
In the game that prompted this review I have never started any wars. I have been attacked three times and two times I seized one city from the opponent in the peace treaty. The second time that happened I was immediately branded as a warmonger by all other nations. I went from carefully cultured friendly relations to being denounced by all other opponents and two of them (former friendly nations) even started a war against me out of the blue, from half a map away, seemingly for no other reason than that they loathed the way I was attacked and conquered a city in my defensive war.
If Firaxis would simply fix this issue I would rank Civ 6 as the best Civ game yet, but as it is now I sadly can't even recommend buying it. Why oh why did the developers ever think that the current system would be an appreciated feature? I can totally accept that you can't steamroll an opponent in wars anymore. If you are attacked and you respond by wiping out an entire civilization or seize half or more of their cities it would be justified to be seen as an aggressor. But the current system doesn't allow for any form of conquest at all, even in defensive wars, without completely breaking the balance of the game.

A game with a LOT of style. A lot of seizure-inducing style. The 16-bit graphics and colors are trippy but oh so enjoyable. The soundtrack is excellent, and the gameplay is REALLY, REALLY damn hard. By far one of the hardest games I have ever played. This is arguably one of the hardest games ever made.
The amount of split-second precision, timing, and reaction speed you need for this game is insane, but at the same time terribly addicting. Every time you fail you just want to try again, knowing now what does and does not work. Eventually, you can take on the entire game strategically. Or, if you are skilled enough, you can run and gun the levels, but that just proved primarily deadly for me.
There are so many ways you can kill and can tackle each situation, with a huge variety of weapons and perks at your disposal. This game should not be passed on, even just for the unique and challenging yet gratifying and satisfying experience. Also it is a blast to play with friends, especially watching them play for the first time and fail miserably after they claimed they can do so much better because it doesn't "look that hard". Oh is it fun to prove them wrong and then get to laugh at them in their face about it.
The story is very unique and intriguing and mysterious. By the end, it is very revelatory and has an awesome twist and message. This game may be violent and absurdly gory and brutal, but it has a point to make.

Okay, this game is not exactly as Civ V, but it doesn't mean it's bad!
Civilization VI is the sixth game in the game serie "Civilization" by Sid Meier. When released Civilization VI they had a hard time competing with Civ V after Civ V huge success. And the fact that the game is not exactly like Civ V did make a lot of their fans and players unhappy I guess. Let's be true, people does not like change, the average person is conservative, and that's the reason for all of these downvotes and negative reviews.
My first impressions of this game was not so great, just because I'd been playing Civ 5 and had a hard time adopt to this new game. But I gave it a while and now I do love it to a 110%. The game does so good!
Pros:
+ Great game mechanics
+ The new way the workers work are great! (They do build instantly but has a limited amout of use per unit.)
+ The new way of handeling culture is great, and the fact that you can build your nation on different ideologics, depending
on ideologic you can have different culture-based features.
+ The possiblity to send envoyjs to other city-states to earn their trust is way better then the old way to earn their trust in
civ v, you can also chose policy (the culture-based features) that make your gain of envoys even better.
+ Trepassing is no longer a thing in Civ VI, you can't even enter a city-states area without being friend or attacking them.
Makes the city-states more like players and less neutral. Makes a more equal game for every participate.
+ Gandhi build nuclear missiles and Montezuma does use a more civilize language xD (refined language).
+ You can now espionage on your enemies (or even allies) without their approval or knowledge. You will benefit in following ways:
1. You will get full vision over the city you do espionage on. Resulting in that you will see all their troops ect. in the city.
2. You can steal money.
3. You can steal scientific boosts.
4. This might be the funniest so far, maybe not most usefull but funniest. You could make their city's population to make a revolt which will summon barbarians of current era in their city. (Happend to me, 3 tanks did summon in my city.)
Cons:
- More advanced (harder to get the hang of than previous games, except beyond earth, this makes the game even funnier
to play when you actually get the hang of it).
- Barbarian are less active, they aren't a problem as they could be in Civ 5 (from my experience so far).
- The AI are dumb, exactly as in previous civilization, it's a problem that all Sid Meier's Civilization suffer from. Their tactics are stupid, doesn't attack when having the advantage etc, but I don't think Civ 5 does it better thou.

There are plenty of other diffenrenties compared with the earlier games for example, luxury resources does not work the same, neither does happiness, but I guess you have and want to experience it yourself.
I give this game a solid 9/10, maybe even 10/10.

This game is a fun game. There are two ways to play this game. The first way is to just luanch rockets and just crash them into the ground, or you can play it like an actual space program. In Kerbal Space Program there are three different game modes there is sandbox, science, and career. In sandbox you can do what ever you want, you can mess around with the physics in the game like crashing rockets into the buildings to make the buildings blow up, or you can make your own station around the Mars like planet named Duna. The science and career game modes are similar. In the science game mode all you do is collect science around the solar system. In career you can do the same things that you can in science, but in career you have money to worry about. To make money you have to do missions that mission control gives you. Some of the missions you will get will tell you to make a rocket with certan items on them. If all of the parameters are met then you complete the mision and you can collect the money you got from that mission. So to sum this game up you can do what ever you wanted to do with rockets in this game. You can run your own space program, or just crash rockets into the ground. I would recommend this game to people who like explosions and rockets.

*Some spoilers included in this review*
The Walking Dead Season 1 was Telltale's take on the Walking Dead franchise. It had a good story, some touching moments to remember, and a great protagonist.
Season 2 is a direct sequel to the first game and tells the tale of Clementine surviving in the apocalypse as a young girl. Having been trained by Lee in the first game, we discover that she is quite adept at survival. Too adept.
To put it lightly, Season 2's narrative, while somewhat believable for the first couple of episodes, forgoes any sense of real direction or character integrity FAST. You realise this at the halfway point, when Clementine is the go-to-gal for any kind of incredibly dangerous task her group requires done.
Clem is unbelievably stealthy, unbelievably brave, unbelievably smart, unbelievably good with weapons, and isn't phased too much even when walking through a giant horde of walkers. The player is merely a click-vessel for a child power fantasy.
This game lacks the single most important Telltale feature - good writing and good character development. Instead, they just seem to be OK with letting the suspense of disbelief run its course on their fans. Over 14,000 positive Steam reviews - and counting - for a game which frankly is a big disappointment for people who wanted a proper sequel to The Walking Dead Season 1.
Do yourself a favour and don't play this if you have an attention span. You will regret it. The ending is terrible, too, by the way.

I feel like I was "supposed" to like this game. I love games with a strong story and well-developed characters, even if that comes at the expense of gameplay, but the story in this game does not hold together.
PROS
* Characters - Many of the characters in the game are well-developed and have distinct personalities and motivations. You get to watch a few of the characters really grow and change throughout the game, and I think that’s the central appeal of the game. The main villain or villains (keeping this spoiler-free) however are generically evil for no particular reason, and midway through the story much of Max's (the main character's) motivations are incoherent.
* Choices - The decisions you make in one episode seem to impact outcomes in every episode afterward. (This is mostly illusion and the plot is actually linear, but it’s sort of fun while it lasts.)
* Premise - The first and second episode had me hooked. I wanted to know how this story would end.
* Music - The soundtrack to this game is great.
CONS
* Story - Starting in Episode 3, the threads holding the story together completely unravel and the game's logic falls apart. Max presumes connections between seemingly unrelated events for no reason. Concepts and storylines introduced in previous episodes remain unexplained or abandoned. As the game progresses, it feels like the writers had no narrative arc in mind for the story, with each writer wresting control of the story as it careens from one distraction to another until, unable to resolve the inconsistencies, it crashes headlong into a stupid and meaningless…
* Ending - One of the primary themes of the game is that every choice you make can have big, unexpected consequences. There was clearly an effort to make the game feel as though each decision could spin off into one of many possible futures. This made it all the more disappointing in the end when you’re given a binary choice between ending A or ending B (neither option makes much sense, but if you’ve played this far it scarcely matters). It’s the game’s final contradiction. Despite the hours of choices and outcomes, in the end regardless of your decisions, it comes down to the same A or B.

Somehow, the AI got even worse compared to Civ 5. This is ridiculous, as it was all ready pretty bad there, but here, it never makes any sense. The cartoony style seems like a step backwards for me, but others seem to not mind, so I might be alone on this one.
The districts system upends the older way to manage, expand and settle cities, which isn't necessarily bad, but it seems a bit arbitrary for me. I'm pretty neutral on this change overall, but it doesn't feel as satisfying as older Civs. Building a mega city with all the buildings and all tiles improved was a fun little mini-game I made for my self in Civ 5, which I even enjoyed on lower difficulties. With the districts, unless I ignore them (and get a worse city than I potentially could have), this isn't fun any-more. Not showing yield icons on districts is annoying, since it makes it difficult to compare them with other tiles, both other districts and more conventional tiles.
Workers (now builders) only having X uses is really annoying, especially as it's as low as three and can't really be raised much, even in the late game (I got 5 uses out of them in the late game once thanks to a policy, maybe you can raise this by one or two more somehow?).
The government types and policies feel much less satisfying compared to Civ 5. Government types seem arbitrary and like they don't really do anything, and the limited number of policy slots compared to the massive amount of policies (half of which seems useless) just makes it annoying to read through. It isn't deep or complex, it doesn't affect much, it's just annoying.
Overall, I prefer the style and gameplay of Civ 5. Hopefully patches and expansions will remedy this over time, but it's been year since release, and it still isn't as fun (for me) compared to Civ 5.

Kerbals are half muppet and half humanoid, and they are a very well suited species for space travel. It's no wonder the developpers picked them to be in this game.
First of all their home planet Kerbin is conveniently small, about 1/3 of the earth, which makes it easier to reach escape velocity.
Then let it be said that Kerbals have no fear. They are always smiling and laughing approximately up to the very moment of the deadly crash.
And then best of all, Kerbals don't need to eat, drink, sleep or breathe, which simplifies a lot of things.  I currently have 2 scientists on the moon. They have been there for 3 years working hard on research. They also have no way of ever going back to Kerbin. They're loving it!
So, the mechanics of KSP are pretty simple, you build rockets, then you fly them.  As you do scientific research to unlock more parts, they get bigger, fly further, and go boldly where no Kerbal has gone before.
The early stages of the game are pretty easy. If you want to know what you're doing, you'll need to have a degree in rocket science. Alternatively, you can also play through the tutorials - which are a bit clunky and rigid but do a good job of explaining the basics.
If you stick to exploring Kerbin and it's 2 beautiful moons, it's a tough yet serene learning curve, enough to give you immense satisfaction each time you reach a milestone (enter space, enter orbit, land on the moon, come back from the moon alive etc..), but never gets frustrating or impossible.
After that point, things get a bit more hairy. Designing a manned vehicle for a return trip to Mars, with a detchable solar-powered rover that actually steers correctly and doesn't just run in circles, is a much more difficult task which the game will not hold your hand for. You'll need to arm yourself with a lot of patience, trial flights and tests, trajectory simulations etc... There are a lot of youtube channels, forums, and mods out there to help you achieve those goals.
The vehicle construction interface can get a little frustrating for those spaceships over 200 moving parts. It tries to snap parts facing the wrong way quite often and can be frustrating, although in the end there is always a way to reach your goal, just remember you'll need a lot of tests before you nail that spaceship.
I consider myself pretty experienced by now, and I think I must fail about 4 out of 5 launches. It can get annoying when you realize you screwed up your ship design when you're already half way to Venus...
Thankfully the game lets you revert each launch to the beginning - which is a good thing otherwise Kerbin would just be a giant graveyard of death. Only problem is for those missions which last 5 years, if you save at any point then you cannot revert anymore.
The game has a time-warp feature which comes in handy for these 5 years mission. It's best avoided during critical phases of the flight, as it will make the physics a bit weird (yes, there certainly is fun to be had deliberately putting the physics engine out of whack!) but otherwise is very much needed. You can bend the time continuum at your leasure: 10x, 100x, 10000x, and what-have-I-done-I-went-too-far-now-I-crashed-and-I-have-to-restart-from-the-beginning x.
KSP's interface is not the shiniest star out there and has it's few frustrating moments, but none of it comes to eclipsing the astronomical amount of fun that there is to be had designing your own rockets, whether you fail hilariously or succeed stellarly.
All in all I learned more about rocket physics from 20 hours of this than from 2 years of High School physics classes. I recommend it heartily to everyone including my ex-teacher.

Have you ever wanted to learn the layman's skills of being an astronaut but without the hastle of actually going into space? Then this is the 'game' for you! I mean, you might actually have to learn the equivalent of a foundation course in basic rocketry and aeroautics to actually play this game well, but surprisigly the payoff seems to be well worth it. Not surprisingly this game has a very steep learning curve, but put in the time and you will (hopefully) find this game is well worth it; I certainly did.
It takes about as much time to learn to play well as Dwarf Fortress but you actually gain some interesting real world knowledge. If you ever find yourself stranded in a spaceship cockpit there might even be a 1% chance mission control could talk you through to a safe landing... and who doesn't expect to find themselves in that situation one day.
In all seriousness I really love this game, though some people will certainly find this game a chore more than entertainment. You probably want to watch/read some let's plays/wiki articles to see if this is the sort of thing you want to put the time into. The modding community for KSP is awesome and active too.
9/10 for me though. Best (maybe only?) space program simulator out there.
P.S. At the time of this review, version 1.2 is in pre-release and it is a massive step forward. If the demo is updated to the same version I highly recommend giving it a whirl to see what you are getting yourself into.

Somehow, the AI got even worse compared to Civ 5. This is ridiculous, as it was all ready pretty bad there, but here, it never makes any sense. The cartoony style seems like a step backwards for me, but others seem to not mind, so I might be alone on this one.
The districts system upends the older way to manage, expand and settle cities, which isn't necessarily bad, but it seems a bit arbitrary for me. I'm pretty neutral on this change overall, but it doesn't feel as satisfying as older Civs. Building a mega city with all the buildings and all tiles improved was a fun little mini-game I made for my self in Civ 5, which I even enjoyed on lower difficulties. With the districts, unless I ignore them (and get a worse city than I potentially could have), this isn't fun any-more. Not showing yield icons on districts is annoying, since it makes it difficult to compare them with other tiles, both other districts and more conventional tiles.
Workers (now builders) only having X uses is really annoying, especially as it's as low as three and can't really be raised much, even in the late game (I got 5 uses out of them in the late game once thanks to a policy, maybe you can raise this by one or two more somehow?).
The government types and policies feel much less satisfying compared to Civ 5. Government types seem arbitrary and like they don't really do anything, and the limited number of policy slots compared to the massive amount of policies (half of which seems useless) just makes it annoying to read through. It isn't deep or complex, it doesn't affect much, it's just annoying.
Overall, I prefer the style and gameplay of Civ 5. Hopefully patches and expansions will remedy this over time, but it's been year since release, and it still isn't as fun (for me) compared to Civ 5.

Kerbal Space Program is truly something unique.
How do you market a game about rocket science -- the default analogy for "something extremely complicated" -- to an audience big enough to justify your budget? Well...there's a lot of little things that make it playable to many people.
First of all, it's a make-your-own-experience sandbox. Just like Minecraft (before there was an End), there's no final goal, no objective arrow. It's just you, an bunch of spaceship parts, a few kerbals, a custom solar system, the infinite expanse of space, and explosions. Lots and lots of explosions.
Second of all, this game about rocket science isn't about ALL of rocket science. There's quite a lot of liberty taken with the laws of physics, all in the name of simplicity. You don't have to worry about fuel flow, or life support, or the speed-of-light delay. All of that is benched in favor of less subtle things, like orbital mechanics, atmospheric shock-heating, and (look this up; it's practically KSP 101) delta-V and Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
But here's the best part; all of these ignored facets of space travel can be added into the game. KSP has a very robust and active modding community, and I'm sure enough mods exist to make the game as realistic as you could possibly demand. Life support? There's a mod for that. Several, actually, in varying degrees of difficulty. Fuel flow? Part of Realism Overhaul. Speed-of-light delay? Check out RemoteTech. There are even mods that replace the stock solar system with our very own, real system, and even mods that add entirely new, dreamed-up systems. (I highly recommend starting out with no mods, then adding them as you become comfortable with what you already have.)
Really, Kerbal Space Program is great for the same reason Minecraft is great. It expects nothing in particular of you, it just wants you to do whatever comes to mind. If that means strapping a hundred boosters together as randomly as possible and watching the fireworks, that's fine. If that means methodically landing on every planet and moon one-by-one, that's fine. If that means brutally murdering your kerbals, well, heck, they're just as surprised to be alive as you are, so go for it.
