Have you ever wanted to learn the layman's skills of being an astronaut but without the hastle of actually going into space? Then this is the 'game' for you! I mean, you might actually have to learn the equivalent of a foundation course in basic rocketry and aeroautics to actually play this game well, but surprisigly the payoff seems to be well worth it. Not surprisingly this game has a very steep learning curve, but put in the time and you will (hopefully) find this game is well worth it; I certainly did.
It takes about as much time to learn to play well as Dwarf Fortress but you actually gain some interesting real world knowledge. If you ever find yourself stranded in a spaceship cockpit there might even be a 1% chance mission control could talk you through to a safe landing... and who doesn't expect to find themselves in that situation one day.
In all seriousness I really love this game, though some people will certainly find this game a chore more than entertainment. You probably want to watch/read some let's plays/wiki articles to see if this is the sort of thing you want to put the time into. The modding community for KSP is awesome and active too.
9/10 for me though. Best (maybe only?) space program simulator out there.
P.S. At the time of this review, version 1.2 is in pre-release and it is a massive step forward. If the demo is updated to the same version I highly recommend giving it a whirl to see what you are getting yourself into.

Kerbal Space Program is truly something unique.
How do you market a game about rocket science -- the default analogy for "something extremely complicated" -- to an audience big enough to justify your budget? Well...there's a lot of little things that make it playable to many people.
First of all, it's a make-your-own-experience sandbox. Just like Minecraft (before there was an End), there's no final goal, no objective arrow. It's just you, an bunch of spaceship parts, a few kerbals, a custom solar system, the infinite expanse of space, and explosions. Lots and lots of explosions.
Second of all, this game about rocket science isn't about ALL of rocket science. There's quite a lot of liberty taken with the laws of physics, all in the name of simplicity. You don't have to worry about fuel flow, or life support, or the speed-of-light delay. All of that is benched in favor of less subtle things, like orbital mechanics, atmospheric shock-heating, and (look this up; it's practically KSP 101) delta-V and Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
But here's the best part; all of these ignored facets of space travel can be added into the game. KSP has a very robust and active modding community, and I'm sure enough mods exist to make the game as realistic as you could possibly demand. Life support? There's a mod for that. Several, actually, in varying degrees of difficulty. Fuel flow? Part of Realism Overhaul. Speed-of-light delay? Check out RemoteTech. There are even mods that replace the stock solar system with our very own, real system, and even mods that add entirely new, dreamed-up systems. (I highly recommend starting out with no mods, then adding them as you become comfortable with what you already have.)
Really, Kerbal Space Program is great for the same reason Minecraft is great. It expects nothing in particular of you, it just wants you to do whatever comes to mind. If that means strapping a hundred boosters together as randomly as possible and watching the fireworks, that's fine. If that means methodically landing on every planet and moon one-by-one, that's fine. If that means brutally murdering your kerbals, well, heck, they're just as surprised to be alive as you are, so go for it.

This game grabbed me in a way I had forgotten that gaming could grab me. It pulled me into a deep and engaging story. It scared the heck out of me. It made me care about the characters and what would become of them. Much has been said about its developmental change from open world to an episodic structure, but after playing this game through twice now, I wouldn't have it any other way. Also, despite the linearity, the game greatly benefits from this open world engine; on a current gaming system, players can see to lush forests and rustic towns to the horizon. This 'Twin Peaks/American Gothic' presentation is what's so gripping. The game feels like a TV drama, down to the 'previously on Alan Wake' montages and the 'closing credits' music between episodes. So much about this game is obviously the product of love and pure creative passion. Remedy: I wish you'd made Max Payne 3.
Technically, the engine is tight, finely tuned and runs beautifully on all detail settings. The lighting and related effects are superb. The motion and control are also responsive and smooth. There was only one bug in which all objects but the lights would be rendered, resulting in an almost entirely black screen. This only occurred twice and restarting the game and the chapter fixed the situation. It must be noted that I have completed the game and its DLC three times; the first time was an all night session into mid morning. The game is worth it.

I came across this game when some friends would not stop raving about it. I promptly checked it out and was not impressed at first and thought "Why buy this game when I can just play Binding of Isaac?" The answer to that question is fairly simple. Nuclear Throne takes the charm and bullet hell fun of BoI and adapts it (or mutates it) into a whole nother experience and game.
I was gifted the game but for a while I did not play the game simply saying "I don't have time for a BoI clone". After putting in 11 hours over 2 weeks I can safely say that I was wrong and I honestly enjoy this game very much.
The Community is very active and very kind to everyone and honestly one of the best gaming commuities I have seen. They're all very excited about the game and very active. Some people have made mods for Nuclear Throne but I have yet to download one.
The lore is currently in the wiki but has not been applied to the game yet. However, the story does not take/give any enjoyment to the game so that is a huge plus. You can load into the game and not have to worry about advancing in the story or missing dialogue.
There are a wide assortment of playable characters, currently at 12. Each character has unique passive and actives so that playing each character is like playing a new game. Each characters active is gamechanging and are useful in their own ways (except Plant's. Because ♥♥♥♥ you Plant. I don't need your stupid snare in my life all you're doing is holding me down)
For the sake of simplicity I'm not going to list each character out but I can say that I have played each character over 20 times and even then I feel as though I only have a basic understanding of how to use them.
My current favorite character to use is Rebel, her healing when you enter portals is one of the most useful passives if you are as reckless as me when playing. Her active ability allows her to sacrifice health to summon a minion who will aid you in your battle before exploding dealing more damage to surrounding enemies.
Some fan favorites are Steroids, Y.V., and Crystal and there are so many well drawn fan art of the game to show people's love for all the different characters.

The music in the game is definitely one good thing amongst a lot of good things about this game. Each level has a unique song that plays while you desperate shoot your way to the throne. Each song fits it's level well and when I first started, I found myself hating the music because at times I find myself being pressured by the music and dying. But now when I play I find myself humming along as I shoot enemies in the face.
Everytime you kill an enemy they drop something called rads (radiation). Each rad you collect goes torward leveling up. If you level up once you finish the level (aka enter the portal) you can pick a mutation (they're like perks). There are weapon based perks (homing bolts, shotgun shells bounce farther, energy weapons deal more damage) and there are basic mutations (more health, enemies have less health, move faster, chance of ammo on kills.
Each mutation will help you get to the throne but like most games there are some mutations that are better than others. Currently, it's advised not to take the weapon mutations unless you are 100% sure that you're going to keep that weapon for the rest of the game.
There are also canisters that give you a lot of rads.
When a character reaches level 10 you can choose a Ultra mutation that are a huge power spike to the character.
At the time of writing this review, there are 104 weapons able to be found in the game. The devs have promised to add more which is incredible. The basic weapon classes are Bullet, Shell, Bolt, Explosive, Energy, and Melee. There are subcatagories in these ammo catagories and each gun feels different to use.
My personal favorites are the Assault Rifle (there are a lot of guns that "outclass  and outdamage this gun but I love the 3 bullet burst) and the Heavy Auto Crossbow (the heavy cross bow is pretty much a 1 shot on all enemy minions and it takes down the bosses in a few shots. The auto portion makes it so that you can kill them faster).
Some weapons are known to be bad such as the smg (too much ammo is being wasted in a non accurate fire) and the laser pistol because the damage feels minisicule and it takes far too long in between shots. You can find ammo and weapons in chests.
The game plays like a Rogue-like, top down shooter. You're expected to die a lot and the game is simple enough to play over and over again in short bursts. When I first started what I used to do was cover shoot from afar. I soon found out that this was not a good tactic because it led to me being able to be swarmed and I could not collect rads/ammo/guns.
The tactic that works best for me is to run around and don't be afraid to get too close to the mobs because most of the time you can dodge what's coming at you and you need to collect all the rads. It's better to find your own playstyle and the game is all about trial and error. Make a mistake once? Don't do it again.
There's also a daily run. Meaning once a day you're given the same seed as everyone else and see how you rank against them. It's pretty fun to wait to play your next daily and see yourself go up the ranks.
There's very little that I can complain about the game. It's fairly polished looks great. However, little does not mean none.
4/10 times you're going to die/get really injured because you spawned in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ place. I once had a run where I spawned in the middle of the map surrounded by scorpions.
The game is on the border of becoming a bullet hell. Enemies will fire at you from halfway across the map often times cornering you.
Sometimes the framerate will go to♥♥♥♥♥♥(mostly during explosions) and might cause you to die.
You can't really change the resolution. I have a 1366x768 monitor but the game does not play in that. The highest resolution I get is 1920x1200 and even that looks a bit meh.
The game looks to have a low learning curve but the first 10-20 runs are going to be you staring at the post death stats screen. You need to push yourself not to give up at first but once the ball gets rolling Nuclear Throne becomes a game that you'll definitely look forward to playing often.
Overall, I think that Nuclear Throne is definitely one of the best rogue-likes I personally, have ever played and it is definitely worth the $15 that the devs ask for. Especially since on release the game will cost more. I highly reccomend you pick this up even if you played Binding of Isaac once and thought it was ok. This game has the potential to become as popular if not more than BoI (not that BoI isn't amazing too). The problems I had with the game were minor and did not take me away from the game.
The devs have promised the community many things and I see them going through with their promises so I think that's really cool of Vlambeer (nearly all of their games are fun to play)
Again, I found myself very pleased by the game and will definitely be playing more of it.

The game is Ok but has a lot of annoyances and flaws in core mechanics which Firaxis has shown very little initiative in addressing. Just as an example it took them over a year to make a trivially simple fix to sorting trades on the trade screen when filtering by yield types and another fix to show a notification when a city is able to bombard enemy units.
Pros:
-City planning is quite engaging due to districts and picking a good place for a city based on water availability, resource tiles, defensibility, and potential district adjacency bonuses (i.e. +1 yield per adjacent mountain) and wonder placements is one of the high points of the game for me.
-Eurekas and Inspirations (you get 50% discount on techs if you meet certain conditions i.e. own 3 archers, kill unit with slinger) make planning tech and culture tree progression engaging and varied. As a result you will often end up advancing somewhat differently through the techs depending on your location, opponents and victory strategy.
-Policy cards system is also engaging and offers a lot of opportunity to engage in planning on when to switch policies in order to reap their benefits (i.e. switching to military production boost for ships just before beefing up your navy)
-Art assets make it much easier than before to identify tile improvements, terrain features, and units at a glance. I also personally enjoy the color palette and find it warm without being gaudy or overbearing.
Cons:
-While the UI is clean and legible at high resolutions, it is very bad at providing much of the information necessary to actively engage with certain game mechanics. For instance district placement only shows adjacency bonus rounded down and only when placing the district. There is no way to see maximum possible adjacency when deciding where to settle so you end up having to calculate the adjacency manually and only use the UI tooltip to verify your work. Every one of the new engaging mechanics is dragged down by the un-accommodating UI.
-AI is miserable at handling the new mechanics. You will often see AI placing cities and districts in very questionable locations as if they are oblivious as to how district adjacency works. They don't seem to go for Eurekas and Inspirations either and it's not really possible to see if they use policy cards in any way other than completely randomly.
-AI has zero ability to wage war effectively. Ok, they will try to surround your city with 5+ warriors on turn 25 on Deity but that is the peak of it's ability. It will concentrate its masses of horribly outdated units in some nonsensical region of the map while you easily siege down it's capital on the other side of the map with the requisite 4 units. Even worse is how it will sometimes ignore military completely after you wipe out their forces and take a couple cities. Overall the AI just fails at this critical aspect of the game.
-The AI is crazy. Seeing a pattern here? Yeah the AI also cannot handle diplomacy in any sensible fashion. The idea of AI civ personalities and agendas is great but the implementation leaves a lot to be desired. A lot of times it does not work as intended and the AI behaviour comes off as arbitrary when it should be predictable and consistent. For example, my last diety game was a domination victory by 1520 AD (fairly standard settings - 8 civs, pangea, etc.) during which time Cleo whose agenda involves respect for a large military kept denouncing me due to a small army even as I took my third or fourth capital. To be fair she praised me once during that game after the 5th capital.
-Lots of unjustifiable downtime. This one is also due in large part to the AI. The AI turns take somewhat too long (not unbearable) even on high end hardware. The more annoying part of this is that during AI turns they will liberally insult you or issue crazy demands, or praise you for not building wonders even as you siege down the captial of your fourth civ. These popups have an animation which takes entirely too long and cannot be skipped. Added together, AI turns can last over a minute and drive you mad especially if you are struggling against the astronomical bonuses AI get on high difficulty to compensate for their lack of ability to play the game.
Conclusion:
While the mechanics at the core of Civ 6 are well done and engaging, the AI and UI drag the whole game experience down too much to recommend. In a game where the focus is on singleplayer and thus necessitates playing against the AI, such an incompetent, slow, cheating, and inconsistent set of opponents combined with a generally irksome and unhelpful UI are unforgivable. Furthermore, the response from the developer in addressing issues has been entirely too slow and half hearted even when dealing with very simple problems. This is in contrast to a fair number of DLCs being released at very questionable price points ($5 for one civ and 60 turn scenario?).

Paladins fans may think I'm being toxic to Paladins, because I'm some sort of diehard Overwatch fan, but that would show a lack of maturity and intelligence on their part. Paladins was a great game during Alpha, but has slowly devolved into simply being a Overwatch clone, with only a few remaining differences, in my opinion.

I feel like I was "supposed" to like this game. I love games with a strong story and well-developed characters, even if that comes at the expense of gameplay, but the story in this game does not hold together.
PROS
* Characters - Many of the characters in the game are well-developed and have distinct personalities and motivations. You get to watch a few of the characters really grow and change throughout the game, and I think that’s the central appeal of the game. The main villain or villains (keeping this spoiler-free) however are generically evil for no particular reason, and midway through the story much of Max's (the main character's) motivations are incoherent.
* Choices - The decisions you make in one episode seem to impact outcomes in every episode afterward. (This is mostly illusion and the plot is actually linear, but it’s sort of fun while it lasts.)
* Premise - The first and second episode had me hooked. I wanted to know how this story would end.
* Music - The soundtrack to this game is great.
CONS
* Story - Starting in Episode 3, the threads holding the story together completely unravel and the game's logic falls apart. Max presumes connections between seemingly unrelated events for no reason. Concepts and storylines introduced in previous episodes remain unexplained or abandoned. As the game progresses, it feels like the writers had no narrative arc in mind for the story, with each writer wresting control of the story as it careens from one distraction to another until, unable to resolve the inconsistencies, it crashes headlong into a stupid and meaningless…
* Ending - One of the primary themes of the game is that every choice you make can have big, unexpected consequences. There was clearly an effort to make the game feel as though each decision could spin off into one of many possible futures. This made it all the more disappointing in the end when you’re given a binary choice between ending A or ending B (neither option makes much sense, but if you’ve played this far it scarcely matters). It’s the game’s final contradiction. Despite the hours of choices and outcomes, in the end regardless of your decisions, it comes down to the same A or B.

Pros:
- Well Optimized
Unlike Overwatch, I can run this game on Max at 100+ FPS and it looks great. All my friends who play on low eng gaming pcs can also play it at 60+ FPS.
- Wide Variety of Champions
I have particular tastes and this game offers fun and unique variations to all the common archetypes, enough to get you into the game and with more I can't imagine the game not being great for everyone. The frontline characters are the wekaest link imo, so if you love tanks... well, better hope you enjoy Fernando and Ruckus, who I find incredibly boring. Other than that though, the flanks are all great, the supports are all incredibly different and fun and the damage dealers, while not perfect has enough variety to keep the people who want a more traditional fps experience happy.
- Very generous Buy Ins and In Game Currency
Founders Pack will grant you all characters(even  unreleased ones) and a bunch of chests. So you can get in this game and have practically everything(outside cards, which you can easily access with the chests you're given). Even if you don't you earn daily gold, gold for leveling up characters, gold for leveling up passively and yes while you will have to focus on a few select characters at first to get the perfect loadout or buy a new character for a F2P model it's still a very generous one.
- Map Design and Items
Less choke points, more traditional free range of movement and more flank routes. Unlike Overwatch, which features choke points from the get go Paladins has much more opened maps in combination with it's characters that don't force you into pushing through boring choke point after choke point. If you want less clumped up shield spam(although it can happen with Ruckus, Fernando and Barrik rushing point on Siege) the game design, with the item system that allows priotization to beat different strats. Which is part of what makes it so good, playing vs shield spammers? Buy Wreckage and boom, your damage does almost double and potentially much more to shields.
- Great Visuals
Clean, unique, colorful and easy to read.
Cons:
- Cheaters
Game seems to have a weak anti-cheat system, so while not common you can run into cheaters from time to time which can be really annoying and frustrating.
- Payload
While the gametype is fine, the map design is a bit odd, the maps at times are great, but sometimes overly cluttered, or more often, too big and spaced out. The gametype is also less fun without a team to coordinate with because dying is punished much harder because if you die early on you have to run 3x as far as the Siege maps to get back to your team, so respawns become desynced and a lot of players will not pay attention to teammate's respawn times and just keep running in and continue the endless cycle.
Summary: Very fun and addictive game, with a lot of variety in gameplay, some solid maps, great optimization, nice visuals and a high emphasis on skill that make the game very rewarding to people looking to be rewarded for skill.

Wide open (quick)sandbox space exploration simulator...  quite a mouthful, I know.
KSP was developed as an indie game at it shows for both the good an bad reason. The bad: There are some minor bugs, the graphics sometimes feel a bit rushed (specially texturing) the game engine is slightly too demanding to the GPU compared to the output and there is hardly any useful tutorial within a game which has quite a steep learning curve.
The good: Virtually EVERYTHING else. The game is addictive, challenging, fun and being completely open ended is as replayable as you want it to be: Want to try out different plane models and see how they fly? Go for it. Want to build a ginormous space station in orbit around Kerbin? Be my guest. Want to explore all of the planets available in the solar system? Will take you a while, but go ahead. Wanna set a permanent base on the moon? Fine by me...  Basically the only limit is your imagination and the (only slightly simplified) physics of the universe. Cobble up whatever contraption you see fit and try it out, it will blow up more often than not, but with careful planning and learning from doing you will end up having something that can (sort of) fly in no time!
Get this game, get it now, learn, have fun and help those little critters get to space!

Wide open (quick)sandbox space exploration simulator...  quite a mouthful, I know.
KSP was developed as an indie game at it shows for both the good an bad reason. The bad: There are some minor bugs, the graphics sometimes feel a bit rushed (specially texturing) the game engine is slightly too demanding to the GPU compared to the output and there is hardly any useful tutorial within a game which has quite a steep learning curve.
The good: Virtually EVERYTHING else. The game is addictive, challenging, fun and being completely open ended is as replayable as you want it to be: Want to try out different plane models and see how they fly? Go for it. Want to build a ginormous space station in orbit around Kerbin? Be my guest. Want to explore all of the planets available in the solar system? Will take you a while, but go ahead. Wanna set a permanent base on the moon? Fine by me...  Basically the only limit is your imagination and the (only slightly simplified) physics of the universe. Cobble up whatever contraption you see fit and try it out, it will blow up more often than not, but with careful planning and learning from doing you will end up having something that can (sort of) fly in no time!
Get this game, get it now, learn, have fun and help those little critters get to space!

Easy Anti Cheat.

This is the same terrible system that plagues many good games and basically ruins everything. Same deal with Robocraft; good game, but uses EAC.
If you like the sound of the game and want to download it, go ahead, but just be aware that EAC is spying on you.

It's up to you to decide whether Kenny is worth sticking around.

Pros:
- Well Optimized
Unlike Overwatch, I can run this game on Max at 100+ FPS and it looks great. All my friends who play on low eng gaming pcs can also play it at 60+ FPS.
- Wide Variety of Champions
I have particular tastes and this game offers fun and unique variations to all the common archetypes, enough to get you into the game and with more I can't imagine the game not being great for everyone. The frontline characters are the wekaest link imo, so if you love tanks... well, better hope you enjoy Fernando and Ruckus, who I find incredibly boring. Other than that though, the flanks are all great, the supports are all incredibly different and fun and the damage dealers, while not perfect has enough variety to keep the people who want a more traditional fps experience happy.
- Very generous Buy Ins and In Game Currency
Founders Pack will grant you all characters(even  unreleased ones) and a bunch of chests. So you can get in this game and have practically everything(outside cards, which you can easily access with the chests you're given). Even if you don't you earn daily gold, gold for leveling up characters, gold for leveling up passively and yes while you will have to focus on a few select characters at first to get the perfect loadout or buy a new character for a F2P model it's still a very generous one.
- Map Design and Items
Less choke points, more traditional free range of movement and more flank routes. Unlike Overwatch, which features choke points from the get go Paladins has much more opened maps in combination with it's characters that don't force you into pushing through boring choke point after choke point. If you want less clumped up shield spam(although it can happen with Ruckus, Fernando and Barrik rushing point on Siege) the game design, with the item system that allows priotization to beat different strats. Which is part of what makes it so good, playing vs shield spammers? Buy Wreckage and boom, your damage does almost double and potentially much more to shields.
- Great Visuals
Clean, unique, colorful and easy to read.
Cons:
- Cheaters
Game seems to have a weak anti-cheat system, so while not common you can run into cheaters from time to time which can be really annoying and frustrating.
- Payload
While the gametype is fine, the map design is a bit odd, the maps at times are great, but sometimes overly cluttered, or more often, too big and spaced out. The gametype is also less fun without a team to coordinate with because dying is punished much harder because if you die early on you have to run 3x as far as the Siege maps to get back to your team, so respawns become desynced and a lot of players will not pay attention to teammate's respawn times and just keep running in and continue the endless cycle.
Summary: Very fun and addictive game, with a lot of variety in gameplay, some solid maps, great optimization, nice visuals and a high emphasis on skill that make the game very rewarding to people looking to be rewarded for skill.

If there is one game in my library I can always find myself coming back to, its Kerbal Space Program.
When I first heard of KSP, it was still in very early alpha, as a free download that was just the bare bones of what it is now. While the bump up in price was unexpected, I find it well worth it for what this game delivers. The game as it is now, offers a wide array of ways to play it. Sandbox to Career, you'll find yourself learning the laws of gravity and rocket engineer dynamics. The amount of depth, from physics to aerodynamics and all the way over to astrometry, requries it in order to advance further in the game. However, the reward is a accomplished feeling of performing the very same missions you'd expect out of the world's space programs, albeit with a little less complication.
The depth of physic-based features in the game is very heavy, forcing critical thinking and in-depth designing of rockets and spaceplanes to achieve your goals. Beyond that, the study of orbital position of planets and their gravitational fields come into play. All this, combined with costs of construction and real finite rescourses require you to work both mentally and physically in achieving the goals you set for yourself.
All and all, this game is a excellent learning tool and rewarding "choose your own path" game, even being used by some school systems in the US and UK as a way of teaching astronomy and physics in school due to its excellent depth in such fields. And for those of us who want a little more, more in-depth aerodynamics, planet diversity, or even a expansive construction system, there is a dedicated modding community adding more and impressive things to the roster of things for your Space Program to do.
In the words of Eugene "Gene" Kranz, "Our place was to raise our aspriations to those things that are possible, if we commit...We have to continue forward; to stop in space, is to surrender."

This game is awesome! The story is engaging, the character's are fleshed out, the visuals look stunning, the voice cast is perfect, and the songs and sounds are fitting. I also enjoyed taking the photos as a completion challenge, but it has no reward that I could find (other than bragging rights), which I didn't mind but is important to know before trying it. It is a more story-driven game with choices throughout that determine how the narrative will unfold. The time rewind mechanic puts an interesting spin on this type of "choose-your-own-adventure" game, as you can look at immediate results of some of your choices and then reverse your decision. Since you can only rewind time back to a certain point, long-reaching consequences may not be evident until you can no loner undo a decision, which adds to the tension. This also gives the game some replayability if you want to see how the game will play out with different choices. The game is long, however, especially if you decide to get all five episodes, so you might be less inclined to replay if you just wanted to change one choice toward the beginning of the game. Overall, if your into story- and choice-driven games, this one is definitely worth your time.

Given the amount of hours put into this and the previous two Civilization games, I thought that I'd might as well give it a short review.
---
I'll start off by pointing out the negatives:
- Single player AI: I don't know if this feature is intentional or not, but diplomacy with the AI is always (not even "almost always") futile. I have never been able to strike a fair trade with the AI, and a good example of this is trading in luxury resources. No matter what your relationship with the AI is, the AI will only accept an unbalanced deal where they come out on top. I don't know whether this is supposed to mimick the AI believing you're struggling, but it makes diplomacy more of a pointless rather than a useful aspect of the game, and the commonly critiqued ridiculous warmongering penalties add to that.
While it is just about noticable that AI combat has been improved in the past couple of updates, it's still pretty... well, sh*t. When the player faces a declaration of war, the AI never bothers to take turns to prepare for an attack, save for the odd units on your borders. In combat, they just don't know how to fight, flinging arrows/cannon balls/probably not missiles at whatever might catch the corner of their eye. In additons to both of these, the AI's forward settling just kills your early game, again due to warmongering penalties. I don't know if it's a recent bug or if it's intentional, but it seems to have only started recently. I tried playing a game as Indonesia, and by turn 12 Nubia had plonked their damn city down with 2 tiles between it and my cap, which doesn't seem to be possible for me to do.
While it has been improved in the most recent update which allows friendly units to stack with foreign religious units, I still cannot bear the way the AI rushes those missionaries towards your cities after you've built up your bomb♥♥♥♥♥religion to help your civilization stand the test of time. This sh*t just tests my goddamn patience. I end up having to DOW them just to kill off their religious units.
- Single player game speeds: Marathon speed is simply unplayable, and epic only just feels playable with highly productive cities. This is purely based on post-turn loading times, with the "Please wait" globe spinning for up to a good minute, and the turns required to train units/ buildings. I've tried these speeds a few times, and I ended up just giving up with scouts, as building my second building or unit just takes too much time without spamming the enter key for about 30-40 turns.
- Multiplayer: Near-broken. While games are great when you get into them, many games usually end between turns 1-40 because either everyone rage quits because of horse-rushes as Scythia, or the game just breaks completely, not to mention the constant in-lobby drops. Don't get me wrong, multiplayer is by far my favourite part of Civ. 6, but I must have actually PROPERLY played about 1/20th of the entire number of games that I've joined. I'd also complain about toxic players, but that isn't really fair as all multiplayer games have them.
---
Moving on to the positive aspects of the game (Don't mistake my short points as not having much to say; My hands are already tired from typing):
- Theme, graphics and art style: Why people complain about this behooves me. I actually really enjoy the art style, and it shows that the developers are trying to spice things up a lil'. As for the theme of exploration and colonisation, this is a personal favourite of mine, and is what makes England my favourite civ to play as in addition to the fun of becoming a major naval superpower (with indonesia in this regard being a close second since the update).
- Gameplay: In contrast to the broken AI, the actual gameplay itself is enjoyable. As many others have said before me, districs make the whole generated world feel a lot more dynamic. It brings a new level of city planning into the game, as wonder terrain requirements for bonuses and tile improvements for city yields must also be taken into account. The automatic generation of great people from these districts feels much better than how great people were managed by its predecessors.
The whole great people system in general feels a lot smoother. I don't know if it's the UI and/or those fancy icons they brought in the new update, or whether I'm just imagining it being better, but the previous games always felt kind of awkward for me in how they handled great people, despite me understanding how they were gotten. I now feel a lot more confident in competing for great people and working towards a certain victory.
Multiplayer: I know it seems like I'm contradicting my previous points about the game's multiplayer, but I stand by the points I made before as I say that multiplayer is fun and less repetitive than you'd expect it to be, despite the frustration of finding a decent game. In my experience, playing against other players and eliminating the AI's irritating hair-trigger agendas allows a whole new level of either co-operation or conflict. My only word of warning is that multiplayer is a LOT more different to single player in how you're playing against ACTUAL people. With that being said, good luck.

If there is one game in my library I can always find myself coming back to, its Kerbal Space Program.
When I first heard of KSP, it was still in very early alpha, as a free download that was just the bare bones of what it is now. While the bump up in price was unexpected, I find it well worth it for what this game delivers. The game as it is now, offers a wide array of ways to play it. Sandbox to Career, you'll find yourself learning the laws of gravity and rocket engineer dynamics. The amount of depth, from physics to aerodynamics and all the way over to astrometry, requries it in order to advance further in the game. However, the reward is a accomplished feeling of performing the very same missions you'd expect out of the world's space programs, albeit with a little less complication.
The depth of physic-based features in the game is very heavy, forcing critical thinking and in-depth designing of rockets and spaceplanes to achieve your goals. Beyond that, the study of orbital position of planets and their gravitational fields come into play. All this, combined with costs of construction and real finite rescourses require you to work both mentally and physically in achieving the goals you set for yourself.
All and all, this game is a excellent learning tool and rewarding "choose your own path" game, even being used by some school systems in the US and UK as a way of teaching astronomy and physics in school due to its excellent depth in such fields. And for those of us who want a little more, more in-depth aerodynamics, planet diversity, or even a expansive construction system, there is a dedicated modding community adding more and impressive things to the roster of things for your Space Program to do.
In the words of Eugene "Gene" Kranz, "Our place was to raise our aspriations to those things that are possible, if we commit...We have to continue forward; to stop in space, is to surrender."

Him and his wife go on vacation and she tries to get him to write again, immediately after his wife disappears and everything turns all strange and monsters start coming. The game is about 8-10 hours long with no multiplayer but two DLC that you had to pay for on Xbox but we get right away for free. The graphics in the game are pretty good and is pretty optimized. The developer did a very good job porting this game to PC. One of my favourite things in this game is the attention to detail with the collectibles. One of the things you can do is watch episodes of a fictional show in the universe that is similar to the episodes of The Twilight Zone. The detail is great and I personally sat through each of the episodes that I found and enjoyed each one. Another great collectible that the game had was manuscript for Alan's work. The writing is fantastic and was an extremely rewarding collectible so I strongly recommend that you explore these great environments to find each one. The light mechanics in Alan Wake are really well done and the system that makes the game feel like a television series is excellent. Each chapter is treated like a new episode to a TV show that you tune in to watch every week even with the "Previously On Alan Wake" section at the beginning. I can't wait for a sequel to this game and I can recommend this game to anyone who enjoys an excellent storyline in a thriller/adventure game. 90/100

This game is awesome! The story is engaging, the character's are fleshed out, the visuals look stunning, the voice cast is perfect, and the songs and sounds are fitting. I also enjoyed taking the photos as a completion challenge, but it has no reward that I could find (other than bragging rights), which I didn't mind but is important to know before trying it. It is a more story-driven game with choices throughout that determine how the narrative will unfold. The time rewind mechanic puts an interesting spin on this type of "choose-your-own-adventure" game, as you can look at immediate results of some of your choices and then reverse your decision. Since you can only rewind time back to a certain point, long-reaching consequences may not be evident until you can no loner undo a decision, which adds to the tension. This also gives the game some replayability if you want to see how the game will play out with different choices. The game is long, however, especially if you decide to get all five episodes, so you might be less inclined to replay if you just wanted to change one choice toward the beginning of the game. Overall, if your into story- and choice-driven games, this one is definitely worth your time.

Nuclear Throne and I have a rather long history. Not only have I put 83 hours into the game myself, I spent at least that much time watching various YouTubers play it for at least a year before taking the plunge. And despite having a working understanding of Nuclear Throne… this game is hard. Hard enough to make me rage quit with some amount of regularity, or exclaim my fair share of foul language.
Nuclear Throne could most easily be classified as a Bullet Hell game. If you’re not familiar with that genre, let me paint you a picture:
Imagine standing in a gymnasium surrounded by about 100 people with dodge balls, each and every one looking at you with murder in their eyes. And then suddenly, and all at once, they launch their dodgeballs at you with the sole intent of pelting you with malicious, unholy, precision. It’s your job to dodge the rubbery onslaught and make it out in one piece. For if you fail, the princess will be eaten… by like, a dragon or something.
Now if that sounds like pure absurdity, it’s probably because it is. Some Bullet Hell games are ridiculous, stupidly over the top, and—in my opinion—for people who are at least part cyborg.  — an example would be Touhhou Project —  However, thankfully for us mortals, Nuclear Throne isn’t nearly as insane as other games. It can be hectic and hard to follow, yes. But it’s certainly beatable.
I should know. I’ve done it four times! In…. 83 hours…
(I’m not going to think about how that’s 20.75 hours between each win. Nope.)
Despite being a Bullet Hell game, Nuclear Throne is also a Rogue-Like in that the world is randomly generated each time and you only have one life. So make it count.
The game is broken up into stages and transition stages. You select your character from a choice of twelve then are sucked through a portal and thrust directly into the chaos. Your only objective: “Reach the Throne”. Starting the game with a revolver, you must kill every enemy in a level before progressing to the next.
Stages are made up of three levels, IE 1-1, 1-2, and 1-3, then followed by a dark transition stage, where your sight is impaired, like 2-1. The next stage begins and the game continues on until you die—I mean win!
On the final level of each stage, you must fight a boss, which is actually fairly difficult until you get the hang of them. I still have trouble with the boss on 5-3. Lil’ Hunter. He’s a real♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ But not impossible to beat! Just believe in yourself.
Once you reach the final boss and beat it, you are taken to a second phase of the fight. If you are mentally prepared and can best this final challenge… then the game starts over and is even more difficult! *Cue confetti and pyrotechnics*
This is known as looping and it’s a main component of the game. The higher score you wish to achieve, the more loops will undoubtedly be necessary. After a loop, the game literally throws everything at you. Enemies are no longer bound to particular stages and can all appear in one giant writhing death ball that would make the Zerg blush. However, as well as having to deal with an unrelenting tide of never ending death constantly trying to pull the very life from you, the game also adds new bosses only available after a loop!
But fear not! The odds aren’t entirely stacked against you.
Although the game certainly throws legions at you. As you get further and further into the game, more and more powerful weapons will drop, giving you the tools you need to fight back. (Although the really cool weapons usually drop after a loop.)
The game also has a leveling mechanic that rewards you with “Mutations” upon each successive level. Most enemies in the game drop “Rads,” this game’s form of experience. In the context of Nuclear Throne, when you level up, you mutate, giving each of the your newly-acquired powers a nice flavorful context.
The different weapons and mutation combinations alone have given me enough reason to continually go back to the game. Some of the mutations are pretty powerful, and can really change the way you play.
On top of the plethora of choices, every character has two ultra mutations to pick from at level 10 that will dramatically alter how you play the character. These are, usually, ridiculously powerful.
One of my favorite aspects of Nuclear Throne is that each one of the twelve characters feel different from each other. And not just artistically or contextually. Each character possesses a unique passive and active ability. The passives change things like the amount of ammo you pick up, your speed, your starting health, or—one of my personal favorites—all weapons becoming automatic, while the various active abilities help you react to the enemies and the world around you. For example one character, Eyes, has the power of telekinesis and can slightly push enemy bullets away from him helping to avoid certain death, while simultaneously pulling items and enemies towards him! Very helpful.
Nuclear Throne’s cast is also quite diverse when it comes to gender without feeling like it’s forced or pandering, which is refreshing to see. Though there isn’t much of a “story” in Nuclear Throne, there is plenty of context and lore, making all of the characters feel right at home.
Most of the “lore” comes from cryptic hints or text on loading screens.
“Welcome to the future.” “There used to be trees here.” “The wind hurts.” “Always wear dry socks.” (Good advice!)
I would be doing Nuclear Throne a disservice if I didn’t talk about the wonderful art style.
It’s cute and minimalist. The game has great artwork and the various locations all look wonderful. Not to mention the characters, all of which have very nice designs and distinctive silhouettes and stand out from the background, making it easy to keep track of where you are when things get crazy.
And trust me they will…
Also, many of the characters have a rare alternate skin that will randomly show up on occasion. And when I say rare, I mean rare. In my 83 hours I’ve only seen some of the “B Skins” and many of them only once!
Along with the game’s great art style, the game is filled with awesome melodies from acoustic and electric guitar that remind me of the wild west, while still feeling modern and contemporary. The consistent, pumping drum lines and sweet♥♥♥♥♥guitar (with some nice twang thrown in for good measure), all comes together in a way that I really dig. The music in this game is reminiscent of the Tristram theme from Diablo, but with pounding drums, funk, and some western twang. I should mention that each level also has a rare “B music” as well.
Here are two great examples are the Main Theme, and the Crystal Caves theme.
The few downsides to Nuclear Throne are that it is one of the few games that will truly make me rage. Once you get a momentum going in the game, and you die it is VERY jarring. And many times it’s from something that you didn’t even see. Or worse, something you did…
I have hit my desk and cursed bitterly more than a few times…
However, the negatives of this game are far outweighed by the positives. Honestly. Maybe I’m biased, but considering I’ve somehow put 83 hours into this game since February. Nuclear Throne does something right.
Or maybe I’m crazy…
This game takes a lot of adjusting. You have to play it in a very particular way, and it requires a lot of attention. It is quite fast, very hectic, and has lots of screen shake. But if you’re willing to give it a try, you’ll also find a game worth coming back to time and time again. Even if it makes you say things that would make your mother faint.

Civ 6 is a solid game. It is a surprisingly complete vanilla game compared to the previous releases and it has the best multiplayer in the franchise yet. Whether you will like this game really boils down to personal preference. I have played all the Civ games since the original, and it saddens me that I can't recommend this recent addtion: It's just not fun.
Buy this game if you like:
- Cartoon graphics
- Pixar-like leader animations
- Uninspiring Wonders
- Depressing soundtrack
- Incompetent AI
- No World Congress or UN
- No diplomatic victory
- Wide instead of tall empire building
- Pointless espionage system
If none of that interests you, you might want to just play Civ 5 instead. Heck, I enjoyed Beyond Earth more than this game. Only get Civ 6 when all of its expansions are released and it becomes a more richer, more competent Civilisation game.

When I am writting this review, Steam shows 354 hours in game. However due to DRM free and moding, I already spent 1400+ hours (KSP is DRM free and is modable - so I play from non Steam-connected copy which is of stable version and specified mod mix - that is why). And I am counting.
What is this game about? Sending green folk (called Kerbals) to space and to another planets. For science. And having TONS and TONS of fun. Well, in case you like rockets, planes, space and explosions. In whatever order. It is so hard to describe the game I advice you to give a check to youtube - e.g. Scott Manleys channel will give you nice view into what KSP is about.
I bought this game back in 1.0.5 (32bit only) only out of boredom and to satisfy my game hoarding habbit. What I buy I do try - so I gave it a quick look before just adding it to my library. I tried to launch a rocket (I was unaware of contracts that time) - the chute deployed instead of expected fireshow. Some testing revealed the problem. I launched Jebediah and landed him back... It was kind of fun... Can I make it to orbit?
After couple hours at 3 AM (working day followed) I maintained very odd, but stable orbit. I literally danced at my darkened man cave-corner. For two weeks straight, I slept only 4 hours a day. I designed rockets in my head while driving, or falling asleep, I was making sketches of new projects while waiting for a meeting at work, I was (and I still am) proactively looking for books and documentaries to study or inspire myself. I have a time to play at PC only around 4 hours a day at max, but KSP takes much much more hours per day. In times before KSP, when on toilet, I would check the smartphone for funny gifs to have some giggles. Now, I am all about space exploration...
In those two weeks I found out I was wrong all my life about microgravity, orbital manneuvers and ascends of rockets. I was actualy learning stuff and I had great time doing so. Then I found out mods. It was like Christmas. Then a 1.1.x versions came and we received completely new engine, 64bit support. I fel in love with superfriendly community around KSP.
And all it took, is lego based rocket building. Behind simple concept of straping a big fuel tank and engine under a crew module lies very complex mechanics of orbital physics. I droped my dream to be an astronaut at age of 5 (bad memory of kindergarden "event" - so I am sure). After more than 20 years later, I am back :)
You can be new Elon Musk, or a reincarnator of Neil Armstrong. Or would you rather be Werner von Braun? You can be all of this. You can build rockets, planes, rovers, or any mad creation of yours (Kerbal mixer to mix actual Kerbals). ANd with mods, you can do really anything. Game can be easened (assisting mods), widened (parts mod, more planets) turned realistic (RSS/RO) and much more.
Well... long text and no actual review of what this game is. Sigh... Ok, go to youtube, check Kerbal Space Program... Does it seem funny? Give it try. I did and it is best game purchase I ever did. I already can play other games, and not touch KSP for two or three days. But I still play, and I still do enjoy it beyond I ever imagined.

Decided to take a chance due to the 50% off coupon.  Long term fan of the series, was very hardcore into Civ III and IV, became more casual with V as work/family commitments make 8+ hrs to play a full game hard to come by and I hate stopping in the middle of a game :D
Pros:
- The addition of districts adds a nice layer of complexity to building up your civilization and managing your cities that was missing from the earlier sequels.
- Religious warfare is awesome.
- While not perfect, the additions to diplomacy and the personalities added to AI civs is nice.  Definitely an area that needs some work, but I can see the potential.
- The game runs better on my computer than Civ V despite it being several years newer and my computer being far better than the recommended specs for Civ V.
- I personally love the art direction in this version.  The game looks wonderful, especially at night if you select the option that turns on the day/night cycle.
- The lenses are awesome, and the strategic overview where everything is flat and represented by icons is actually useful in this version, whereas I found it painful to use in previous versions.
Cons:
- I'd like to see more Civilizations to choose from.  I assume these will continue to be added with DLC, but even with all current DLC the selection is prerty light.
- I'm not a fan of the civics card system.  It's a bit cumbersome, especially in the late game when you've unlocked a bunch.  It would be nice to be able to group the cards by eras (specifically the military ones.  I really don't need to see 50% boost to production of medieval units when I'm rolling modern armor around the map)
- The AI needs work, specifically in combat.  Winning wars is laughably easy.  I'm not some grand strategist who can stomp the AI on the highest levels, I usually get a decent challenge out of playing on Prince/King level, but I was able to steamroll everyone quite easily on my first playthrough, despite being very inefficient with my city layouts and production.  Had two civilizations declare war on me at the same time, which should have led to a challenging two front war, but instead the enemy on my western front didn't do anything at all and after some light resistance in the east I was able to move deep within their territory and force them to sue for peace in no time at all.
- No matter what you do diplomatically or how friendly you get with a civilization, once you start winning, all AI civs will hate you.  They'll denounce you for anything and everything, even if it's got nothing to do with them.  I'm sure this is something that will be improved by Firaxis over time, but it's a little disappointing.  It would be great to build a meaningful relationship with another civilization and be able to win with an ally instead of being one Civ vs the world once you reach the modern era.
- The micromanagement once you get into the late game is a real pain in the balls.  The lack of a production queue is a serious flaw.  Don't even really need a big one, just let me queue up 3 things while I'm in the middle of a war instead of having every turn take 15-20 minutes because I'm forced to micromanage production of 10+ cities while also pushing armies around the map.
- Building "tall" (fewer, larger cities) is a less feasable play style due to the district changes.  If you want to succeed you're going to need a decent amount of cities, otherwise you'll find yourself limited in the late game.
Overall:
A fun game with some flaws that don't really detract from the experience too much.  Hardcore fans of the series will either love or hate some of the changes, so keep that in mind when reading reviews.  Casual fans and newbies will find a lot to enjoy here, and it will only get better as Firaxis and modders continue to improve on the game.

tl;dr

I don't often write reviews however I feel like writing my thoughts on this game. I have put quite a few hours into Civ 5, despite my Steam account saying 260~ hours upon the time I am writing this review its probably at least twice as much as I had a non Steam copy for the longest time. Anyways, Civ 6 is a very nice game to play, its very pretty, it feels new and updated, however its lacking certain "Civ" characteristics that make it fun for more intense players. As someone who splits the difference between "casual" and "try hard" when it comes to a civ player its really hard for me to decide where I am landing on this game. I'm sure many people are like me when it comes to this so hopefully this review can clear the air. I play Civ 5 with the Vox Pop mod, it does a great job of making Civ 5 a little more intense, and forces you to try a little harder, this game seems to miss those marks.
t
AI
The AI seems much less intelligent than it does in Civ 5, not playing to its strengths (at all) and making trade and any other diplomacy next to useless. It seems like gaining friends and alliances is done by spinning an arrow and it landing on whoever wants to be your friend. If you have a different government than a different Civ, chances are they will denounce you. Having friends with other civs doesn't seem to really help much either, it makes spreading tourists and religious units a little easier at some points but if you are attacked in war they won't come help even if you are allies. They often do random pointless things and make absolutely stupid trade offers that either totally give you the shaft or help you way too much. For example, one turn I was offered a peace deal where I was to give up several great works and luxuries the next turn they gave me some gold. The only feasible victory I have seen for the computer is science or religion, however the AI doesn't seem capable of finishing a religious victory.
Gameplay
The core gameplay of this game seems to be very much improved, the new "districts" system is brand new and in my opinion works very well for the game. However it has been tricky to really plan and maximize each city, oftentimes you need to heavily plan out district and wonder placement to maximize each tile. Certain wonders and districts provide bonuses to other districts and tiles so you need to really think about where you are putting things in order to get the most bang for your buck. City growth has been tweaked, you now need housing to supplement the food growth, you can't just plant down a city in the middle of a bunch of grass and wheat so you can explode a city in a few turns. Coastal tiles are not nearly as valuable as in previous games so you are encouraged to settle inland as opposed to on the water. Certain bonuses wonders aren't worth the massive time sink you need to build them. Great people seem to be more or less useless as well, there aren't enough of them in certain categories, and late game some of them provide bonuses that don't really pay off in the long run.
Maps
In my opinion, there is very little variety in the maps available right now. Civ 5 had a million possible maps, and even if you played a game you had the chance to see a plethora of different layouts. With Civ 6 I have played on continents, Island Plates, and TSL Earth. Continents seems similar to Pangea, however has the possibility of several smaller seas, Small continents almost always ends with two reasonably small islands with a MASSIVE body of water between them on one side leaving most of the map dead. TSL Earth is incredibly unbalanced, civs like America, Rome, China, and Arabia have massive advantages in terms of land. They end up being able to take entire continents without much resitance, Civs like Indonesia (played one TSL game with them, theres 0 space to grow if you don't get Australia/India) recieve almost no land and need to rely on bum rushing sailing and shipbuilding to get your units to bigger bits of land.
Civs
Coming from Civ 5, I am feeling a little lacking in the number of Civs, however considering how much DLC that has been released for Civ 5 over the years its unfair to judge Civ 6 for not having so many. The ones available now have some fun unique advantages that are well thought out, however learning each civ takes some time and multiple playthroughs to maximize benefits. In civ 5, it seemed that I was better able to hop into a game with a new Civ and do well using a new civ. As far as balance goes it definitely seems there are some Civs that are more OP than others, however that is unsurprising as well, hopefully some mods will be available to balance things better but only time will tell.
Graphics
I personally am in love with the visuals of the new game, compared to Civ 5 yes, some might say they are "cartooney" but they are growing on me fast. The wonders and districts are incredibly detailed, and the leader screens show much more attention to detail than I originally noticed and anticipated. The animations are very well done and vary depending on the unit, early game melee units have some good animations (see spearmen vaulting over defeated units). Overall I love the new look of everything.
Conclusion
Rating this game at its current state I would give it a 7-8/10. It is a very very strong base game that will need to be improved in similar ways that civ 5 will need to be improved, new maps, civs, balancing tweaks, gameplay changes (give me a ♥♥♥♥ing production queue ffs) to stand the test of time. The late game still needs some work, becoming more and more tiresome depending on victory conditions that can easily get boring depending on how you like to play. Civ 5 had some similar problems but again mods often allieviated some of that. I bought the game with one of the 50% off coupons that everyone got and at the 40 dollar point for the deluxe edition I think it's worth it. At 60 for the regular or 80 for the deluxe I would say wait a bit, but if you have the coupon I would pull the trigger.

Alan Wake is a game set in a world of darkness and mystery. Within that darkness, Mr. Alan Wake (a horror fiction writer who gets his inspiration from the great Stephen King) decides he needs a more intriguing location to get his creative writing juices flowing. He and his wife leave Manhattan and visit a very old styled town somewhere in the sticks of a New England state.
Without spoiling too much, let me get into the gameplay.
As Alan Wake you are tasked with finding your wife at all costs. Having to work your way through the forests and buldings in this foreign town. The catch? There are tons of dark shadow figures lurking about. You find that light is the only weapon that can defeat them. Your best way to fight them? Flashlights! Naturally the first thought that comes to mind is that flashlights as a weapon is a very cool and new idea. You weaken the enemies with flashlights and finish them off with a gun. After a while, the shock and awe of this innovative concept does lose its "Shine" (get it?). However, it still keeps you on your toes at all times. Having to find batteries to keep your flashlight going can be ver intense at crucial times.
Overall? The story and gameplay are both very engaging, and most certainly unforgettable. You WILL remember this game years from now.
Story - Great story = 4 Points
Visuals - Very visually appealing = 2 Points
Sound - With songs from artists like Roy Orbison and David bowie, this soundtrack is music to the ears = 2 points
Gameplay - While this game had an interesting combat system, at times Alan Wakes movement seemed sluggish and not as responsive and fluent as one would hope. Unfortunately it loses one point in my book. = 1 Point
Final Score: 9/10

An year after initial release, after a set of DLC and patches, and traditionally reworked mechanics (in Civ V, that was diplomacy, in Civ VI — religion), I still can't really recommend it.
The core gameplay is decent, the districts/wonders and policies are nice development of Civ V features. Religion is still overcomplicated, though. The game lacks overall quality, and the most miserable feature is user interface. It is still a bit buggy, somewhat unclear, and misses some important information, though it certainly has been improved since the release. The AI is still mediocre, wastes workers/settlers, picks bad postitions, chooses targets incorrectly (like healthy weaker units instead of heavily wounded, for example). Overall art style became even more cartoony which I don't like, the map doesn't resemble the real world even remotely, especially with those districts and wonders it looks like a pure wargame now, and not a grand strategy. The graphics are good, day/night changing is a beatiful idea, but because the interface doesn't change its color with the daylight, it's harder to see anything at night under the icons, so in the end you'll want to set some fixed time of the day. Leaders also look good, but they are overacting badly, and different animations are separated by fade-out/fade-in effect. This is cheap as hell. Also, no fancy backgrounds anymore. Voice acting is boring, including most of the quotes, but it's already gone bad since Civ IV (even worse now).
Thus, no, don't waste your time and money getting this even on sale. At this time, Civ V with its own flaws is still better.

Nuclear Throne is a rougelike, top-down, point and click shooter developed by Vlambeer, A Dutch independent game studio by Rami Ismail and Jan Willem Nijman. It is considered to be the early access game that does it right. Stable gameplay and weekly updates, this game is a fun time, but takes a bit of practice and feel for the game at first. The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic world filled with mutants. You play as 12 different mutant characters who fight through this wasteland of destruction while collecting radiation and leveling up or "mutating" with 28 base mutations, choosing between 4 random ones, and with the choice between 2 (3 with another playable mutant) character specific mutation obtained once max level is reached.  I, being a fan of these types of games, love the characters with special abilities and hindrances, leveling up and getting certain perks, the enormous variety of weapons, and the randomness of the levels. All this combined will make most of every run unique,

In my opinion the main part of the game is something called looping. In Nuclear Throne you progress through portals to get to the next level while fighting fixed enemy variants. After the main boss is defeated,  you go back to the first level and all the enemy types fought (not including bosses) get thrown into your game at one time. This is called looping. While you are looping the game turns into a survival mode of sorts while revisiting all previous levels and defeating enemies and previous bosses that have higher health with every loop. The game also has daily runs where you compete against other players to get as far as you can. There are daily leaderboards at
that tally up the scores and rank players.
Nuclear Throne changes with every week and when the game is released (no set release date) it will be out on PC, PS4, and PS Vita (possibly will release on Xbox One). Vlambeer also hosts development streams every Tuesday and Thrusday on Twitch.tv where the Steam build can be bought as well by subscribing for $12.99. Any fans of famous rougelikes such as The Binding of Issac, Spelunky, Faster Than Light, Don't Starve and more will enjoy this game. Good luck and have fun Throning.

While this is an alright Civilization game, with potential to be better (and probably will be with some proper updates), I can't recommend it.
Why, you might wonder? I'll tell you.
Because even if it's an alright game, it's also a game where the devs have a skewed focus. There's very little in terms of QoL improvements in the updates, and the end-game is nothing but tedious.
Take Espionage, for example. Unlike previous iterations of Civilization, you can't turn the system off. And they've expanded it, so enemy spies can target not only cities, but also districts. So you'll want to cover a lot with counter-spies to not have havoc wrecked throughout your Empire. The problem? You can't set permanent counter-spying assignments, so in the end-game you will spend a lot of your time reassigning counter-spies because hell, apparently this is the devs opinion of fun. I don't share it. It breaks the late game since it means you've got the choice between doing something that is outright not fun, or allowing the enemy spies to do whatever they want. Stupid, to say the least.
Or take the fact that they implemented an Alert function that, in fact, does not function. When you station a troop next to some mines and set it to Alert you'd expect it to actually wake up if a barbarian comes close, right? But it doesn't. Troop remains soundly asleep while the world burns around them, not waking up until said barbarian pokes them with a stick to see if they contain coins. Stupid, to say the least.
Or just something as basic as the fact that THERE IS NO PRODUCTION QUEUE. Let that sink in, for a moment. Couple this up with the fact that your cities MUST, at every given point of the game, produce something... You see the problem? Especially when there's nothing left you want to build, so you have to build projects. But if your city have decent production, you have to re-set that project production every 3 turns. Multiply this with ten cities. Then add the aforementioned spies on top of that. Sounds fun to you? I didn't think so.
As it stands, this game got too many things that is bound to rub you the wrong way, and make playing tedious instead of fun. It's dumb. Go play Civilization 5 instead, which is a much more polished game, but that, most importantly, isn't outright trying to annoy you.

When I am writting this review, Steam shows 354 hours in game. However due to DRM free and moding, I already spent 1400+ hours (KSP is DRM free and is modable - so I play from non Steam-connected copy which is of stable version and specified mod mix - that is why). And I am counting.
What is this game about? Sending green folk (called Kerbals) to space and to another planets. For science. And having TONS and TONS of fun. Well, in case you like rockets, planes, space and explosions. In whatever order. It is so hard to describe the game I advice you to give a check to youtube - e.g. Scott Manleys channel will give you nice view into what KSP is about.
I bought this game back in 1.0.5 (32bit only) only out of boredom and to satisfy my game hoarding habbit. What I buy I do try - so I gave it a quick look before just adding it to my library. I tried to launch a rocket (I was unaware of contracts that time) - the chute deployed instead of expected fireshow. Some testing revealed the problem. I launched Jebediah and landed him back... It was kind of fun... Can I make it to orbit?
After couple hours at 3 AM (working day followed) I maintained very odd, but stable orbit. I literally danced at my darkened man cave-corner. For two weeks straight, I slept only 4 hours a day. I designed rockets in my head while driving, or falling asleep, I was making sketches of new projects while waiting for a meeting at work, I was (and I still am) proactively looking for books and documentaries to study or inspire myself. I have a time to play at PC only around 4 hours a day at max, but KSP takes much much more hours per day. In times before KSP, when on toilet, I would check the smartphone for funny gifs to have some giggles. Now, I am all about space exploration...
In those two weeks I found out I was wrong all my life about microgravity, orbital manneuvers and ascends of rockets. I was actualy learning stuff and I had great time doing so. Then I found out mods. It was like Christmas. Then a 1.1.x versions came and we received completely new engine, 64bit support. I fel in love with superfriendly community around KSP.
And all it took, is lego based rocket building. Behind simple concept of straping a big fuel tank and engine under a crew module lies very complex mechanics of orbital physics. I droped my dream to be an astronaut at age of 5 (bad memory of kindergarden "event" - so I am sure). After more than 20 years later, I am back :)
You can be new Elon Musk, or a reincarnator of Neil Armstrong. Or would you rather be Werner von Braun? You can be all of this. You can build rockets, planes, rovers, or any mad creation of yours (Kerbal mixer to mix actual Kerbals). ANd with mods, you can do really anything. Game can be easened (assisting mods), widened (parts mod, more planets) turned realistic (RSS/RO) and much more.
Well... long text and no actual review of what this game is. Sigh... Ok, go to youtube, check Kerbal Space Program... Does it seem funny? Give it try. I did and it is best game purchase I ever did. I already can play other games, and not touch KSP for two or three days. But I still play, and I still do enjoy it beyond I ever imagined.

All in all, buy this game! But do so knowing that it will be frustrating and time-consuming to master.

This game has truly been the over-appreciated Crystal of a game of mine lately; Melting hours upon hours away as it has fixed my Steroids-infused adrenaline rushes in a manner truly only achieved by harsh, fast Rogue-likes - just like this.
In essence, it's difficulty can seem overwhelmingly punishing at times and at points it feels like only a Robot could attain the proper level of dodging-skill; yet, once one gets the hang of it (after several fast-paced game-overs), it is a truly rewarding experience.
One's skill is like a Plant: A small, meager bud at first, nurtured by the sweat, blood and tears to grow tremendously and brilliate. The game is well-balanced in that regard; that it does not entirely rely on lucky circumstances regarding power-ups (Mutations), Spawn-areas, Weapons, etc. This feature makes it somewhat of a Rebel in it's genre, which is a neat thing, considering the vagueness of the genre in the first place.
The true Horror of the game comes upon completion, which, without any forms of spoilation, is a love-hate relationship, but fits the whole theme of the game rather well.
Remember to keep your Eyes peeled for the huge amounts of updates constantly pumped out of Vlambeer HQ; truly showing their passion for the game.
Final Verdict: Brutal adrenaline-rush that demands your full-on attention; but don't be no Chicken and disconcern it because of this. The game believes in you, even if it might not at first.

As some other reviewers mentioned, don't bother with this when you can just get your Civ fix with 5. In comparison, Civ V is far more streamlined than Civ VI. This game adds "complexity" in the form of extra micromanagement; turns take longer but I don't gain any enjoyment from that. In particular, I'm not fond of the new city management. It bogs everything down. Happiness, while a bit simple, was far better than this nonsense.
I also don't like the new tile management, with placing districts and wonders. Districts is okay, I guess, but having to deal with both districts and wonder placement just takes too much extra effort and foresight. In order to optimize each city, you have to have each tile it currently has and will have planned out for at least a few dozen turns, though 100 or more is ideal. Oh, and how each of those plans fit into your empire as a whole is important too.
I feel like I need to start taking notes or make a spreadsheet while playing this game. . . And, to me, that isn't Civ. The franchise has always been on the lighter end of 4x games, particularly if you are playing single player. And that's what I liked: I like being able to open a relatively easy game of Civ to pass the time, or play when I'm tired, or to run while I'm watching a show. It's relaxing. But Civ VI takes that away from me without really giving me anything worthwhile in return.
Is this a popular opinion? I don't know. Have I played it a bunch? No. I'm staring at my 6.6 hours thinking about how much crap I'm going to get for a negative review with under 20 hours in a 4x game, but guess what? It didn't take long to figure out that the game just isn't my thing. I have no interest in playing the current game. And, based on playtime, my friends seem to feel the same way.
If you like it, well, great! But I can't recommend a game when I'd rather be playing the previous game in the series.

Civ 6 receives ALOT of flack for whatever reason; the bugs, the leader DLC, hating the art style or being a noob.
But IMO its a great addition to the franchise. "Unstacking the cities" makes city placement more diverse and dynamic. The different leaders introduce new play styles and challenges. Mods are better suppoprted with integration meant from engine. So there's definately some great improvements to this rendition of Civ.
That being said it isn't without its quirks, bugs and issues. Finding a game that will last longer than 20 mins when people decide they hate their start is difficult and really should be addressed. I reccommend joining CPL if you're serious about playing Civ because people are less likely to leave a CPL game. Games can sometimes lose connection for no reason, personally I'd like to see the possibility for dedicated servers and good old pit boss (who knows it may come) for better flexibility when it comes to playing.
But the important thing is that the developer is continuing to improve the game! As with EVERY Civ game there were issues at launch. And there still maybe, but they're getting worked on and Mods provide great relief in the meantime.

pros
- the unpacked cities give more dynamics to the game
- special unit upgrades give diff types of units purpose

cons
