The Walking Dead: Season 2 is the continuing story about a young girl struggling to survive in a post-apocalyptic world where trusting other survivors are difficult, zombies are a secondary threat, and conflicted leaderships turn into violence against themselves. You play as Clementine, a secondary, major character from the legendary first season from Telltale's, The Walking Dead: Season 1. After the events from Season One, you trek throughout the American South to find refuge and rely on new characters in Season 2 as well as a few (surprising) characters from Season 1 to benefit or hinder your decisions throughout Season 2.
The story in Season 2 was solid, but not as high-pumping or intense as it was on Season 1. Character developments for new characters in Season 2 were decent or pretty good in most cases. Unfortunately, most characters were "rushed" off or didn't have an direct impact as the player (or potential buyer) would expect. Some of your decisions in Season 2 does not have an impact at all. You would probably ask yourself: "Does that choice even matter?". Later episodes in Season 2 seems to have a "forced narrative" for the player to make the choice to choose that one particular character even though you have the freedom to select (won't go any further than that).
The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a game that many players from Season 1 would expect, but expect the story's pacing in the game to be a bit slow. Certain parts in the story is a drag while others do keep you on the edge of your seat. If the player was expecting this game to live up the expectations from Season 1, the player would be disappointed but Season 2 is still a great game and the later episodes was the ultimate shocker. To be honest, The Walking Dead: Season 2 was a mixed bag. The main issues that I've experienced was its pacing, lack of character development for a few characters that should have its own development, and "forced narrative". Despite of these negative attributes, Season 2 was actually a solid game on its own merits especially with Episode IV and V. The Walking Dead: Season 2 is
recommended to players and potential buyers who already played Season One. It's a good game, but don't expect too much from it until the later episodes. Season 2 has my cautious recommendation.

Life is strange is made by Dontnode, the same people that made Remember Me. That game was an ok fighting game, with a great concept where you could alter memory. There would be scenes where you would be altering somebody's memory in that game. You could be rewind the scene back and forth, and there would be things you could change, which could cause a different effect.
This game basically took that concept, but made their next game an adventure game. Except that the main character in the game can rewind time rather than alter memories. I hope you see the range of possibilities you can have with that?
But enough of that. This game is trully a masterpiece of game cinematrography. The music, the camera, the details of the environment. Don't believe me? Play the first episode which is free.
Believe me, if that won't grip you, then nothing will.

Don't buy this game.
In all seriousness, find some way to play it without buying it first so you can work out whether you're going to enjoy/be frustrated with it or not before you spend/waste money on it. 160hrs of playtime, and it feels like 150hrs of that were nothing but frustration, annoyance, restarting, taking wild stabs in the dark, and getting nowhere. I'd ask for a refund if I could.
This isn't to say it's a bad game, but it's NOT a fun game unless you're willing to spend hours working out how to do some of the simplest things while getting more and more frustrated because you don't understand what's happening, or have things go wrong for no reason.
The game itself won't tell you what's happening, what you're doing, what you should be doing, or why. The game won't tell you if you could be doing things better or how. It won't congratulate you for doing things wrong OR right, has no 'goal' other than what you set for yourself, is an INCREDIBLE bore and waste of time INTENTIONALLY, at times. There are so many negative aspects to actually playing the game that they start to all mesh together after a while.
At the same time, it can be fun. And if it turns out to be your sort of thing it's DEFINITELY going to be fun, because it's got a sort of cheery feeling to it, and a sense of accomplishment.
It's just that there's a lot of 'but's attached to any sort of enjoyment of the game.
So try it first, and not the incredibly cut down demo that doesn't really show you anything, or the YouTube channels where people who know every little thing about the game show you how easy it is for THEM to play it, and make up your mind before spending money on it.
And be prepared to be disappointed. It's just that sort of game.

An American teenage girl (Maxine/Max, a shy girl with normal life and normal problems) returns back to her hometown after 5 years, to pursue arts/photography. (In game description, not a spoiler) She reunites with her best childhood friend, Chloe, who has lost her father, and hence is having a hard time settling in with her step dad.
In past 5 years, when Max was away from Chloe, Chloe had become BFF with Rachel Amber, who is currently missing. So, Max and Chloe investigate the mysterious disappearance of Rachel, which takes their lives on one hell of a roller coaster ride.
You get to play Maxine's role in the game, who can rewind time! The dev team has tailored the game in such a way that, You totally get immersed into Maxine's character. The effort that the development team has put in the details of the game and story line is just amazing, period!

Every major or minor choices (optional or mandatory) You make, every time You use time rewinding power, Your every action, has an impact! The way the game describes/shows alternate realities is also good.
Time Taken to finish:
If You just stick to the story line, It might take around 1.5 hours of game play per episode(total of 5 episodes). If You choose to explore everything, Around 2 to 3 hours per episode. Steam achievements are also 100% achievable in one go, "Provided You explore everything in game".

As some other reviewers mentioned, don't bother with this when you can just get your Civ fix with 5. In comparison, Civ V is far more streamlined than Civ VI. This game adds "complexity" in the form of extra micromanagement; turns take longer but I don't gain any enjoyment from that. In particular, I'm not fond of the new city management. It bogs everything down. Happiness, while a bit simple, was far better than this nonsense.
I also don't like the new tile management, with placing districts and wonders. Districts is okay, I guess, but having to deal with both districts and wonder placement just takes too much extra effort and foresight. In order to optimize each city, you have to have each tile it currently has and will have planned out for at least a few dozen turns, though 100 or more is ideal. Oh, and how each of those plans fit into your empire as a whole is important too.
I feel like I need to start taking notes or make a spreadsheet while playing this game. . . And, to me, that isn't Civ. The franchise has always been on the lighter end of 4x games, particularly if you are playing single player. And that's what I liked: I like being able to open a relatively easy game of Civ to pass the time, or play when I'm tired, or to run while I'm watching a show. It's relaxing. But Civ VI takes that away from me without really giving me anything worthwhile in return.
Is this a popular opinion? I don't know. Have I played it a bunch? No. I'm staring at my 6.6 hours thinking about how much crap I'm going to get for a negative review with under 20 hours in a 4x game, but guess what? It didn't take long to figure out that the game just isn't my thing. I have no interest in playing the current game. And, based on playtime, my friends seem to feel the same way.
If you like it, well, great! But I can't recommend a game when I'd rather be playing the previous game in the series.

I love this game. I love it so much that I have nearly 500 hours into it. I wouldn't so much call this a review, just some (hopefully) objective experiences I personally had for the game I love so much while explaining a bit of the game in general.
Nuclear Throne sports a roster of 12 playable characters, diverse with their own unique passive and active ability. From shielding to bullet-time, to air strikes to rolling, every character offers up a variable play-style each go around. The art for the game suits the game's overall direction and is generally nice to look at. Remember this is still early access: We've had some hilarious placeholder ms-paint stick-figure art that would be redrawn into worthwhile, lovely pixel portraits. You can watch the developer stream to see just how great the art assets become as it's being done live.
Despite its seemingly very simplistic design, the game coddles a sinking depth in terms of mutation selection, weapon diversity and character synergy that overlaps well with one another.
The core component of your journeys in the wasteland. I'd categorize mutations in the following categories:
Mutations are randomly generated out of a mix of 4 (5 for a specific character) which can provide you with a mixed variety of mutations. Each mutation handles, generally, fairly better or fairly worse for every character and finding a good synergy is key. Aside from the regular mutations, each character that reaches Level 10 (Ultra) gets to choose from 2 (3 for a specific character) Ultra Mutations. These are generally better than regular mutations and, generally, are a power spike to the character.
As of now, there are over 100 weapons in the game, categorized in 6 different weapon types, with multiple subcategories:
Many weapons perform differently under many circumstances and get better by taking the mutation for the specified weapon. Weapons are tiered and drop according to how far you have progressed in the game. To go into the details of every weapon would be exhausting and I will not do that for the sake of this already wall-of-text-y piece. (but we all know there's only one true energy weapon)
At its core, Nuclear Throne is a rogue-like, twinstick shooter bolstered by the accompanying variants and mechanics the game brings to the table. It's a really fast paced action shooter  with split-second decision making keeping you on your feet. Unlike most games with randomly generated variables, you don't totally live and die by the RNG. It does indeed factor into the game and what weapons, mutations, etc you get throughout a run, but usually player skill will often trump in a nerve-wracking circumstance.
Nuclear Throne is a game about trial and error. That is, in order to get better at the game, you will need to lose. A lot. Like I mean it, a LOT. I can recount a fair number of times I have died in situations similar to my 5th hour in the game in my nearly 500 hours of it. Half of your first few hours with the game will be spent looking at your post-death stats screen. That is how often you will be dead. You have to realize and understand how everything went wrong and learn from it.
But that's it for this review, I've spent more time than I originally planned typing this up. I hope something in this post inspires you to try the game out despite it being in early access. It's a game that is really worth the money.

DISCLAIMER: I've played WAY more than 58 hours, I play alot offline while I'm on the road or at a friends house. It's probably closer to 200-300 hours. I've had around 500 hours on CIV 5 also, (on my other account.) Okay, now that we got out the way, here's my review:
TLDR: If you like the way CIV 5 is right now, stay there for a while. CIV 5 is funner than this at this moment, but CIV 6 has way more potential once all of the bugs are straightened out. Remember, CIV 5 was released in 2010, it has most of it's bugs fixed and had its greatest DLC released years later (BNW.) However, this game will be better in a few years time.
*POSITIVES*
- Art style is awesome! I guess a huge reason why I buy new games in franchises is for their graphics, and I am loving this artwork.
- I've had fun with this new district/wonder system. It really focuses in on what you want to do with your empire. Want to focus on science? Build a campus! Want to focus on culture? Build a Theatre Square! It hones in on what YOU want to do and I enjoy that.
- Eureka! Many people do not like this feature due to you having to "play to the mold" but I love science rushes, and this is what it gives you! Get the eureka's and it really rushes your progress on both Science and Cultural.
- Bug Fixes. After the Fall update, you can really tell that they smoothed this game out a ton. One of my biggest bug problems is that I play mostly epic speed, so I turn on autoturn. You weren't able to send Envoys to city-states with auto turn on, and it would end the turn before you got the chance do to so. Thank goodness they fixed this. Small point, but it's good they are constantly refining the game.
- Barbarians are sad they had little impact in CIV 5, and they are coming to fight you. A constant pain in my side in early eras, they FINALLY made barbarians a bit of a challenge in the early stages of the game. I usually like to build my empire without the use of building any military units, but now I have to decide if I want to build military units to defeat these blood-thirsty barbarians, or have one of my cities seiged until I have enough gold to buy a warrior.
- Has the same addicting gameplay that we are all used to. I said "one more turn" at 9:00, it turned 3 AM QUICK. Speaking of, why did they put a clock into the game. It just shows how much time I dumped into this game. Screw you Firaxis, anyway..
As I said, as the years progress, this game will get better. However, the negatives RIGHT NOW outweight the positives.
*NEGATIVES*
- The denouncing.. holy guacamole. I think the worst feature they put in the game is the "Agendas." If someone has the agenda of wanting Great People, and you get 2-3 Great People, they will denounce you for it. If you build one more wonder than someone who is a Wonder Hog, you will be denounced. If you don't have a strong military you will be denounced. If you don't have a strong Navy you will be denounced. If put one point in a City-State, you will get denounced. Do you see the trend here? Denouncing is supposed to happen when your military is too close to their territory or when you are "Warmongering" (more on this later), not for something as silly as "YOU HAVE A MILITARY OF 2 WARRIORS? I'M GONNA DENOUNCE YOU." Fix this pls.
- If I try to retake my city that is owned by a denounced enemy, I will be classified as a "severe warmonger," even if I use the Casus Belli. Everything you do you will be classified as a warmonger. An ally wants you to take up arms and help in a fight? They will denounce you two turns into the war for being a warmonger. Goodness..
- The territorial expansion the AI have is kind of ridiculous. If THEY settle too close to me, they will say that I am getting too close to their settlements.. like.. come on. I was here. That's your fault. Go away.
- The spies are lackluster. If they have a 5% chance of being captured or killed? Guess what, they'll be captured and killed. Even in the off chance that they FINALLY do actually achieve a mission, it's also lackluster. Trying to siphon funds from America? It'll take you 14 turns to take 400 gold. Trying to "steal" Chemistry from Egypt? Nah son, you got the Eureka, not the technology. And the escape routes all feel the same. They say that escaping by foot is the safest way, but you die anyway. I actually got safely back to my capital more by going by boat instead of by foot. Whatever.
- Lack of visual interface with luxury resources. This one is aggravating at times. You have to keep track of how much sugar or spices or whatever resource you are trading away to another civilization because there is no visual number of how much you actually have in the main interface. Again, another tick-tack thing but still irritating.
- Pace of the game. The pace is too fast going towards the end of the game. It ramps up QUICK.
- THIS MEANS WAR! I feel like war on this CIV is weird. The AI want to attack you 20 turns in even though all you've done is built a scout and a monument. Then, when the war is done, they want to trade you the farm to negotiate peace? Weird AI in wartime.. Their movement isn't too great, it looks like a five year old is at the helm of the Indian empire. Their strategy to attack is poor. It has gotten better since the Fall Update, but it's not quite there yet.
- Can't help but feel this is a bit of a cash grab? The DLC is $5 a pop, I would much rather have an expansion of $30 and it actually put new things in place rather than another bloodthirsty AI.
I guess.. I guess that's all I can say about that...
Again, it WILL be a very fun game in 2018 or 2019, when more DLC comes out (hopefully not this stupid singular scenario DLC we have been getting, and more of an overhaul like BNW.)
It has SO much potential, but it's not quite there yet. It's the DayZ standalone of the strategy world.
I DO recommend this game, however. If it is on sale, get it. But at it's current $60 price? I would wait a few years. Play Civ 5 instead.

I've waited for all the episodes to come out before playing The Walking Dead: Season 2 since playing all 5 episodes from season 1 in one sitting was probably the best way to experience the game. Heard a couple of rumors about season 2 in the meantime, about it not being as deep as season 1, not many big choices to make et cetera.

Don't get me wrong, season 1 was really awesome and I've played the entire game 3 times to see what other storyline choices I could make. Lee was a great character
. Season 2 however has more character development, especially from the main character (Clementine). During this season I really started to hate/love some characters, which tore me up inside during the final episode. It's really impressive how this game makes you feel when making tough choices, which is all the more reason to play each episode/season more than once.

It's like watching a movie on TV, but making the choices yourself and for me as a gamer that's all I ever wanted since I was a little kid playing videogames.

ok, but seriously though, let me preface this by saying that it took me a long time to warm up to Life Is Strange. I always saw it as just another Telltale lookalike, trying to carve out a spot in their niche brand of episodic choices-have-consequences-styled storytelling games. the thing is, Life Is Strange is exactly that; it's just so, so much more lovingly crafted.
the gist is you're Max, a high-school girl who comes back to her old hometown after five years, only to find out she has the power to rewind time. that's the central gameplay mechanic, and it's such a smart way of dealing with the whole idea of branching dialog options that plagues Telltale games - you no longer have to restart your save when the mechanic is baked into the game. seriously, whoever thought that♥♥♥♥♥♥up - you're a genius. also, that's one of the big themes of the game: going back in time. we'll get back to that.
this review is gonna be LONG, so i'll break it down into points.
point one: i binge-played all fifteen hours of this game over the course of one and a half days. that should speak for itself, really.
point two: what makes Life Is Strange work - at least, for me - so cohesively more than any of its contemporaries is that it feels so real. the characters are simultaneously caricatures and subversions of their stereotypes that are slowly unpacked and shaped over the course of the game. in particular, the dynamic between the two main characters - Chloe and Max - is written really well, and does a great job of getting you to understand their weird limbo of finally-being-reunited-with-the-best -friend-from-your-childhood-only-you're-not-best-friends-anymore. like, you KNOW these two have history, and we see it from the way they behave around each other, from the pictures they have, from the way Max recognizes Chloe's old pirate towel hanging in her bathroom - the whole idea of going back in time isn't just a gimmick here, but the thematic and narrative heart of the game - but i won't spoil that any further. that's something you have to experience yourself.
point three: the moment-to-moment mundanity of so many of its situations, as well as hearing Max's internal monologue as she comments on literally everything, are the best parts of this game - waking up with Max, watching her start her day, watching a movie with a best friend, eating lunch at the local diner, going swimming after dark, sitting down for a moment on a bench to force things to a stop as you contemplate the present. those moments ground the game in reality, giving the story a moment to catch its breath, immersing us in the world that's being created here - Arcadia Bay lives and breathes, as do its residents - and makes us feel like it really has a history, that we've been there before too.
point four: there are a lot of small touches that really make the game feel polished; in particular, the soundtrack and the voice acting - there are some great musical choices here with some real raw emotional punch, and the VAs did an amazing job of bringing each character into their own. serious props to Ashley Burch (chloe's VA) for killing it.
point five: i just remembered the little opening sequences where the logo slowly fades in and music plays. Telltale does that, and those are always a nice touch. they're here too, don't worry - but they're less of an opening montage, and more of a way to frame the episode. kinda makes it feel like you're watching a TV show.
point six (five and a half?): actually though, life is strange would be such a good TV show.
point seven: admittedly, the game isn't perfect - there are some narrative decisions that are incredibly questionable, the rewind mechanic isn't utilized as well as it could have been, the lip syncing is kinda jarring at times - but all those are small nitpicks that don't really detract from the experience as a whole. so not really a point, i guess.
point eight: the dialogue is really not as cringy as people say it is. in fact, it kinda grows on you, makes the lines more memorable. some people are just not ready for the mosh pit, shaka brah.
point nine: look, Life Is Strange is a lot of things: it's a brilliant coming-of-age tale with a setting that pays obvious homage to its influences - Twin Peaks supernatural suburbia mixed with the charm of Groundhog Day and other 90s depictions of rural America - and it tackles some social taboos in a surprisingly mature way, despite looking like a surface-level melodrama. even if you're not into unraveling its literary merits, it's still a gripping, visceral read that never lets up until the end credits roll. what more can a story ask for?
point ten: i miss it already.

I truly adore this game, not because of the really cool gameplay or the pretty nice graphics, but because it does its job of truly immersing you in the story and atmosphere. It truly gives you the feeling that you are genuinely trapped inside a twisted nightmare fueled by your own mind.
It's a horror game not from jumpscares or loud noises or demented monsters, but from the dark atmosphere combined with enemies that take some work to put down. It's one of those games that deserve to be put on the hardest difficulty, not exactly for a challenging game, but to make it feel like you're scavenging for every bullet and every battery just to get to the next safepoint.
The characters are wonderfully developed and put together, except for Alan's wife, she seems rather shallow and empty, not very well developed, but other than that the characters are very well written. There's even moments of actual humor from Barry, the comic relief character.
Gameplay: 8/10
Atmosphere/Immersion: 10/10
Story: 9.5/10
High recommendation.

This game could have been a masterpiece but it was ruined by 3 major issues. I will start by listing the problems and then give an example of how they spoil the game.
By far the biggest problem with the game is the AI or lack of it. It completely ruins the game. It should be the most developed part of the game and central to everything, but it makes the game unplayable.
The bad AI makes diplomacy impossible so I don't bother with it in the game. The other leaders act completely at random. One turn they're your mate, the next turn they denounce you.
AI military tactics are non-existant. They couldn't fight their way out of a wet paper bag.
Inevitabley the AI will declare war on you at some point. You are then branded a warmonger for defending yourself. When you come to make peace, the AI will give an excessive amount away to make peace and totally take them out of the game.
City placement is not thought out. Middle to late game the AI will pop a city right on the corner of a continent squeezed in between two of your cities with access to no water and possible one amenity if they're lucky. Completely pointless.
When you take a city of the AI, it's often not developed and needs work.
In most of the games I've played one civilization is always overpowered and wins a cultural victory with 200 turns to spare. This often means I have to declare war on them to reign then in a bit, this then leads to being a warmonger.
It's clear the AI hasn't been well developed and it's the worst part about the game.
Although there have been some additions to the game I like, such as districs and wonder placements. This is outweighed by other issues with the game mechanics.
How can a crossbow corps inflict damage on a tank?
Why does it take 50 years of an infantry unit to cross my territory?
Why does it take over 100 years to build an aerodrome?
Why do cities keep growing to the point where their surroundings cant sustain them and they run out of amenities and houising?
The majority of cities I have will always run out of amenities in middle to late game and there's only so much one can do to resolve it. JUST STOP GROWING.
It takes far too long to the "other players" turns to be calcualted and taken. It makes the games drag. This has always been an issue in other civiliziation games I have played. Why is this still an issue on the 6th installment?
Clearly the person who developed the UI has never played this game, or any game like it. It makes the game so annoying.
I am interrupted every turn by leaders denouncing me or whatever. The game has to show me 10 seconds of Ghandi kicking off at me? why? I don't care. Stop interrupting my game play. Luckily there is a mod to cut these screens down.
When I make a trade deal with another civilization, My delegate informs me that I have just made a trade deal. Seriously?
The screen overflows with useless and annoying information about every little thing that's going on in the world.
It's a terrible UI.
Game is steady away. I am around mid table score. By pereclies of Greece wins a culture victory before we reach 300 turns out of 500. Nothing I could have done to stop this realistically. I couldn't build up a big enough army in time to take some cities off him and affect his culture. If the AI was decent, they would have seen he was going to win and all attacked him to balance the game out.
Anyway, I continue to play for a bit. Throughout the game I was denounced every other turn by at least one civilization because I had a different governement to them. The only person who was ok was Ghandi.
At this point I had not declared any war on anyone or had a war declared on me.
Suddenly, Japan attacks one of my city states. I declare a war of protectorate on Japan with a warmonger penalty of "none". Anyway, next turn Ghandi denounces me as a warmonger..... as does someone else I can't remember.
I protect my city state and seriously weaken Japan's army but don't touch their cities.
When I come to make peace with Japan, I take around 5 cities off his hands at the negotiating table as well as gold.
I now gain 5 cities which all need work as Japan had done a crap job.
Japan now has around 4 cities left and a weak army. Not longer after we made peace. Japan and Ghandi both declare war on me. Bear in mind ghandi hates war and people who declare war. This is seriously messed up. I end up decimating Japan as they have no army and they are out of the game.
Ghandi is on the other side of the continent to me and poses no real threat. He sends about 5 medievil era units to one of my cities (I am in the information era) and they are quickly dealt with. We come to negotiate peace and he gives me the city of mumbai! How is 5 medievil land units worth a full city with several districs?
The game makes no sense and is completely unpredictable.
I don't think I will be buying Civ 7.

There are a LOT of different things in this version of Civilizaton than previous. Which is the cause of most of the bad reviews, as people tend to be overly attached to the past.
Nearly every change TBO is great. From the way builders (workers) now work, to Districting.
However.
There are three really bad things, that just make the game nearly unplayable to me.
1. Map size. The maps are WAY smaller than previous versions. A lot of the reason for this is likely due to Districts. The game has to generate a map, with that thought in mind. Which you will notice when even starting on the smallest of maps that it takes a lot of time before you actually get into the game. All of that in and of itself is not the issue until you get to 2...
2. You got to 2. The AI initial cities are too close, and the AI too aggressive. I am used to actually having a decent amount of room to expand prior to making contact with an AI player. In this version of Civilization, you nearly always make contact immediately, with at least 2 AIs.
Furthermore, 1-2 of them will declare war almost always around turn 75. Which pretty much means you just start to grow your first town, and have founded a second that really hasn't even started, then are at war.
A war that usually means your initial city is surrounded by 5-8 units attacking it. And you have 2 cities. 1 that can make units at a decent pace which is 1 every 2-5 turns, and one that can make them even slower.
Which in turn means you have now lost the game.
3. Diplomacy. You seem to have decent options. All of which seem to do nothing, or very little. Furthermore, the various AIs all seem to be unstable diplomatically. Changing their minds on a whim. And making random comments and threats (...lot about city-states) that you can not interpret in any meaningful way. In one case, and only in 1, I managed to make an ally before getting attacked. And the ally did nothing at all to help me prior while I was getting destroyed. (Not that the ally had much time to react. I had 2 cities, and they were taken out in like 6 turns.)
In previous version of Civ, if I needed more room, I would go to a larger map, or reduce the number of AI players. Hasn't helped one bit in this version. They ALWAYS are placed too close to you, and ALWAYS attack. No matter how it is set up.
I really really really like this game. More than previous versions. All the changes except the two I remarked upon are great. Makes it worth the money, as you actually feel not only that the game has been improved, but also that you are getting a *NEW* game, instead of more of the same ole.
BUT.
After 2 dozen attempts to get to Turn 100 even, let alone get past 2 cities without getting wiped, I've gone back to Civ 5.
As the game is unplayable as is.
Love the feel for the game and how it works. Wish there were more game modes but I like the potential!!

I like several of the new features that Civ 6 has to offer.
- The new district design makes each city feel more unique and forces you to make genuinly interesting decisions about how to customize your cities.
- I like the way that Wonders show up on the map and the look of some of the nation specific improvements - it helps me get into the game.
- Initially I didn't like the way the units were modeled because they are a little cartoony.  However, I have become used to the art style and actually like the animations now.
- I like the seperate trees for Culture and Science and I like that they have slightly reduced the number of units on the tech trees which means that you actually get to use your unique units for a little while before they are obsolete.
There are a few things that I don't like as well as civ 5.

- I had a hard time getting into the initial civs that were offered because many of the most famous leaders and civs had not been included in favor of lesser known civs and leaders.   However, the newer DLC's have added a lot of interesting civs (including several famous ones that I had missed) so I am much happier with the civ selection now - though I still miss a few of the civs from Civ 5.
- I personally liked the Civ 5 leader animations better because they were slightly more realistic and I loved the throne room in the background which made each civ a little more unique.  The civ 6 animations focus on a much more zoomed in view of the slightly cartoony looking leaders.

This game is more of a personal exploration than an interactive experience. It tries to present a scenario that ties you in and makes you feel emotionally connected, and when it's decision time, your morals, philosophy, and subconscious will be put to the test. Unfortunately, you can't change the course of the game much at all, and the thing that season 1 did well, allowing you to make different friends based on who you were as a person, was almost entirely taken out.
At this point, this game is all about you; what would you do in this situation? Given certain options, you will find out how you handle incredible pressure and at times be horrified by your own decisions, even if it would have happened either way (and it probably would have). Think about what you would do, and think about who you are while playing this game.
tl;dr: This game is about internal moral contemplation, and fantastic story telling, not exactly survival, just with themes presented in a survival scenario.

I get that it is unfair to compare this to Overwatch, but bare with me anyway.
I bought OW back in July and have really enjoyed the game since i've bought it. There are regular updates with an active community and some really fantastic dev's behind a glass wall. Overwatch itself is a game the does it's very best to be balanced. Maps feel like they are crafted with care and every character has a background and an interesting and unique personality.
Of course, this review is for Paladins, a game I really didn't enjoy from my first experience through to my last.
My negative perception starts before I even got into the game. Logging in was a chore as Hi-Rez did not recognize my account so I had to make a new one which also didn't work. Luckily, my third one did. However, this may have just been a really unlucky experience that only i've gotten so don't let that excerpt sway you.
As soon as I got into the game I noticed that the main menu feels extremely cluttered with a lot of elements that I am not used to seeing as I rarely play MOBAs.
The actual visuals of Paladins are a mixed bag. Some of the textures look really well crafted while other elements look like complete garbage. The game seems to mash them all together and that makes for a strange ambiance that didn't feel inviting. As a result I was never immersed into the game. However, I think my biggest complaint about the visuals was the bloom. They need a specific slider for that as it always felt like it was cranked up to 11 and really did not look that good in my opinion.
Gameplay wise the characters handled pretty well. Skills felt decent but not unique. Certain characters felt as though they were overpowered versus others in the same tier. I will say that I liked the element of purchasing upgrades for your hero with money made from performing well in the game. Game modes were very similar to Overwatch and TF2.
The Heroes themselves, left much to be desired. While there were all technically different, I never found myself really knowing who i was or who any of the other characters were on my team. There is little life to them and almost no personality. Their catchphrases and dialogue are easily forgetable, and this is something I think blizzard definitely did a better job at crafting.
I'm sure I've left out a few things I wanted to say when I first thought about leaving a review but I feel as though i've gotten my negativity across.
TLDR: In the end, yes, Paladins is a free game. For a free game it has a pretty solid amount of content I could imagine people investing a sizable chunk of time into. However it's ambiance is easily forgettable and I never once felt immersed into the game. It's gameplay is fairly tight but definitely needs a few adjustments before it can be taken too seriously. And I definitely see no reason to play this over a similar shooter like Overwatch. Thus I can not recommend it.
My takeaway comment is that the game lacks the polish that Overwatch has and feels more like a mobile game rather than a PC title.

This game sent me on a emotional roller coaster ride. I laughed. I cried. At some time, I did not know what was going on. I became one of the characters in the story and fell in love with rest of them.

(*NO* Spoilers)
An American teenage girl (Maxine/Max, a shy girl with normal life and normal problems) returns back to her hometown after 5 years, to pursue arts/photography. However, once she joins the college, she finds out that she has power to rewind time!! (In game description, not a spoiler) She reunites with her best childhood friend, Chloe, who has lost her father, and hence is having a hard time settling in with her step dad.
In past 5 years, when Max was away from Chloe, Chloe had become BFF with Rachel Amber, who is currently missing. So, Max and Chloe investigate the mysterious disappearance of Rachel, which takes their lives on one hell of a roller coaster ride.
You get to play Maxine's role in the game, who can rewind time! The dev team has tailored the game in such a way that, You totally get immersed into Maxine's character. The effort that the development team has put in the details of the game and story line is just amazing, period!

Every major or minor choices (optional or mandatory) You make, every time You use time rewinding power, Your every action, has an impact! The way the game describes/shows alternate realities is also good.
Time Taken to finish:
If You just stick to the story line, It might take around 1.5 hours of game play per episode(total of 5 episodes). If You choose to explore everything, Around 2 to 3 hours per episode. Steam achievements are also 100% achievable in one go, "Provided You explore everything in game".

As the second installment of one of my favorite games, the Walking Dead Season Two falls short in terms of depth, gameplay, and production. The TellTale version of the Walking Dead series is a point and click adventure, with a strong focus on narrative exposition requiring investment or at least knowledge of the previous game in order to enjoy the sequel. Unfortunately this sequel feels rushed and lacking, in both content and depth of characters which retroactively works to tarnish the previous work. So unlike most games (such as the Assassin’s Creed Series) that get more gameplay with more games, this sequel is not enjoyable because players of TellTale games are not invested in gameplay but rather the story.
In all the things I feel where TellTale falls short, their choice of making Clementine the protagonist is the most glaring and the topic I want to focus on in this review. If there were to be a sequel to the original Walking Dead, Clementine had to be in it. They did a great job with her, in transforming her from a soft child into a hardened teen. It was especially powerful to watch Omid’s death be the beginning of her transformation into a more serious character, as Omid’s personality was playful and childish and his death acted as a symbol for Clementine’s loss of innocence. Omid’s absence plays a huge toll on Christa, who solely raises Clementine and shapes her into a solemn person, but Clementine still is a child. Playing as a child in a choose-your-own adventure game is extremely ineffective because children don’t have control over their situations, which make the choices of the player feel less significant. Furthermore Clementine doesn’t have an agenda, and because of her lack of overarching goals or investments, there is a lack of tension and significance in her actions. Because Clementine is the protagonist of the story, her lack of influence and significance to the plot makes the plot itself weaker.
This is completely opposite of what TellTale has done in the Walking Dead Season One, where Lee (an adult) wanted to find Clementine’s parents (goal), and keep Clementine safe (investment).  This strong sense of plot is what kept us rooting for Lee despite all the hardships and questionably morale choices he had to make, and what made us feel tense when either Lee or Clementine was in danger. Season Two Clementine is a child and things happen to her, and while the game seems to be going towards her own survival as an independent teen, she seems to always need help from other people. In fact, it feels that the writers of the game understood that Clementine lacks these major plot elements, and has inserted a baby for Clementine to fend for; but because this responsibility is thrust upon her, the player inherently feels no sympathy for the baby nor responsibility for it.
While the game has its own plot, throughout the story the subplot is in answering the question, “Who is Clementine’s guardian?” This is not a problem, this is THE problem. This subplot works to undermine the plot when the audience has to keep this question in the back of their minds while making every choice because the audience is already assuming that Clementine needs someone. All the characters generally seem to be interested in Clementine’s wellbeing, even the main antagonist, Carver. With this in mind, Clementine is again put in the backseat while the adults tend to her wellbeing to group politics, taking the player out from a position of choosing their-own-adventure but rather choosing their version of angry response or happy response from whoever is in charge of taking care of Clementine for the scene.  The only moment where Clementine gets enough control to make a decision in leading her own life is at the end, but then the game forces you to choose Clementine’s guardian, which gives closure to the subplot but a lack of closure for the real plot. Whatever decision you choose at the end feels non-canon, because the plot could have gone so many different ways due to a SUBPLOT.
This game is one of many TallTale games that feel generally rushed to make mad bucks. With a few simple changes they could have expelled the terrible subplot or changed the protagonist to a character that the players can actually choose-their-own adventures with. The beginning chapters of The Walking Dead Season two are actually really good (when Clementine is alone), but it quickly goes downhill as a cast of Big Brothers and Big Sisters guide you in watching-your-own weak plot adventure.

Fish, Crystal, Steroids etc.
All of the characters in this game bring their own style and flow of gameplay. Want to roll around like a madman? Play Fish. Want to laugh as your enemies pitifully try and break through your defenses? Play Crystal. Want to go full-auto YOLO? Play Steroids. Want to show the world the meaning of bullet hell? Play the Gun God himself, Yung Venuz.
Every character has his/her/its own personality, and I just adore that in games. No one wants a bland military special operative. They want floating triangles and fish.
And the characters is only breaking the surface.
The gameplay is where this game truly shines. It's a pulse-pounding survival-of-the-fittest shooter that rewards risk and brutally punishes mistakes. It's easy to assume that when you click on a character, you're unstoppable. Every character is a hurricane of death, but so are your enemies. Damage is what it should be in this game: killer (Sorry my puns are just dead today!) In a game where bullets flying everywhere, fire traps around every corner, huge♥♥♥♥♥dogs shooting rockets at your face. You'll frantically search for little packs of ammo just to continue your quest for the throne, and pray to every single deity in the universe for a miniature health pack. The world is dying, and you're the last son-of-a-♥♥♥♥♥ left.
Yeah, that's Nuclear Throne.
This is by no means an easy game, but when you make it to the throne, you'll understand why people rave about this epic adventure filled with endless fun and destruction.

Worth full price. Now that I have the attention of those of you with low attention span, let me explain why my first sentence applies to this game.
After being attacked by strange people acting possessed, you quickly realize how simple yet magnificantly tense the combat is. In order to kill an enemy, you must "melt" the darkness controller them via your flashlight (they are bulletproof otherwise). This becomes a game of prioritizing targets and "focusing" your flashlight to both keep the dark hordes away as well as make them vulnerable. This mechanic, coupled with the dark and opaque forest adds the kind of tension you don't see in many horror games, let alone American ones.
Furthermore, the story is compelling in both the twists and turns it takes and how cleverly it breaks the "ingame 4th wall". The story and how the game interwines raises the bar for how storytelling should be in a horror game.
Lastly, this game (originally on 360) ran beautfiully. No hitches or crashes.

I have mixed feelings about this game.  I recommend it, but have some complaints.  I typically play Single player/Marathon from ancient/ shuffled map/Immortal difficulty/chosen civ.  It meets all the requirements of a civilazation game, but it feels kinda empty.  It feels like it needs an expansion.  Big issues are: all victory conditions are kinda the same- meaning you have to be one of the top civs in score to complete any of them.  There really isn't a chance to complete science or culture without also being one of the dominant civs, and then you can just get a domination victory anyway.  Religious victory is war without war.  I guess I don't mind it, it's a nice twist, but still the same style or play.  I would want a more cutting mechanic, something that forces you to choose war or religion or culture and you can't go back because you;ve dedicated yourself to that victory.  The pacing is slow.  Can't describe why or how to fix it, but it just feels slower than previous civ games.  The AI is crap, especially late game.  I can wipe a civization with 5-6 units of their similar tech level.  Diplomacy is a joke.  I wish there was a way to turn off the cut screens.  I'll tell you when I want to talk to you- asking for friendship every 5 turns really kills flow- game turns take long enough.  It's fun- I guess, but gameplay at higher difficulty levels tends to be all the same.  Be the dominant civ (can only be done through war) and then pick your victory condition.  Ussually you can do them all save religious, which takes a little more planning earlier on.

Civ 6 is a great civilization game. Noticeable new things:
- Districts: used to specialize a city (military, science, culture, industry etc). All districts can be built in any one city but they take up one tile!
- Wonders: they now, like districts, take up a whole tile! Plan ahead
- Workers: workers now have 'uses', and will build instantly but will be expended after their uses are up. You need to build more workers as you go, not just go a whole game with just those workers you captured at the start.
I can only recommend this game, this next paragraph is adressing the mindset of many bad reviewers.
Every Civilization game had to suffer the "last civ was better"-disease. Many of the bad reviews are from people that played Civ 1 and Civ 2, and are of the impression that the series gets worse and worse. They are however just being nostalgic. Games change and evolve, some people can't handle new and improved.
Civ 4 many remember with love because of the great score 'Baba Yetu', and the game really had a much more modern feel than the previous 3.
When Civ 5 came everyone lost their mind because with it they apparently messed everything up (they didn't). Hexagonal tiles instead of squares!? What sorcery is that!? Too many changes at once, and most were confident they'd always prefer Civ 4 before Civ 5. That soon changed
and now everyone's cheering for their one true love Civilization 5 and how much better it is than this garbage that is Civ 6 (it's not garbage, it's awesome). When Civ 7 comes out, we'll hear great tales about how fantastic Civ 6 was and so on, so forth.
tl;dr
Sid Meier's Civilization VI is great, I've spent over 300 hours on it and looking forward to spending many more! Don't listen to any review mentioning Civ 1 or Civ 2 as they are just being nostalgic.

It's a fact of life that change is hard.  I do applaud Firaxis and company for branching out and trying something new in an attempt to innovate in the long saga of Civilization titles.  But, Civ 6 jarringly veers from the tried-and-true path that its predecessors engrained in the very essence of what it means to be Civilzation game.
Realism aside, the prior model focused on cities and their growth.  Every city could have arsenals and research and their cake and eat it, too.  You did everything you could to expand their borders, claim additional tile territories and expand your empire in order to achieve this.  Meaning your empire was more a coalition of super city states than anything else
This game decentralizes the experience in a way that shifts the focus away from cities as production centers and focuses more on tile development/expansion working in synergy with your cities.  Again, from a practical standpoint, it makes sense -- it's more realistic.  Military bases aren't in every city.  Howver, from a historical fan's take on the series, it's a wild departure from the standard M.O.
Overall, the game is aesthetically pleasing and still contains many familiar game elements to prior titles.  Take it with a grain of salt when you see that Gamespot rates the game as "superb" -- perhaps collectively their review teams have as many hours in the Civ titles as I do (4,000+).  Whereas they gave it a 9/10, I think it's more like a solid 6/10.

It has now been a few weeks since I've played Season 2 and I'm still not really sure how I felt about it.
As a whole the game is fine.  I got a solid eight hours out of it, less than the ten or so it took me to complete 1 but still comparable.
The music is still great and so is the animation style.  Choices are difficult and having a timer on them creates the illusion of tension: you need to act and you need to act now.  It plays like 1.
Unlike Season 1 the episode transitions are more jarring.  The story is much, much more linear this time around than it was in S1 and each episode effectively starts where the last one ended without missing a beat.  Additionally, each episode ends on a pretty strong cliffhanger giving it a very television feel, suiting the game well considering it's labeling system of episodes and seasons.  Because of this tightness between the episodes, however, I very early on began wondering why this was produced in an episodic format.  While the transitions work well to support that, the narrative does not.  Episodic gameplay does not seem necessary and perhaps even devalues the core experience of playing Season 2.  Oh, and at the end of each episode are unskippable credits.  Yeah, I could have crashed the game to get around that but come on.  I get that some people may not have worked on the same episodes but would it have been so hard to remove these, or at least add a skip function?
Gameplay wise not much as changed.  There is much, much less walking around, exploring small areas and interacting with the environment/characters.  Instead you spend the majority of your play time in chat cutscenes.  In that regard S2 feels much less like a game than 1 but it also focuses on the strong points of 1 as opposed to the weak navigation and point and click puzzle solving.
Discard any concerns you have for Clementine serving as the player character as she fits the role pretty damn perfectly and much better than Lee in many circumstances.  Making tough choices with her has a lot more weight as you're now working with much more of a blank slate, and that's the beauty of these games.  They're not about zombies, or the story or the characters: they're about you, your choices and the story you want to tell with the character you're making.  Trust me when I say Clem is a much better fit for that role than Lee ever was.
As an aside, the plot of episode 1 is pretty weak.  It very much felt like I was being manipulated with cheap story elements to feel a certain way.  After a few chapters the game picks up but the very early parts are extremely weak.  As a whole the plot is fine though it did feel like it was just shuffling about and wasting opportunities at times, which summarizes my feelings for the game.  It was alright and a good form of entertainment but compared to the long strides that S1 took, s2 felt like it was just killing time while setting up a much better S3.
Do I recommend it?  Sure.  It may have overall felt like a weaker game than Season 1 but that's not saying much.  It's still a good game.

Dont get me wrong, I adore The Walking Dead Game franchise. I love the concept, the characters, and TellTale are great in what they did. I've got a HUGE emotional attatchment to each and every character.
I played the first game (which is a MUST if you're planning on playing the second) and I loved it.
Now, this is why I wont rate Season 2 as good as season 1- Season one took me 20 hours to complete. Season Two took me 8.
This isnt because of lack of storyline, the actual story is the same length, and I have no problems with the story. This is because of the lack of the ability to talk and get to know characters.
Season One. At the farm. You can go and talk to Katjaa, when shes with Clem. You can talk to Kenny. You can learn about their backstory, where they used to live, and so on.
Season Two, without giving away any spoilers, you simply cant.
You dont get to learn about the groups past, and a lot of them die off before you get a chance to ask. I'm the type of player who will spend time to talk to every person in between the action scenes. But in SSN2, you dont get the oppourtinity.
It sucks, becasue I like finding out about characters. I like knowing about them. But they end up dying, and im left like "So... What ever happened to them?"
One more thing. The ending of SSN1 was powerful, and hit home for most players, because everyone loved Lee. I dont think there was ANYONE who didnt like him at the end. But in season two, without trying to give away the ending- as much as they tried to make a big ending, if you didnt like the characters at the end, the choice wasnt so difficult at all.
Like I said, I love the game, and I would still reccomend it to people who want to follow Clementines story. But, I feel like it was rushed, and it could of been thought out a lot more thoroughly before release.
If there was a mixed feelings button to post this review as, it would be that, but Im still going to rate it up- becasue at the end of the day- Clementine is great and I still like to know how shes going to follow her story.

Season Two was an incredible addition to the series. Everything was up to the impossible standards of the first season, and in a lot of cases actually improved upon it.
Storyline:
With Lee gone, Clementine must fend for herself. She starts out with two characters from the last game but quickly unites with a different group of people. She used everything that she learnt from Lee to help herself and the new members of her group. As always with the Walking Dead, nothing and no one is safe. The story moves forward based on decisions made by you throughout. However, I felt as though no matter what choice I made, something would happen anyway. For example, if I did something to save someone, that person would just die in a slightly different way shortly after. Even though there were multiple endings, this was the most emotional ending that I have ever played through, and I can honestly say, I was crying way before the final credits.
Graphics:
The graphics were stunning as usual. I spent plenty of extra time exploring everything and generally just looking around. The background always matched and enhanced what was happening at that moment in the game.
Characters:
Clementine was the main character for this season. She was well developed from the last season, but in this game, they expanded on her a considerable amount. The way she grew as a person was noticeable and made you feel more connected to her and her journey. I could feel the change in her as well as in myself as the story moved forward and different events.
With intense graphics and an emotional storyline, this game is incredible and I would highly recommend this game to anyone.

If you ae buying this as the next step from Civ V.... Don't. You'll be thoroughly disappointed.
I usually ease myself into a game by starting with a couple of AIs and on the simplest settings. get to know the mechanics and then the next campaign pump up the difficulty, etc.
I ended up playing 10 hours, running 4 senarios at the settler level, 4 different leaders, against AIs ranging from 3 to 7 opponents. I couldn't figure it out, after playing 600 hours of Civ V, I was expecting there to be some level of progression linking. I was wrong.
- The AIs were schizophrenic in their actions, even at settler level, heaven forbid what the inequality boons are like at prince/king/immortal is like... I played against America in 3 scenarios, completely random personalities each time,  its almost as if Rosavelt had a gandhi complex in one senario (the age old, "lets all be friends!... and i'll nuke you")
- The game mechanic forces your playstyle towards domination due to the random nature of the AIs,  if you dont keep a balenced policy tree and build a reasonable defence, you'll end up in generational wars you wont be able to keep up with or dominate the opponents... I personally dont want to be winning the game using domination every time, it would be nice to adapt to the situation once in a while.
- Which takes me to the civic and science trees. if you are looking for a playstyle like civ 5, dont bother. there is little to no ability to adapt the game to your own playstyle or adapting your playstyle to victory conditions of certain leaders. for example; in Civ 5 you could rush to medieval era pushing through one line of science (usually i did through stonehenge, boosting faith, establishing a foothold.)... rushing through either of the tech trees will leave you at a great disadvantage... i then tried going through the science tree normally on two scenarios, boosted science in campuses, still ended up behind the other AIs in tech... I dont expect the game to be a cake-walk, however, this was at settler level.
- The use of faith in this game is just half-arsed compared to Civ V. It hardly has any scope of boons. There is no UI toggle to view faith influence on cities (like when you are on a missionary or apostle) generally. accessing the faith purchasing is tedius, and im sure that unless it was pointed out to brand new players, they wouldnt know how to access it.
- shortcut keys dont always work.  I played this on 3 different PCs.... all three I had issues toggling yields (Y key) I can only assume its the game.
- whats this with taking away build queues? ok, so due to the irritation of random AIs you need to change your builds often. but sometimes you have that city pottering along, pumping out stuff
-the balance of amenities, housing and production focus is odd. there isnt a thoroughly explained section in the tutorial why housing and amenities are so important, and there isnt a quick explination as to what conditions you will lose if you dont have enough housing/amenities, without opening the civ wiki. I do think making larger housing and amenity icons on builds/tech tree items would be beneficial.
What I do like
- the concept of districts are good
- the animation is very cartoony, but also very good quality, the graphics overall levels the playing field as opposed to Civ V
Really, this game left me frustrated that I spent a hell of a lot of money for something i am really not going to play.

I'm reluctant to purchase early access titles due to the rampant abuse of greenlight - you know the story. But with a reputable developer like Vlambeer, who have delivered games that feel like, well, actual games, I was pretty sure I would get my moneys worth. And if I were to stop playing the game now, it still would have made it worth the purchase. Luckily, Vlambeer has been consistently updating the game on an (almost always) weekly basis with new content being added all the time. They take criticism to heart and listen to the players.
The action roguelite gameplay allows for a variety of gameplay styles within the somewhat limited top-down shooter style, but a variety of "Mutations"(that function like perks which alter your statistics, abilities and expands and also limits how you play) which you are given the choice between when you level up can dramatically alter your plans. Even if you decided on a "melee" character, the selection of mutations you are given as you level up might not cater to that playstyle at all, nor might you get the preferred weapons for how you intended to play in the first place, so the game is dynamic and spontaneous in that it can crash your plans and force you to re-consider your strategy throughout your game.
Permadeath keeps you at your toes. You can forget about checkpoints. This is good because modern games are plagued with these and they make your actions have less consequences. Vlambeer brings back the thrill of old school gaming, and the high-risk/high-reward mechanics is something that draws people to roguelites.
Now to the negatives.
There are balancing issues in the game, sometimes game breaking generation parameters that can give you a seemingly impossible spawn. This has been heavily debated on the forums. This is an obvious problem area when you combine a bullet-hell shooter with a randomly generated roguelite, but Vlambeer have taken the criticism to heart and have improved on the generation parameters throughout the game development and continue to do so consistently.
There are also the obvious limitations and confines of the gamemaker engine, which Vlambeer insists on using. The game is locked to 30fps which is downright horrible on the eyes for extended playing sessions. The slideshow effect and clumsiness of this low a framerate is very detrimental to a genre that requires the player to be observant and react quickly. What makes it problematic for gamemaker creators to increase the framerate is that a lot of events are executed per-frame through the step event. This basically means that the devs have to re-write every part of the code that utilizes the step event and change it if the game was to run at, say 60fps. It is a shame that on a dynamic platform like the PC that a game is locked to perform like that.
There are also balancing issues between characters. Vlambeer seem stubborn on keeping some characters underpowered(Fish being the number one example) because they insist on keeping useless active abilities that nobody actually finds useful which becomes ridiculously underpowered in comparison to other characters abilities. At one point, some characters were ridiculously overpowered, like Rebel and Chicken. They were both nerfed, which somehow changed completely the way people play and sort of took away the novelty and personality of said characters. But I must add that criticism like this is aimed at something that takes time to perfect and that there is no one right answer to. You always give some and lose some with such decisions.
To sum it up, I have gotten my moneys worth at least two times over and I intend to also purchase the game again for the PS4 platform, even with the negatives mentioned because the game is still very fun to play.
The game keeps becoming more polished and new features are always added, so I am confident that the game will be great at release. It's just a shame about the framerate. I think it's important to know that a game is locked to 30fps before purchasing.

When Civilization VI was announced a lot of people including me were very excited for how Firaxis would expand the series, the district systems and such were extremely promising even though we sort of had districts in Civ V already with the great person improvements.
When the first few gameplay videos came a massive wave of disappointment was already being announced and when we finally got to play the game we got even more disappointed in how awfully designed the game is.
I have 1037 hours in Civilization V and too many thousands to count in Civ IV but Civ VI is just too boring and I will explain why.
The district system is an interesting idea do not get me wrong but the fact that they actually made building tall (high population per city) pointless and you can basically spam as many cities as you want unlimited whereas in Civ V you at least had a form of balance to prevent that.
In all Civilization games there were rewards and downsides in going tall and wide (lots of cities) whereas in Civ VI the only benefit is going wide and not tall at all.
The districts do not help with this either making your low population cities extremely overpowered. all you need is the commercial, industrial and there you go, the harbour if coastal and/or Holy Site or Campus and basically your city wont have to grow any larger because Civ VI is all about money and production, you rule those you own the game.
This is the dumbest way of designing a game the fact that production costs SCALE with how much you produce something is even more idiotic.
This was their idea of preventing you spamming cities but it turns out its working against you, want to make more infantry and tanks to fight the wars the dumb AI starts all the time? Oh sorry, you already made too many tanks, its 40 turns to make one now.
They also completely ruined culture, its pointless now, I cannot tell whether it has an effect on border growth because they completely butchered the interface and dumbed it so much down its counterproductive.
The policy idea is also another great idea but poorly implemented, the idea of enacting your own policies is very nice indeed but it basically costs you nothing, everytime you research a culture policy you can to change your government.
This is silly so what is the point of culture? Its basically just like science, its only there to make you progress and the theater square is pretty much pointless as you already can amaze good culture output through buildings and religion.
Then we get to the real big ugly flaw of this game, the AI itself, its the worst AI I have seen in a strategy game and believe me I play and have played a LOT of strategy games, I seen AI's from 2002 that are smarter than this and that is sad.
The AI was very smart in Civilization IV after the final expansion pack, the AI was pretty dumb in Civ V but even then it was still capable of doing SOMETHING.
In Civ VI the AI is utterly useless in war, even with mods the AI is so crippled it scares me, it cannot do basic manouvers it just spams units at you which is pretty silly at least in previous Civ games the AI would try to come up with basic tactics.
The AI is also really bad at economy and city placement, early games the AI may be ahead of you but then you suddenly start getting ahead of the AI really fast.
As for the graphics this is a matter of taste, but I always prefered the more realistic art look of the previous games than this new cartoon look which looks silly in my opinion, are we playing a game for kids now? You may think so considering how dumbed down the game is in general.
I have also noticed how Firaxis are releasing lots of small DLC's, seeing how this is going it looks like they have adopted the Paradox Interactive strategy of just spamming lots of tiny DLC's for what may appear like small prices but when you start adding all these tiny DLC's together you suddenly end up with prices like 100 euro or 300 euro, Europa Universalis IV is probably 400 euro by now if you want all the DLC's.
This new strategy by game developers is disgusting and frankly puts me off completely from buying their games in the future, it was bad enough with the death of Expansion Packs and the beginning of DLC's but Firaxis still kept making good DLC's for Civ V.
And finally, I want to give Firaxis my middle finger, Civilization V is the most successful strategy game of our time so far, and there still more people playing Civ V today than VI, you could have made MORE profits making DLC's for Civ V and expanding the game further, a lot of people may not realise this but the district system could EASILY been implemented in Civ V, you could have fleshed out the future era, you could have made space colonisation a thing, the fact that Civilization Beyond Earth was not made a DLC for Civ V puzzles me.
Game developers today are extremely lazy and it seems Firaxis have joined the club, expanding already extremely successfully game franchises with more content is too much effort these days, Firaxis promised us many years ago to fix Multiplayer in Civ V and add mod support what do we get? An entire new game that costs 60 euro at launch, thank you Firaxis for sinking to a level even EA Games have yet to reach.

Telltale comes back to The Walking Dead series with much of the same game mechanics that comprised the first season. This time around though, it feels even less puzzle driven and more adventure/story focused than before. Not that the original one had that many puzzles to deal with. TWD brings a few more tricks to the field with some new QTEs to keep the character busy. The most noticeable addition is a “sliding” QTE that feels touch inspired, though designed with a mouse in mind. A tich clunky but effective. There’s one particular scene where you’re healing Clementine’s wound that got a little too eye wincing for me. *shudder*. I know QTEs are generally frowned upon (and I share that attitude pretty often) but I have to admit that games such as TWD create them in such a way that keeps me involved without feeling tacked on or unnecessarily finicky. You’ll find a few items for your inventory now and again but their usage is usually restricted to the level you’re on. Nothing that’s changed from Season 1, though their importance feels reduced. Each "level" of the game tends to have a bit of exploration and the option to interact with objects or converse with other characters.
The story picks up some time after season one had finished. The main protagonist is now Clementine which I think is a fantastic choice. Clementine was clearly the standout character last season and seeing the apocalypse from her perspective is a change of pace for the universe. Seeing Clementine’s character mature in this season is also great to see. She feels like one of the best implementations of combining a “blank slate” for the player and still having a personal agenda/character yet. She still commands the player’s respect both mechanically and in the story itself. Furthermore, she remains my favorite character to come out of TWD. Which still surprises me to this day as I write this review. That said, I have to wonder if Telltale are going to let the player decide her personality in Season 3 or fast forward enough years for it to not matter too much. Or, if they’re even going to cover her story at all, as crazy as that might seem. It’ll be interesting to see how she stands in S3.
It’s mostly a new cast that you get thrust into this season. That’s due to what happened in the last season. However, there are a few characters that make a surprising return from season one. As the game is a narrative-driven experience, I find myself unwilling to talk about the story in fear of spoiling it. That said, I will talk about how the story works overall. For the most part, it follows how TWD S1 worked. Your actions do have an immediate and short-term effect on the story, but the long term effects are mostly corrected for or worked into the overall goals of the narrative. While your experience will differ somewhat every time you play and make different choices, there’s no real way to take the story off its rails. Telltale really isn’t kidding around when they say that the story adapts to the choices of the players. And for the most part this works. Though I did notice at times that the delivery of voice lines after you make choices can come off a bit odd or over/underacted.
Still, the story is a dark one of survival. Much of the focus this season is dealing with people close With characters trying to protect what remains of their families, their hope and their humanity. Each struggling with demons that some contain, while others unleash it on those around them. I think all of this helps to keep the story grounded and personable. It feels like these are real situations and dramas that rarely feel forced or unnecessary for the sake of having drama.
I once again abstained from buying The Walking Dead S2 until the entire season was available for release. Though, I did keep my finger on the pulse of what people were saying about each episode. There were numerous delays for many of the episodes of S2, creating some doubts as to whether an episodic model is worth buying into. For myself, I still have mixed feelings on the business model. It still feels a bit too much like pre-ordering at this point. There’s the other problem that having to wait months between episodic releases can cause you to forget what happened in the last episode. But, if people still prefer it, then I don’t have any reason to say you shouldn’t do it. Just realize you may be waiting a long time between episodes. I myself prefer the Netflix approach of being able to enjoy the entire season in “one sitting”. So, I guess having choice is better than not.
From my playthrough, TWD S2 ran about as well as Season One of The Walking Dead, which was pretty darn good. I didn’t notice any glaring bugs or performance difficulties. The only thing I did notice are relatively minor animation glitches during transitions but I honestly feel like that’s nitpicking to even point them out. Compared to S1, S2’s settings are a lot more limited. Texture quality is the only low/high slider compared to three changeable visual settings of the previous entry. Anti-aliasing and full screen can be turned on or off. Resolutions have a decent selection to choose from which is unchanged from before. Overall, a little disappointing to have less choice in tweaking the game’s graphics but unless you’re running on a really old machine, you’re probably going to set everything to high and call it good. Master volume and music sliders are here though it would have been nice to have a speech audio slider considering how much talking is going on.
The Walking Dead Season 2 improves upon the original season while still remembering what it’s about. It’s character-driven narrative, involving the player as much as possible even during what would otherwise be “boring” cutscenes. There is one thing I found really refreshing though. Telltale shows us that they can still have a very character driven story with dramatic moments that are personable and realistic without giant explosions or deus ex machinas getting in the way. It keeps the universe’s bite throughout the five episodes, no pun intended. I am slightly concerned that Telltale may be biting off more than they can chew with the many series they are running  concurrently right now. There are a few odd moments in the series where it felt like the writers might not be on the same page. That or maybe it was the naivety of certain characters that made them say one thing only to do something that contradicted themselves.
Ultimately, should you get The Walking Dead Season 2? Yes if you’re entering the series new and yes if you’re wanting to follow up on Season 1. The characters, overall story and continued improvements on what Telltale started in S1 are worth enjoying in this sequel.

=I really wanted to give this game a thumbs down.  Played through it until the last episode, sure I was going to, but unable to stop because I wanted closure.  Then I got to the last episode, and about halfway through the series re-won my love.  This game doesn't live up to the original.  In fact I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who did not play the original.  But for those of us who did this game will be irresistable- in fact the best parts of this game are carried over from the original.  But those parts are enough.
+Suceeds in generating "feels" for those who played the original.
+They fixed problems with the control sceme, I was able to use the controller throughout the entirity and was not frustrated doing so.
+Still can't run, but can kind of shuffle slightly faster.
+UI much more clever, rewind feature better implemented.
-Plot holes plot holes plot holes!  Some are big and we can hope will be filled in later in the series.  Actually the more unforgivable ones for me are the small ones.  This game makes even less pretense at being a point and click puzzler than the original, but when it feels like the items you need to complete a task are placed there just so that you can complete the task and don't really have any reason to be in the rooms they're in as far as the plot is concerned- well, it's just sad.
-Signifigantly shorter than the original.
-Maybe my sense of fatalism has increased, maybe this is just a darker game, but I never felt any real pressure to make the right decision.  People seem to forgive you no matter what because you are a child.  You are also always the one to do tasks and make decisions.  A big change from the original where people ask a lot for their trust and you are seldom if ever the leader.
-New interactions sometimes over the top.  OK, pressing "A" rapidly again.  They did sometimes add to the immersion, but in particualr I never felt the "hold 'A' and push in a direction" added anything.  I also imagine much of the playtime lost from the original went to rendering death scenes where interactions were failed.
=Overall I love the game series and what it's added to the genre.  I won't lie.  I'm going to keep buying these games pretty much no matter what.  But I hope Telltale moves back towards the slow, thoughtful, heartbreaking original and away from the fast, gimmicky, gore-festiness of the sequil.
=Worth a buy at $9.99, but only if you've played the original.
