Was excited about this game since it was announced in 2006 by one of my favorite developers and can say it was worth the wait after finally playing it in 2012.  Alan Wake was in development for so long Left 4 Dead may have been partially influenced by demonstrations of it, with Alan Wake being influenced by it in return.  The number of parallels that can be drawn between them is surprising.
If you want a triple-A game with TV series-like presentation of a mysterious, spooky and twisting plot driven by creative gameplay design then this is right down your alley.  Excellent voice acting, soundtrack, pacing, variety, level design, transitions and special effects.
It's broken into 8 episodes which are about 2-3 hours long each.  6 are the base story and 2 specials which continue the story with crazier level design, leading into the next Alan Wake game.  The 2 specials have to be started by going under the Episodes menu, as ending episode 6 doesn't automatically roll you into special 1.

The graphics are cartoony and honestly not a good look for a strategy game.
Some things I did like were the fact that you had to use up a tile to build wonders and several types of buildings called districts. I also liked how you had to compete with other civs for the same great person, however I think that this could allow people to dominate in abttle too much given that great generals are a huge part of winning a land war and the same goes for sea wars and great admirals. I personally hated the tourism mechanic in brave new world expansion along with the repetitiveness of the ultra late game where your capital had nothing to do besides be put on gold production this game deals with it in a strange way by introducing district projects which give great person points.
Overall i'd give it a 4/10. There are some good things about it, but coming from Civ V I can't recommend it for anyone

“I know Lee would die for this game”
Speed 3.5/5 - Speed varies depending on how fast you want to complete the game, I felt like this season was shorter than the last one but sometimes speed isn’t that much of a factor when playing. Some episodes felt like they were taking forever to finish but overall it was not that bad.
Graphics 5/5 - Graphics for this game were slightly better than the last game but mainly stayed on the same level. I haven’t played as many games as other gamers have but I though the graphics for both games were amazing, I give props to the designers.
Story line 6/5- Amazing storyline, just as good as the last one but I felt that this one went more into depth with certain characters. More of the characters had back story which really makes this game a must play. Compared to the first game it has more suspense and what I felt was an overall better story progression in where they tried to tell what happened to every character.
Horror2/5- Some jump scares but they are very slight, it’s not really a horror game like Outlast. I am a fan of Horror and love blood and gore, and while there was some blood and gore I felt like there could have been more.
Action 4.5/5 -While this is not like a typical action (being where you are doing the moves yourself) game I found that it had its moments, most of the actions came from the decisions you made both verbally and physically. The more decisions you make the more action you tend to receive depending on the story.
Suspense 5/5- Very suspenseful, makes you question what is going to happen next just like in the first installment. Playing the game while the stores were still being release made me mad because I wanted to find out what happened next. It was frustrating because when I was on the edge of my seat the on the next episode of the game would pop up. To make things my frustrating there is news of a Walking Dead Season 3 game said to be released in December so the means more waiting for us.
If you are a fan of the Walking Dead video game then I recommend the second installment of the series, I have played both and personally I believe season 2 is something that can definitely compete with season 1. I have spent up to forty five hours playing both games and have gotten all of the achievements for both of the games, and it was worth every second that I played.
If you remember in the first walking dead you played as Lee, a father like figure who is constantly watching out for Clementine, a small girl whose parents left her at home when they went on vacation. As the story progressed you grow attached to the characters especially Lee and Clementine but depending on which root you choose you are left seeing Clementine surviving on her own. In this season you play as Clementine as she survives through new dangers and experiences while she grows up in this apocalyptic society.  She is constantly outsmarting the adults around her, which in my opinion shows that she adapted well to the society and that Lees death wasn’t in vain. In each danger or crisis you once again have to make decisions that will not only affect Clementine but the other characters around her. Overall it was an amazing game for both the first and second seasons and I recommend this game to all of my family and friends. Here were some things that I thought the gamer could expect when playing the Season 2 of the Walking Dead game:
What to expect
-	Blood and gore, while not as bad as the game Outlast there is still slight blood and gore
-	A child constantly outsmarting the adults that she is around
-	New characters will great back stories that make us question the decisions that we make
-	Zombies, as the mentions this is the Walking Dead so zombies are a given
-	Tears , keep a box of tissues handy people trust me it can be sad at times
What not to expect
-	Do not expect it to be like the TV series, they are two separate matters and have completely different characters. Sorry but there will be no Daryl Dixon, or Rick Grimes in this game.
-	Butterflies and sunshine, it’s a Zombie apocalypse the only way you get that is if you die.
-	A season three anytime soon, the earliest they stated its going to be released is by December 2015 and knowing them it will probably be longer than that.
-	Lee coming back riding on a horse like a knight to save clementine.
-	MMO and competitive game play, this is not like CSGO or COD, if you are looking for this , it’s not your game

It's a mixed bag.  There are some great design decisions, like the addition of districts and wonders that occupy individual tiles.  And then there are a whole lot of awful decisions.  For example, instead of diplomatic victory they added religious victory.  Yet they don't allow every player to create a religion (in fact, one civ's unique ability explicitly prevents them from founding a religion).  So if you're not quick to found one before all the Great Prophets dry up (usually around 500 AD in my experience), too bad, an entire victory condition is lost.
Why not let everyone found a religion and make them spread more vigorously to weed out the weak ones?  Why not allow players to seize control of a religion they didn't create (like western Europe did to Christianity) to allow late bloomers a shot at religious victory?  The developers obviously care about religion, considering they tried to make a lot of improvements with the Fall 2017 Update, but it's baffling to me that they focus so much on a mechanic that only a select portion of players will use in any given game.

Several paid DLCs have been released over the last year adding some new civilizations and small amounts of content. Despite the extra content Firaxis has been selling, they have completely neglected fixing all of the bugs, crashes, and issues plaguing their game. Countless crash reports and bugs have been submitted to the developers, and nearly none of these issues have been resolved. Firaxis only concern is pushing out minimal effort DLC for extra profit. There is no long-term plan to create a fanbase. Firaxis is milking the sid meyers cow for all its worth before burying the name with this bug riddled game.
I am a big fan of strategy games, TBS and RTS alike. Civ6 has a great deal of potential, but has far too many issues and nearly none have been fixed since release. A vast majority of my game time is in multiplayer, but many of these issues with the game affect single and multiplayer.
Major issues:
-The game is always crashing, or forcing players to disconnect from multiplayer games when they still have a stable internet connection. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-There is no reason to ever play a "Tall" empire. Wide is always better than tall. The ammenities/happiness mechanic is weak, and disctrics+structures all give flat yields making tall cities never better but almost always worse than a wide empire.
-Multiplayer lobbies are very unstable and players often disconnect or get errors joining lobbies. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Units can erroneously stack when moving to hidden tiles. This is common when scouting the map early game. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Units teleport outside of borders if at war with a city state while the city state suzerain changes. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Team games cause nukes to not function properly.
-Team games break the game demographics so they never update past the turn the game was loaded in on.
-AI can't manage combat. It Suicides units frequently, and often moves units instead of attacking with them. The AI doesn't upgrade units to new eras and is entirely worthless at war.
-AI makes terrible diplomatic decisions like constantly declaring war and then giving the player all its gold for peace.
-AI is practically a random number generator. Units move in arbitrary directions even when at war. AI cities build random items. AI chooses strange tech paths. DEITY is barely even a challenge when you figure out the game.
-Hot joining and reconnecting to a game frequently generates an error and prevents players from doing so. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-City ranged attack is bugged and takes multiple clicks to activate as well as forcing the player camera to move sometimes. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Unit combat sometimes displays incorrectly, showing unit strength in the 1000s. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Hoplites were bugged so they always had +10 combat strength even when not adjacent to other Hoplites. This was fixed 1 year after release. Likely a single line of code that needed to be adjusted, took 1 year to be adjusted.
-Finding a city state before settling your first city results in the player receiving no benefit from its first envoy in that city state. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Pantheons and wonders that affect tile yields may sometimes break in the middle of the game and cease to provide their benefit until the game is reloaded. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-If a player disconnects from a multiplayer game, the AI instantly takes over and moves all of the players units, spends their gold, and changes their civics--forcing players to load a previous save. Since players frequently disconnect due to game instability, this is a big deal. This is a well known issue and has been ongoing for 1 year.
-Cities than change owner multiple times can get stuck as being permanently occupied even after the other empire is entirely wiped off the map or the city has been ceded in a peace deal. This bug was introduced in the Nubia DLC.
Minor issues (Mostly multiplayer balance concerns):
-Unit balance is extremely poor. Horsemen beat spearmen.
-Completing a wonder or reaching enough great people points to earn a great person at the same time as another player always gives the wonder or great person to the player in the highest game slot.
-City states are far too easy to capture early game.
-Upgrading units from previous eras does not cost nearly enough gold resulting in the odd situation where you should  never build current era units--you build previous era units and upgrade them with gold.
-The tech tree is not well designed and players only have 2 logical options--go for field cannons, or go for cavalry, and in both cases you go straight to tanks next.
-Districs are not well balanced. Theatre squares and Holy Sites are very underpowered except in rare situations.
-Great generals can stack.
Overall, I have had fun playing this game, but I cannot recommend it. Firaxis does not fix issues with the game. They design some DLC to sell, and then sell it with nearly no testing done at all. Each DLC has introduced additional bugs to the game. The latest DLC completely broke the script that determines where civilizations can spawn on the map causing civilizations to sometimes spawn in the arctic, or within 3 tiles of another civilization. This problem can be identified in 15 minutes of testing. Any competent developer would realize that if he modifies the script affecting civiliazation spawn locations, its worth testing the script by starting the game a few times, revealing the entire map, and checking that all spawn locations are reasonable--This did not happen. The script was changed, and then sold as part of the DLC.

Great game, love it so far. A very small critique is that the game has very few decisions and/or scenarios that you need to do multiple steps to go through in a specific way like a Hitman game with the glory kills. I feel like those moments really lifts the game and makes it very rewarding and fun to explore and seek the details of the game.
Overall, I am recommending this game and I am enjoying it very much. Huge props to the team for the very apropriate pricing, as the game not is a AAA title and it feels really fair and unlike some other games this doesn't feel in any way like a ripoff, but actually like a really priceworthy game easly worth it's price (don't tell the dev team, but I think the game might actually do for a slight increase in price). The free demo also adds to the feeling of good care of customers. All of this toghether makes me smile, even before opening the game.
Another thing that I feel this game does good for the industry is that it is a very good game for people to get into gaming. Its almost the perfect way to enter into gaming. It's well formatet so you can pause or do something else while you play, as there is many checkpoints, and you know, time traveling. Also the game has somee really easy and convinient controlls. The mouse is really simple to use, and there isnt alot of controll.
Another detail that I have to give HUGE props to is the fact that you can use WASD and the arrow keys by default. This is one of the biggest things for people that havent played much on the PC, usually the first thing they do is reaching for the arrow keys.
As mention abow, their pricing and the free demo is great. But also, this really helps bringing new gamers as the price is not a problem, you can play for free and if you get hooked you can buy the expansion. The game is not to heavy on the computer either, which obviosly is a plus for new PC players. The games genre is also really good for this purpose. Despite the much bigger budget, "GTA V" will for an example be harder to push to non gamers than "Life Is Strange", im certain.
So, if any of you gamers out there want to do something to make games more "acceptable" and bring a even larger amount of people into gaming, please share this to your none gaming friends or hey, your parents. This is just the perfect entry for non gamers.

I'll preface by admitting that I'm a grumpy old civ4 elitist, but this game just isn't worth buying in its current state.
There are a lot of very cool systems the designers have put up a rough foundation for, but it's still just too empty to really enjoy.  You can really see the potential in this game, but there's still just so many little things missing or buggy that drive you nuts.
And as always, the AI is dumb as rocks.  They keep making the combat engine more and more complicated without adapting the AI to handle it at all.  As a result, you can win wars with maybe 4-5 units.  The AI is just not good enough to handle the system.  All the depth of the combat mechanics just aren't satisfying because of this.
It's like beating a dog in Chess.  Your great strategy and tactics are simply wasted on an opponent that has no idea what it's doing.
And a full year after release, there are still missing hotkeys for actions you will do *EVERY TURN*.
The art is gorgeous.  The soundtrack is amazing.  The district system and the armies/fleets system show so much promise.  But the game's just not deep enough, and the AI so poor that it's simply not enjoyable after one or two playthroughs.
I cranked the difficulty up to diety on my 2nd playthrough, and still got bored and quit 200 turns in because of how far ahead of the AI I was.  I played on Emperor in civ5, and I think Monarch in civ4.  It's not like I've magically gotten better at the game.  The AI is just *that* bad.  It is utterly incapable of threatening you militarily, and does not know how to pursue win conditions at all.
Again, there's a TON of potential.  Really disappointing game as it stands though.  Maybe with a couple of expansions it'll reach its full potential, but until then I cannot recommend this game.

Telltale Games did it again, raising the technical bar in the process.
We can now enjoy cell-shaded post-processing, as well as reflections, depth of field and highly-defined textures. Animations are somewhat improved and coupled with a nice assortment of in-game facial animations. There are some added gameplay features, and the interface has been revamped for keyboard and mouse users. Although voice acting is appropriate most of the time, there are some levelling and quality issues, specially for a certain character. Thankfully, music keeps its outstanding level.
Story-wise, this season is brutal from beginning to end.
Unfortunately, being put in the shoes of a young girl while also being given mature choices through the majority of the dialogues can be a little off-putting. During the first season we were introduced to a really smart kid, but even so dialogue options are often too mature or denote a certain amount of knowledge that isn't always suitable in the context.
However, the story is awesome, and it develops with such an intensity and pace that will surely keep you on the edge for its entire rather-short duration. Yes, compared to the first season, playtime is considerable shorter in this sequel.
To the negative points mentioned so far, I would add the annoyance and lack of purpose of the Civil War Museum level, and the hole in a certain character's face that seems to have fooled the quality assurance team on every episode release.
Achievements are once again very easy to get, even easier than in season one. On the other hand, there are no game cards this time. I wanted my badge!

As a huge fan of horror fiction, I was more than a little interested in Alan Wake when news first started circulating about it. Luckily, I have finally been able to play the game as it is no longer an Xbox exclusive.
First of all, Alan Wake looks amazing. I can't remember the last time I played a game from start to finish whilst being in awe of the graphics all the way through! The lighting effects are truly out of this world and make walking through spooky forests all the more immersive. The level design is also fantastic with huge draw distances and a really detailed countryside to explore in its entirety. This is all backed up by a really decent story, that whilst not incredibly scary, is still a good horror tale in its own right. There's no hiding the fact that this story has been inspired by Stephen King. The writers mention his name several times throughout - but the brilliant thing about it is that Alan Wake is both a homage and a parody of King's work.

The retro styled top down shooter that is Hotline Miami offers an amazing gaming experience. This game will frustrate you, but in a good way. If and when you get caught on a level, you are forced to take a second look at your approach. Nothing is more satisfying then completing a tough level seemlessly after experimenting with every aspect of the game. Hotline Miami offers an experience similar to older games that incited excitement through getting through hard levels, Whether your an older gamer, or a new generation of gamer you will enjoy this game! Buy it already!

Synopsis: My rating of this game would be a 8.5/10, because of the creative potential, mods, community, and knowledge gained from playing the game.
This game, like many others that I had baught in 2014, is a very deep and special game to me. Ever since I first got KSP in 2014, I have been playing it almost non-stop and trust me, I enjoy it thuroughly. Although there may be some snags in the coding or crashes due to CPU usage or RAM overusage, the Squad team really did it with the previous update and have finally released a stable, smooth, and stronger 64-bit, which, I should mention, may scratch out many of the negative comments about the game on how the game used to constantly crash for CPU or RAM usage.
Don't get me wrong, this game CAN... repeat, CAN... get repetative. If, let's say, you want to go to a far planet then you take a bunch of fuel tanks and a nuclear engine and go there quite easily, which can degrade the "fin" of the game; Yet, that's where breaks come in. As of recently, I took a rather long break from KSP and I finally realized then that it had become a very important part of me.
On to a side note,
KSP can be absolutely fantastic for crude education in Aerospace engineering. Someone in KSP will learn some simple terms such as "Delta V" or "Prograde", "Retrograde", "Antinormal", "Normal" etc. Someone playing KSP will learn concepts of how rockets work, how boosters work, and how flow of air works. An example, is when someone makes a lander to go to the Mun or somewhere farther, they will soon learn why exactly Saturn VII used the fairing between the mothership and the lander; Or the player will learn soon enough that a square is less Aerosynamic than an Elipsoid. With the new 1.2 update coming around the corner, a player of KSP will also soon learn that Radio communication is essential, and will learn how exactly a "Satelite Constelation" is essential to ANY kind of mission to space.
In all honesty, I'd rate this game a solid 8.5/10, due to it's engaging atmosphere (Pls get the reference ;-;), potential for creativity, knowledge, and community. The only downside is, When I got the game I was hoping for a more "procedural" solar system, for a bit of a challenge, or even Star Systems that one could travel to. I also expected to see the modding community as a friendly one, but I realized that if you make one wrong click, then your "mod page" will become an endless list of bug reports. Don't get me wrong, though, the mods are to die for (On the Mun). If the developers could keep up with Space Engineers, though, then I'd rate the game a 9/10 (SE gets updated every Thursday for thos of you who don't know).

Civ VI is a good game, though imperfect.
I have not looked back at (the excellent) Civ V since playing this game, and I honestly don't know why anyone would. The district system is innovative, making you think about how you place your cities more, and unlocking both the ability to strategize and roleplay more. The changes to city-states are an amazing breath of fresh air. There are many interesting civilizations with cool bonuses that drive you to play the game in a unique way, and I've had a great time pumping hundereds of hours into this latest installment.
Lately, there have been many critical reviews, which is fine; everyone is entitled to their own opinion. However, I find that a lot of these reviews strike me as incredibly possesive of the product. Some people have their vision of where the franchise should go, and are disappointed that their view doesn't match up with reality. Some complaints I see are:
- The diplomacy is broken! I was attacked, and when I conquered the aggressor, everyone hated me! (Remember, the allies never 'conquered' Germany; conquest is generally looked down upon.)
- I can't use nukes, because they ruin the city I'm trying to conquer, or there's never a large enough standing target that I'd want to! (Maybe that's why people aren't constantly nuking people irl.)
- All the cool civs are behind a DLC wall! (Fair criticism.)
I enjoy the h*ck out of this game, and it's worth saying that I have a pretty good computer, so I've never had a problem with long load times, and I've never experienced bugs or crashes, certainly fewer than I had with Civ V. I also don't play much multiplayer, and generally go through games trying to win, but in a more role-play fashion. So that's the perspective I'm coming from through my review, and I have a great time.
The concerns I do have are these:
- AI isn't great, but the more complicated a game becomes the worse the AI is going to be, because it cannot efficiently play the same way the player does.
- Some games hit a point where it feels like you're just filling different buckets with gold, faith, culture, or whatever, and are mostly clicking next turn. This isn't the whole game, and not every game, however.
- I wish some civilizations had bonuses more tied to specific ways of playing or winning, instead of feeling like a stack of unrelated bonuses.
Overall, I do recommend the game.

Hotline Miami is the best worst trip of your life. The nightmare begins in a dingy 1989 Miami apartment, as you listen to the first in a long line of mysterious messages left on your answering machine. For whatever reason, you feel compelled to do as you're told, a task that usually involves brutally murdering dozens of armed gunmen with hair triggers. Pressing on in a search for answers only further blurs the lines between reality and rampant psychosis, and you're left wondering which possibility is the least horrifying. Vigilante gone overboard? Contract killer? Maybe you're just a delivery driver losing himself in increasingly improbable power fantasies. Maybe it doesn't matter. Maybe you don't care.
The game presents an impressive array of weapons and animal masks, each augmenting your abilities or changing the gameplay in some way. It's more of a twitchy, reflex-based puzzler than a mindless rampage, and a single misstep will lead to a messy death at the hands of your adrenaline-fueled enemies. However, any feelings of frustration that might arise are quickly washed away in a tsunami of 16bit blood and gore, and the fast-paced, addictive gameplay will have you hitting the "retry" button out of pure reflex.
The soundtrack fits the game like a glass slipper, ghosts of acid-washed synthesizers and contemporary electronica comprising one of the best video game soundtracks you'll ever hear.

Alan Wake came as a shock to me. From what I had read, it seemed as though it were a linear game with limited features and a sub-par plot.
I was wrong. This game has you gripping your mouse and smashing your keyboard the entire time. Its intense gameplay is based on eradicating darkness from your enemies before you can finally end there suffering with a loaded gun. It has a horror-esque feel to it, as you are constantly trapped in darkness and swarmed by enemies. Combine that with a plot that follows Alan in his nightmarish days in the Pacific Northwest and is assembled like a TV show (you play through "episodes"), and you have one hell of a concept for a video game.
Plus, it was executed beautifully.
Recommended for fans of thriller and heavily plot based games.

Although it pains me to do so, with all the thousands of hours I've put into its 5 mighty predecessors, I click the thumb down on recommending this game. I got like 1500+ hours in Civ5, and I've played the sixth one for 73 hours now, but it just cannot keep me going. It's just too buggy to keep me immersed. The bugs range from the mildly irritating ones in the UI, to the rather disturbing ones in AI, to completely ridiculous ones in especially diplomacy.
I got denounced for not having a strong navy by Norway while being landlocked... who were just as landlocked without a navy themselves. I got huge culture by just trading every piece of art of every other player because they seem to put no value whatsoever in them anyway. I get trade offers all the time which are unacceptable by the offering opponent right away. And on... and on.... and on....
The game itself is fine, but overcomplicates itself by offering way too many mechanics, and executing many of them halfwittedly. In graphical view it's nigh on impossible to discern which districts are where, despite placement being vital to many decisions on the map.
And where are my management statistics? There is no military report, so in practice no usable way to find accidentally "lost" units that you fortified a while back in a backward part of the kingdom. Other reports are too concise to be as useful as they could be... and should be in a globe-spanning strategy game.
Sorry, but this needs 6 months of bug fixes this winter, not a feature update.

You start the game out with a revolver and some bullets and work through randomly generated levels trying to manage your health and ammo while collecting pieces of radiation from the corpses of your fallen enemies and canisters that are placed on the map.  Collecting enough will eventualy allpw you to level up....but only once you beat the current level.  Once you beat the level, youll be given several randomly generated "mutations" or perks to choose from that do various things like modfy your special ability, give you more health, increase your ammo cap, increase drop rates, allow you to pick up items from further away, or countless others.  There are clear mutations that are better for certain characters and some that are just good choices overall.
This game shines in comparisn to other rougelike games in its ability for you to cater a run and have the objectives to be to try and get x or y weapon and get a, b, and c mutations.  Unlike in games like th binng of issac where you will just get random weapons and there are too many for you to be able to realiably make a plan, there are enough to provide variety while not being so much that its overwhelming to understand and providing enough oppertunitie to switch weapons on levels.  Its also really important to understand that while you can "plan" your runs to do something in particular, it is still hard to execute because you have to stay on your feet the entire time and one stray bullet, misfired rocket, or graze against the wrong enemy is enough to end even the most promsing of runs.
While nuclear thorne is still in early access, the game has more going for it than many games that are already published in the same price range.  Unlike other games with different playable classes and  characters, there is no clearly best character and every character has their own unique playstyle that can be played effectively.  The game has constantly been recieving updates and Im looking forward to even more in the future!

Without any further delay, I present to you my review of The Walking Dead, season 2.
I'll be making a considerable ammount of comparisons to season 1, as I'm expecting people to have played that one before considering season 2.
As expected, season 2 picks off a little while after season 1 ends, and if you did, in fact, play season 1, you'll be able to use that save so that the game adapts to the choices you made in the past.
From the get-go the story is more focused on the human side of what's left, and not just run/hide/kill zombies. Obviously, there will still be zombies to kill, and zombies to hide or run from, but it won't feel as important. You'll have to make choices, some harder than others, and they will tailor the game as you go along, or this wouldn't be a Telltale game.
You can expect the same graphics you had one season 1, with some tweaks to the graphical hiccups you might have felt while playing the previous season.
You can also expect an incredible soundtrack, which adapts effortlessly to the scenario at hand.

as I just don't feel it's as fluid as season 1, and the life/death situations aren't as exhilarating.

I like the game, but unless you're playing with friends you're going to have a bad time as most players in this game are new to this kind of genre, and don't really know how to play this game. But obviously thats not the developers fault, but simply the community.
The game itself is fun. The maps are designed smoothly so bug free gameplay is possible.
Now the characters themself all feel kind of like frankenstein creations. All abilities you will find in OV will also be found in this game. But it doesn't bother me. Because in this game you can actually easily defeat every character with every other character. It's not a game of who can bite whos tail the best (*cough* overwatch *cough*) but more who can outplay the otherone the best.
I also like that just playing the game gives you money which you can use to then to buy customisation parts for you characters.
This game also has a really clever card system, which basicly works that you can unpack cards from boxes or straight up just buy them, and then put them in your card deck for each character to strenghen certain abilitys or even add special traits that e.g. the explosives of your characters harm yourself 20% less.
Another cool thing is that when you spawn into the match, you can buy special perks that only affect you during that game. These momentary perks can be bought through coins, which you collect overtime buy getting points. The perks can give you more direct damage, reduce the direct damage you take, reduce crowd control effects on you, etc...
Overall i definetly recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a team based game.

This is literally the very first Civ game I've played where I have not felt the draw of "Just One More Turn". Even Civilization Beyond Earth had that a little bit for me.
Every single good "new" feature of Civ6 has existed in some form in past versions of Civ and/or their mods: districts have existed as the improvement-heavy strategies of Civ4, amenities have existed as Civ4's happiness and health metrics, the great person special abilities system is ripped entirely from Civilization Colonization, the culture tech tree / policies system has been done many times in Civ4 mods with great person abilities that put you down particular paths, harvesting resources has been done in both Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri and a large amount of Civ4 and Civ5 mods, and most of what is good about the unit management system is ripped straight from Civ5.
Worse yet, as an avid Civ5 modder, I can safely say that Civ6 has had some of the worst modding support from a Civ game to date. It took months after release to just get modding tools out, and 2K have made Firaxis pull the same thing with Civ6's DLL Source Code as they did with Civ5 (which is one of the big reasons we didn't get a lot of big mods for Civ5 like we did with Civ4).
A thorough disappointment. Just play Civ5, Civ4, or one of those two's mods instead.

Simply amazing!  This is the successor to the hugely popular Walking dead Season 1.
This time around you play as Clementine, much older and much tougher.  As usual from the start you are thrown into the nightmare the world has become.  Right away you find yourself making decisions and just trying to survive.
The character development in this game is slightly different to the first game, i suspect telltale made it this way to reflect the large time gap between this and the first game.  Basically people are much less trusting or to be trusted, because the world is a different place now right?
I found myself struggling to decide what to say and do and mainly got by on my gut feeling putting myself in Clems shoes, again this seemed much different to the first game because each character seemed emotionally numb after living in the zombie apocalypse for so long.  Each person much like the first game you feel is a real person, they make mistakes and they certainly have an opinion.
The quicktime events slightly changed at times in this game i wont explain it but i'll leave you discover that for yourself, they work very well im my opinion but take a few moments to get used to.
Storylines this time around has changed pace, it just seemed that with each and every moment things can change and the pace of the game certainly did at times.
As per the last game you find that decisions you made earlier in the game effect things later on, with every decision you make it can have a negative or positive effect.  I wrote a review for season 1 where i explained that i felt a deep connection to the characters, this time around it was pretty much the same and much like the first game i just didnt want the story to end it was so good.
With each chapter of the season you will make good and bad decisions its just how the game is, my advice is try just not to do the right thing but just try to become the character and decide for yourself, the story works best this way in the long run.
I cannot praise telltale enough for making these amazing games with the amazing storylines and character progression.
9.5/10 if you havent played these games yet do so already!  You don't know what you're missing.
Cant wait for Season 3!!!

This game reminds me of Civ5 at the same point in its lifecycle: incredibly innovative ideas but missing the interstitial components that always get added later in the lifecycle of a civ game. Ex: Civ5 cultural victory used to be about unlocking all the policy trees and then building a wonder, tourism and artifacts were added much later. Firaxis have been doing a good job of fixing the bugs and annoyances, but they haven't gotten to full system reworks beyond religion.
The disaggregation of cities is comparable to the disaggregation of armies in 5 in impact on the franchise. For me, it's as impossible to go back to 5's stacked cities as it was to go back to 4's stacked armies.
I usually play at Emperor difficulty in the Civ franchise and that's no different here. I'd say the AI is pretty comparable to 5. A little better in some areas, a little worse in others. The lack of AI mods is a pain, and we're all hoping the SDK gets released soon. If I remember right it took a couple years for the 5 one to get released, so I wouldn't be shocked if it'll still be a bit for 6.
The DLC for me is supremely uninteresting. I got Poland for personal reasons, but the rest of them are kind of irrelevant just like the Civ 5 DLCs. Maybe get Australia if you want to have all the luxuries. I'm waiting for them to all go on heavy discount.
If you can get it for half off, go nuts. In terms of enjoyment I've gotten out of it, it's already pretty comparable to 5 (which was for me second worst in franchise after release 3, but is now near the top with Civ 2 CTP). Otherwise, wait for the first or second expansion.

An example of a good sequel. Crueler, more interesting and with tougher choices.
At first I was reluctant to play as Clementine, knowing that Lee taught her to be a good little girl with high moral standards which would be kinda boring. But in a year long gap between two season Clementine matured a lot and became tougher. Even though everyone says that she's just a child and can't survive on her own, she constantly proves them wrong and shows that she clearly adapts better to zombie apocalypse than adults. Can't say much about other characters in this game. Some are good-written, some aren't and some are killed before you can begin to sympathize with them.
And this brings us to the main flaw of Telltale Games' games - your choices do not matter as much as you may think. Yeah, sometimes your choice would lead to the death of some character but about 2/3 of them die anyway and you can't do anything about that, so if you play the game again you may find out that that one time, when you were desperately thinking should you rob a guy with medicine or not, does not matter - that guy is still being robbed, if not by you, than by your partner.
Gameplay-wise it's the same game, since there is no point in changing working mechanics of story-driven interactive movie. And once again I want to note an amazing soundtrack by Jared Emerson-Johnson which blends really well with storytelling and beautiful on it's own. A real shame Telltale Games still haven't released it or the one from the previous game for sale.
Overall it's a good experience, still better than TV series, season 3 when?

70% Stephen King (the good stuff), 28% Twin Peaks, 2% H.P. Lovecraft. If that is a mix you like, you'll like Alan Wake. The game is quite "cinematic" in that you don't have much freedom. You'll have to follow the (very good) story without making any kind of choice but the mechanics of the game are compelling enough to keep you entertained.
PROs:
- The way you have to fight the monsters is very fun and original, and will keep fresh throughout the game.
- The game manages to be scary without being gory.
- A good story which (usually) manages to avoid the worst clichés.
- The way Alan moves is great for the fights, giving a great feel to dodges and narrow escapes and making everything more frantic, but is imprecise for the rare occasion in which you need to jump over something or move on something narrow.
CONs:
- The scenery could use some more variety. The dark woods get old after a while and the variations are too few and too far between.
- The protagonist is an idiot and a jerk.
For a free to play shooter it's very fun!

Alan Wake is a gorgeous, plot-driven third person shooter by Remedy. Because the game is so plot-heavy, I will entirely avoid discussing the story in this review.
The one gameplay element that separates Alan Wake from other shooters is that enemies must be weakened by light sources before becoming vulnerable to bullets. This adds a layer of strategy by forcing the player to be wary of his environment and resource management. Unfortunately, the fight sequences do get repetitive.
Only $29.99, what makes this purchase even more worthwhile is that it comes bundled with two additional pieces of downloadable content. The first, titled "The Signal", is more action oriented. The second, titled "The Writer", presents itself as more of a platformer.
If you're hungering for an engrossing story and exciting gameplay, Alan Wake will fill that niche perfectly. The variety of solid gameplay is refreshing and welcomed. It makes me eager to see what Remedy has in store for the sequel.
Grade: B+

Telltale had both a very difficult and a very easy job with The Walking Dead: Season 2. They didn't really need to change much; at the same time, the game would be judged very harshly, since it would have to live up to the legend of Season 1. Fortunately, the game does not disappoint and retains its predecessor's strengths: great story, told with an abundance of emotions, meaningful choices and a cast of interesting characters. It's everything Season 1 was, and that's enough. Basically, if you loved the first game, Season 2 will not disappoint. Just play Season 1 first.
Pros:
+ Brilliant story and gripping atmosphere - one of the best narratives in video game history
+ Varied cast of characters and numerous meaningful choices
+ Strong visuals and sounds
+ If you loved the first game, you'll love Season 2
+ What more do you really need?
Cons:
- More of the same, so if you did not like it the first time, Season 2 will not change your mind
- Some textures and animations could be of better quality; however, it does not detract from the story a whole lot
- Poor optimization - the game often had trouble hitting 30 FPS on a pretty powerfull rig, even during slower scenes
- Goddamit, where is Season 3?!

Like all Telltale reviews, by now you should know what you're getting. It's a playable story with limited decisions that you play for the story and good voice acting. So what's up with TWD Season 2? It's good. Not quite as good as Season 1, TWD2 is still a worthy title.
I don't think you can call this game "fun". After all, the choices are depressing. Your ability to actually change things is exceptionally limited. It's more of an interactive story than a game. Still, I find this series compelling to play and the narrative gripping. Clem is one of my most favorite characters in all my gaming years (stretching back to Pong). The voice acting continues to be a major strength of the series.
I found Season 2's quality more variable than Season 1. There were far more gut-punches in #1, far more difficult decisions in #1 than in this season. Still, this has it's moments. But frankly perhaps the biggest flaw is that there are too many characters that you don't really get to know them. They seem - and often are - expendible whereas in Season #1 the group was tighter and better fleshed out.
If you haven't played Season 1, get that first. But these titles are really worth your time because they tell such great stories.

*As a note before you read this, there may be some spoilers to the first game. If you are reading this with no prior knowledge to the game, please read a review for the first game. you have been warned
Ah, The Walking Dead. A game which, although I haven't played in a while, I can still remember every detail of.
The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a sequel from the game The Walking Dead (quite self explanatory really). You asume the role of Clementine, a young teenager (aging up from the previous game) who was left with a babysitter while her parents went to Savannah for a vacation. Little did they know that there vacation was to be cut short. As the name suggests, the dead become the undead and begin walking around and grunting in the usual zombie way, leaving Clementine in a world of death and torment. She leaves the safety of her home to travel with a man called Lee who does everything in his power to protect her. You are faced with many different characters and personalities, much like real life and are forced to make decisions based on the situation. The best part about it, you're in control of those choices.
As I've given the story, I may as well review that element first.
The story is the main element of this game and makes it into what it is. The choices that you make affect the story heavily and drive to connect with the characters that you have been presented with, be it that you feel like being a complete badass throughout the whole of the game, threatening to kill someone for trying to tickle you or being the friendly and conserved type. Lets be honest though. who plays nice in these games?
The emotional connection that you get with some of the characters is absolutely phenomenal. When you start playing this, chances are you will probably end up caring for some people more than you care about some of your so-clled 'friends' that you swear that you have but always seem to be busy when you want to do something with them. Lets be real though. Who needs real-life friends when you've got all the people you could ever want to talk to here?
Next up is the gameplay.
The Walking Dead has a rather different style of play to most games. It's a break from the old FPS and MOBA genres which now appear to steal the show. However, the actual gameplay is very limited. Remember I said that the story is the main element? Yep, that's what this game is. The Walking dead has been from the first game 3 different modes of gameplay. A mode where everyone is calm and has no problem going on at that particular time and so you have all the time in the world. A mode where the previous mode requires you to make a fast decision and finally a mode where you mash buttons. The first and second mode play out like a game of detective. You move the mouse until you find what it is you're looking for to progress with the story. I guess you could say there are technically 4 if you include parts where there are 4 diffferent dialogue options for you to choose from. This is also usually timed but in some cases is not. In Season 2, there are quick-time events which require you to do things such as using the arrows to move left and right or pressing a specific key in order to do certain actions.
As you can currently see, not much in terms of technicality. But that's the beauty of it. The simplicity really does make this game better as it focuses on the finer details of the game as opposed to games that rely on their complex mechanics to which the game-devs scratch their heads in confusion. The Walking Dead focuses in on the story, using the timer and the atmosphere to put the player at an emotional disadvantage and make them reall consider their choices in-game.
The best part about this game is the way in which it is meant to be played over many times to get the different outcomes and to play in different ways to which the player gets to choose. Also, thank TellTale Games for placing 3 save slots so that you get to do a playthrough of to get the different endings, all ready for the next game to come out. If it does that is.
The art style of this game is also very creative, using hand-drawn textures which suit the games style and mood. This also makes it much easier to run for those who don't have good PC's meaning that the game's experiences are to be shared with everyone.
These are the overall Scores:-
Story:- 9/10 - Very memorable and really hits the player hard. Draws emotional attachment out of the player. My only criticism is the way in which the majority of the choices have no bearing on what happens in the end
Gameplay:- 7/10 - I had a lot of fun playing through this game and even cried towards the end, but sequences eventually become easy and there is no difficulty in the completion. It is very rare you will fail. Also, trying to find what you need to do to progress can become annoying.
Textures/Art-style:- 9/10 - A beautiful game with stunning scenes that make an impact on its own. The scenes in this game really show off the atmophere and feeling.Can't ask for much more than that.
Replayability:- 10/10 - This is where this game really excels. The multiple choice element to this game makes you want to go back and redo the whole game again, leaving your mind with the 'What-if?' thought constantly after you make a decision.
Overall:- 9/10 - Overall, this game is a must buy. It is one of the biggest emotional rollrcoasters you are likely to go on. Hell, I think I would have cried less if you had made me chop onions. If you locked me in a room with this game, I'd cry every time you put me through having to watch the closing scenes.
I hope this gave you some insight as to whether you would want to buy this game (please do) and I hope it helps :)

I dont normally write reviews but this game has moved me so much that I am absolutely compelled to write a review about it.
I dont know even where to begin about this game. But I'll start with this. This has probably been the best game I have ever played and I have played a lot out there trust me. I have a particular affinity to games that have deep and rich stories and I have never developed such a deep and emotional connection as I have with the characters of this game. This game feels so fleshed out and beautifully directed and created. There is a raw connection that feels like I am living someone else's life for a change and this game has fundamentally affected my philosophy on life. Prior to playing this I felt cocooned and detached to the world like I have my life to live and my problems to worry about. But after playing this and experiencing the life and problems of the protagonist, I am forever changed. Never has a game affected me so profoundly. I realize now that we each live and play out our own lives even if it doesnt conciously feel that way to us. The developer has made this game in such a way that I am connected to humanity as a whole and that I am not alone in this crowd. I feel like this is a hallmark/milestone on how games should be made! It has made a significant impact on my life and I definitely recommend it to everyone who loves deep and meaningful stories. Its an easy enough game and can be finished in one weekend but its impact will last a lifetime.
TL;DR: I definitely reccomend this game to anyone looking for some feels and what a great game ought to be and I am not the same person because of it!

While these graphics imply a dumbing down they have actually taken the fully expanded civ v and added on to it with the flagship feature being the "unstackng" of cities i.e. one needs to expand districts onto further tiles to add building for each resource: holy site for faith, campus for science, theatre district for culture, etc. Devs seem to listen to fans, as a pricing error in the season pass lead them to add more dlc packs to the pass when they could have just said "sucks to be not american." Most of the Telltale games gets you really invested in the story and it's safe to say, that the story plays with your emotions. The Walking Dead: Season 2 is not an exception.
When I played the first episode, I thought to myself, that Telltale Games will not pull off something like the original game and I was right at first. The first episode and maybe, half of the second didn't make me attached to the characters. As the game progresses, you start caring about several characters, about the events going on without even noticing. If you are left with a choice where you have to pick a side or do something, you will wish you had that extra 10 seconds to think about it, while at the start of the game it didn't feel as important. You will feel even more attached and invested in the story after each episode, so don't jump in conclusions right when you start playing it. Trust me, I didn't want to play like a little girl at first either.
I recommend TWD:S2 not because it is a good game, but because it is one of the few games that actually makes you feel something inside, makes you think about morals. Pretty much shows the human side of you. While on games like Postal, Manhunt, Killing Floor etc. you'll feel anger and no remorse. Some games make you absolutely neutral. It's safe to say that both The Walking Dead games are worth your time and the full price.

Note: I have only played 23 hours of civ vi. I have repeatedly tried to play this game more, but I just can't.
Pro's:
-The district system is a neat idea, and I'm excited to see where they intend to take it.
-I really like how you can send a fighter to patrol a tile (the animation is quite neat as well). Too bad air power is useless...
-The idea of city-state diplomacy is promising. This, however, was also poorly implemented.
-Small detail, but still cool: nuclear subs can attack coasts. This is a fun aspect to the game that I think makes submarines actually useful to have many of.
Con's:
-The ai is objectively all the same. They really only differ in the specific reason that they hate you, but they will all hate you by mid game. They will also all have terrible military abilities. No more legitimately powerful nations like in Civ V that can actually defeat a player (it's not likely, but possible).
-Diplomacy in general doesn't work like it would make sense to work. I don't really have any ellaboration to this; it all feels awkward and annoying.
-This might just be me, but the model for missile cruiser is completely pathetic. I actually dislike the game substantially more because of it. Naval ranged goes from the mighty battleship model to this tiny, patrol boat looking missile cruiser that still has greater strength. No thank you - Fireaxis, make missile cruisers look like missile cruisers....
-PREDATORY DLC MG! Like, I'm fine with morally questionable dlc practices that probably most other games have, but Civ VI boasts what, 5 tiny dlc's that cost way too much? The game is largely broken, yet Fireaxis is putting more than zero effort into pumping out more civs that ultimately act the same (see my first point).
-Civ V complete>Civ VI. I know some people say that the base Civ VI shouldn't compare with the fully complete Civ V, but that doesn't really make sense. Why does Civ VI have a tiny fraction of the features that Fireaxis already included in the previous game? I understand some things don't carry over that easily due to mechanics, but it honestly feels like they are trying to go The Sims route where literally the same base game gets released and is then improved by the same set of dlc (as if EA had trouble putting pets in Sims 4 when they were already in sims 3).
-Religion is just terrible (moreso than usual). Nothing else to really ellaborate on, it just doesn't work at all.
-The world seems smaller. Even on huge, you can only fit a few cities at most. I understand, and actually agree, that this is needed because of the new city mechanics, but I think they could have still made the world smaller while still making it feel "huge".
-The style is just annoying. Everything is comical. The art style is bright and reminds me of a free mobile game. The writing is cringe inducing. Too many quotes about the techs are from contemporary funny people that have no qualifications to speak about the things they are quoted for.
Conclusion:
Honestly, if it's your cup of tea, it's your cup of tea. This is definitely not a game for those that love the previous civs - that game would be Civ V. However, Civ VI isn't done yet, and should have 3 or so expansion packs coming in the next few years; Fireaxis can still recover. Would I recommend this game? Yes, but not for $60; buy Civ V for $60. CIv VI is worth probably $15 in its current state.

For the price tag, I wish I could say I really enjoyed this game. Unless you have a lot of patience, the late game becomes frustrating very quickly. Few things that make this game unplayable for me
- Spastic pathfinds requires you to constantly re-route the same units over and over again every turn if you attempt to move many units in the same direction.
- Inability to cross borders + pathfinding in fog causes your units to get in circular loops unless you manually move them every turn. (to be expected I guess, but still frustrating)
- You constantly get "AI cutscenes" such as Civilizations denouncing you as a warmonger. If you play as a warmonger, you'll get interrupted by more than one of these every turn.
- Managing many cities becomes a tedious chore of building the same stuff over and over. It gets to the point where you wish you could just have the cities build on autopilot, because you don't even really care what they're building anymore.
I played 2 games up until the 20th century, in neither game did any Civ ever declare war on me, even if it was a good idea for the Civ to do so. As a result you can play extremely passive and there isn't much point to warmongering (and it's not fun to do so), as was the case in my second game where I decided to start some wars around the 17th century.
Turns become extremely long in the midgame and for me that just makes it unplayable. I'm not really new to Civ, I've played them all since Civ II when I was a kid, but something about this game just felt more tedious and boring than the others. I can't recommend it, especially not for the price tag.

The Walking Dead kind of straddles that line between Video Game and Interactive Fiction, in that there isn't really much gaming to be done here beyond selecting dialogue choices or walking around investigating things. Most of the game is carried by the story, the weight of the choices you make, and the interactions between the characters.
Unfortunate that Season Two is a display of some of the problems with interactive fiction. Ultimately, you can't really change much throughout the story, and while there are technically five endings, you aren't really influencing much in the game. A lot of the time is spent waiting between major moments, and then these seemingly big things turn out to be nothing.
I still had a good time with it, but Season One was better and I'm kind of questioning Season Three. There's still a lot of fun to be had, though, and if you're a fan of the gameplay formula that Telltale uses for their games, you're going to have a great time.

Nuclear Throne had a rocky release as it left Early Access with Update 98. There were quite a few bugs and it looked like Vlambeer had abandoned it. With Update 99 this game is truely finished, and in no small part thanks to modder Yellowafterlife. No, you wont have to download a 3rd party mod to have a complete game. Vlambeer hired YA to officially release Update 99, and with that I can finally give my review:
It's hard to believe the early access game I bought on a whim several years ago would be one I still play on a daily basis. Whether its to do the daily, weekly, or just a random run, there's always something to keep me coming back to this game almost every single day. It's hard to describe to people what makes Nuclear Throne so special. The gameplay is satisfying and challenging, the art is gorgeous, the sound design perfectly fits the theme, the weapons and characters are totally unique, and crowns can completely change the way you play the game on the fly.
For me it's easy to see why Nuclear Throne is one of my top played and most favorite games I own, but for you who may be curious I say why not give it a chance? It may be tough at first, but dont give up. In time you too will reach the Nuclear Throne.

Seeing it as it's own game, it's an okay 4X turn based strategy. If you've never played a Civ game, it's alright, I guess.
The majority of the hate comes down to two things, which both I agree with. The first point is that as an entry to the Civilization franchise, it's pretty weak: the district system is... interesting, but I wouldn't neccisarily call anything an improvment since the last entry to Civ, just... different. It's a good game, but it doesn't have a soul.
The second reason being the malicious DLC pricing and releasing. The unfortunate trend of "Triple A" games being priced at $60 dollars has infected the new Civ entry. Likewise, 2K has decided to also emulate the practice of DLCs with barely any content for $5, only containing a single civilization. For those who didn't want to pay almost one hundred dollars on a single game, the DLC amounts to another half a game at the time of this review, and more is to come. While it sounds like a good idea to put each civ in it's own DLC (only buy the one you want, right?), all it does is make people want to purchase NONE of the DLCs, as 6 dollars for what's equivlant to a new face, a single unit, maybe one building, and a special ability for that face doesn't sound particuarlly interesting, especially since you will probably play that civ once (maybe twice if you're an acheivement hunter).
I dunno, I don't like the direction where Civ 6 and Beyond Earth is painting the Civilization series, but I'm keeping hope for now. By all means by the game if it looks interesting, and if you enjoy it, I'm glad you got more fun out of it than I did. It isn't even bad, it just isn't great, which is what I had come to expect from the Civilization series.

I guess if I had to sum up Alan Wake, I would call it Stephen King the game.  Anybody who is a fan of horror movies/novels should play this game, you will appreciate it and that's not even mentioning the twilight zone and other pop culture references.  Basically the game centers around a writer who, as the story progresses realizes he is basically living in one of this stories.... or is he?  The line between what is real and what is not is often blurred, and you will find pages from your story that will hint at things to come.  The story is the really great thing about the game, but the gameplay is also interesting.  The fighting is based on a whole light vs darkness type thing in which you have to shine light on enemies to make them vulnerable to gun fire.  There are also some "chase" parts where you will have no weapon and are forced to just run.  The music adds to the tension as well, always making you weary of exploring around the next corner.  Overall a great game worth the money.

This has been my go-to game for months now!  There's an incredible amount of variety in the weapons and abilities that you can find, and they get crazier as you go on!  Revolver.  Sledgehammer.  Laser rifle.  Minigun.  Energy sword.  Auto grenade shotgun.  Lightning cannon.  Each character is also completely unique, and plays very differently.  One revolves around spawning minions to assist you, while another can dual wield, an yet another can explode the corpses of defeated enemies!  You can become absurdly powerful, but you're still always vulnerable, and it's PERFECT.  If you have played some of the modern action-roguelikes that are so popular today (Binding of Isaac, Crypt of the Necrodancer), you have likely noticed that you become nearly unstoppable after a while.  In Isaac, you get Brimstone, tammy's head, and holy mantle?  You can't die.  This is not the case with Nuclear Throne!  You can launch nukes into crowds of enemies, you can spawn an entire army of allies to protect you, you can use telekinesis to push away projectiles, and yet the slightest misstep leads to a yeti hurling a car at you, putting your rampage to an explosive end.  And that explosion is going to look good, sound good, and feel good, because the visual and audio design is extremely on point.  You can really feel the power in a gun when you're shooting it.  The only reason I can think of to pass up this game is if you're just not into the challenge of it.  As I said, you can die in an instant at any moment.  You'll generally have 8 HP tops, and a standard bullet does 3 damage.  Many things deal more than that.  You do not get invincibility frames upon being hit (I THINK.  If you do, it's like 2 or 3 frames tops).  If that sounds like a dealbreaker to you, I guess this isn't your kind of game.  If that sounds exciting to you, get the game NOW!  I honestly can't recommend it enough.  Have fun!

Edit after full release: I'm still playing this, and it's still glorious fun!  Lots of content and tweaks have been added over the last several months, and I think it lead up to an incredibly solid final product.  If I was told right now that I could only play one game for the rest of my life, I'd probably pick Nuclear Throne.

In its current state I unfortunately have no choice but to give this game a thumbs down. And the ironic thing is that when I first started playing this game in Spring 2017, I was actually very happy with it. I played something like 160 hours, and after some very enjoyable games was ready to attempt the hardest difficulty level. And then out of the blue came the compulsory Summer 2017 patch which introduced so many absurd bugs that I haven't played at all since. AI diplomacy is quite simply broken now. For instance, the AI civs now spam you with proposals which right from the outset they aren't willing to accept. Even worse, the AI now drastically overvalues resources, and is now willing to trade multiple cities for just a single resource. In the course of only a few turns, I managed to gain more than 50 cities from three different AI civilizations, and all it cost me was a few resources and a small amount of gold. These are the worst bugs I've personally experienced, and judging from other reviews there are plenty more besides.
I just can't fathom how Firaxis ever thought it was a good idea to bring the Summer patch out in its current state and ruin an otherwise good game. The aforementioned bugs should have been uncovered after only a few turns of very basic playtesting. Which means that either the developers essentially didn't test the patch at all, or that they knew about the bugs and decided to release the patch anyway. Not only this, but it's been nearly three months and these issues still haven't been acknowledged by them, let alone fixed. Very disappointing from a software house that released other excellent games such as XCOM2, and patched them in a much more professional manner.

In my review of season one I touched on a couple of points that still hold true in season two. The game still has a comic book style for graphics, the game is still very much on rails and the choices you make don’t have any meaning to the rest of the story what so ever, even though the game tries its best to convince you that they do. This was probably my biggest annoyance with season one and it’s disappointing to see that no attempt to improve the story system was made at all. If you don’t make the ‘right’ decisions, the game will simply correct itself and continue with the story the way it was intended. The story does not have multiple paths or multiple endings.
The story we’re given is pretty terrible. Plot twists can be seen coming from a mile away, the dialog is mediocre and where we had a pretty good cast of interesting characters in season one, the characters in season two are mostly dumb and annoying. The group Clementine ends up with makes one stupid decision after another. The few times Clementine gets to respond to these decisions and give an opinion, the only options are mild agreements or disagreements which then, of course, are promptly ignored by absolutely everyone. For me it got to a point where I started going against the group at every opportunity because the offered alternative was simply insane given the circumstances. Unlike season one, where losing a member of the group was often a sad and emotional moment, losing a group member in season two feels more like a relief each time it happens. It means one of the idiots was dead, which hopefully meant less stupid decisions and less group drama that the player can’t do anything about.
Overall you as a player will get invested into the story. You will care for Clementine and you will get frustrated by the group. But that doesn’t take away the fact that the story arcs itself are incredibly boring.
Right off the bat it should be said that yes, the comic book style is expected to be a little cartoony in its animation and Telltale isn’t a very a large studio. One does not expect to see the same level of animation as in certain triple A titles. Despite all that, the animation and scene direction in season two are still pretty bad. The cinematography in particular could have been done much better with minimal effort. There were certain scenes that absolutely had the potential to be very tense and exciting despite the lame characters, bad voice acting and horrible writing. Sadly the cut scenes are put together so badly that any excitement is quickly lost. Whenever something exciting happens it is often immediately followed by a five second pause to show all the characters reacting to it individually (somewhat like an anime), killing off all momentum the scene had going. Things like this are lethal to the overall perception of the story which is pretty horrible as it is.
It’s sad to see The Walking Dead fall victim to the age old sequel trap. Season one was great despite its faults and for season two Tell Tale had plenty of opportunity to get those things right. Instead the game is made into a cheap carbon copy that does very little effort to produce an exciting story or produce interesting characters. In all five episodes there are only one or two tense moments, the ending being one of them. It’s really the only thing season two has going for it.
Despite how bad the season was, I’ll still be buying season three if and when it ever comes out. But because of how boring season two turned out to be I will be getting it during a sale. I can’t justify a €23,- price tag on something that I only occasionally enjoyed over its five episode run.

Alan Wake may be a port from the Xbox 360 release, but it is by no means a bad port. With a good amount of control over graphics options (including FoV), and an easy on-the-fly swap from a controller to the mouse and keyboard, Alan Wake is one of the more notable re-releases on the PC.
With it's eerie writing, Alan Wake provides a strange "WTF is going on" story that tends to suck up hours as you promise yourself to finish the last portion of "the episode" that you are on. This not-really-a-shooter provides for a unique experience all with a strange subliminal message to collect as much coffee as possible.
While there are some minor control issues (as there is not a 1:1 input at the moment since Alan Wake himself does actually take time to turn), it still feels quite nice to play overall. Combine this with the lower introductory price tag of $35 along with "The Signal" and "The Writer" makes this a very valuable addition to your library. It's a great one, reward great ports.

3,100 hours in, I believe it's time to create a fair, interesting review for this game.
When I first bought this game, I did not know what I was doing, I spent most likely 200 hours on the gamemode Jailbreak, and that was just the beginning of my time on Garry's Mod.
As any other kiddo would do, you donate to the server you loved playing on because you want to help it stay alive... only to be banned the next day. Amazing.
Any who, the majority of my time playing this game was in the lovely gamemode called starwarsRP. I've most likely spent 2,000 hour alone in this gamemode, and by far I can say it has changed from what I originally experienced a couple years back.
I was exposed to a small community named NOM, this small star wars server grew on me, and I wanted to stay with it until my downfall, but like all things GMOD related, it eventually shutdown.
I began to freelance around the gamemode community, assisting wherever I could with small bug fixes, development, and management. From experiencing being insulted by 10 year olds for not listening to their "orders," to being praised by server owners for my aid, I still have to say even though I've spent over 3,000 hours on this game it still does not bore me.
The memories I've created playing this game have stuck with me forever. The people I've met, the people I despise, and even the people who were just a blur are all remembered. Being mistakened for Sono all the time, starring in a Zuthar youtube video as the infamous Major Cool, and even just marching with 20 willing troopers in your battalion who listen to all the garbage you spew, these memories are precious to me. Garry's Mod is more than autistic screeching, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ roleplay servers, and mass rdming youtubers, it's about creating memories with people who you enjoy playing with, not taking things too seriously when roleplaying, and just remembering to have a good time on the servers you join.
So, for those who don't already have this game, but want to purchase it, of course I recommend this game, I highly recommend this game. Find a community you can enjoy. Find people who will stay by your side and make everlasting friendships with them. Raid a bank and hold off against 12 cops with your 3 man crew in a DarkRP server. Accidently kill another terrorist as a terrorist in TTT. Yell at your officer in starwarsRP if they're being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The game has the freedom for you to do whatever you want.
+ The Community is amazing, but there is always those people in every game who ruin it. The overwhelming majority of the community heavily outnumber those people though.
+ Limitless amounts of gamemodes, currently the gamemodes are mostly starwarsrp and darkrp, but explore the smaller gamemodes to get a taste of how they are.
+ Become a rockman in DarkRP when a server has a great "Developer."
- Lots of addons to download sometimes
- People are too serious at times, especially staff on roleplay servers.
Just remember, this is a game. Let's all have fun together.
Thank you for taking the time to read this review if you've made it down this far.
TL;DR - This game can honestly make you go crazy, but it's worth every second.

In its current state I unfortunately have no choice but to give this game a thumbs down. And the ironic thing is that when I first started playing this game in Spring 2017, I was actually very happy with it. I played something like 160 hours, and after some very enjoyable games was ready to attempt the hardest difficulty level. And then out of the blue came the compulsory Summer 2017 patch which introduced so many absurd bugs that I haven't played at all since. AI diplomacy is quite simply broken now. For instance, the AI civs now spam you with proposals which right from the outset they aren't willing to accept. Even worse, the AI now drastically overvalues resources, and is now willing to trade multiple cities for just a single resource. In the course of only a few turns, I managed to gain more than 50 cities from three different AI civilizations, and all it cost me was a few resources and a small amount of gold. These are the worst bugs I've personally experienced, and judging from other reviews there are plenty more besides.
I just can't fathom how Firaxis ever thought it was a good idea to bring the Summer patch out in its current state and ruin an otherwise good game. The aforementioned bugs should have been uncovered after only a few turns of very basic playtesting. Which means that either the developers essentially didn't test the patch at all, or that they knew about the bugs and decided to release the patch anyway. Not only this, but it's been nearly three months and these issues still haven't been acknowledged by them, let alone fixed. Very disappointing from a software house that released other excellent games such as XCOM2, and patched them in a much more professional manner.
