Simply the most phenomenal game ever created.
You will fail. You will get frustrated. You will get angry. The learning curve in Kerbal Space Program is astronomical. It took me days of playing before I put my first craft into orbit. A week before I reached the Mun. A month before I mastered rendezvous and docking. Never once, however, was I ever bored. You are, after all, developing your own space program. One small step for man, one giant step for Kerbal kind.
You build, you launch, you fly, and you crash. You conduct SCIENCE and develop new rocket parts to build, and fly, and crash. And, eventually, in one moment, you sit back and take in the overwhelmingly divine view of your space station that took 30 launches and countless hours to create as the Sun comes across the horizon of Kerban and illuminates your incredible feat of engineering. It is then that you take in the full breadth of space exploration in the real world, and in one massive, clarifying moment, you applaud the scientists, astronauts, and engineers for their breath taking accomplishments in exploring our own solar system.
If you find yourself on the academic path to the space industry, you quickly realize how many parallels you can draw between Kerbal Space Program gameplay and the real world. Suddenly, you are more qualified than others around you to answer fundamental questions about space flight. Even more so than your colleagues that are studying the topic.
Kerbal Space Program is more than just a video game. It teaches you. I have never before, and probably never again will, encounter a video game that will help develop my skillset as an engineer. The intuition for space travel that this game has given me is unparalleled, and is more than any classroom can teach.
If you are in any college and have any intent on working in the space industry in the future, buy this game. Now.
If you are at all interested in space, buy this game. Now.

Nuclear Throne is simply put, the greatest rogue-lite I've ever played. Despite investing more time into The Binding of Isaac and finding Rogue Legacy to be phenomenal, Nuclear Throne has impressed me more than any other. It has a colorful, charismatic art style that's gorgeous. A badass soundtrack with a fantastic mix of kick♥♥♥♥♥action pieces and haunting, desperate melodies. The sound effects are top-notch and have a satisfying crunch to them. The gameplay is brutally difficult and unforgiving. It has an ultra-addictive nature due to the quick rounds (you'll die within 10 minutes a lot) and also thanks to a multitude of characters, weapons, and upgrades that give each run a unique vibe. Moreover, the game is very cathartic thanks to the sound effects and punch of the weapons. All of these aspects put together creates a brilliant experience that is more satisfying than almost any other game out there. If you're looking for a good rogue-lite, you can't go wrong here. Just be ready to die A LOT.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 continues the story of Clementine from Season 1, who is forced to grow up in harsh world filled with man-eating zombies and other desperate humans trying to survive.
I'll start off by saying that TWD: Season 2 is a much darker and grittier tale than Season 1, with things moving much faster and the world looking more grim than ever. Even though the story told in Season 1 was sad, it never really resonated with me fully. Season 2 does.
You will see a few familiar faces from Season 1 and one of which is a sight for sore eyes. One of the scenes with Clementine and a returning character from the first season made me so gutted that tears streaked down my cheeks. It was a really heartbreaking moment. The story of this game is one of the best I've witnessed in a video game.
Graphically, the game remains unchanged from the previous entry with comic-book styled graphics which capture the facial expressions and detail of the characters excellently. A few tweaks here and there were made with the UI to make it easier to recognise who's talking, with a different colour for each character's subtitles.
In the sound department, the game developers have done a superb job. The voice acting is spot-on, with many characters giving off believable and emotional performances. The soundtrack is similarly great, it is subtle yet captures the grim and hopeless ambiance to near perfection.
Gameplay is the standard point and click of many other Telltale Games. It mainly involves the player moving around to inspect the environment, talk to different characters or on occasion initiate a quick-time event (QTE) whereby the player must quickly mash a button or flick the left analog stick in a particular direction. I feel the QTEs add a good dimension to the game, capturing the intense and fast-paced nature of the story really well.
In summary, The Walking Dead: Season 2 is one of the best point-and-click adventure games I've ever played with a story that takes you on a wild emotional rollercoaster and nearly never lets you go.

Playing as 11 year old Clementine makes gives you a different perspective on the post-apocalypse. Clem is not the innocent child she is in season 1. Now she is a survivor. This is a good thing, a she can now handle herself quite well, but it's also heartbreaking as she is forced to do things that no girl should ever have to do. While I liked Clen in season 1, I loved her in season 2. She has now solidified herself as one of my favorite video game characters of all time.
The gameplay is similar to the previous season but with a cleaner interface. There is noticeably less interactivity and less scene exploration which can sometimes make you feel a bit useless during long scenes where Clem walks everywhere herself. The game also makes it seem like the decisions you make are having a more significant effect than they really are. This was also a problem in season 1 where your decisions always lead to the same outcome anyway. I can forgive this problem because the story and characters are so good. I wanted to keep playing after I'd finished an episode and I was so upset when it was all over.
This season came with so many shocking moments, tearful scenes, and unwinnable decision-making moments that stuck in my mind long after I played. If I had to compare both seasons, I would say I prefer season 2 purely for Clementine's character. You may not be playing as Lee anymore, but you will still feel insanely protective of her and want to make sure she comes out of situations unharmed.
People who finished season 1 should get season 2 without a doubt. Unless you're bitten.

I decided to write this review after all the negative reviews and comments I read.

I really do not understand why. Most of them seems to originated from old Civ5 players that compare Civ6 Vanilla with a Civ5 that has been retrofitted 2 times with 2 massive expansion packs. Well this is not fair, if you want to compare Civ 6 with something you will compare it with the plain Civ5 - thus with a game without religion, great works  of art and a silly unit upgrade system with which you end up with lots of melee units that had 2 or 3 (useless for them) ranged unit  promotions .
But even if you decide to compare it with the complete civ5  the game have all the elements and less flaws of a fully developed Cv5. It has religion, great works of art and also have interesting new concepts that vastly improve the game. Concepts such as districts (districts with their adjutancy bonuses bring a whole new way of city planning), consumable workers (no more Idle worker at the end of the game), an improved Great people system taken from the founding fathers of colonization, (I still remember myself laughing with Picasso appearance in ancient era in Civ5), the ability to create armies and armadas (a lost civ4 concept) and more. To be honest the only new concept that I do not like is the way roads created in the game.
So even if  you decide to compare the Civ6 vanilla with the Civ5 including both its expansion packs, thus compare a game that has 1 year of development with a game that has 6, the verdict still goes to CIV 6.
Sure there are bugs (all games have them) sure the AI is silly (It was more silly in Civ5 when it first released) but all those can be corrected  in the future .So  If you see things with a clear mind Civilization 6 starts from a better position and with a greater potential  from all its predecessors. It is more complete and It has lots of new  elements that bring a fresh approach to the series. Some people just wanted a Civ5 with new graphics. Well thank god Firaxis did not listen to them.

Civilization VI is the first Civ game I have played, and so far I am not disapointed. Don't get me wrong, this game has plenty of faults especially in multiplayer, but I still enjoyed it!
- What I like about the game -
The gameplay it fun and addictive, and is fun to play with friends, after the previous update, trading with the AI is now possible! The different leaders have fun and unique abilites, some of which are better than others, but they're equally fun to play. (Personaly, I prefer Catherine de' Medici and Montezuma).
Pros:
Unique leaders and abilities
Multiplayer, w/ teams (optional)
Fun and addictive gameplay
Strategy game
But, as in many games there are always "cons", and there aren't a few here:
Cons:
Multiplayer bugs
Singelplayer bugs
Bad and "simple to beat" AI
Boring map generation
Payed DLC leaders
- Things I don't like about this game -
There are many, and I mean many bugs in CIv VI. Everything from trading bugs, to annoying sound loops. Trading in Civ multiplayer, is the biggest problem. When you propose a deal, for example; 1 iron for 4 gold per turn, the receiver will only see the deal as; 1 iron per turn for nothing. Meaning the receiver will get it for free, and you sit there with -1 iron and 0+ gold.
Sound loop are also very annoying. Not a big problem, but something that should be fixed. The AI is bad and too simple to fool, and all the maps feel the same.
Conclusion:
If I were to buy this game again, I would wait until some of these game-breaking bugs had been fixed.

The Walking Dead Season 2 went further into what I would call it, the "Crying Simulator". Season 1 was already exceptionally good and with Season 2, the hard choices kept coming and harsh decisions came afterwards.
As of now, I would say TWD: S2 is the best of all Telltale games; the epitome I have played in their pedigree.
Without spoiling anything, I can only say that this Season picks up directly where it left us from Season 1 and now you take control of Clementine. You'll see that being a small child doesn't have only negative aspects but many good ones as well.
+Strong protagonist.
+Incredible gritty story.
+Witnessing Clementine become a real survivor.
+Every "important" decisions taken from the start to the end matters.
+Strong voice acting.
+Fantastic credits songs played at every episodes ending.
+Michael Madsen as Carver character! Just love that actor!
-At times, you feel the illusion of choice by making a decision, or lack thereoff of other possible decisions.
-Pacing felt weird from Episode 4 till the finale.
-Cliffhanger finale.
While the main story is vague and mostly secondary in this Season, the main focus and appeal are between the characters interaction. Decisions matter and when you least expect it, a decision could have a badder impact than another. I loved this game from start to finish even if it seemed to lack the proper pacing around Episode 4 till the Finale but if you're a fan of TWD in general, you will just love this game anyway!
If you're a fan of The Walking Dead, you OUGHT it to yourself to get this game and play it ASAP. Love great storied point&click interactive games? Then startup TWD: Season 1 and play this Season 2 right after!

Recently the reviews being posted regarding this game have been quite strongly negative. I am inclined to disagree with a lot of whats been said and disagree that this game should be given a poor review.
Me and friends after playing civilization 5 to death using different multiplayer settings and exhausting the workshop were very pessimistic in trying out this latest installment due to all the negativity that was surrounding the game. After having purchased the game recently in a sale we thought to give it a shot and try out the multiplayer too which was said to be bug riddled.
Before we had the chance to start a multiplayer game, i thought i would start a game myself and get used to the new way the game is played. I picked the English and played on a true start location Earth map. Needless to say later on in the game i regretted this and with France also being chosen there was not much room to manouever. However my overall goal halfway through the game was a cultural victory, and well i wont this ridiciously easy. I was not shocked due to the difficulty i had placed the game at, but i was suprised at how much i had enjoyed actually winnning through culture. Previous cultural victories on the previous civ game, didnt feel rewarding or great when pulled off. However winning through actual tourism, i thought was satisfying.
Moving onto looking at all the victory types, i think the science victory has been worked substantially better than in any other previous civ game. Having to create a district (yes i will come to this later) to create the componenets for a space victory, having a city work on specific edicts to pass to progress in space exploration, just made the game feeling a bit more tactical and involving. Domination is the same as it always has been, and i maintain the bets way to play a multiplayer civ game. Score victory i just ignore as i think this is one that should be removed as it is meaningless. Finally coming to the Religious victory, this has been improved greatly, and everything to do with religion has had its improvements making it something actually useful and worthwhile rather than something i ignored because it felt like a bit of a gimmick in the previous civ game.
The new way to create and build up your civilzations cities is through districts. This way creates new challenges in running your civilization. Early on in the game you have to decide what is more important to you as you are only allowed to build some many districts depending on population. This adds a whole new element to the challenging strategy, especially when played against friends. For example a friend of mine is the English Empire with a stupidly large navy. This is countered however by a few of us building airports and aerodromes to house aircraft close to the coast and defend from sea attacks. Diplomacy could use a look at, but that isnt the be all and end all of the game, and to anyone who thinks they can just take everything for essentially nothing are wrong or havent played multiple games to see this isnt the case. The new way to build wonders is interesting and i for one love it. Requiring a stone resource in your empire and close by to build stonehenge is intuitive and also would be neccesary at the stage of the civilizations development.
The highest difficulty we have currently played on is having one civilization on Emperor, and while it starts off difficult it becomes mildly easier and frankly we were lucky it was the Russians who were the highest difficulty because they seemed to lack the capacity to build anything other than knights. A staple it seems onany civ game from them...
To the dlc point, while i agree the dlc for civ 6 is comparably poor and pricey to civ 5, dlc that create massive changes to the games core mechanic take time to produce. Funnily enough i dont buy a game expecting amazing dlc to be added to pay for later. Its always a nice bonus, but a game like this in its base form should provide more than enough entertainement.
The game takes a big step in adapting the core formula around building the cities, and creating armies where you can put multiple units together to create a stronger force. Changing from familliarity and something that works, to something that changes the way you think about the game is not always easy and i do think there is room for improvement in some aspects, such as maps avaliable, game settings and some of the victory types. I do believe however this is a good addition to the series and will not be going back to play the last generation fo the game. The best way for a game like this that relies on gamers input and feedback, is to suport and that is what i shall be doing and hope you will too!

A punishing roguelike shooter with a surprising amount of nuanced gameplay. You play as one of several mutants in a post-apocalyptic setting. Your goal is to fight through throngs of enemies until you reach the Nuclear Throne. Along the way, you'll pick up different weapons and XP in the form of radiation. Each level you earn, you can choose a new mutation that helps you progress through the game.
It sounds simple enough, and the basic jist of gameplay is. If you shoot things and don't get hit, you win. That's much easier said than done, though, especially as you spawn into levels randomly--something surrounded by enemies. Many times you'll have to go in guns blazing and run for cover. Others you'll weave in and out of bullet sprays while popping off a few well-aimed shots of your own. It's challenging and engaging, even in level 1-1. And that's a good thing, because you'll find yourself back there a lot.
I thought this game would frustrate me, but so far I've had a smile on my face every time I've died. It's such a fun game that the only thing keeping me from hitting R to do a quick restart is other commitments.
If roguelikes are your thing and you're a fan of punishing games, give it a whirl. Even though it's EA, it's extremely polished thus far and the develop updates it frequently.

Mere words cannot express how much I love this game. This story, these characters, everything draws you in and immerses you into a dangerous world where you truly feel that all hope is lost. Some parts will make you laugh, or simply crack a smile, while others will send tears running down your eyes as you witness the death of yet another beloved character...yet another comrade taken by things far worst then zombies. If your a fan of season one then you should need no convincing! Season two is just as good or I dare say even better then the first, and this is coming from someone who is only on episode 2 of the second season, and already its been an emotional roller coaster. If your a fan of the show then I will just be blunt with you, in my honest opinion, this game is 10x better then the show is or most likely ever will be. It might just be a game, but the characters are just so much more interesting, you feel drawn to them and when one of them is forever silenced not only do you feel sadness, but a burning anger as well.
Your choices mold the story, you decided who to befriend and at times who lives and who dies. The decisions are hard, the consequences even harder, but in the end it all comes down to survival of the fittest, and as you steer young Clementine through this dangerous world and watch her grow into a young women you'll start to look back on your past decisions with regret. The fact that once you make the choices their set in stone is what makes the game so fun, just like in realy life once you make a choice there is no going back.
EDIT: After finally completing the game I must say that the ending was very satisfying indeed, you actually get to decide how it ends unlike the first one where what happens at the end of the game is set in stone. As a man, I'm not afraid to admit that tears were shed towards the end of this game, and the fact that a videogame can make me shed tears at all makes this one of the best games out there in my book.

While not as good as the marvelous Season 1, The Walking Dead Season 2 is still a prime example of great story telling in video games that only continues the amazing streak Telltale is on. Now in the role of Clementine, we see just how much she's changed from Season 1 as a result of the seriousness of her surroundings. As a child, her abilities are greatly underestimated, but she proves to be a strong survivor in a world that requires this or else you die. Clementine has had to abandon her entire childhood and grow up faster than children should have to, making her somewhat of an adult in the body of a child, but still maintaining that childhood innocence of Season 1. Overall, if I had to grade Season 2, I'd give it a 9.2/10. While the writing quality was a tad better and more consistent in Season 1, Season 2 delivers an enjoyable experience and continues the story of Clementine through the apocalypse.

This is one of the reasons Nuclear Throne is such an amazing game, and it's simply because the dev team truely cares for it. The insane gameplay gives no time to rest as you are forced to each level in an infinite loop constantly finding better loot, and harder enemies. The game takes a while to learn, and it will be a good week before you even reach the frozen city, or big dog, but when you do it's the best feeling in the world. Nuclear Throne features a huge roster of characters that have no gimmicks that force you into a certain gamestyle, but rather unique features that you can addapt within your own game style. (Instead of doing more melee damage and less gun damage slo mo) The game never seems to punish you for exploring a new game style and instead seems to encourage that there truely isn't a meta and that you must discover your own. Sadly the free copy of the game I recieved was given to someone who has ill taste for these sorts of games but even with that he still had a hell of a lot of fun. Overall it's a game that even with it's bugs, is so much fun it's easy to ignore. Easy 10 outta 10

Recently the reviews being posted regarding this game have been quite strongly negative. I am inclined to disagree with a lot of whats been said and disagree that this game should be given a poor review.
Me and friends after playing civilization 5 to death using different multiplayer settings and exhausting the workshop were very pessimistic in trying out this latest installment due to all the negativity that was surrounding the game. After having purchased the game recently in a sale we thought to give it a shot and try out the multiplayer too which was said to be bug riddled.
Before we had the chance to start a multiplayer game, i thought i would start a game myself and get used to the new way the game is played. I picked the English and played on a true start location Earth map. Needless to say later on in the game i regretted this and with France also being chosen there was not much room to manouever. However my overall goal halfway through the game was a cultural victory, and well i wont this ridiciously easy. I was not shocked due to the difficulty i had placed the game at, but i was suprised at how much i had enjoyed actually winnning through culture. Previous cultural victories on the previous civ game, didnt feel rewarding or great when pulled off. However winning through actual tourism, i thought was satisfying.
Moving onto looking at all the victory types, i think the science victory has been worked substantially better than in any other previous civ game. Having to create a district (yes i will come to this later) to create the componenets for a space victory, having a city work on specific edicts to pass to progress in space exploration, just made the game feeling a bit more tactical and involving. Domination is the same as it always has been, and i maintain the bets way to play a multiplayer civ game. Score victory i just ignore as i think this is one that should be removed as it is meaningless. Finally coming to the Religious victory, this has been improved greatly, and everything to do with religion has had its improvements making it something actually useful and worthwhile rather than something i ignored because it felt like a bit of a gimmick in the previous civ game.
The new way to create and build up your civilzations cities is through districts. This way creates new challenges in running your civilization. Early on in the game you have to decide what is more important to you as you are only allowed to build some many districts depending on population. This adds a whole new element to the challenging strategy, especially when played against friends. For example a friend of mine is the English Empire with a stupidly large navy. This is countered however by a few of us building airports and aerodromes to house aircraft close to the coast and defend from sea attacks. Diplomacy could use a look at, but that isnt the be all and end all of the game, and to anyone who thinks they can just take everything for essentially nothing are wrong or havent played multiple games to see this isnt the case. The new way to build wonders is interesting and i for one love it. Requiring a stone resource in your empire and close by to build stonehenge is intuitive and also would be neccesary at the stage of the civilizations development.
The highest difficulty we have currently played on is having one civilization on Emperor, and while it starts off difficult it becomes mildly easier and frankly we were lucky it was the Russians who were the highest difficulty because they seemed to lack the capacity to build anything other than knights. A staple it seems onany civ game from them...
To the dlc point, while i agree the dlc for civ 6 is comparably poor and pricey to civ 5, dlc that create massive changes to the games core mechanic take time to produce. Funnily enough i dont buy a game expecting amazing dlc to be added to pay for later. Its always a nice bonus, but a game like this in its base form should provide more than enough entertainement.
The game takes a big step in adapting the core formula around building the cities, and creating armies where you can put multiple units together to create a stronger force. Changing from familliarity and something that works, to something that changes the way you think about the game is not always easy and i do think there is room for improvement in some aspects, such as maps avaliable, game settings and some of the victory types. I do believe however this is a good addition to the series and will not be going back to play the last generation fo the game. The best way for a game like this that relies on gamers input and feedback, is to suport and that is what i shall be doing and hope you will too!

Another masterpiece by Telltale.
Like the first season of Walking Dead, the game pulls no punches when it comes to delivering quality story-telling, and invoking all sorts of emotions from players.
The game captures the desperate feeling of the post-apocalyptic zombie world perfectly, where morality is often tested and people do not always have the luxury of doing the right thing.
The game is still played in a point-and-click manner, and you have a time limit to make a decision, creating a sense of urgency and adding to the story.
Games of this nature are often quality over quantity, where a full playthrough only takes about 9 hours. But the 9 hours are definitely worth the price of admission. If the game is too short for your liking, you could always wait till a sale to buy it.
A must-buy for story lovers.

**Spoiler free and unbiased review**
Life is strange is truly one gem of a videogame in the truest sense of the word. The game is in essence a cinematic experience and its riveting shady plot takes you for an emotional rollercoaster ride with its mindblowing plot twists, nerve racking moments of disbelief and devastating consequences. It is one of those rare games that gets you hooked right off the bat and makes you feel more important and emotionally attached as the story progresses. The game bestows on you a great power and as the famous saying goes "With great power comes great responsibility", that is justified well and truly throughout the game's entirety because the choices that you make in game alters the course of events in past, present and future. So being wise and judicious while making your decisions is imperative to say the least. The gameplay is pretty much linear yet not banal. The pacing of the story is quite impressive as well. The subtle and somewhat elusive elements directly related to the story is hard to decipher or comprehend at first but eventually it gets to you as the game gradually progresses towards the climax. The ambient music and soundtrack of the game coupled with impeccable voice acting are like the icing on an already well baked cake. Makes the overall experience so much better. Despite having some negligible and infinitesimal flaws, it didn't really detract from the experience even remotely. All in all, in a world full of flashy AAA titles not living upto the billing these days mostly, Life is strange has hit the sweet spot that leaves an indelible mark and has set a benchmark of its own. Highly recommended!

Wow, what can I say about Nuclear Throne? Let me give you my gaming context for this review, I am an adult gamer, I have been gaming since I was in first grade and my parents bought me an NES. I've played through the subsequent console generations and of course I have always been a PC gamer.
So it is within that context that I saw Nuclear Throne easily makes my top 20 games of all time list. This game is still in early access yet has a great amount of depth, polish, and "feel".
It is a top down shooter, you can play it as a twn stick though mouse and keyboard is recommended. You choose from among several class all with unique abilities that will inform your play style. As befits a rogue-lite it has random generation, punishing difficulty, and leveling with each level allowing you to choose from among a small pool of mutations.
This game has sucked me in, I am fast approaching 300 hours in it. Even as you die you will be hitting R to restart and get right back into the action. Eventually you will learn how to play well and even defeat the throne and start looping. If you like old school games, if you like fast paced games, if you like addictive games designed by people who really know what moment to moment gameplay should feel like, then buy this game. This is an instant classic.

What if The Longest Journey and the Telltale's Walking Dead games had a child that was raised by Square Enix? This short game (2 hours for the first episode) is 10% cringe, 30% interactive fiction, 30% old-school adventure gaming, 10% girl power - and 100% awesome and free.
The innovative and unique design of the game feels like a breath of fresh air in a genre that has been struggling to get on with the times. It's the perfect mix of casual and hardcore gaming, in the sense that only a real gamer will find himself immersed enough in the story. And let's be honest here: no one is hardcore enough to appreciate ye olde puzzles and game logic from the classic adventure titles from Sierra or Lucas Arts, so the compromise is definitely a step in the right direction.
Now for the negative points. As I've said, there's a definite cringe factor as you play a teenage girl who is heavy on her "wowzers" and "oh my gods", which has obviously been written by an adult man. It's not as bad as it sounds though, as you can rely on that Square Enix sensibility where even men with spiked hair and oversized swords can be endearing and passionate. The game also tries to be set in 2015 but is stuck halfway in the 90s some of the time, which makes it odd.
The greatest shame here is that although the main mechanic of the game is very interesting, it is seriously underutilized when it comes to puzzles, which are the bread and butter of adventure games. You'll be using it to do the most menial tasks ever, as if the designer came up with this amazing idea but wasn't quite ready to put it into action just yet. I hope this is solved on the following episodes.
Anyway, none of this will detract from the gameplay if you're not one to be held back by details. The story is pretty linear but it makes up for it with great exploration and plenty of contextual voice acting, plus much more meaningful decisions than you'll see even on big RPG titles that claim to have them.
EDIT I have written at some length here about how Life is Strange managed to fix all flaws inherent to point-and-click adventure game design.since they first came out in the late 80s and early 90s

Before I begin my review, I have to clarify that I've never read the comic books nor seen the tv show The Walking Dead.
The strongest point of this title is its story. Even though it might not be as good as Season 1, the story of The Walking Dead: Season 2 still manages to capture your curiosity. I was completely absorbed by Clementine's adventures and always wanted to see what was going to happend next. You can see that the writers tried their best to make a story that was coherent with Season 1. If you can invest a little bit of yourself into the story you might enjoy it a lot.
Like most Telltale games, you have to make choices during the game. However, I felt like the repercussions of your choices were less important in this season.
The core game in itself isn't revolutionary. There are some Quick Time Events, but they're not annoying. There's very little of actual gameplay. It's basically the same thing as Season 1. It's one of those "cinematic experience" game and it's really good at it.
In the end, The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a very interesting game. I recommend that you play this game along with Season 1 and make your own opinion about this game.

Civ 5, and even Beyond Earth, I can still manage to play.  And of course Civ 4, because honestly, who doesn't enjoy the soothing intonations of the late, lamented, Leonard Nimoy?
I have been waiting for some kind of gameplay overhaul that would make Civ 6 anything but a feckless slogfest at every turn - simply put, the things that have historically made Civ fun and make you want to take one more turn are lacking.
More comprehensive critiques have been made, but echoing them suffices.  There is no rhyme or reason to the AI's approach on diplomacy or trade.  The interruptions from AI leaders concerning their hidden agendas are needless and shouldn't even be a factor when the tech level at which they'd be relevant has yet to be reached.  Why, for example, is Gandhi consistently berating me in 2500 BC for lacking a nuclear arsenal?  Why is Harald Hardrada damning me for being devoid of a fleet on a land-locked map?
There is no equilibrium in the religion game.   You are free to found your own religion, of course, but you will without doubt be swarmed by foreign missionaries with no recourse to dissuade them save war.  As with diplomacy and trade, the options available to the AI to penalize you on this front are vast and weighed heavily in their favor, whereas any expectation the player has of being able to reciprocate in kind will instead yield the somber reality that your only options are open hostilities, or simply rolling over and accepting whatever the AI decides to do to you once they have a religion of their own.
On the subject of warfare, it is painfully easy to decimate an enemy AI regardless of circumstance - circumstance that will be presented, in spades, to a player on account of the AI's proclivity to punish any unfavorable action with a military response.  And yet, no opposing Civ has the capacity to mount a convincing assault by land or sea, and it only takes a handful of ranged and melee units to unilaterally annihilate an opponent.
City planning and tile improvement is an utter joke.  Any choices you may have had in your build order in previous series titles evaporate here, as there are ideal city locations and preferential build orders that you inevitably find yourself railroaded into (despite the lack of actual ♥♥♥♥ing railroads in the game!) regardless of starting variables.  You will build certain districts, and only those districts and associated buildings, in the same order, every time.  You will only build certain Wonders, and only those Wonders, every game, every time. The other terrible thing about this is that game turns become painfully, unbearably slow due to choices governing the movement of units.  Whereas in the past military and civil units could at least move over a river or into hilly terrain so long as they had a point of movement remaining, all units must now pay their full movement cost to do so, or otherwise be prohibited from taking that action.  This only accomplishes two things: padding out turn duration and making the starting game unnecessarily slow, and cutting off what have otherwise been viable strategic options in previous games.
The biggest nail in the coffin, however, is the nickel-and-dime DLC being released piecemeal for this game.  Rather than civilizations arriving in expansion packs balanced and adjusted around other civilizations from the initial release and their associated expansion, new Civs now feature, generally, a single gimmick that is either overpowered or underpowered in comparison to existing Civs, and does nothing to help the persistent gameplay problems that already exist.  Simply because a number of high-profile developers have consigned themselves to this utter garbage approach in content design and release does not mean that every single game needs to follow suit, and is only helping contribute to broader malaise and ambivalence towards titles that, while looking quite pretty on the surface, expect players to pay out the nose for what is ultimately a pothole of an experience, filled in with loose gravel after the fact.  If you find yourself fondly reminicisng about the Video Game Crash of 1983 either from first-hand experience or academic interest, take heart, you may not have to reminisce for much longer - season passes, single-item DLC, and the like are keeping us on track for a repeat.
My advice? Wait for a sale.  Wait a few years when the whole shrink-wrapped♥♥♥♥♥♥heap is on sale for a few bucks, because none of the individual DLC, nor the base product, are worth the asking price in comparison to previous Civ titles.

I really liked the game. TL;DR: Pro: fun, well scripted and interesting story! Con: Drags on slightly too long.
I collected about 80-90% of all collectibles and played it through on normal difficulty. Final endtime is around 13h. I died roughly 8 times, give or take.
Story and execution is good. I really liked the episodic format, giving you an few clear points where you can take a break and let go of the game. The episode start recap is welcome as well. However, they did not provide a quit button and when i tried quitting at the "end of episode" screen, the game hadn't saved. Which was VERY bad. Why have an end of the episode, if you cant quit the game when it ends?
Environments are beautiful. Lightning is good, most characters are acceptable but the lipsyncing is horrible, especially on Alice. Alan have quite good animations and he feels quite believable in his actions.
Its quite intense and somewhat scary in the beginning, with excellent scripting and events happening. But after a while you get used to it and when youre on the final stretch, you kind of just want it to be short so it can be intensive and end. But it drags on just slighty too long.
The game is split into 6 episodes, each are designed to take around 2 hours to play, if you explore it will take longer, if you go along the path, it will take less time. Last episode is slightly shorter, but due to heavy driving sections and exploration it can be quite boring.
All in all I enjoyed it quite a lot and might try and do a 100% run on nightmare to do some achievement whoring. But for me, 13 hours or more for a non-RPG game is quite a lot, nightmare with collectables will probably take longer due to deaths.

It's either over powered or if you’re lucky it works the way you would expect it. This seems like a rushed production. It's a disappointing release and I would avoid this game for the time being because they need to do a lot of patching. The one good thing is that they made a lot of changes to the game mechanics from previous releases for city building. There are districts now that provide a specific function like improving industry, culture, or science. They are very useful for your city and require you to use a plot of land within the city limit to construct one. Building in the game is more fun and requires much more planning than in previous releases. Military fighting has improved from the previous civ5 release, but still similar in many ways. Religion is still annoying to deal with, although, there is a MOD that prevents religions from spreading as long as you don’t have open borders with a civ. One would assume that is how it should be by default in civilization since all other units can’t access your territory, but for some reason they decided to make it annoying like in previous releases. Diplomacy is still wacky and doesn’t make a lot of sense with the AI. If you already bought it than enjoy it, but if your on the fense I would wait until they release more patches or the price goes down. It wasn't worth the $60.

Minor quips aside (the vehicle handling leaves a bit to be desired), this is a great game, and provided you have the hardware to back it up, you should be quite satisfied with it by the end of its 10-hour story.

This is a truly unique game.
This is a truly infuriating game.
There's nothing I can say bad about this game because
1: I'd call it about 90% stable (compared to a bethesda game that's about 70%). This alone wouldn't matter. Just cuz the game loads and doesn't crash while you play it doesn't mean it's not bad. But for how much time the average Kerbal will play this game, it's a huge factor (Also, the game takes about 10 minutes to load if you have anywhere near 100 mods installed, like me.)
2: It's unique. There is no game like this. ANywhere. It simulates a solar system (simplified, of course, because truly doing this in real time is beyond any home computer.) so that you can build, fly and crash rockets, planes, boats and... anything. The limitations are almost nonexistent. Some youtubes build completely stock (No mods) helicopters even though there are no parts designed to build a helicopter.
3: You HAVE to think. You can slap rockets together and hope for the best and plenty of people have mastered this game from doing that. But if you don't learn and try, this game will lose appeal fast. If you manage to get over the steep learning curve, though, you'll never get bored of this game. Minecraft let you let your artistry go wild. This game will refine it into a diamond as you struggle to meld Form and Function into spacecraft that can literally go beyond the Moon. I can't be serious enough in saying that this is a truly fascinating and amazing game.
4: Mod support. There are mods that give you exactly the type of experience you're looking for. The stock game is wonderful and enough for most people to sink their teeth into for a good minute. If you want more, there are mods that enhance and maintain a stock-a-like experience and mods that add completely new systems.
Or bananas. Hell, there's a mod that lets you make a Hamburger that you can launch into space. Why? I dunno.
Anyways, this game is worth playing for anybody. It's unique, offers limitless challenge and, if you're patient, it will actually teach you about aerospace. It won't make you an astronaut, but if you show up to space camp after a few hundred hours of this game you'll definitely have some knowledge to show off.

An interesting simulation with bad controls, and a physics engine that's been upgraded to "mostly okay."
The game is fairly enjoyable with simple ideas, but gets buggy way before you get to all of the most interesting parts.
Sadly, far more time is spent in the game fighting with (or looking up solutions to) the design system and bad controls than actually enjoying the game. Figure out what you want to do, then figure out why the game won't let it work, spend a few hours looking up and watching videos trying to figure out what the game wants you to do to achieve your goal, try and fail, watch videos and look on the forums to find out what they changed and the new solution, then actually maybe accomplish something. Rinse and repeat.
Trying to build a rocket (or worse - a plane)? Hope the game doesn't decide you want to install parts upside down or sideways. Once it's built, even using the in-game symetry system, the game might decide one side is heavier or less aerodynamic. Nothing will show up as being unbalanced, but you'll spin out of control until you take it all apart and build it the exact same way again. Any wheeled vehicle (rovers or rocket cars) will have a 100% chance of being unbalanced and making unplanned turns, assuming they don't explode first.
The collision detection will cause things to explode when they shouldn't, especially anything on or near the ground.
Once you manage to make orbit, you're expected to use waypoints you set by hand experimentally (they show you where you will end up if you've got enough fuel), in real time while flying. There is a way to remove waypoints when you've flown past where you wanted to be or the angle got screwed up, and it works almost half of the time if you keep clicking. I say expected to, because there are nearly-mandatory mods to automate the process. Any attempts to use the jetpack will result in only frustration.

First, a little background on myself, so you know where I’m coming from. I had seen a few videos of Nuclear Throne gameplay, and it looked really good. I had planned on purchasing the game when it officially gets released. I didn’t watch any LP’s or streamers aside from the initial 30ish minutes of gameplay that made the game catch my attention last year, and I didn’t want to purchase Early Access to the game, because I think the early access process is more harmful to consumers as a whole in the long run. Despite that, I did manage to acquire one of the free copies of the game that were gifted at the start of 2015, and proceeded to play, as of this writing, 12 hours of it, which is what this feedback is based on. I wasn’t planning on leaving feedback, but after seeing how the devs seem to really value feedback, I decided to man up and finally say what’s on my mind.
(Keep in mind this is mostly criticism. I’ll save my praise for the game for when it is officially released.)
Now, onto the game itself. My very first issue is what must hit each and every player, is the 4:3 perspective. I’ve read enough to see that JW has compromised in this, as he envisioned a 1:1 play-space, and I seem to recall Rami being more towards the full-screen side of the issue. I understand that the argument is that you want don’t want players to favor a left-right exploration tactic.
I’m just one man, but I call bullsh-, because I explore 100% of each level, not favoring one axis of exploration for another. Furthermore, this can be balanced if world generation is wider than it is tall. The fact is we all have wide-screen monitors. This game is being made for monitors and TV’s, not for an arcade box. Not only is it a waste of screen-space that we’ve been conditioned into needing filling, but go look in the mirror ... unless you suffer from birth-defects or some horrific accident, your eyes are next to each other and your field of view is wider than it is tall … it feels better to watch and play something that matches your natural FOV, which is why reasonable people film things in what is called “landscape mode” and anyone filming in portrait orientation would be drawn and quartered.
My second issue - framerate. I’m an old Binding of Isaac addict. Since Rebirth came out I’ve been losing countless hours of my life playing that (at 60fps), but every once in a while I boot up original BOI, and wow … the framerate on that game is horrifically bad to the point of it actually making the game unnecessarily more difficult and I just can’t play it anymore. This is pretty much how I feel about Nuclear Throne. Having it locked down to a 30fps cap is a big handicap that actually prevents me from playing the game. It feels like the game is cheating by only showing me half the frames I’m used to seeing and reacting to in almost every other PC game ever. Unless (until?) this gets fixed I can’t see myself playing the game very much at all. Please please PLEASE make this game run at 60fps.
Item descriptions. I understand the temptation to follow in the footsteps of the Binding of Isaac and others like it by giving vague descriptions of power-ups and items. Most of the stuff in Nuclear Throne is clearly labeled or described, which makes it all the more frustrating when things are really poorly explained. I still don’t know what “Brrrrapp” is supposed to mean in context of its power-up. And do alternate skins to characters or weapons affect the gameplay? What level am I on? How many levels are there? Etc. Overall, I’d like to see a clear and consistent philosophy regarding telling plays what the heck stuff is.
The options menu, I understand, is non-functional. At the very least if gamepad is enabled, put a line of text on the menu screen telling us that we need to press “g” to reset settings, because I lost A LOT of time thinking I’d never be able to play with mouse and keyboard after experimenting with the heinousness that is playing NT with a gamepad, until I scoured the Steam forums for help.
Level generation. Sometimes you’re dropped into an survivable firefight. That’s unfair and it sucks.
Well, that’s the major stuff. My main issue with the game that will prevent me from playing or recommending it is the screen ratio and frame rate. What if The Longest Journey and the Telltale's Walking Dead games had a child that was raised by Square Enix? This short game (2 hours for the first episode) is 10% cringe, 30% interactive fiction, 30% old-school adventure gaming, 10% girl power - and 100% awesome and free.
The innovative and unique design of the game feels like a breath of fresh air in a genre that has been struggling to get on with the times. It's the perfect mix of casual and hardcore gaming, in the sense that only a real gamer will find himself immersed enough in the story. And let's be honest here: no one is hardcore enough to appreciate ye olde puzzles and game logic from the classic adventure titles from Sierra or Lucas Arts, so the compromise is definitely a step in the right direction.
Now for the negative points. As I've said, there's a definite cringe factor as you play a teenage girl who is heavy on her "wowzers" and "oh my gods", which has obviously been written by an adult man. It's not as bad as it sounds though, as you can rely on that Square Enix sensibility where even men with spiked hair and oversized swords can be endearing and passionate. The game also tries to be set in 2015 but is stuck halfway in the 90s some of the time, which makes it odd.
The greatest shame here is that although the main mechanic of the game is very interesting, it is seriously underutilized when it comes to puzzles, which are the bread and butter of adventure games. You'll be using it to do the most menial tasks ever, as if the designer came up with this amazing idea but wasn't quite ready to put it into action just yet. I hope this is solved on the following episodes.
Anyway, none of this will detract from the gameplay if you're not one to be held back by details. The story is pretty linear but it makes up for it with great exploration and plenty of contextual voice acting, plus much more meaningful decisions than you'll see even on big RPG titles that claim to have them.
EDIT I have written at some length here about how Life is Strange managed to fix all flaws inherent to point-and-click adventure game design.since they first came out in the late 80s and early 90s

**Spoiler free and unbiased review**
Life is strange is truly one gem of a videogame in the truest sense of the word. The game is in essence a cinematic experience and its riveting shady plot takes you for an emotional rollercoaster ride with its mindblowing plot twists, nerve racking moments of disbelief and devastating consequences. It is one of those rare games that gets you hooked right off the bat and makes you feel more important and emotionally attached as the story progresses. The game bestows on you a great power and as the famous saying goes "With great power comes great responsibility", that is justified well and truly throughout the game's entirety because the choices that you make in game alters the course of events in past, present and future. So being wise and judicious while making your decisions is imperative to say the least. The gameplay is pretty much linear yet not banal. The pacing of the story is quite impressive as well. The subtle and somewhat elusive elements directly related to the story is hard to decipher or comprehend at first but eventually it gets to you as the game gradually progresses towards the climax. The ambient music and soundtrack of the game coupled with impeccable voice acting are like the icing on an already well baked cake. Makes the overall experience so much better. Despite having some negligible and infinitesimal flaws, it didn't really detract from the experience even remotely. All in all, in a world full of flashy AAA titles not living upto the billing these days mostly, Life is strange has hit the sweet spot that leaves an indelible mark and has set a benchmark of its own. Highly recommended!

This is a truly unique game.
This is a truly infuriating game.
There's nothing I can say bad about this game because
1: I'd call it about 90% stable (compared to a bethesda game that's about 70%). This alone wouldn't matter. Just cuz the game loads and doesn't crash while you play it doesn't mean it's not bad. But for how much time the average Kerbal will play this game, it's a huge factor (Also, the game takes about 10 minutes to load if you have anywhere near 100 mods installed, like me.)
2: It's unique. There is no game like this. ANywhere. It simulates a solar system (simplified, of course, because truly doing this in real time is beyond any home computer.) so that you can build, fly and crash rockets, planes, boats and... anything. The limitations are almost nonexistent. Some youtubes build completely stock (No mods) helicopters even though there are no parts designed to build a helicopter.
3: You HAVE to think. You can slap rockets together and hope for the best and plenty of people have mastered this game from doing that. But if you don't learn and try, this game will lose appeal fast. If you manage to get over the steep learning curve, though, you'll never get bored of this game. Minecraft let you let your artistry go wild. This game will refine it into a diamond as you struggle to meld Form and Function into spacecraft that can literally go beyond the Moon. I can't be serious enough in saying that this is a truly fascinating and amazing game.
4: Mod support. There are mods that give you exactly the type of experience you're looking for. The stock game is wonderful and enough for most people to sink their teeth into for a good minute. If you want more, there are mods that enhance and maintain a stock-a-like experience and mods that add completely new systems.
Or bananas. Hell, there's a mod that lets you make a Hamburger that you can launch into space. Why? I dunno.
Anyways, this game is worth playing for anybody. It's unique, offers limitless challenge and, if you're patient, it will actually teach you about aerospace. It won't make you an astronaut, but if you show up to space camp after a few hundred hours of this game you'll definitely have some knowledge to show off.

An interesting simulation with bad controls, and a physics engine that's been upgraded to "mostly okay."
The game is fairly enjoyable with simple ideas, but gets buggy way before you get to all of the most interesting parts.
Sadly, far more time is spent in the game fighting with (or looking up solutions to) the design system and bad controls than actually enjoying the game. Figure out what you want to do, then figure out why the game won't let it work, spend a few hours looking up and watching videos trying to figure out what the game wants you to do to achieve your goal, try and fail, watch videos and look on the forums to find out what they changed and the new solution, then actually maybe accomplish something. Rinse and repeat.
Trying to build a rocket (or worse - a plane)? Hope the game doesn't decide you want to install parts upside down or sideways. Once it's built, even using the in-game symetry system, the game might decide one side is heavier or less aerodynamic. Nothing will show up as being unbalanced, but you'll spin out of control until you take it all apart and build it the exact same way again. Any wheeled vehicle (rovers or rocket cars) will have a 100% chance of being unbalanced and making unplanned turns, assuming they don't explode first.
The collision detection will cause things to explode when they shouldn't, especially anything on or near the ground.
Once you manage to make orbit, you're expected to use waypoints you set by hand experimentally (they show you where you will end up if you've got enough fuel), in real time while flying. There is a way to remove waypoints when you've flown past where you wanted to be or the angle got screwed up, and it works almost half of the time if you keep clicking. I say expected to, because there are nearly-mandatory mods to automate the process. Any attempts to use the jetpack will result in only frustration.

Overall a waste of a game.
The difficulty levels aren't fun. Prince level is way too easy. King level is still too easy. Above King (and maybe even sooner), the AI cheats. You'll send your initial scout out to explore, and the first other civ that they encounter will be already rolling with a couple other settlers and warriors. Then, within a few turns, magically all of the other civs get an advanced government style all at the same time. And, since I don't have the same government (apparently, that enrages other civs), they all band against me.
The AI doesn't make smart moves. Just rushes with no tactics. So, even though the AI cheats, and they all unite together against me, I can usually take them out.

What if The Longest Journey and the Telltale's Walking Dead games had a child that was raised by Square Enix? This short game (2 hours for the first episode) is 10% cringe, 30% interactive fiction, 30% old-school adventure gaming, 10% girl power - and 100% awesome and free.
The innovative and unique design of the game feels like a breath of fresh air in a genre that has been struggling to get on with the times. It's the perfect mix of casual and hardcore gaming, in the sense that only a real gamer will find himself immersed enough in the story. And let's be honest here: no one is hardcore enough to appreciate ye olde puzzles and game logic from the classic adventure titles from Sierra or Lucas Arts, so the compromise is definitely a step in the right direction.
Now for the negative points. As I've said, there's a definite cringe factor as you play a teenage girl who is heavy on her "wowzers" and "oh my gods", which has obviously been written by an adult man. It's not as bad as it sounds though, as you can rely on that Square Enix sensibility where even men with spiked hair and oversized swords can be endearing and passionate. The game also tries to be set in 2015 but is stuck halfway in the 90s some of the time, which makes it odd.
The greatest shame here is that although the main mechanic of the game is very interesting, it is seriously underutilized when it comes to puzzles, which are the bread and butter of adventure games. You'll be using it to do the most menial tasks ever, as if the designer came up with this amazing idea but wasn't quite ready to put it into action just yet. I hope this is solved on the following episodes.
Anyway, none of this will detract from the gameplay if you're not one to be held back by details. The story is pretty linear but it makes up for it with great exploration and plenty of contextual voice acting, plus much more meaningful decisions than you'll see even on big RPG titles that claim to have them.
EDIT I have written at some length here about how Life is Strange managed to fix all flaws inherent to point-and-click adventure game design.since they first came out in the late 80s and early 90s

The core concept of Civilization VI is strong, but the execution is weak. I love the idea of creating civilizations and interacting with leaders of another country, but the leaders lack personality and the static images come off as boring. 12 hours in and the dialogue options are stale. If you don't comply with everything they say they will just plain not like you. With the exception of Ghandi, Cleopatra, Montezuma, and a few others, I have no clue who the others are and I don't get a sense of excitement when I discover them in the world.
However, my main gripe with this game is that it's boring. The point is to advance from era to era, but it doesn't feel like you are advancing in this game. The pacing is way too slow and the payoff is thin. I also wish there was less clutter and more clarity in the menus. Being my first entry in the series, the tutorial wasn't great either.
Although it sounds I hate Civilization VI, there is a charm to it. It has the potential to be fun and great, but currently the game is just boring. Most people recommended Civilization V, and seeing the reviews and the gameplay, there's more life and love put in that game.
I've yet to try playing online, but if, like me, you were planning to play with the A.I. (or a story mode--there's no story mode T_T), you'll come out disappointed.

I’ve played way to much civilization, and my first impression of this new civilization game was not a good one. I was comparing it to all the previous games and not just looking at it as a standalone game.
After many hours of play, without the comparison to other versions, I still can't decide If would recommend this game to others.
Some Pros: The districts concept create a fun new way to think about cities and I enjoy being able to see each individual building in the district it belongs to. One note I do have is that in old civ games I felt a more tangible reward from buildings, and in many cases, the most tangible reward in this civilization is the little graphic fun building you get to see. Which is no comparison. I’d rather know the specific benefit of that building and have it be worthwhile then get a cute building graphic and have a vague understanding of what that building is doing. As I’ve played the game I’ve jotted down specific things that I believe may be holding Civ 6 back from being as satisfying as the other games. These random notes are below. I apologize in advance.
I should also note that I have not purchased any expansion other than the Aztecs. This is so because of all the flaws in the game. The usual gameplay overhauling expansion is what I want. Not a map or a new civ with a new wonder.
Unequal distribution of turn worth. 18 turns for spy mission yielding 4000 gold when my civilization makes over 1000 gold per turn.
Spies have 3 promotion levels with benefits, then they claim to have more as they complete missions BUT there is no option to pick another upgrade and the actual level and effectiveness of the spy doesn’t seem to change at all.
Lies about spy promotions
Spy cannot see the cities current production.
The “victory progress” world rankings gives inadequate explanation to why science victory progress bar is slowly increasing in stage 3. Also spies are unable to gather relevant information too
There are very vague building benefits in both the civlopedia and when you hover to discover more information. Ex: what does “faster” fleet and armada training mean? (Also says 125% combat experience to all naval units trained in this city. +2gold from costal tiles, which are specific)
Subjective district project yields. (what does “large amount of gold” vs “gold” mean?! Give me Numbers!)
Unclear tile range modifiers. It says +6 and then under it says +3from mod. Does that total 9 or total 6?
There is no useful filter for trade routes, unable to sort them by most gold or most of anything, just if it contains that thing
Does one uranium create infinite nukes? Same question for all units that require strategic resources.
AI doesn’t understand how to use naturalists. Their naturalists wander the globe aimlessly for all eternity.
AI does not understand how to use inquisitors, they seem to believe that they can also be used on a foreign city and will send them there in mass.
Cannot make a joint war and use a Casus Belli to declare war.
Great people are far too limited. I consistently run out of all great people before game is over which renders a major part of a good number of building and districts useless. (Accumulating great people points for nothing)
Not nearly enough great artists, musicians, and writers to even fill a fraction of the buildings that house them on larger maps.
On lower difficulties I constantly run out of techs AND civics to research. On harder difficulties most the AI players and I run out of techs and civics and just “future tech” it up until the game resolves.
This means by the endgame, all buildings the create science and great people points are obsolete.
Why does a national park have to have all tiles owned by the same city? This is ridiculous.
Many wonders are very much underpowered comparted to how much time to take the build. It makes for some easy choices when picking between units/buildings or wonders.
•	The amount of tourism from a fully upgraded theatre square district with a themed archology museum dwarfs wonders into obsolescence (16 tourism for big ben vs 157 for upgraded theatre square with all buildings and themed museum.
Relics apparently are limited so if you built the Mount St. Michel wonder, all of your apostles will still say they will create a relic if they die on religious combat, but that is a lie. You will just stop getting them at some point with absolutely no explanation or substitute.
View gallery button in the great works menu is broken and only displays the very first item in the top left hand side of screen
THE CITY PRODUCTION STATUS DOES NOT GIVE ENOUGH INFORMATION.
•	YOU CAN SEE HOW MUCH TOTAL PRODUCTION A CITY MAKES
•	YOU CAN SEE THAT CHOPPING A FOREST OR IMPROVEMENT DOWN WILL YIELD A SPECIFIC NUMBERS
•	YOU CAN SEE HOW MANY TURNS AN ITEM WILL TAKE TO COMPLTETE
•	IT DOES NOT HOWEEVER TELL YOU HOW MUCH TOTAL PRODUCTION AN ITEM NEEDS
•	ALSO IT APPEARS THAT REMOVING A FOREST WILL DRASTICALLY SPEED THE CONTRUCTION OF A DISTRICT, BUT ONLY KINDA HELP MAKE A UNIT (EVEN IT MAKES SENSE THAT WOOD WOULD HELP THIS UNIT, LIKE A CATAPULT). I CANNOT BE MORE SPECIFIC BECAUSE I AM NOT GIVEN THE DETAILS.
City state benefits take a turn to reflect when you become their suzerain
Inquisitors are overpowered. My two 4000 faith apostle should not be able to be undone by one measly inquisitor
Game doesn’t understand what 75% of existing religion means. Or I don’t understand.  But it reduces religion by less than 75percent of current religion.
Very effeminate horn honk for the missile cruiser. A very powerful late game unit.
This is the first civilization game that I could be drunk and still kick the computers♥♥♥♥♥ (Up to Immortal difficulty)
Every time you purchase a unit with gold/faith, the next one becomes more expensive (workers, apostles, inquisitors) plus they will just get more expensive as the turns go by.  I understand this is for balance purposes, but it is a bit to dramatic for my tastes.
At the end/beginning of the turn, notifications scroll across the screen quickly. This blocks some combat that is happening, and in order to see a list of what scrolled through you have to go through and click the diplomatic screen of every civilization and they may or may not have had something on that list from the turn in question. This is a truly unique game.
This is a truly infuriating game.
There's nothing I can say bad about this game because
1: I'd call it about 90% stable (compared to a bethesda game that's about 70%). This alone wouldn't matter. Just cuz the game loads and doesn't crash while you play it doesn't mean it's not bad. But for how much time the average Kerbal will play this game, it's a huge factor (Also, the game takes about 10 minutes to load if you have anywhere near 100 mods installed, like me.)
2: It's unique. There is no game like this. ANywhere. It simulates a solar system (simplified, of course, because truly doing this in real time is beyond any home computer.) so that you can build, fly and crash rockets, planes, boats and... anything. The limitations are almost nonexistent. Some youtubes build completely stock (No mods) helicopters even though there are no parts designed to build a helicopter.
3: You HAVE to think. You can slap rockets together and hope for the best and plenty of people have mastered this game from doing that. But if you don't learn and try, this game will lose appeal fast. If you manage to get over the steep learning curve, though, you'll never get bored of this game. Minecraft let you let your artistry go wild. This game will refine it into a diamond as you struggle to meld Form and Function into spacecraft that can literally go beyond the Moon. I can't be serious enough in saying that this is a truly fascinating and amazing game.
4: Mod support. There are mods that give you exactly the type of experience you're looking for. The stock game is wonderful and enough for most people to sink their teeth into for a good minute. If you want more, there are mods that enhance and maintain a stock-a-like experience and mods that add completely new systems.
Or bananas. Hell, there's a mod that lets you make a Hamburger that you can launch into space. Why? I dunno.
Anyways, this game is worth playing for anybody. It's unique, offers limitless challenge and, if you're patient, it will actually teach you about aerospace. It won't make you an astronaut, but if you show up to space camp after a few hundred hours of this game you'll definitely have some knowledge to show off.

An interesting simulation with bad controls, and a physics engine that's been upgraded to "mostly okay."
The game is fairly enjoyable with simple ideas, but gets buggy way before you get to all of the most interesting parts.
Sadly, far more time is spent in the game fighting with (or looking up solutions to) the design system and bad controls than actually enjoying the game. Figure out what you want to do, then figure out why the game won't let it work, spend a few hours looking up and watching videos trying to figure out what the game wants you to do to achieve your goal, try and fail, watch videos and look on the forums to find out what they changed and the new solution, then actually maybe accomplish something. Rinse and repeat.
Trying to build a rocket (or worse - a plane)? Hope the game doesn't decide you want to install parts upside down or sideways. Once it's built, even using the in-game symetry system, the game might decide one side is heavier or less aerodynamic. Nothing will show up as being unbalanced, but you'll spin out of control until you take it all apart and build it the exact same way again. Any wheeled vehicle (rovers or rocket cars) will have a 100% chance of being unbalanced and making unplanned turns, assuming they don't explode first.
The collision detection will cause things to explode when they shouldn't, especially anything on or near the ground.
Once you manage to make orbit, you're expected to use waypoints you set by hand experimentally (they show you where you will end up if you've got enough fuel), in real time while flying. There is a way to remove waypoints when you've flown past where you wanted to be or the angle got screwed up, and it works almost half of the time if you keep clicking. I say expected to, because there are nearly-mandatory mods to automate the process. Any attempts to use the jetpack will result in only frustration.

If you like fast-paced, randomly generated rogue-likes, then this is the perfect game for you. Nuclear Throne is another great game by one of my favorite developer teams, Vlambeer. You're a mutant stuck in the wasteland with all of your friends, and you've all heard the tale of the Nuclear Throne. Some think it's a bunch of baloney, others think that it really exists, and a few mutants are going to go out of their way to get to it. You are one of those few mutants. One of those few mutants, who is also really well balanced with the other mutants in terms of power.
NOTE: If the character's name has a star (*) next to it in the list, then it means it's one of my favorites.
FISH*: Once a police officer, now turned into a scaly fish-man on the last day before his retirement. He gets more ammo from all sources of the stuff, and can roll out of danger.
CRYSTAL: An okay mutant for the new players, Crystal gets more HP and can briefly shield herself to block almost all attacks. After all, "Crystal can handle this." Though, don't get too attached to her shield, or you might not be the best at dodging.
EYES*: He has a deep backstory, according to the devs, but he doesn't have a mouth to speak about it. He can see much clearer in the dark levels like the Sewers, and he can use telekinesis to drag enemies towards him and projectiles away from him. He is super underrated.
MELTING: The wind hurts. Everything hurts. Melting is tired. Melting starts out with 2 HP (keep in mind, most projectiles do 3 damage), but to balance that out, he gets more radiation (in other words, experience), and can blow up corpses for immense damage potential. You should really get acquainted with the game before you try him out!
PLANT*: Assuming you've gotten pretty good at this game, Plant is basically the anti-bad RNG character. He's extra fast, and can also trap enemies with vine snares. KILL KILL KILL.
YUNG VENUZ*: Ladies and gentlemen, the one and only Gun God! He has a faster rate of fire, as well as being able to fire two shots at once (with double the reload time, of course). Also, he doesn't even die. Whenever you reach 0 HP, he just gets frustrated with himself and goes home to his mansion.
STEROIDS*: He was the only human who came prepared. He predicted the apocalypse and pumped himself full of steroids to survive. Every weapon he holds is fully automatic and he can dual-wield, but he has less accuracy to compensate.
ROBOT: An automaton straight from the future. He finds better weapons earlier, and can eat guns if he doesn't like 'em (robots can digest anything, according to the game).
CHICKEN: A samurai chicken. Enough said. She's another good mutant to start with (yes, SHE), as she starts out with her good ol' sword and can throw her weapons! If her health reaches zero, she simply becomes beheaded and you will need to collect a medkit within 3 seconds! During this time, the screen does not move and you can kill everything you'd like to. Upon getting beheaded, you'll have two less max HP, and lost max HP can be restored with the mutation "Last Wish" or by getting a big medkit.
REBEL: A bandit who detached from the group, she's found home around the campfire of mutants. She's probably one of the most fun to play as if you can get her late game. She heals when she goes through portals, and she can spawn allies to help her.
ROGUE: Similar to Rebel, Rogue is a cop that, as her name says, went rogue and left the Interdimensional Police Department (I.D.P.D). As a result, she is constantly being hunted throughout the adventure by the po-po. To combat them, she comes equipped with a weapon she stole after leaving, the Portal Strike, which has potential for immense damage.
[CLASSIFIED]: A living blob of [CLASSIFIED], [CLASSIFIED] can fire a beam of [CLASSIFIED] to kill stuff. He also gets an extra [CLASSIFIED] to choose from. He's a secret!
[CLASSIFIED]: Basically the worst character in the game. He's a super secret that you get while playing as [CLASSIFIED] if you die inside of a [CLASSIFIED]. He starts out with less health, speed, and accuracy, and his ability allows him to [CLASSIFIED] with a chance of taking 1 point of damage.
[CLASSIFIED]*: One of my favorites, he is immune to [CLASSIFIED], and can fart out the stuff he's immune to! Sadly, he can never stop [CLASSIFIED]. You get him by damaging [CLASSIFIED] at least once with a golden weapon, keeping that golden weapon to the end of the fight, and picking up the [CLASSIFIED] that the [CLASSIFIED] drops. Take it to a [CLASSIFIED] and put it in a [CLASSIFIED], then go to the same [CLASSIFIED] with a different character and open up the [CLASSIFIED] to get a [CLASSIFIED]. Keep it to the next level and you will be able to play as [CLASSIFIED] once you select the [CLASSIFIED]!
PROS:
-Replayability is off the charts!
-Graphics, gameplay, and music are all really enjoyable.
-Good variety of... everything!
-Nice team of developers.
CONS:
-RNG can screw you over, and does so way too often.
-Has a chronic disease of NEVER TELLING YOU WHAT ANYTHING DOES (I.E. snipers are OBVIOUSLY suicide-bombers, obviously...)
-Don't have quick reflexes? You're dead already.
If you're a fan of rogue-likes, buy this game. Go. Buy it.
