Almost a year after it’s release, let’s see how Sid Meier’s Civilization VI fares. Is it a great game? Is it a bad game? Is it a disappoi- DING! Correct! It’s a @#$%ing disappointment! …Let me see if I can explain why.
This review was made possible with the help of
. Thanks for the help.
Civilization VI (or Civ VI for short) introduces a neat change to the policy gameplay, by adding its own research tree known as a Civic Tree.
The Civic Tree, which uses culture, focuses on researching policies that helps your civilization in various ways as it has done in the previous games of the series. Of course, you can only have so much policies in effect for a period of time, but after researching certain civics in the Civic Tree, you will be able to use more policies.
I really like this addition to the game. For one, this puts players on a different focus, in which they can’t just focus on science all the time, they now need to focus on culture. And two, when playing Civilization, I usually play a cultural style and to see the developers increase the uses for culture is a big plus in my book.
The AI for the opposing civilizations in Civ VI is easily the most frustrating experience I’ve had to deal with to date. They’re very sensitive to the actions that you make, or don’t make, and they critique your army a lot in this game.
When playing against AIs, you can view their agendas, which tells you what they like or dislike from their opponents. Problem is, the majority of them prefer seeing a strong military. In the case you don’t have a strong army, your enemies will let you know by contacting you, denouncing you and eventually, declaring war on you.
One example of poor AI that I want to share. One game, I had a group of enemy units next to my borders. Eventually, war was declared, but instead of attacking my units, the enemy turned their units around back towards their city.
Another new addition that Civ VI introduces is Districts. Districts focuses on the key elements of the game, science, culture, money, production, you name it. They are essential in advancing in the game. Problem here is that it cuts down the pace of the game.
If you were to look at this game’s predecessor, Civ V, you could build any type of buildings & wonders at anytime in the game. In Civ VI, you need to have the specified district built if you want to build specific buildings, and wonders suffers more problems as well. Some of them needs a particular district and maybe another building before you can start constructing it.
Another thing to note is that the first few Districts will take time to build. Adding insult to injury, the Industrial District, which specializes in production, is among the last districts you will research as it’s far from the start of the game.
It saddens me to make the move of not recommending this game. I want to like this game and I want to recommend it to friends & various people, but considering the negative points that I made, which can’t be ignored that easily, this is a game you should avoid. There are much better 4x strategy games out there that won’t frustrate you like this one.

KSP is a blank slate waiting to be populated with your own creations and designs. As someone who is interested in real orbital mechanics and rocketry, it was very exciting to see a game that incorporates this on a smaller, easier to tackle scale. Arcade space games that allow you fly as if you were in the atmosphere are fun, however lack a challenge, as you just point your ship where you want to go, and you're there. Planning your trajectories, conserving fuel, and keeping Jeb alive makes for a unique, challenging, and rewarding experience. It is often the missions where issues arise that are the most interesting. Landing on the Mun is plenty fun, but creating a ship to save Jeb with is always the most entertaining. The mod support is great as well, as the developers openly support modding and endorse creators on their social media and other outlets.
9.5/10, would save Jeb from Mun again and again.

I would recomend civ 6  as a good game for most part but there are caveeats here and I will not shun from going over a few of them. Lets start with some of the pros..
Pros; The districts outside of the city square works great and makes you question what you want to do with each city and why you place it were you put them. Ai is decent at this as well for most part aside from sometimes putting districs down where the bonuses are greatest at the moment  ( not thinking long term ). It keeps the whole hex system from civ 5 and civ beyond earth but allow support units such as anti air cannons, medics, battling rams, settlers etc to share a square with military units giving them some protection. Also makes you think about which unit that is best were on the battlefield unlike civ 4 which had death stacks on a single sqaure roaming around.
The civic cards that replace the civic trees from civ 5 and beyond earth work pretty well too. The splitting of the science tree into a civic and a tech focused one is a good move as well to open up more options on what to get in what order for civ ( certain civs get major benefits from specific techs ). Graphics is good enough too but some might find it cartoonish, I however don't and actually prefer civ 6/civ  beyond earth over the civ 5 graphics but that is just me.
Now for the cons then....
Con; the ai is better than it used to be but the recent summer patch broke it to some degrees....needs fixes both in unit controll and diplomacy. I have bought great art of ai civs for 1-2 gold each if they were happy enough with me basicly handing me culture wins on a platter. Just meeting you and finding your follow a diffrent goverment = instant loss in reputation with them does happen as well so be aware.
The eurekas for civics and tech trees have to be rebalanced. Basicly an eureka for ironworking for example ( 50% of the science/culture cost given for free ) is haveing a mine on iron. The sailing eureka is a city on the coast and so forth but giving 50% is to much and it speeds science up to ludacris degrees at times....I have seen anti tank infantery among the ai troops before we even got the idea for tanks. It needs lower % bonuses or a rework system similat to civ beyond earth's science webb that allowed you to jump start sciences early in an area ahead of time for the cost of being behind in others. It is not a bad idea and an improvement over civ 5's stiffer build orders so it can do its intended effect though. It is just that sometimes you will see things so ahead of time it is stupid.
multiplayer is honestly broken, it works better than civ 5's multiplayer with the boatload of issues it had but it still feels tacked on as a last effort. If buying the game for multiplayer only avoid this game....it is not worth it from a pure multiplayer view. DLC's for the new civs are interesting and comes with scenarios you can play but the prices might be to high. 5 dollars for civ and a scenario ( allthough fun experiences ) is on the pricier side.
Overall it is good enough for me to like it over civ 5 which I found stiff and it to some extent tapped into civ beyond earths each playthrough is unique territory but some things need more work. If you are fine with that you will probably like what civ 6 has to offer.

Torn on this one. It's good, but not great. Maybe my expectations were too high, or maybe I just need to wait a few years until they add enough content and patches to bring it up to par with V.
Gripes so far: seriously unbalanced, frustrating, and feels very closed-off and limited compared to previous versions. This is a personal opinion but I *hate* the art style. World leaders are rendered as silly, cartoony goofs (who want to nuke you, by the way), the map is an utter visual disaster...it's like a pixel lasagna, layer after layer of graphics that look good on their own, but turn into a melted mush when combined; the net effect is that it's difficult to tell at a glance exactly what or who you're looking at. Music is so-so; probably an odd thing to complain about, but since you're stuck with it for hours and hours at a given time, it'd be nice if it wasn't so grating (seriously, banjos have little place in the real world, let alone in a video game). And worst of all...it's kinda boring. Never before in the series have I felt so robotic in every task I was doing. I feel less like a leader playing this game and more like an overworked shift supervisor at a toy-soldier factory.
There are good things to say about this game...though at the moment they all escape me. To be fair, I will probably revisit this game in a few years, and either it will have improved, or my tastes will have evolved, but for now, I'm going back to Civ V.

I finally got around to playing TWD: Season 2 (I always buy them once all 5 episodes are already out, screw waiting months in between each one!), and it was just as compelling as the first.
Stepping into the shoes of the now 11-year-old Clementine felt natural
. But she seems to embody him in everything she does, and Telltale gives you the opportunity to make ballsy and often heart wrenching choices the way you think is right, same as the first season.
One of the complaints of the first season is it's a tad linear. Don't get me wrong, it's an amazing game, but the dozens of decisions we agonized over in Season 1 all ended up taking us to the same ending anyway. It was disappointing to make a tough call, be curious what direction the other choices would have taken me, reload the save and redo the decision, only to find out I ended up in the same place anyway.
Season 2 rectifies the linearity of the first one, especially in the ending department. In fact, if Telltale continues with the Clementine storyline, Season 3 is going to be one hell of an undertaking, considering the multiple different places (and people!) you had the possibility to end with in S2. It's almost for this reason I feel a third season wouldn't pick up directly where the second season left off. Sure, there will always be the people you can't save, and I'd reload a save file only to watch my favorite character die a different way, but overall, I was happy in feeling my decisions had an impact on the outcome.
When reading through some other reviews, one thing a lot of players agreed on is not feeling as connected to the cast as the first season. I can definitely see this, and I do agree I wasn't as invested in most of the characters, and didn't care about many of their inevitable deaths (sounds terrible, but it's true). However, there are enough characters I did find myself caring deeply about. Those are the ones TWD centers on, and that's what's important.
To quote another reviewer,
I do too, but Season 2 does a great job in convincing me everything I did last season wasn't in vain.

The Walking Dead season 2 takes place 16 months after the events of the first season. You now control a 11 year old Clementine which makes the world feel even more dangerous since taking down a single walker takes multiple strikes because she lacks the strength to destroy the brain. It is a shame we don't get to play as 9 year old Clem and suddenly get a jump cut saying “16 months later”  with nothing else added on how she survived or what she went through when she was most vulnerable. That doesn't mean she won't be in danger though, as she will be receiving plenty of horrific injuries. Her voice is no longer high pitched and cute like in Season 1, she now sounds depressed after all the stuff she has been through. And since it has been so long after the outbreak most of the survivors are very selfish and jaded or just flatout insane.
Nothing has really changed from Season 1 besides the story and a few new inputs during quick time events.  There are much less puzzles and less chances to talk to characters while walking around. They will usually just repeat one line and tell you to do something which helps keep up the pace of the game but also has less time to flesh out the characters.  It makes sense that they wouldn't want to converse with a little girl but it comes off as a bit silly how dependent they are on her at times. This time around they focus a lot more on human evil and pull it off very well. You will frequently feel intimidated by the insane people and more so by the people at your side as they start to lose it. Which brings me to the choices. It makes since that most people will ignore what you want to do but when you do make a choice it feels a lot less satisfying than in Season 1. They just feel lazy and the outcome will feel the same no matter what you pick, making it feel less like a choose your own adventure game and more like a point and click game with occasional dialogue choices.
The game feels like it was rushed out before they could fine tune it to the quality of the first. Not that I'm saying it is a bad sequel though. I personally enjoyed it more than the first due to the helplessness of playing as a child. It is a very “fun” and tragic journey that I refuse to spoil here.  Not bad at all if you don't compare it to the original. Though one thing I just have to mention is that they make you sit through the credits that lists the whole staff and their pets five times. That's just unnecessary but at the very least they throw in some good music each time. Still if you liked the first season and want to know what happens next this is a very solid purchase that is every bit as emotional as the last season.

After the great success that the first "season" of The Walking Dead was, I was totally hyped and ready for round 2 with this game. Sadly, Season 2 fails on just about every level to surpass or even meet the original's quality. Telltale's Walking Dead now suffers from the same issues that the TV show is burdened by: overall terrible writing with characters who have very generic motivations who get killed off when the writers run out of ideas for their storylines. Unlike the original, the characters have no clear direction or plans for survival beyond finding food and shelter for the day; while this is reasonably realistic, its also incredibly boring. A domino effect of hurt feelings goes through this story, with characters behaving erratically (often contradicting their previous motivations and ignoring friendships) because other characters were behaving erratically. Everytime something bad happens, Clementine has to save the day while the adults bicker and threaten to kill each other. Most character's actions in these episodes are illogical and your choices and actions have even less consequences than in the original game.
Even with Telltale behind the wheel, TWD: Season 2 has already fallen into the shallow strides set by the TV show. While I still recommend the original, Season 2 is a decidedly phoned in 8 hours of "gameplay" that isn't worth wasting your time on.

This is my first time reviewing a game on  steam! For starters, civilization VI is an unbelievable game that has compelled me to right a review. 9.5/10

The enhanced graphics look incredible when compared to other civ games. Next, the technology tree albeit seemingly straightforward at first has a ton of depth as players begin to realize the advantages one can receive by rushing certain techs at certain stages of the game; it is well thought out and begs players to experiment and comeback to discover new strategies with multiple factions.
After the 50-100 hour mark this game really took off as a dove into the world of online multiplayer. The new dynamic timer was a good fitt at first but as expansionist factions like the romans or russians have begun there routine the dynamic timer drags the game on and on; perhaps this is the only flaw, however, for beginners it serves as a great tool. Online play ranges from soft play to hardcore ranked matches that are arranged by top players from the public matches and the competitive league is largely organized through discord. If you are looking for high tier gameplay it wouldnt hurt to ask people in your public match where you could get started.
100-150 hours. This game is a true gem and deserves recognition as the top Civilization game in the history of the franchise.

TLDR: Civ 6 is a solid and fun addition to the civ series. Pro - Polished, features complement each other, civ gameplay that gives the "one-more-turn-phenomenon." Con - AI cannot handle features and 1 unit per tile. Diplomacy is still bad. Late game usually falls flat like previous Civ games. The UI is worse than Civ 5 UI.
Civ 6 pros and cons, and mixed feelings...
Pros:
Cons:
Mixed feelings:
Civ 6 is a solid civ game. I have been playing civilization series since civ 3, and I have enjoyed all of them. Its hard for me to pick a favorite, but if forced to I would have to pick civ 4. I have put hundreds of hours into each, and I think each of them had strengths and weaknesses.
Civ 6 was probably the best launch of any civ game I played. It was a complete game from the start. People say it is missing features, but honestly it has a ton of features. It added a lot of new mechanics, kept most old mechanics/systems, has good graphics, and maintained the hex grid/1 unit per tile game play that made civ 5 unique and complex.
With all this in mind, I want to address the complaint most people bring up with every civ game. The AI. From this point, I will mainly be discussing the Civ 6 AI, and it is more of a discussion rather than a review.
The civ 6 AI sucks. I suspected it would suck. Every civ AI has sucked horribly since I started playing civ 3. However, in Civ 3-4, the horrible AI got to stack all their units and it was not quite as apparent how bad the AI was in those games because the game was "simpler." With 1 unit per tile and increasing # of features/mechanics that have been implemented in Civ over time, the flaws in AI become obvious.
Civ 6 is by far the most complex civ game I have played in the series. This is not a complement. I think it is a bit too complex. AI cannot handle complexity, and it makes the game look silly sometimes. I don't think people realize how complex it is to make a game that is 1 unit per tile with all the features included in civ 6. Every new game the map is randomized. Each tile has random features. Now, you throw ~8 civs on this new random map, with some random city-states, random barbarian placements, and resources.
Now the map is generated and the civs (with their unique special bonuses) are placed on a map relatively randomly. You will begin to move through a tech tree where the units/districts/resources available are always changing at a different pace for each civ on the map. New to civ 6, your research/progress is map-dependent. You have to find things/accomplish things to speed up your research. Also new to civ 6 you're placing districts and wonders on the map. The AI has to have some sort of programing to make decisions. The game is complex, and I am not sure that AI that can be run on computers that meet the min requirements is robust enough to handle it.
So what happens? In order to make the AI competitive, high difficulty civ AI cheats. The AI cheats in every Civ title. In Civ 6 they spam districts and units, but they do it poorly. They throw units away in war. They cannot handle 1 unit per tile combat. This is a huge negative in my opinion. However, it does NOT ruin the game.
The game is still fun, it still has the civ charm. You can still min/max your civ making super power economy, high-tech military, or a tourist culture. I played it day after day at launch and really did enjoy it. At launch, I was playing on diety and winning most games. However, after one of the first big patches I had trouble on immortal and always lost on diety. Considering I always played civ 5 on immortal, I feel like the developers already had a sense of how to start changing (or buffing?) the AI to properly challenge hardcore civ fanatics. I am assuming I would still struggle to win on diety now. This does not mean the AI got "better" it just means the developers made changes to higher difficulty AI to appropriately challenge the hardcore gamer. I typed up this review because I honestly felt the huge number of negative reviews does not really reflect the quality of this game.
Civ 6, in spite of its flaws, is good. Worth buying on sale for sure. I bought it at launch, and I do not regret it.

So, starting out, I think Civ 5 is better (with all of its expansions).  However, I've put many hours now into Civ 6 and I do think it is fun, and overall I would recommend. I think the game can be much better, and I do hope they fix stuff moving forward.
Positives:
- Graphics/art direction are really nice
- Loooove Sean Bean in this
- Gameplay is overall easy to learn and at its most fun when playing against other humans.
- I like the idea of the religious war/victory
- I really like the districts and the fact that you can't spam wonders (that they take a tile per each). I like the increased strategy that comes along with the district and wonder building and planning out your cities.
- I like the different civilizations in the game so far, they each are pretty fun and each has a slightly different play style which has been fun to learn and try to do well with.
- I think tile strategy has been improved with the amenity and appeal systems.
Negatives
- The religious victory and fighting is too simplistic.
- The AI is the biggest drawback IMO. They are really stupid about diplomacy, will often give you their great works for pennies, are weird about trading, and dumb about war. The way the AI agendas are implemented by them seems to be poorly thought out. How the AI treats religion is one of the most annoying aspects of this game. As soon as they get religion, they will generate somehow like 3000 missionaries and spam your cities. The only way to deal with this is to either work to up your faith output so as to buy apostles (which may or may not even win trying to kill them before they die themselves), or you have to declare war on them to kill them with military units. If you are trying for a cultural or scientific victory, this is an incredibly annoying distraction.
- The city/empire size balance is non-existent. Civ 5 allowed you to win with just one city. Civ 6 basically demands you build a ton of cities.
- Cultural and scientific victories can take too long and be a little boring. They both need to be a little more special or have more nuance.
- There is no production queue like there was in Civ 5. I would really love to see that make its way into this game.
- Like Civ 5, team play is not well implemented.
- The espionage system needs help - the spies rarely seem that useful.

I just wanted it to be good, so damn bad.
I played the hell of of Civ V, it was a great game. I eventually got tired, there were a few little niggling bits that annoyed me, wasted potential etc., but it was a good game.
I wanted Civ VI to be good, if they'd taken Civ V, changed the civs around, added in their new districts mechanics, new artwork etc., I wouldn't have minded too much. If they could have improved the AI, that would have been great. I visualised great wars, alliances! Some kind of 3rd 4th 5th 6th Coalition against a great foe! Or at least, AT THE VERY LEAST, the same as Civ V, just with smarter AI.
None of this came true, of course. You can't bribe wars like in Civ V (okay maybe there's some other similar mechanic, secret alliances, maybe intertwine them with the new agenda system?), nope, you either go on a joint war (you can only do this if you're friends with the joint war partner, which is incredibily unlikely), or no war at all, unless you're gonna do it yourself. You have to just sit there, as you watch one, two, three civs run away, with no way to stop them, unless you've got a large army hidden somewhere up the backside of one of your cities.
I like the amenities, building an empire of more than four cities doesn't feel anywhere near as restrictive and ruinous as it was in Civ V.
The agenda system is terrible. Good concept, badly, badly executed. I was playing a game on Immortal difficulty as Brazil, and found myself denounced on turn 5 by Rome, because I 'controlled very little territory'. I was in a state of constant denouncement for the rest of the game, even as I settled my sixth city, in a futile attempt to appease my Roman overlords. I won't get into the other two denouncements I received within 5-10 turns of meeting the next two civs, because they "Just plain don't like you"- it was funny the first time, haha lol a bit of comedy, but when every civ seems to do it, it's just frustrating. I feel like I spend every game trying to please every civ in the game, or one of them at least, but I just can't. I look at all their relations with eachother, and they're all besties, all having fun denouncing me. And once they decide they hate you, it seems that's it, no second chances.
There's so much more I could say but I've wasted so much of my life on this game already, hoping I was wrong, that until it gets a COMPLETE overhaul (the diplomacy, at least), I'm gonna expel all thoughts of it from my mind. It just frustrates me.

A review on Life is Strange
Life is Strange is in many ways one of the best games I've ever played, from the characters to the world but most of all because of the amazing and immersive story. In Life is Strange you play as photography student Max Caulfield, a who's life goes crazy when she finds out she can reverse time and change the past, present and future. The gameplay in Life is Strange is your standard Telltale story driven gameplay with of course the bonus feature of being able to reverse time, which makes for some amazing options in your own story. Don't like the choice you made? Just reverse time and choose another option! Life is Strange is set in the fictional town of Arcadia Bay. A cozy town at the coast of Oregon. The town feels alive for so many reasons, from the believable scenery to ambient noises but most of all because of the characters. The characters in Life is Strange, even the smaller ones, have a story and a specific drive to them that makes them unique. The art style is fantastic, the game has plenty of colors which makes the world pop out at you. Again the story is one of the best stories I've ever played, every episode I finished left me wanting more. If something bad happened to a character I liked I would react angry or even sad. If a character I didn't like had something bad happen to them I would be happy because they probably deserved it in one way or another. And the amazing voice acting by the voice actors only immerses you more into the story. The only thing I would've liked to see Life is Strange do was the ending, in my opinion the ending was good but it wasn't on par with the rest of the story.
Summary:
Pros
- Fantastic story
- Amazing characters
- Beautiful scenery
- Time travel is a great gameplay element
- Amazing voice acting
Cons
- Ending could be better
Final verdict: Life is Strange is an amazing game that pulls you in on every single aspect and I'd love to revisit Arcadia Bay many times again. 9.5/10

Played episode 1, and then played the rest on a friend's account.
Haven't looked at it a second time, but here is what I feel about the game.
Really great game, no doubt about that.
+ Characters
LiS's strongest aspect in my opinion. The game gets you really attached to it's characters. Max is absolutely adorable and she gets quite a good deal of character development(always a plus). The supporting characters are fleshed out enough for me to not think that they are just throwaway characters, and also enough for me to get at least a little invested in them. One complain I have will be how little they expanded on Warren's character for the sake of Chloe.
- Chloe
Chloe is a likeable character, you get a lot of beautiful interactions with her. But I really can't help but feel that there are a lot of wasted potential on her character. We obviously know that she's a fairly depressed person(as her mom mentioned she's never really happy), with the situations concerning Max, her dad and Rachel. All these changed her a lot, and I really think that it's wasting as we don't get much exploration into it, sure we get a few lines from her mentioning these situations, but it's really not enough in my opinion.
- Story and closure
Imo, it feels as though the writers do not have a clear focus on how they want to conclude the story. We do a lot of things towards the end of the game, at no point did it made me feel like I was getting somewhere close to the end, and this may not be bad if it was building up to a gigantic closure, but the ending really doesn't show that. We were doing this and that, and oh man, we can't do this because of this, not much buildup. The ending feels like the writers wrote themselves to a corner and thought of a bad way out, or that, they were trying hard to make the story a tragedy. And it does feel that sometimes the writers are trying a little too hard . For instance,
.
All in all, I can't praise the story that much, I feel like a lot of things could have been better executed. Ending is not really well thought out. While I would really love a better closure, the characters made the game for me, the journey is pretty sweet and just for that, I would recommend this game.

Overall, it's a decent game, if you want to spend $60 on it. Honestly though, it's very meh. One of the problems is that there's simply too much going on. I appreciate the depth and complextity Civ 6 brings to the table compared to the previous ones, but it frequently feels to cluttered. I would be ok with this except it feels too much like work and the payout isn't all that satisfying. As far as gameply, there are some mechanics that are questionable. For instance, after a certian point, fairly early into the game, you can move land units directly into the water and they have their own self-contained transport. It does make it substantially easier, but in that case whats the point of even having an ocean besides you can't build on it? On top of that, I have a bigger issue with the gameplay: It's too easy and doesnt feel at all interesting or satisfying. I played several times on the hardest mode and each time I was able to take over the world or at least get close before i won by other means. This may relate exclusivly to combat, but every time I took a city instead of feeling elated after a hard-fought campaign, I found myself thinking "ugh what a waste of time." All of the units feel pretty much the same, either they're meele or you can bombard a target from a few hexes away using an asthetically horrible red arrow, and the only thing that changes is hp, damage, and when you get to nukes(actually one of the better parts of the game). Finally, the graphics aren't bad per se, but the game is from 2016, not 2006. The graphics could stand to be improved, but the UI is a real weak point. Parts of it are clearly designed to be old-fashioned style but it would work better if it decided wheter to go that route or make it sleek and modern with intuitave controls. Last point- It takes ridiculously long to load or take a turn compared to previous Civ games. I have a pretty good laptop that can handle first-person shooters with ease, so this is likley on the developer's end.
My point: Don't play it if you're looking for a quick game. Do get it if you want complex gameplay and dont care terribly much about graphics/UI or performance.

Nuclear Throne is an action shoot em' up roguelike game made by Vlambeer, where your objective is to reach the Nuclear Throne, your main enemy in the game.
 
Some people might not know this, but this game actually has a background story. But, since this is not the main "star of the show", it's okay for the game to have a lack of detailed storyline.
There are some more details, but it could be considered a spoiler at some point. If you're interested in knowing more about it, you could simply check the game's Wikia and find out yourself.
 
Nuclear Throne is a game with a big focus on gameplay and it would be a shame if it weren't good, right? This game has playstyle similar to the well-known Binding of Isaac, but way faster. The controls are easy to understand and are really responsive. At first, it will be a little bit boring because of the lack of things happening, but as you progress through levels, things get better and way faster! Fun and challenging.
In a nutshell: You shoot things. Things die. Get weapon upgrades and new mutations to power yourself up. Progress to the next area. Repeat until you reach the Nuclear Throne.
The sad thing about this game is that it lacks an online Multiplayer, only a local Multiplayer option, which is not that bad, but since this game requires a lot of precision and quick responses, using a gamepad to play with someone else is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ unless you manage to use two keyboards and two mices.
 
Vlambeer did an awesome job with the soundtrack the same way they did with
and their other games, the musics and songs fit really well. Boss battles, areas and everything else. And the mutants' voices and sound effects, like weapons and such are really well made as well.
 
You can probably tell that this game has pixelated graphics and, if you're a fan of super detailed and realistic graphics, this is not for you. The sprites in the game are well-made, the scenarios are great and suit each enemey very well. Also, their promotional art is awesome!
 
Okay, so, if there's a negative review out there, it probably is because of the difficulty and learning curve on this game. This is a really punishing game and little mistakes will make you get to the start of the game within a second, you must be cautious and think fast. As mentioned above, if you're a person that gets mad really fast or dislike games that are really difficult, you should probably avoid this.
 
It's a "short" game and you are going to die
, I assure you, if this game didn't have a great replay value, it would be absolute sh*t. If you enjoyed your first runs, you're probably going to enjoy the rest of it, since you're always progressing through the game, learning new things, trying out other mutants and mutations, yada, yada.
 
More like a TL;DR, I guess. It's an awesome game with fast gameplay, charming graphics, responsive controls and incredible replay value, I highly recommend it if you're a big fan of the genre, and, since it finally released, there's no need for you to be hesitant about the early access part. Vlambeer will probably keep updating the game, so, there's much more content to come and much more to enjoy. Also, if you know and enjoyed the abovementioned Binding of Isaac and want to "spice things up" and have a more "breathtaking" experience, give this game a shot.
There are also some other aspects of this game that might be a turnoff to some people, such as: no widescreen option and 30 fps cap. Just wanted to point it out, since some dislike this.

TLDR: Some interesting innovations but not as good as Civ5 yet. Buy this game if on discount
At the time of writing this, I have played approximately 200 hours of Civilization 6. I have not purchased any of the DLC because it is overpriced and most of it should have been included in the base game. I don't feel that any of the DLC reaches the same level as the expansions to Civilization 5, which I think remains the superior game.
Positive Innovations:
- Builders vs Workers: Having a temporary unit that expends charges to build things is better, in my opinion, than having a permanent unit that takes a long time to build things. This is especially useful in managing the weakness of an AI, because a clever player can prevent worker capture much better and thus over time get a lot more out of their workers than an AI can.
- Envoys: This is the best way of handling city-state interaction that I have seen. The shifting alignment system in Civ5 was much more vulnerable to exploitation. I like that even if you aren't their suzerain, you can still get benefits from having sent envoys to that city-state. Just all-round better way of handling things.
- Government + Policy Cards: This is a cool way of allowing customized government. The player can tinker with their government to match their own plans. I think the AI could use some help on picking the best cards for their nation, but overall a good innovation.
- Civics and Tech: I like having two tech trees; one for true technology and one for ideas/civics based on culture output. It works very well and the inspirations/eurekas system makes it so that if you are doing related activities, you advance faster. This is very good.
- Unit Management: Breaking things out into primary units, support units, great people units works great. Much less map clogging going on. Grouping into armies/armadas works well. In general this part of the game is improved.
Mixed Innovations:
- Districts are interesting. I like that they take up a hex on the map, so that a bigger city takes up literally more space. However, they can become a straight jacket for a city. If you don't build an industrial district, your build times are huge. If you don't build a holy district essentially as your first district, you will likely lose the religious race and end up with no prophet. I just feel like having districts puts big constraints on your strategic choices. They also take way too long to build, in my opinion.
- Wonders: They are less useful than in the past and many times you can't even build one due to the constraints (need a flat desert tile near a river adjacent to city center.... yikes!). I think they could be improved a lot with some simply tweaking.
- Trade Routes & Roads: I like how trade routes work, but I don't know that I think it is a good idea to tie road building to trade units. I understand the historical/thematic reasoning, I just think it doesn't work that well in the game. It results in a lot fewer roads. I would rather build roads and pay a maintenance cost (like in Civ5).
- The map: The tan map concept is cool, but it can be very hard to tell what is there once you explore it. There might be a region in the fog-of-war that looks like a desert at first glance, but it is actually plains. They just need to improve the quality of the map in the fog-of-war areas.
Negative Innovations:
- Movement Points: Blocking unit movement when they lack enough movement points really screws up the game. A unit with 2 movement points cannot move across a plains, then a forest. This makes pursuit of other units very clunky. Civ5 management of movement points was much better. Nothing is more frustrating than chasing a barbarian scout unit around hopelessly because you can't move/attack into a neighboring hex due to insufficient movement points.
- Barbarians: Barbarians are totally fubar. They send out a scout to find your cities, and if you kill the scout that is fine. But it can be difficult (see above discussion of movement points). Then once they find a city, they raise a huge force and come bash you. This changes barbarians from a nuissance to a huge problem to deal with. I have played games where I churned out three warriors immediately and I still get seriously hamstrung by barbarians early on. I just turn them off in a lot of games. It is just much better handled in Civ5.
- Diplomacy is feast or famine. If you develop a commanding lead early on, the AI will all beg for your friendship. If not, they will prey upon you. That's fine, I think. But because of the way that they account for warmongering, if you get into just a single war over a single city, nearly every AI will become hostile to you and it becomes a vicious cycle. They attack you and defending yourself will count towards additional warmongering which makes them hate you more. You have to either commit to a domination victory, endless defensive war, or just be a pacifist. You cannot have a mix of wars and diplomacy. It just won't happen.
- Defensive AI: The AI is just not optimized for defensive war. It does a good job of concentrating forces when on the attack. I have observed the AI several times moving a large force into position near my borders, then I build a bunch of units and they back down. And when they invade, they do a good job of attacking. But they can't defend worth a damn. It is so easy to take a city in this game. Offensive war vs the AI is way way too easy (unless you are attacking INTO a concentrated force that they assembled for another purpose).
- Naval power: Civilization just sucks at this, even in Civ5. It is clear that the designers spend a lot of time thinking about land warfare interactions. Naval power was so important in history, but it just has a minimal role in Civilization games.
- Civilization/Leader Imbalance: Some leaders are fantastic. Others are near useless. Some are so super specific that is radically constrains gameplay (Scythia, for example). They also made bizarre choices about which civilizations to include. Many great civilizations were not implemented so that they could include what are clearly diversity-influenced decisions. Having a Civilization from Sub-Saharan Africa that played almost no role in history (Kongo) or a minor barbarian group that left almost no trace behind (Scythia) while leaving out Persia, the Mongols, the Turks, and others is just disgraceful.
- Game Progression: Time flows way too fast on standard speed. If you want any time to actually enjoy a particular time (WW2 combat, for example), you really have to be on Marathon speed. I have (on standard difficulty) passed through research so fast that I may only get 20-30 turns with a particular unit before it is obsolete. The AI (as is common for many Civilization variations) has a hard time upgrading their units fast enough so they are frequently using units from a previous age. It's not as bad as Civ3 where I could be fighting a spearman with a tank, but it isn't pretty. I almost never even build air units because by the time I get an aerodome district built, I am about to land on Mars.
- Inquisition is too strong: Inquisitors are cheap to produce and can completely purge all your religious progress in another nation. This leads to most nations having a religion of their own, purging all others from their own lands, and maybe fighting over the handful of nations without a religion. The religious combat idea is awesome, inquisitors just ruin it all.

Civ VI's district system is, in my opinion, a great innovation in city management, as it means that one city can't produce everything for the empire. The fact that wonders now take up a tile slot adds to this, and the result is that turtling isn't as effective a strategy anymore and one city can't house literally 90% of the world's wonders. District management means planning is paramount.
This game launched with few leaders, some of whom were near reskins of existing ones. Firaxis has decided that it's okay to ship the same civ with a different leader, which only changes
of the unique characteristics of a civ, and call that differentiation. The game is also unbalanced. If you don't have DLC, you will always square off against either Sumeria or Scythia in the late-game, because they are extremely powerful civs. If you
have DLC, you will face whatever civ is a DLC civ.
Each game feels hardly different than any other because the civ variety is so low. Each game feels like you're fighting the same seven enemies with the same two always coming out on top.
Civ VI employs a predatory system of DLC release. DLC civs are objectively more powerful than base-civs, making Civ VI essentially pay-to-win. A
will cost you $5 since it comes bundled with a bunch of useless crap like scenario packs that you'll never play. FURTHERMORE, and this deserves its own paragraph:
-----
-----
You'll notice that my profile has ~99 hours of gameplay in Civ VI. At least 5 of that is just bug fixing. Here is a list of bugs I have had that is in no way complete, but what I can remember off my head:
* Crashing from launch screen
* Build/Culture/Bottom-Right button not working at all
* Units not moving to the space I click on
* Almost every single patch to this game will require you to not only disable, but UNINSTALL FROM THE FILE FOLDER every single piece of Workshop DLC content you have ever downloaded, and chances are you still won't be able to use DLC content even with a reinstallation.
* Unit icons not displaying
And lastly, the single most ugly thing about this entire game, worse even than the frequent crashes, predatory DLC policy, and inability to use Workshop content:
Every single time you complete a production, you need to do another. It's incredibly micro-intensive. "But wait!" I hear you say, "I can just get a UI mod from the Workshop to fix that!" To which I say, no, you can't. Civ VI won't run Workshop content without breaking instantly.
Go buy Civ V.
Edit: To those that are saying Endless Legend started the district system, they didn't-- at least not as it's used here. Endless Legend's districts allow the city to utilize all benefits of extra tiles or adjacencies. There is nothing preventing you from building any building you want in any city in EL. Civ's district system is innovative because it prohibits building certain buildings without the prerequisite district.

The game is fun and challenging at times, but a few things annoy me.
The main thing that bugs me is being denounced by people for stupid reasons like not having a navy 10 turns into a game on a map of pangea where everyone is on the same continent (♥♥♥♥ norway). Another thing thats weird is you will start a game, meet india, and then a few turns later ghandi shows up talking about how nukes are the future and you both just have warriors with sticks and rocks. I have noticed the AI does 1 of 2 things. They either try to♥♥♥♥♥♥you every chance they get, be it send an army of priests to your lands and convert all your citys, or settleing citys all around your land giving you no room to grow. Or the dont bother you the whole game until you have almost won. I have recently done 3 complete playthroughs. This review was conducted on 4 Feb 2015 and is subject to change as content is added to the game.
Edit* love the additions to the title and in game sound track. Already warrants changing to an upvote, keep it up.
This is a fun game for the first 30-45 minutes that it takes to unlock all the characters, but falls flat during the player's arduous struggle to reach the highest floor. I'm aware that this game is in early access and that things are bound to change. My issue with it is that the only replayability in its current state,  stems from the incredibly difficult task of reaching the nuclear throne. I myself have only reached floor 8 or so, but I'm finding the runs tediously repetitive rather than exciting.
So many people claim that the game is similar to the binding of isaac, but with guns. I'm very familiar with the binding of isaac (Over 120+ hours between BoI and Rebirth), and I can't say that this game is remotely related to BoI other than the fact that the levels are randomly generated. What the Binding of Isaac has that this game is missing is constant unlockables that give the player a sense that they are progressing rather than grinding for nothing. Another really neat feature in BoI is the fact that the player can get thousands upon thousands of completely different item combinations that lead to unique effects and are often hilarious or overpowered.
I think the biggest issue comes from the fact that this game feels like it doesn't have enough substance after you've completed the first few unlocks. After this point, there is a 4 hour (and counting) block of repetitive dying with no further unlocks or progress. The game is also missing that ability to be broken that everyone loves in The Binding of Isaac. The only way to get to the end, is to be patient and practice by doing a ton of runs. I have no issue with dying a lot, although in this case, the game may be slightly too unforgiving. You can get to the final floor with full health (not an easy task) and a single misfire of your explosive weapon or an unlucky spawn can result in your instant death from full health to zero, which is extremely aggravating.
I understand that the binding of Isaac is similar in that beating the game takes a ton of practice, but BoI also has the occasional run where, due to RNG in item drops, you become the bane of all that is horrible and wreak havoc. I think that if the dev removed this parameter that inhibits you from becoming op, perhaps by adding quite a few more upgrades, I might enjoy the game more. As a sidenote idea, if each of the weapons themselves could have multiple levels of upgrades or effects (on top of the mutations), I feel that the game's replay value would go up ten fold.
The game's wiki features a plethora of awesome looking weapons and cool features, but these features are hard to appreciate because of how difficult it is to access the floors that hold them. Ultimately the game is enjoyable for what it is in its current state. It has a fun soundtrack and decent pixel graphics.
I look forward to future updates to see what the dev does with the game and I will gladly change my review if the game fulfills its potential.

Great game! Nuclear Throne takes a serious subject (a post-apocalyptic world) and makes it into an awesome and quickly accelerating game. In a similar fashion to many other games, there are unlockable characters with different abilites and skills. It gets gradually harder with each passing level. Instead of the overused 'coins' or 'experience', the game uses an upgrade system that requires you to collect radiation points, whch are dropped by dead enemies. Between each level, you can use these radiation points to gain mutations, which can change the whole game for you. I personally enjoy the game, even though I have yet to complete it. Here are some pros and cons:
PROS:
*A quick game that you can play any time.
*Requires skill, but also practice. You won't beat it on your first try, is all I'm saying.
*The unlockable characters have a set of skills unique to them, and can make the game easier for you depending on your level of expertise.
*The storyline of Nuclear Throne is quite dark, but the gameplay is fun and the characters are reminiscent of classic, 8-bit players from original arcade games.
*The game is FUN!
CONS:
*It can be frustrating at times when you are at full health just starting out on level 5_2 and you get hit by the ONE THING THAT CAN KILL YOU INSTANTLY AND YOU TOTALLY RAGE AND HURT YOUR HEAD ON YOUR DESK. Just one example that comes to mind.
*The game is adddicting. Sometimes I sit down to play just one level, and an hour and a half later I realize I'm late for something or another.
*Every time you update the game, ypu lose all your progress. This includes your unlocked characters, your furthest level, and your golden weapons (some weapons can be found as golden weapons, and can be saved as your starting gun).
*There is a co-op, but no online multiplayer mode.
All in all, I love the game and hope you will too. Rating : 95 eyeballls out of 100 eyeballs.

TLDR: Some interesting innovations but not as good as Civ5 yet. Buy this game if on discount
At the time of writing this, I have played approximately 200 hours of Civilization 6. I have not purchased any of the DLC because it is overpriced and most of it should have been included in the base game. I don't feel that any of the DLC reaches the same level as the expansions to Civilization 5, which I think remains the superior game.
Positive Innovations:
- Builders vs Workers: Having a temporary unit that expends charges to build things is better, in my opinion, than having a permanent unit that takes a long time to build things. This is especially useful in managing the weakness of an AI, because a clever player can prevent worker capture much better and thus over time get a lot more out of their workers than an AI can.
- Envoys: This is the best way of handling city-state interaction that I have seen. The shifting alignment system in Civ5 was much more vulnerable to exploitation. I like that even if you aren't their suzerain, you can still get benefits from having sent envoys to that city-state. Just all-round better way of handling things.
- Government + Policy Cards: This is a cool way of allowing customized government. The player can tinker with their government to match their own plans. I think the AI could use some help on picking the best cards for their nation, but overall a good innovation.
- Civics and Tech: I like having two tech trees; one for true technology and one for ideas/civics based on culture output. It works very well and the inspirations/eurekas system makes it so that if you are doing related activities, you advance faster. This is very good.
- Unit Management: Breaking things out into primary units, support units, great people units works great. Much less map clogging going on. Grouping into armies/armadas works well. In general this part of the game is improved.
Mixed Innovations:
- Districts are interesting. I like that they take up a hex on the map, so that a bigger city takes up literally more space. However, they can become a straight jacket for a city. If you don't build an industrial district, your build times are huge. If you don't build a holy district essentially as your first district, you will likely lose the religious race and end up with no prophet. I just feel like having districts puts big constraints on your strategic choices. They also take way too long to build, in my opinion.
- Wonders: They are less useful than in the past and many times you can't even build one due to the constraints (need a flat desert tile near a river adjacent to city center.... yikes!). I think they could be improved a lot with some simply tweaking.
- Trade Routes & Roads: I like how trade routes work, but I don't know that I think it is a good idea to tie road building to trade units. I understand the historical/thematic reasoning, I just think it doesn't work that well in the game. It results in a lot fewer roads. I would rather build roads and pay a maintenance cost (like in Civ5).
- The map: The tan map concept is cool, but it can be very hard to tell what is there once you explore it. There might be a region in the fog-of-war that looks like a desert at first glance, but it is actually plains. They just need to improve the quality of the map in the fog-of-war areas.
Negative Innovations:
- Movement Points: Blocking unit movement when they lack enough movement points really screws up the game. A unit with 2 movement points cannot move across a plains, then a forest. This makes pursuit of other units very clunky. Civ5 management of movement points was much better. Nothing is more frustrating than chasing a barbarian scout unit around hopelessly because you can't move/attack into a neighboring hex due to insufficient movement points.
- Barbarians: Barbarians are totally fubar. They send out a scout to find your cities, and if you kill the scout that is fine. But it can be difficult (see above discussion of movement points). Then once they find a city, they raise a huge force and come bash you. This changes barbarians from a nuissance to a huge problem to deal with. I have played games where I churned out three warriors immediately and I still get seriously hamstrung by barbarians early on. I just turn them off in a lot of games. It is just much better handled in Civ5.
- Diplomacy is feast or famine. If you develop a commanding lead early on, the AI will all beg for your friendship. If not, they will prey upon you. That's fine, I think. But because of the way that they account for warmongering, if you get into just a single war over a single city, nearly every AI will become hostile to you and it becomes a vicious cycle. They attack you and defending yourself will count towards additional warmongering which makes them hate you more. You have to either commit to a domination victory, endless defensive war, or just be a pacifist. You cannot have a mix of wars and diplomacy. It just won't happen.
- Defensive AI: The AI is just not optimized for defensive war. It does a good job of concentrating forces when on the attack. I have observed the AI several times moving a large force into position near my borders, then I build a bunch of units and they back down. And when they invade, they do a good job of attacking. But they can't defend worth a damn. It is so easy to take a city in this game. Offensive war vs the AI is way way too easy (unless you are attacking INTO a concentrated force that they assembled for another purpose).
- Naval power: Civilization just sucks at this, even in Civ5. It is clear that the designers spend a lot of time thinking about land warfare interactions. Naval power was so important in history, but it just has a minimal role in Civilization games.
- Civilization/Leader Imbalance: Some leaders are fantastic. Others are near useless. Some are so super specific that is radically constrains gameplay (Scythia, for example). They also made bizarre choices about which civilizations to include. Many great civilizations were not implemented so that they could include what are clearly diversity-influenced decisions. Having a Civilization from Sub-Saharan Africa that played almost no role in history (Kongo) or a minor barbarian group that left almost no trace behind (Scythia) while leaving out Persia, the Mongols, the Turks, and others is just disgraceful.
- Game Progression: Time flows way too fast on standard speed. If you want any time to actually enjoy a particular time (WW2 combat, for example), you really have to be on Marathon speed. I have (on standard difficulty) passed through research so fast that I may only get 20-30 turns with a particular unit before it is obsolete. The AI (as is common for many Civilization variations) has a hard time upgrading their units fast enough so they are frequently using units from a previous age. It's not as bad as Civ3 where I could be fighting a spearman with a tank, but it isn't pretty. I almost never even build air units because by the time I get an aerodome district built, I am about to land on Mars.
- Inquisition is too strong: Inquisitors are cheap to produce and can completely purge all your religious progress in another nation. This leads to most nations having a religion of their own, purging all others from their own lands, and maybe fighting over the handful of nations without a religion. The religious combat idea is awesome, inquisitors just ruin it all.

Civ VI's district system is, in my opinion, a great innovation in city management, as it means that one city can't produce everything for the empire. The fact that wonders now take up a tile slot adds to this, and the result is that turtling isn't as effective a strategy anymore and one city can't house literally 90% of the world's wonders. District management means planning is paramount.
This game launched with few leaders, some of whom were near reskins of existing ones. Firaxis has decided that it's okay to ship the same civ with a different leader, which only changes
of the unique characteristics of a civ, and call that differentiation. The game is also unbalanced. If you don't have DLC, you will always square off against either Sumeria or Scythia in the late-game, because they are extremely powerful civs. If you
have DLC, you will face whatever civ is a DLC civ.
Each game feels hardly different than any other because the civ variety is so low. Each game feels like you're fighting the same seven enemies with the same two always coming out on top.
Civ VI employs a predatory system of DLC release. DLC civs are objectively more powerful than base-civs, making Civ VI essentially pay-to-win. A
will cost you $5 since it comes bundled with a bunch of useless crap like scenario packs that you'll never play. FURTHERMORE, and this deserves its own paragraph:
-----
-----
You'll notice that my profile has ~99 hours of gameplay in Civ VI. At least 5 of that is just bug fixing. Here is a list of bugs I have had that is in no way complete, but what I can remember off my head:
* Crashing from launch screen
* Build/Culture/Bottom-Right button not working at all
* Units not moving to the space I click on
* Almost every single patch to this game will require you to not only disable, but UNINSTALL FROM THE FILE FOLDER every single piece of Workshop DLC content you have ever downloaded, and chances are you still won't be able to use DLC content even with a reinstallation.
* Unit icons not displaying
And lastly, the single most ugly thing about this entire game, worse even than the frequent crashes, predatory DLC policy, and inability to use Workshop content:
Every single time you complete a production, you need to do another. It's incredibly micro-intensive. "But wait!" I hear you say, "I can just get a UI mod from the Workshop to fix that!" To which I say, no, you can't. Civ VI won't run Workshop content without breaking instantly.
Go buy Civ V.
Edit: To those that are saying Endless Legend started the district system, they didn't-- at least not as it's used here. Endless Legend's districts allow the city to utilize all benefits of extra tiles or adjacencies. There is nothing preventing you from building any building you want in any city in EL. Civ's district system is innovative because it prohibits building certain buildings without the prerequisite district.

I’m playing Life is Strange, the stunning episodic game from DONTNOD Entertainment. I think I knew I was going to love it from the opening credits, as the protagonist steps into her high school hallway, sighs momentarily, and drowns out the gossip and hubbub with exactly the right indie song. Her internal dialog runs over the smooth lyrics and burbling guitar as she makes her way through the flowing river of students.
Back in the day, games were always about the gameplay. A game was good if it had fun combat or interesting mechanics. Gaming itself was still fresh and new, and the process of interacting with a computer and overcoming challenges was entertaining in its own right. Lately, though, that hasn’t been enough for me. A shooter where the plot only exists to keep you moving down the path towards the end of the game while both your gear and the enemies incrementally improve… it feels stale at this point. More and more, I’ve been moving towards games that skip the ‘action’ entirely in favor of the story.
The central mechanic of Life is Strange is a key reason it works so well. Max, the hero, gains the ability to rewind time in short bursts. Most games would use this as a way to liven up a combat system or to create intricate puzzles to navigate, but in Life is Strange, you use it to make choices. Everyday, normal decisions, at first — should you raise your hand with the correct answer in class or not? You see people’s immediate reactions, and if you don’t like them, you can go back and pick another option. Once your choice is locked in, though, there’s no going back.
This isn’t Fallout 4 — it soon becomes very clear that your choices have large and growing impacts on the world around you. Friendships and romances begin and end, lives are threatened, and you start to learn more about the characters, the world, and your powers. The ability to rewind time and change your choices leads to long moments of contemplation, exploring all of the options and carefully considering the ramifications, but other than your movement and the decisions, the game plays like an interactive movie. The perfectly selected indie rock soundtrack adds depth and feeling to the scenes and the voice acting is spot on. It takes place in a fictional town in Oregon, and it feels so much like the Pacific Northwest that it’s making me homesick.
I’m only a few hours into the game, and I’ve already completely screwed everything up. I was trying to save someone, but I just couldn’t make it happen. All my decisions have come home to roost. The haunting sound of Jose Gonzalez’s Crosses plays in my ears as the results of my decisions play out on the screen. I’m powerless to stop it.
It’s one of the few times a game has made me roll back in my chair and just sit, staring blankly at the screen and feeling the sick, sinking sensation of every poor choice I’ve made piling up on me, my good intentions useless in the face of what’s unfolding.
And, suddenly, the game isn’t about the game anymore. I’m transported back through my own life, reliving my pivotal decisions: dropping out of college, moving to Costa Rica on a whim, moving to Japan on another. The branching path of the choices that have shaped my life has never been as apparent to me as it is right now. I’m not distraught because of what’s happening in the plot. I’m mourning for all the other versions of me that I’m not — the ones who bounced down a different path because of an offhand decision, a minor, momentary, careless impulse that sent them spiraling off in another direction. The ones who worked harder, the ones who took more chances, the ones who played it safer…
I shake my head, jarring myself out of my reverie. I chase it away for good with the rest of the glass, the smooth burn searing my throat as I pull myself back into position, enthralled, gutted. All I can do is keep going.

The graphics and sound are impressive. Additionally, the game is much more stable than Civ V even is currently. However, the team responsible for the game's mechanics greatly undermined those improvements. The new mechanics are often confusing, nonsensical and infuriating in the extreme. The addition of districts sounds good on paper but their implementation makes city placement an absolute headache. Expansion is now completely at the mercy of map randomization instead of just your first city like previous tiles. Additionally, districts are not explained well anywhere and the game will simply insist that "there is no suitable location for this district" without ever really explaining exactly what IS suitable. I gave up on building a harbor after seeing that message on a half dozen different maps building cities near, but not actually on the water, in spite of the fact that this is what the game explains that harbors are for. Finally, the new movement mechanics make no sense and are completely unintuitive. For instance: if you 3 hexes of movement left and you're one hex from a river, you can move 3 hexes up or down the bank, but if you want to cross you have to use 1 of your 3 moves, stopping at the water, and then waiting a whole turn to actually cross, and there's no refund of the lost movement you could have used to start crossing the water. This change was absolutely unnecessary and made something that was straight forward  and turned it into something confusing for no logical reason whatsoever. There is more, but this is already long... It comes down to the mechanics designer having done a terrible, over-complicated job.

I own both Civ V & VI. Personally, I prefer Civ V, but Civ VI still has some positive aspects about it.
For starters, Civ VI has better graphics, and different features. If you're thinking of purchasing the game, you will have to consider both the positive & negative factors.
We have diplomatic relation options with other civilizations, the ability to send envoys to increase relationships with city-states, and different options to select the cause of war for minimal warmongering.
Having said that, some of the AI initiatives are ridiculous, like the ridiculous spawn of Apostles from other civilizations. You will probably get denounced a lot and most likely will not be able to have peace in the game.
We have the ability to build districts on a tile which makes it different that Civ V. It makes it somewhat harder for you to manage your civilization, but at the same time makes it more realistic than ever before.
The challenge you get from Civ VI is mainly at the early stages of your game (if you start by Ancient Era) and as you go on further into the game, it becomes less challenging. Early on, some of the AI get a ridiculous amount of military units for a domination victory, so you have to be really careful with your defense.
On the other hand, there also aren't many mods available at this time as compared to Civ V. (Civ VI is still fairly new anyways).
I have also seen many people complaining about the game having lots of bugs, but I have yet to experience one yet.
Anyways, if you are a huge Civ fan, I would recommend this game. However, I would buy this when it goes on sale. The game needs more mods too!

Okay, going to do half of this as a non-spoiler review then a spoiler review. Then just a final overview which doesn't contain spoilers.
NON-SPOILER REVIEW
The game starts from the past events from Season 1, making the decisions you made in the 1st game matter to an extent. This does make it interesting however it does not affect the game greatly. It does matter when you go through flashbacks or mention names from Season 1. You play as Clementine after again following the events of the first one. Let's just say she's not doing great for now
Okay, now time for the begged question "Is it better than Season 1?"
Well, it's hard to tell. I approached this with caution as generally sequels aren't as good as the originals. Telltale had time to work on this and improve on Season 1's faults. And in some ways they did. The graphic style is better but still keeps the comic book type graphics, better action sequences. It is a more interesting world. However there are things that bugged me in the first one which they didn't fix, this includes poorly peformed animations, one case an animation of fire looked like a orange blob, and the thing that annoys me the most is the talking animations, i found it through where dialogue could be heard and it was displaying subtitles but the characters mouth movement were simply not corresponding with the words or not moving AT ALL, also i did wish there would have been a wider selection of ways to carry out a co-ordinated attack.
What i found out was also unlike the first one it wasn't option A and option B. But you could also delay the activity till the next day for reasons depending on the status of the group.
HOWEVER,  the deaths of certain characters are in some way worse and in some way better. Some deaths you could save character A or B or just left defenseless, which i do like because like Season 1 there was at least a character death which was decided by you every season however it is a LOT more unpredictable in this one. However when some characters get killed off it's just not as affective anymore
The game still keeps the two scenarios ;♥♥♥♥♥♥is not hitting the fan or♥♥♥♥♥♥IS HITTING THE FAN. However, it is quite rare we see our characters get a break which i personally see better and just makes the brakes so much better.
SPOILER REVIEW
You have been warned
At the start of the game literally made me hit my head against of the wall due to the poor writing because right at the start they straight away kill of Omid and Christa, and this literally did not make it affecting anyway what so ever, and then just skips to another time period which is such a waste of decent characters, i was not asking for a decent well thought death but literally killing them off within 5 minutes of the game just makes no sense. Within time we meet a new group which at first don't trust you due to a dog bite earlier that day. You are locked in a shed and are forced to escape as you need immediate medical care, and this bit is actually good as it shows human nature and you find trust within the group.
However you don't get to know characters much as straight away you are put in a "save A or B" situation, in the end i chose Nick which i felt was the right decision. Soon after this we have a brief encounter with the bad guy BIll as he questions Clementine when we the others are out,  we which immeiately abandon the safe house as even though he lied it is obvious he is after us due to a story which the characters are foreshadowing for later on involving the group escaping the camp which they were held in which Bill ran
Before we move on i want to talk about Clementine. I was VERY skeptical about her being the protagonist. She was lovely and awesome in the first game however i'm not sure i wanted to play her as a character, i will give a hands down to Telltale but they ♥♥♥♥ing nailed Clementine's progression. I know a lot of other reviews talk about this but how she's handled by her own and by other characters if fantastic. To some she's just another little dansel in distress who is going to die the next time there's a walker, but to others she's a tough son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ which she is.
When we are escaping from Bill's gang we meet a familiar face, Kenny!  was absolutely thrilled when we saw him again as he was my Top 3 favourite characters in Season 1. Depending on what you do you find out more or confer with your group i decided to find out more about Kenny. We learn what happend after he was "killed off" whilst trying to save Ben.  We find out he wasn't doing too well until he found his new wife.
We are then taken to a new work place by force from Bill which we then escape with a few new characters like Mike and Jane and i am strongly sure that Jane is a mirrored version of Carol of AMC's The Walking Dead. We then have to take care of Alvin's baby as the mother died soon after childbirth. We then run into Argo's group who Jane and Clementine robbed Argo before, this then leads to some dificulties resulting in Luke's death. One things leads to another and you get betrayed by Mike, Argo and Bonne betray you resuting running away. Which leaves us to the final decision, who do you kill, Jane or Kenny or both. I personally chose Kenny, as i still trusted him no matter what but that's me.
SPOILERS OVER

Wow... how do I start? The Walking Dead: Season 2 was one of the most emotional and gut-wrenching games that I have played in a while. The game has all the usual scenarios from the first; allies betraying you, zombie hordes or 'herds' overrunning locations, Kenny being a psycopath/ badass, and unavoidable deaths of main characters. If watching people being eaten alive or stabbed repetitively is your thing, then this game has plenty to satisfy you.
However, this game is not one of the usual hack, slash and shoot zombie games that you have come to expect. The crew at Telltale Games have really outdone themselves this time round, producing a story that is much darker and more refined than the original. Whilst Season 2 is indeed shorter than the first, the story is much more action-packed and entertaining. There is little of the long discussions and 'boring' character development that bogged down the first chapter in the trilogy. Lee also returns for a dream sequence, providing an emotional insight into Clementines mind, once again reminding us that despite all she's done, she's still only a kid at heart. And lastly, you are forced to make a difficult decision at the end of the game, one that I assume will have a major impact on the third season.
My Score: 90/100.

There is no other video game series that gives me a sense of the grand scope of human accomplishment that the civilization series has given me. Now days the market is saturated with games that focus on violence and war, these games have their prominent place in the market and rightly so. Out of the amazing civ games I believe the sixth is the strongest yet. Civ 6 adds the city tile system that allows city micromanaging to be more complex than it has in the past, which gives you options on what you want your city to specialize in. The government and religion systems have been redone to make a better and unique gameplay experience every time you play. Most people complain about the new art style but I rather enjoy the fresh take on the cartoony art style.
I am highly recommending civ six to all players of all ages for it is a deep and rich gaming experience that only Sid Meier and the folks at firaxis games could achieve.
