A most emotional rollercoaster-ride (Spoiler-free)
To write a review for Life is Strange is quite a challenge, as it is a game that's difficult to describe without spoiling the story. I try to do so, though, and still express what's so special about this game.
Story: Again, no spoilers here. You play Max, a rather shy and insecure college student, who wants to become a photographer. At the beginning of the game you discover that you have the power to reverse time and try to use this power in order to do the right thing. The story that evolves is a mixture of college-drama, coming of age story with a bit of crime and some mystery elements. Ultimately though, it's a story about friendship.
More I'll not tell. In fact it's best if you have as little clue about the game as possible.  I had seen no Let's Plays and forgotten everything I read about it when I finally found the time to play it. And that was a blessing, as it was due to this fact that I was could completely absorb myself into the story.
Gameplay: To be honest, there isn't so much of a game here and it's important to know about that before you start to play. You have no health bar, no combat mechanism, no experience points or equipment. It's neither shooter, nor action-adventure or RPG. Yet it's no adventure with proper puzzles either. There are a handful of situations in the game where you need to collect some items, but that's it. Apart from that you run around, look at things, talk to people and experience the story. Life is Strange is more like an interactive movie. You have no real HUD either, but that's a blessing as it only enhances your immersion in the game's world.
What sets Life is Strange apart though, is that you decide what is going to happen.
In each episode you have up to 5 major and around 10 smaller decisions to make and they decide the outcome of certain parts of the game. Many games now advertise themselves with free decision making. Everyone was/is praising CD Projects Witcher 3 for its difficult choices (it's a great game, mind you), but Life is Strange knocks Geralt & Co. out of the park. Period. All the choices were more difficult than anyone I had to pick in Witcher 3 – because they felt more like real-life-choices – and as soon as you start to care about the characters, you will bite your nails in order to guess the outcome of what you're doing.
Graphics: Nothing special here. The Unreal 4-Engine is working, but it's nothing fancy. There is no lip-synchronization either, but for most parts it doesn't really matter. I found the style and in general the art design to be quite appealing and in fact enhancing my experience of the game.
Music/Sound: A proper highlight of the game. The score and the songs are amazing and quite fitting and draw you into the scenery and the world of the small town of Arcadia Bay. And the voice cast is second to none, probably one of the best  I've seen in a video game and so so fitting for the roles. The chemistry is also incredible great. All the voice actors do a stunning job and really bring the characters to life.
So far that sounds like a good game, but nothing special. But believe me, it is. I've never been more affected by a game. The story and the way it is told is one of the best and clearly THE most emotional I've ever experienced.
If you're just a touch into well told and emotional stories and don't need fights around every corner, then Life is Strange probably will mesmerize you. It will make you laugh and smile and think about your youth, your friends, your family. It will warm your heart and it will hurt. You will bite your nails about some decisions and you will cry. There's serious tissue-alarm here, so be forewarned.
This game is meant to linger in your minds for quite some time. And it does. It may not be the best game ever (a rather subjective term, but even for me it isn't – I'm looking at you there, Baldur's Gate 2). But it is one hell of an emotional rollercoaster-ride – and clearly the most intense and most emotional gaming experience I've ever made.
If you like interactive storytelling, PLAY IT! If you like coming-of-age stories, PLAY IT! If you are into well written and believable characters, PLAY IT! If you want to have a once-in-a-lifetime-gaming-experience, PLAY IT!
Don't miss out on this gem. Even though Life is Strange has pushed my emotional limits really hard, I wouldn't trade the experience I had with this game for a million dollars. That's how good this one is.

Good as vanilla, great with mods.
This is basically a space rocket simulator with nice looking guys and some jokes.
There is a real sense of achievement in this game.
There is a steep learning curve (I love complicated games, this one must be in the top 3 in that sense).
Read wiki, watch Twitch / tutorials.
Assume you will need around 20 hours (yes... 20 hours) to be at ease with the game.
The first 10 hours will be enlightening, but not incredibly fun. Not a chore either :)
Then, it is a *blast*. A blast. I don't play many other games than Kerbal these days.
It's sandbox, the solar system is your oyster.
To name a few mods that make the game a real gem (no need to pick them all, the first is very very usefull, the rest is to give examples) :
- Kerbal Engineer Redux. Must-have if you want to know what you are doing. Install it out of the box
- Remote tech : all your satellites must have a working radio connection with home base to work. Build a satellite network
- TAC : Your astronauts (Kerbal) need supplies of air & food & water. Stock and equipments to provide these included
- K&K Base building : nice looking buidings to build base on the surface of any moon / planet
There are tons of other mods, from trivial to crazy ones.

With the current 83 662 positive reviews on Steam, my opinion feels highly irrelevant. Still, Life is Strange carved itself a special place in my heart and deserves another vote : mine.
Life is Strange is simply a masterpiece. I'm very fond of games in which your choices actually matter and have a real impact on the course of events ; now I have only one desire : play it over and see what could have happened with alternative actions. Until now, I have sadly experienced so few games with such a level of immersion : I sometimes felt as if I were Max Caulfield herself and developped affection, hatred or mixed feelings for every single character. All aboard the feel train : the game is so intense and emotional, I dare you not to cry !
Besides the fantastic personalities, the story is one of the highlights of this game. Many serious themes and problems of everyday life are cleverly evoked, different perspectives and life lessons to value. The gameplay is rather simple but unique, as you can "rewind" and change your actions or dialogues, which makes the story progression so captivating. You'll come across a couple of puzzles, nothing very complicated though, but the investigation with Watson (Chloe) is thrilling. Since the game is about Art, I would like to add that even if the graphics aren't out of this world, I truly find them particular and beautiful, and it perfectly fits. Let's not leave the wonderful and unmatched soundtrack besides.
We need more gaming experiences like this and I can totally picture a movie inspired by Life is Strange. At least this announcement should reassure the fans : "[...] we can indeed confirm that the original Life is Strange team at DONTNOD are working on a brand new Life is Strange game.". Hella hyped !
If I had to recommend one interactive story game, it would be without a doubt Life is Strange.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a great follow-up to the fantastic TWD: Season 1 from Telltale. TWD: Season 2 does improve over TWD: Season 1 in some ways, while the experience is still littered w/ fantastic storytelling, character development, and important decisions to make. If you weren't a fan of TWD: S1, I don't think S2 will sway you into becoming a fan of the series, as this series and these style of games just might not be for you (i.e. adventure games mixed with a lot of interactive story elements - such as Fahrenheit / Indigo Prophecy and The Walking Dead: Season 1).
Often, a lot of the decisions the player makes as Clementine during this zombie-apocalypse, you will have very limited time to make a decision, which makes often for a very gripping & intense experience. Like the previous season, things are often very intense here. You will have to make decisions here in this bleak game-world, which will cause rifts between yourself and the other people in the group that are trying to survive in this zombie-apocalypse - and this is where a lot of the tension comes from. Also, adding to the tension is that this game is so focused on story + character development, that characters you will care about - well, you'll have to make a decision on what to do. Since this is TWD - expect making bleak + dark decisions, which often are in the realm of choosing b/t gray-clouded areas. Often, players will be choosing b/t the lesser of a few evils; or making what feels like a the morally good decision where the outcome is just still down-right horrible.
Just like with S1, S2's story + character, & decision-making stuff is pushed into the forefront. In this Season, you are Clementine (who returns from Season 1, but is now fully playable this time around). Clementine is stuck with a group of mostly new survivors, who are trying to stay alive in this zombie-apocalypse. This is what the game actually is. If you're looking for a typical type of game with challenge put forth in combat, puzzles, and things of that nature - don't. This is not that kind of game.
Though, S2 feels like it often offers up more action sequences in the previous season.  If you were hoping for more action sequences in S2, you'll probably be happy with that change. With that change, though - it feels like there are less puzzles offered than what was in the previous Season. S2 feels a bit more on-rails, less areas to explore, and less items often in the inventory - which can makes these puzzles a lot easier than what was in Season 1. While this is labeled as an adventure game, do not expect mind-numbing puzzles: most of these puzzles are very logical and very easy to figure out. If you were hoping they'd improve that by having more difficult puzzles or another difficulty to offer up tougher puzzles, don't. Actually, the puzzles in S1 - which weren't even remotely hard, anyways - were a bit more challenging.
When you make choices + decisions, they will often shape the journey of the experience itself in certain ways. They might even make the final outcome of the game different even. Having a bit of a different journey itself and final outcome, for fans - this could make the game worth any replays they would want to give the game. Since you can import directly from S1 + 400 Days DLC, in which your decisions can matter from those - there could even be reasons to replay and start from S1, play 400 Days, and then run S2.
When it comes down all to it, after around 9.5 hours w/ this game (according to Steam), The Walking Dead: Season 2 is an excellent adventure game + interactive story. If you were not a fan of TWD: Season 1, then I don't think TWD: S2 will turn you into a fan of the series. While the experience is fantastic, it still offers up a lot more of the same greatness that came forth in S1. Great characters, storytelling, voice-acting, dialogue, and decision-making are what make this game as great as it is. If you haven't played S1, well - you should start with S1 and then play 400 Days DLC b/c your saved-games can be imported right into S2. While TWD: S2 does not have the freshness of a new experience that Season 1 offered up, TWD: S2 is still great and most definitely worth experiencing for fans of TWD: Season 1 and those into a mix of adventure games + interactive stories.
Final Grade = A-.

The UI, compared to 5 at least, is absolutely dreadful and the Diplomacy is completely broken at time of writing (other AI nations will propose a deal to me then refuse to accept it, for example). It forces Full-screen play and doesn't play nice with Alt-Tab'ing out to change your podcast or whatever (it doesn't crash but it'll put up a fight).
The art style has gone from simplistic realism to children's game. I like how the map is actually like a ye olde sailor's chart, but the animation of the visibility fog and such just makes it feel... childish. So it looks like a kid's game, BUT...
There are so many mechanics, plenty of new ones. I like the new Districts thing, and the new layout to the tech and culture trees, and the Eureka mechanic. But the new way you tangle with City-States, the religion, all the new diplomatic options just make it overwhelming for anyone who doesn't plan on diving in and tearing it up.
Mechanically, I like this game. But the crap AI, UI, pacing, optimization, and childish art style just put me off. I'll go back to 5, I think.

- How do I condense the fact that the game is an all-around blast into bullet points?
- There are very few games attempting to simulate realistic space exploration, and KSP is by far the best that I'm aware of. Even without mods, there is plenty to do, plenty to learn about orbital mechanics, and a lot of satisfaction to be had from knowing that you've created something that could more or less work in real life. With mods, it gets even better.
- The game can be played in Campaign, Science, and Sandbox modes, and each is its own kind of fun, letting you indulge in your choice of space agency fantasy, whether it be themed after SpaceX, NASA, or the Federation of Planets.
- The community is very active, and you will find no shortage of tutorials, videos, mods, and whatever else you might want from a game community. If you're afraid you've missed the train, don't; you'll still find people eager to share KSP stories years from now.
- It's not just for space travel! Even in the unmodded game, you have plenty of opportunity to experiment with land vehicles and aircraft, and recent updates have opened the door to water craft as well.
- The game can be a bit buggy even before adding mods to the mix. I get bad stuttering near large space stations, and this is on a computer that can eat AAA shooters for breakfast. Vessels will occasionally load improperly and break on the launch pad.
- When you get deeper into the game, you start to notice physics kludges that take away from the realism, such as the fact that two vessels will phase through each other undamaged if their relative velocity is high enough. The way vessels are composed of "parts," while it does make design fun and streamlined, also causes oddities such as the way damage is handled, with a part being either destroyed or left undamaged (a part cannot, for instance, be sheared in half).
- The game is starting to add mod support, but when an update breaks a mod, I basically lose access to all the saves I used the mod with, because if I load the save, KSP will delete any modded vessels and kill all the crew. It would be very nice to see something like Civ V's mod menu, associating saves with mods.
- The altitude restriction on time warp gets a little ridiculous at times. If I have a vessel orbiting Kerbin at 200km, and I want to transfer it to another planet at the lowest possible dV cost, I have to either wait literal hours of real time for the node or go to the tracking center and try not to advance time too far to miss my window. The Alarm Clock mod mitigates this issue somewhat, and while I haven't been able to find a mod that turns off the restriction, I'm sure it's out there somewhere, so this problem is a little nitpicky, but cut me some slack; I'd look like a fawning KSP zealot if I didn't try to balance out the "pros" somehow.
You will learn firsthand why and how space travel is dangerous as you send legions of kerbonauts to their untimely deaths. You will recreate the early successes and failures of the world's space agencies. You will experience the thrill that runs through mission control in the movies after a milestone mission. You will conquer the solar system and create another one to do it again. You will--hey, why are you still reading this when you could be playing KSP?

A most emotional rollercoaster-ride (Spoiler-free)
To write a review for Life is Strange is quite a challenge, as it is a game that's difficult to describe without spoiling the story. I try to do so, though, and still express what's so special about this game.
Story: Again, no spoilers here. You play Max, a rather shy and insecure college student, who wants to become a photographer. At the beginning of the game you discover that you have the power to reverse time and try to use this power in order to do the right thing. The story that evolves is a mixture of college-drama, coming of age story with a bit of crime and some mystery elements. Ultimately though, it's a story about friendship.
More I'll not tell. In fact it's best if you have as little clue about the game as possible.  I had seen no Let's Plays and forgotten everything I read about it when I finally found the time to play it. And that was a blessing, as it was due to this fact that I was could completely absorb myself into the story.
Gameplay: To be honest, there isn't so much of a game here and it's important to know about that before you start to play. You have no health bar, no combat mechanism, no experience points or equipment. It's neither shooter, nor action-adventure or RPG. Yet it's no adventure with proper puzzles either. There are a handful of situations in the game where you need to collect some items, but that's it. Apart from that you run around, look at things, talk to people and experience the story. Life is Strange is more like an interactive movie. You have no real HUD either, but that's a blessing as it only enhances your immersion in the game's world.
What sets Life is Strange apart though, is that you decide what is going to happen.
In each episode you have up to 5 major and around 10 smaller decisions to make and they decide the outcome of certain parts of the game. Many games now advertise themselves with free decision making. Everyone was/is praising CD Projects Witcher 3 for its difficult choices (it's a great game, mind you), but Life is Strange knocks Geralt & Co. out of the park. Period. All the choices were more difficult than anyone I had to pick in Witcher 3 – because they felt more like real-life-choices – and as soon as you start to care about the characters, you will bite your nails in order to guess the outcome of what you're doing.
Graphics: Nothing special here. The Unreal 4-Engine is working, but it's nothing fancy. There is no lip-synchronization either, but for most parts it doesn't really matter. I found the style and in general the art design to be quite appealing and in fact enhancing my experience of the game.
Music/Sound: A proper highlight of the game. The score and the songs are amazing and quite fitting and draw you into the scenery and the world of the small town of Arcadia Bay. And the voice cast is second to none, probably one of the best  I've seen in a video game and so so fitting for the roles. The chemistry is also incredible great. All the voice actors do a stunning job and really bring the characters to life.
So far that sounds like a good game, but nothing special. But believe me, it is. I've never been more affected by a game. The story and the way it is told is one of the best and clearly THE most emotional I've ever experienced.
If you're just a touch into well told and emotional stories and don't need fights around every corner, then Life is Strange probably will mesmerize you. It will make you laugh and smile and think about your youth, your friends, your family. It will warm your heart and it will hurt. You will bite your nails about some decisions and you will cry. There's serious tissue-alarm here, so be forewarned.
This game is meant to linger in your minds for quite some time. And it does. It may not be the best game ever (a rather subjective term, but even for me it isn't – I'm looking at you there, Baldur's Gate 2). But it is one hell of an emotional rollercoaster-ride – and clearly the most intense and most emotional gaming experience I've ever made.
If you like interactive storytelling, PLAY IT! If you like coming-of-age stories, PLAY IT! If you are into well written and believable characters, PLAY IT! If you want to have a once-in-a-lifetime-gaming-experience, PLAY IT!
Don't miss out on this gem. Even though Life is Strange has pushed my emotional limits really hard, I wouldn't trade the experience I had with this game for a million dollars. That's how good this one is.

If this is your first Civ game, welcome to the franchise! Hope you enjoy it! This is probably the best one to start with.
I've been playing Civ since 4. I have 5 and Beyond Earth in my Steam library as well. Each have their pros and cons, natch. But it seems to me that Civ 6 has a worse pro-to-con ratio than previous installments. The UI, compared to 5 at least, is absolutely dreadful and the Diplomacy is completely broken at time of writing (other AI nations will propose a deal to me then refuse to accept it, for example). And it all moves so slowly, it is such a boring experience. Sometimes clicks don't register properly. It forces Full-screen play and doesn't play nice with Alt-Tab'ing out to change your podcast or whatever (it doesn't crash but it'll put up a fight).
The art style has gone from simplistic realism to children's game. I like how the map is actually like a ye olde sailor's chart, but the animation of the visibility fog and such just makes it feel... childish. So it looks like a kid's game, BUT...
There are so many mechanics, plenty of new ones. I like the new Districts thing, and the new layout to the tech and culture trees, and the Eureka mechanic. But the new way you tangle with City-States, the religion, all the new diplomatic options just make it overwhelming for anyone who doesn't plan on diving in and tearing it up.
Mechanically, I like this game. But the crap AI, UI, pacing, optimization, and childish art style just put me off. I'll go back to 5, I think.

Writing-wise, this certainly isn't up to par with TWDS1 or even TWAU. There's no coherent narrative, the cast members die off too quickly to leave an impact and there's no real resolution to be had.
Honestly at this point, I really wish Telltale would abandon the episodic format... it does not serve what they want to do well. You can't have a purely linear story and also emphasize choice. I bet they could make something really amazing if they released one big game with a branching story, multiple paths and endings, different outcomes determined by the way the players play the game. The fact that they have to release in an episodic format is holding them back, a lot. Almost every problem of this game can be traced to that.
Because a character *could* die at some point in time, they *must* die before the game ends. The only real exceptions come right at the very end of the game (and the way the game "ends" makes sure that Clementine herself cannot be an important character in the narrative of the already-announced Season 3... great work there.) There's not even any real puzzles this time around, like TWDS1 and TWAU at least brushed with.
That being said. I like this game, even still. There's plenty of suspense and although a lot of things are predictable as hell there's still enough twists and turns in the story, though it never leads to anything in the end. Heck, there's a 9 day gap at the end of the game where nothing is implied to have happened of significance; 9 days is longer than the main plot of the game. But... yeah. I'm still on board with this in spite of its flaws. It's on the short side, again, compared to TWDS1 (both this and TWAU have this issue, but TWDS2 doesn't even have the excuse of having several different investigation scenarios like TWAU did). $25 is probably too high for this, probably too high for any Telltale game. But on sale? Sure, it's worth your time. The art direction's still good, the music's fine enough and the voice acting is fine enough (save for one character who, thankfully, is killed within half an episode's span.)

KSP is a physics game which means its not for everyone. It is somewhat technical but thanks to its cartoonish approach funny at the same time.
You build your rocket or your plane in the hangar, go to the launchpad/runway and watch it fly ( or die trying ).

The graphics are pretty basic but that has no negative impact on the game for me (i for one prefer a good game to good looks).
It can be somewhat repetitive. You're going to repeat ALOT of your flights until they yield the results you set out for but with the tinkering in between trying to optimize your design its okay for me.
There are 3 gameplay-modes to choose from.
1) Sandbox: just build what you want and let it fly.
2) Science: Get scientific data from different locations to advance your rockets like various climate zones of your own planet, in flight, in orbit, heck even swimming in the ocean and in space of course. Just worry about the data no matter the costs.
3) Career: You pretty much run the whole show yourself if its science/piloting/managing/work on contracts etc.
For me it was totally worth it and im not done yet. :D

Most of the other reiews already say it, but this game is a massive letdown. While it has plenty of fun mechanics that have been revamped from civ 5, such as the new wonder system, the game all around does not compete with it's predecessor, especially in terms of the DLC policy. This game has been out for nearly a year now, and all the people who bought the Digital Deluxe edition feel scammed. Why? Because unlike civ 5, which was pumping out a plethora of great dlc, that expanded the mechanics and added more civs for reasonable prices in nearly every one, we are getting severely overpriced civilization packs, that include underwhelming civilizations, with no clear priority on the more important or interesting ones throughout history. A lot of people hated the Poland DLC, because all it added was a civ, but I felt it was well needed, however, later in the DLC line, we have gotten nothing but scenarios and civilzations. We have Australia, which is an underwhelming choice for a civ, as they have only been independant for about a hundred years. I could forgive this, however afterwards, rather than releasing an in depth, well made dlc, they made a dual pack with Persia, and for some reason Greece for a third time. That's right folks, Greece is in this game 3 times, but it's ok because Alexander's greece is "Macedon". And lastly, we have the Nubia DLC, which adds Nubia, an extremely vague, and odd choice for a civilzation in a game that is missing some of the most historically rich countries in history, such as the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, and Austria. Even though I do have 140 hours in the game, and have forced myself to have a positive outlook, on it, the DLC is making me more and more pessimistic by the release. Absolutely not worth the $80 I spent on the digital deluxe. Only consider getting this game if heavily on sale.

Everything changes for her in the moment when she saw something she wasn’t supposed to see and she discovers her power to rewind time. And that is the beginning of a great adventure of Max and her best friend Chloe. You will meet allies but also make enemies. You have a choice to be nice and friendly and stay out of trouble, or choose to make trouble everywhere possible. Max will also try to collect evidence for three different stories she wants to solve, which is accomplished, but not everything is as you thought it was.

It can be fun in short 30 minute bursts, but it gets super boring after second match because of low quality map desings, akward, disjointed and unbalanced hero designs( for example why does Evie has two mobility skills? it just bothers me so much ) and very strange and raw art design.
No matter what the fans of this game says, this game is clearly a Overwatch clone. Character designs, game modes, abilites,  sound effects, even small things like play of the game screen, crosshairs, classes...
I've played Paladins before I played Overwatch, and the difference of quality just left me speechless. For example Pharah from Overwatch and Drogoz from Paladins are very similar heroes but when I played them one after the other, Drogoz is just a very trashy, half a**ed version of Pharah. Drogoz's rockets are very slow, they don't have a knockback effect, you cant control his jetpack with short bursts and his ult is ridiculously lazy (one punch an enemy to death) and he is just ugly af.
Some heroes have overlapping abilities as I mentioned before. Like Evie's teleport and soar, Tyra's molotof and grenade, Shalin's invis-dodge and invis ult.
Some heroes are wastly op while others are ok-ish. Victor for example, is a Soldier 76 clone without any recoil. 76 is already an easy hero to begin with, so copying him and giving Victor close to 0 recoil is just cheap.
Another big turn off for me is that how GIANT hitboxes are in this game. Not only there is no recoil for any weapon, you don't have to have any aiming skills at all, everybody just holds left mouse button and game plays itself.
Oh did I mention that art design SUCKS in this game. There is no time period, no setting like sci-fi, futurism, medieval, realistic, steam-punk etc, instead it's just a mix of everything but there is nothing for your eye and soul to set on. A talking turtle, a russian soldier, a body builder with monk uniform and a shotgun, a talking jumping fox, an italian knight with a flame thrower.. its all so random, yet there is not one single paladin in this game. Why is this games name Paladins btw????
To sum it up, this game will satisfy your needs if you have very VERY low expectations from a game, otherwise ist's a very cheap, half a**ed copy of games like Overwatch and TF2. If you can't afford Overwatch, play TF2, this game will reduce your IQ to 0, lower your FPS skills into 0, shrink your artistic perspective into 0 or worse, bore you to death.

A most emotional rollercoaster-ride (Spoiler-free)
To write a review for Life is Strange is quite a challenge, as it is a game that's difficult to describe without spoiling the story. I try to do so, though, and still express what's so special about this game.
Story: Again, no spoilers here. You play Max, a rather shy and insecure college student, who wants to become a photographer. At the beginning of the game you discover that you have the power to reverse time and try to use this power in order to do the right thing. The story that evolves is a mixture of college-drama, coming of age story with a bit of crime and some mystery elements. Ultimately though, it's a story about friendship.
More I'll not tell. In fact it's best if you have as little clue about the game as possible.  I had seen no Let's Plays and forgotten everything I read about it when I finally found the time to play it. And that was a blessing, as it was due to this fact that I was could completely absorb myself into the story.
Gameplay: To be honest, there isn't so much of a game here and it's important to know about that before you start to play. You have no health bar, no combat mechanism, no experience points or equipment. It's neither shooter, nor action-adventure or RPG. Yet it's no adventure with proper puzzles either. There are a handful of situations in the game where you need to collect some items, but that's it. Apart from that you run around, look at things, talk to people and experience the story. Life is Strange is more like an interactive movie. You have no real HUD either, but that's a blessing as it only enhances your immersion in the game's world.
What sets Life is Strange apart though, is that you decide what is going to happen.
In each episode you have up to 5 major and around 10 smaller decisions to make and they decide the outcome of certain parts of the game. Many games now advertise themselves with free decision making. Everyone was/is praising CD Projects Witcher 3 for its difficult choices (it's a great game, mind you), but Life is Strange knocks Geralt & Co. out of the park. Period. All the choices were more difficult than anyone I had to pick in Witcher 3 – because they felt more like real-life-choices – and as soon as you start to care about the characters, you will bite your nails in order to guess the outcome of what you're doing.
Graphics: Nothing special here. The Unreal 4-Engine is working, but it's nothing fancy. There is no lip-synchronization either, but for most parts it doesn't really matter. I found the style and in general the art design to be quite appealing and in fact enhancing my experience of the game.
Music/Sound: A proper highlight of the game. The score and the songs are amazing and quite fitting and draw you into the scenery and the world of the small town of Arcadia Bay. And the voice cast is second to none, probably one of the best  I've seen in a video game and so so fitting for the roles. The chemistry is also incredible great. All the voice actors do a stunning job and really bring the characters to life.
So far that sounds like a good game, but nothing special. But believe me, it is. I've never been more affected by a game. The story and the way it is told is one of the best and clearly THE most emotional I've ever experienced.
If you're just a touch into well told and emotional stories and don't need fights around every corner, then Life is Strange probably will mesmerize you. It will make you laugh and smile and think about your youth, your friends, your family. It will warm your heart and it will hurt. You will bite your nails about some decisions and you will cry. There's serious tissue-alarm here, so be forewarned.
This game is meant to linger in your minds for quite some time. And it does. It may not be the best game ever (a rather subjective term, but even for me it isn't – I'm looking at you there, Baldur's Gate 2). But it is one hell of an emotional rollercoaster-ride – and clearly the most intense and most emotional gaming experience I've ever made.
If you like interactive storytelling, PLAY IT! If you like coming-of-age stories, PLAY IT! If you are into well written and believable characters, PLAY IT! If you want to have a once-in-a-lifetime-gaming-experience, PLAY IT!
Don't miss out on this gem. Even though Life is Strange has pushed my emotional limits really hard, I wouldn't trade the experience I had with this game for a million dollars. That's how good this one is.

KSP is a physics game which means its not for everyone. It is somewhat technical but thanks to its cartoonish approach funny at the same time.
You build your rocket or your plane in the hangar, go to the launchpad/runway and watch it fly ( or die trying ).

The graphics are pretty basic but that has no negative impact on the game for me (i for one prefer a good game to good looks).
It can be somewhat repetitive. You're going to repeat ALOT of your flights until they yield the results you set out for but with the tinkering in between trying to optimize your design its okay for me.
There are 3 gameplay-modes to choose from.
1) Sandbox: just build what you want and let it fly.
2) Science: Get scientific data from different locations to advance your rockets like various climate zones of your own planet, in flight, in orbit, heck even swimming in the ocean and in space of course. Just worry about the data no matter the costs.
3) Career: You pretty much run the whole show yourself if its science/piloting/managing/work on contracts etc.
For me it was totally worth it and im not done yet. :D

With the current 83 662 positive reviews on Steam, my opinion feels highly irrelevant. Still, Life is Strange carved itself a special place in my heart and deserves another vote : mine.
Life is Strange is simply a masterpiece. I'm very fond of games in which your choices actually matter and have a real impact on the course of events ; now I have only one desire : play it over and see what could have happened with alternative actions. Until now, I have sadly experienced so few games with such a level of immersion : I sometimes felt as if I were Max Caulfield herself and developped affection, hatred or mixed feelings for every single character. All aboard the feel train : the game is so intense and emotional, I dare you not to cry !
Besides the fantastic personalities, the story is one of the highlights of this game. Many serious themes and problems of everyday life are cleverly evoked, different perspectives and life lessons to value. The gameplay is rather simple but unique, as you can "rewind" and change your actions or dialogues, which makes the story progression so captivating. You'll come across a couple of puzzles, nothing very complicated though, but the investigation with Watson (Chloe) is thrilling. Since the game is about Art, I would like to add that even if the graphics aren't out of this world, I truly find them particular and beautiful, and it perfectly fits. Let's not leave the wonderful and unmatched soundtrack besides.
We need more gaming experiences like this and I can totally picture a movie inspired by Life is Strange. At least this announcement should reassure the fans : "[...] we can indeed confirm that the original Life is Strange team at DONTNOD are working on a brand new Life is Strange game.". Hella hyped !
If I had to recommend one interactive story game, it would be without a doubt Life is Strange.

I've been a civ fan since civ 3 and have easily played 1000 hours for every installment.  So it is with great sadness that I say this game is terrible.  My hope is that the next expansion 2k/Sid Meier decide to release (and I hope much sooner than the year it took to make War of Chosen for X-Com 2 which was great) will fix alot of the issues plaguing this game.
tl;dr if you look at steam stats civ 5 is being played far more than civ 6 so wait for a sale and buy that game for $10 because 6 is no where near as good.
A few issues off the top of my head are:
Pacing - its terrible.  Eras and units are far too short and this maybe due to the eureka mechanic in the game.  I like the idea  of playing around these bursts of science and civics but they affect the pacing of the game so much.  For instance you could finish a game in 1700AD with stealth bombers on Emperor (3rd hardest difficulty) which takes away from the immersiveness you might want.
UI - The UI is terrible at the moment and mods are required to make it playable.  There's no production queue, trade routes are better with the most recent patch but still awful.  Diplomacy tab is just cumbersome; to see the quests required to complete to get an envoy is painful to scroll through.  All cities status requires you to click through 3 tabs instead of pressing one god damn button and even then to change production queues quickly you have to zoom onto the city EVERY TIME.
District removal - I love the concept of districts and playing around it.  Really makes city building and perhaps going tall interesting but lack of district removal is a severe oversight.  Even in the real world parcels of land get re-zoned all the time so why can't we remove districts.  The only time a district might not have the right to be removed is through some grandfathered idea (like 50 turns perhaps longer).  Especially due to populations limiting your ability to make new districts its crucial in strategy game to re-appropriate the land as you need it although it should be at a great expense.  Adding this feature could change the game alot and how you adapt and if tied in with government it would diversify your playstyle greatly (for ex. communists governments could remove districts with fewer penalties).
AI - This is probably the issue most people complain about and with good reason.  AI is incredibly difficult to program especially in an intricate strategy so I can understand there will be hiccups.  However, diplomacy is just a joke and often times just SPAM so much damn spam.  Refusing a deal only to have the same deal pop up 3-5 turns later is infuriating; ALL SPAM IS BAD.  The combat is questionable.  Sometimes the AI has clear advantage and walks past your city while your at war witht hem.  Their units are spaced out all over their land when it should be fighting on whatever front it should be fighting on.  Barbarian spam is unreal and can overrun you so fast even if your constantly building units.  The fact that barb camps can overrun you so quickly with horseman and slow down your progress so damn much can force a re-roll.
This game has so much potential to be great but it pains me to say that this is the worst civ game its released in awhile.  Here's hoping the developers will release an actual expansion instead of these money-gouging dlc's but for now this is straight trash and needs to be uninstalled.
10/10 highly recommended if you want to give up your life entirely

The follow up to the critically acclaimed Walking Dead season 1 game by Telltale, Season 2 keeps you incredibly invested in its story and characters.
You can see my review of season 1 for the usual details, but essentially it's the same old Telltale gameplay. The game is more like an interactive story, focusing more on storytelling rather than moment-to-moment action. Thus, this game is not for you if you're looking for the next innovative, fast-paced, gameplay. If you're looking for a strong story that may or may not leave you emotionally devastated, this is for you.
Like the first game, the gameplay is more of a classic "point and click" adventure style game. Throughout the game you'll be able to move around in a very limited area and investigate points of interest by highlighting them with the cursor and using a few different action keys. There are also plenty of quick time events, although unlike other games they feel..."right" for the genre rather than out of place and annoying. The gameplay is nothing to be excited about - instead, it is a means of interaction, allowing you as a player to move the story along and make key decisions.
Again however, the story is what you're here for. Season 2 picks up after the events of Season 1 and its small DLC, 400 Days. You have the option of importing decisions you made in the first game over to new games in Season 2, although this is not necessary (but I recommend it nonetheless of course).
You play as Clementine this time, one of the primary characters from Season 1. The gameplay/story differs a bit because unlike last time, you are now a little girl in a zombie apocalypse. Characters amy underestimate you or treat you differently due to the large age difference, along with giving you as a player a fairly different perspective when it comes to making decisions and interacting with characters.
Other minor details is the appreciated addition of a "move faster" button that you can hold down, so that plodding nature of your character doesn't slow things down too much. In addition, the artwork and graphics seems to have improved compared to Season 1, and there is a greater variety of environments and colours used.
For those who played through Season 1, Season 2 is definitely worth getting. Aside from continuing the story and potentially crying some more, Season 2 doesn't feel any weaker and continues to hold up Telltale's golden storytelling standards.
If you haven't played any of the Telltale Walking Dead games (or many of their other games for that matter, such as Wolf Among Us), I highly recommend this series if you're at all interested in good story and don't mind a much simpler gameplay.

I really enjoyed Season 1.
Season 2... no.
I'm not a delicate flower, but bluntly this is more or less torture-porn starring an 11-year-old girl - the relentlessly severe first episode of Season 2 establishes this with no room for uncertainty.  Season 2 just left a bad taste in my mouth right from the start, that just got worse.
The premise of this season is that you have to choose who to trust to ensure your survival, but the reality is that you'll repeatedly have to make decisions to do things that even the most inept party of survivors wouldn't even begin to think of leaving to a little girl, so the premise is flawed and immersion-breaking.
In keeping with the tradition of the worst survivalist fantasies, any morally-positive decision WILL hurt someone's chances for survival, unlike the more nuanced co-operative spirit of Season 1 where, particularly, the Lee-Clementine relationship at least functioned frequently to reward less selfish decisions.  No matter, as it seems that no decision you think you're making in Season 2 will really have any effect on the story anyway.
There are no persistent likeable characters and very few of those quiet bonding moments that were the highlights of Season 1 - and why bother bonding with anyone anyway?  Forgettable characters drift in and out of the story; you will quickly notice the pattern that if anyone seems nice, then they will die horribly and entirely futiley, very very soon...
